title: F · Problems
text:
Executed in: Python · Book: ADM Appendix F
This page collects every problem used on the site, implemented in both Python (adm/problems/) and Julia (julia/src/problems/), with tests that check the two languages agree. It has two parts: the benchmark problems from Appendix F of the book, implemented from their descriptions, and the small original problems built for this site’s chapters. Each problem was added when a chapter first used it, so the five Appendix F problems that no chapter needed (2048, cart-pole, machine replacement, catch and collaborative predator-prey) are not implemented. The table shows the status of each.

title: F · Problems
text:
How problems are packaged
Every finite MDP comes as a DiscreteMDP with five fields:



Table 2: Fields of a DiscreteMDP. The arrays use the same layout as Chapter 7.









Field
Meaning




T
Transition array: T[s, a, s′] \(= T(s' \mid s, a)\)


R
Reward array: R[s, a] \(= R(s, a)\)


gamma (Python), γ (Julia)
Discount factor


states
A readable label for each state index, such as a tile’s (row, col)


actions
A readable label for each action index, such as "NE"






So any solver written for (T, R, γ) works on any problem. For example, here is Chapter 7’s value iteration solving Hex World:

PythonJulia



from adm.mdp import greedy, value_iteration
from adm.problems.hex_world import hex_world

mdp = hex_world()
U, _ = value_iteration(mdp.T, mdp.R, mdp.gamma)
policy, _ = greedy(mdp.T, mdp.R, mdp.gamma, U)



using ADM

mdp = hex_world()    # fields: T, R, γ, states, actions

# Value iteration (Ch 7): repeat Bellman backups until the values settle.
function solve(m; δ = 1e-6)
    U = zeros(length(m.states))
    while true
        Q = [m.R[s, a] + m.γ * sum(m.T[s, a, :] .* U) for s in axes(m.R, 1), a in axes(m.R, 2)]
        U′ = vec(maximum(Q, dims = 2))
        maximum(abs.(U′ - U)) < δ && return U′, argmax.(eachrow(Q))
        U = U′
    end
end
U, policy = solve(mdp)
@assert mdp.states[argmax(U)] == (2, 9)    # the +10 tile is worth the most





25 states (24 tiles + terminal), 6 actions, γ = 0.9
Most valuable tile: (2, 9) with U* = 10.00

title: F · Problems
text:
Hex World
The story. A robot crosses a floor of hexagonal tiles. Three tiles are special: one pays +10, one pays +5, and one costs −10. Acting on a special tile collects its value and ends the episode. The floor is slippery, so a move sometimes veers off course, and walking into the edge of the map wastes a turn and costs 1.
It is a good first benchmark because it is small enough to solve exactly (25 states), yet it has real trade-offs. The +5 is closer than the +10 for part of the map, and the −10 sits beside a useful path.



Table 3: Hex World at a glance (ADM §F.1).









States
24 tiles, plus one terminal state reached after collecting a reward


Actions
Move in one of 6 directions: E, NE, NW, W, SW, SE


Rewards
+10, +5 and −10 on three tiles; −1 for bumping into the edge


Discount
\(\gamma = 0.9\)







\[
T(s' \mid s, a) = 0.7\,\big[s' = \mathrm{step}(s, a)\big] + 0.15\,\big[s' = \mathrm{step}(s, a^{-})\big] + 0.15\,\big[s' = \mathrm{step}(s, a^{+})\big]
\tag{1}\]

In words. The robot goes the way it chose 70% of the time. Otherwise it veers 60° to the left or to the right, 15% each.
Term by term.

\(\mathrm{step}(s, a)\) is the tile one step from \(s\) in direction \(a\). If that step would leave the map, \(\mathrm{step}(s, a) = s\): the robot stays put.
\(a^{-}\) and \(a^{+}\) are the two directions next to \(a\). For \(a = \text{E}\) they are NE and SE.
\([\cdot]\) is 1 if the condition inside is true and 0 otherwise, so the three terms add up the ways of landing on \(s'\).
On a reward tile, every action instead moves to the terminal state with probability 1.

The reward is \(R(s, a) = r(s)\) on a reward tile. Elsewhere it is \(-1\) times the probability of bumping into the edge. For example, heading east from the top-left tile veers off the map with probability 0.15, so \(R = -0.15\).
Figure 1 shows the map and its optimal policy.








Figure 1: Hex World. Left: the map, with the three reward tiles colored. Right: the optimal values (color) and policy (arrows) from value iteration with γ = 0.9.






Straight-line Hex World
A smaller variant has seven tiles in a row, with +10 on the rightmost tile. Its only purpose is to make one thing visible: how value iteration spreads reward backward, one tile per sweep (Figure 2).








Figure 2: Value iteration on straight-line Hex World (γ = 0.9). Each row is one sweep. The +10 reaches one more tile to the left per sweep, fading as it goes. Tiles it hasn’t reached yet are slightly negative: in a single row every move risks veering off the edge, which costs 1. The values settle after 26 sweeps.





Where it’s used. Ch 9: every online planner is scored against the exact solution. Ch 13: a tabular policy and value table learned from guided tree search. optimistic_values in adm/problems/hex_world.py gives an upper bound on the optimal values (each positive reward discounted by the fewest moves to reach it), used by branch and bound and heuristic search.

title: F · Problems
text:
Mountain car
The story. A car sits in a valley between two hills and must reach the top of the right one. Its engine is too weak to drive straight up, so it has to rock back and forth, using gravity to build speed. It is the classic example of a delayed reward: every step costs the same, and the only way to do well is to first drive away from the goal. The problem goes back to A. Moore’s 1990 PhD thesis; this discrete-action version is from S. Singh and R. Sutton, “Reinforcement Learning with Replacing Eligibility Traces,” Machine Learning, 1996.



Table 4: Mountain car. The cos(3x) term is gravity along a valley shaped like sin(3x).









Part
Definition




State
position \(x \in [-1.2, 0.6]\) and speed \(v \in [-0.07, 0.07]\)


Actions
accelerate left (\(a = -1\)), coast (\(0\)), accelerate right (\(+1\))


Transition (deterministic)
\(v' = v + 0.001a - 0.0025\cos(3x)\), then \(x' = x + v'\); both clamped to their ranges


Reward
\(-1\) per step; the episode ends when \(x\) reaches \(0.6\)


Discount
\(\gamma = 1\) on this site, so a state’s value is minus the number of steps to the goal







PythonJulia



from adm.problems import mountain_car as mc
s = mc.step([-0.5, 0.0], 1)          # one step accelerating right from rest at x = -0.5
# mc.step also works on arrays of states: s[..., 0] is x and s[..., 1] is v



using ADM
s = mountain_car_step([-0.5, 0.0], 1)          # s = [x, v]
@assert s[2] ≈ 0.001 - 0.0025cos(-1.5) && !mountain_car_goal(s)



Where it’s used. Ch 8: approximate value iteration with seven kinds of value function approximation. From rest at \(x = -0.5\), a policy from a fine 201 × 201 grid takes 106 steps: right, then left, then right. Ch 9: receding-horizon forward search, with and without Ch 8’s value function beyond the horizon. Ch 10: policy search over the two-parameter rule “accelerate right if \(v + \theta_1 x + \theta_2 > 0\)” (switching_rule), scored from ten standard starts at rest (STANDARD_STARTS).

title: F · Problems
text:
Simple regulator
The story. Keep a single number \(s\) close to zero. Each step you choose an amount \(a\) to add to it, and the world adds a little noise of its own. It is the smallest possible linear-quadratic control problem, and small enough that the value of any linear policy can be written down exactly. That makes it a clean benchmark for policy search: every method’s answer can be scored without simulation noise.



Table 5: The simple regulator. With a linear Gaussian policy, E[s²] evolves as (1 + θ₁)² E[s²] + θ₂² + 0.1², which gives the exact value.









Part
Definition




State and action
real numbers \(s\) and \(a\)


Transition
\(s' \sim \mathcal{N}(s + a,\ 0.1^2)\)


Reward
\(R(s, a) = -s^2\) (the action is free)


Start
\(s \sim \mathcal{N}(0.3,\ 0.1^2)\)


Discount, horizon
\(\gamma = 0.9\) and 10 steps on this site


Policy family used
\(a \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_1 s,\ \theta_2^2)\); best: \(\theta = (-1, 0)\)







PythonJulia



from adm.problems import simple_regulator as sr
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
estimate = sr.rollout_returns(np.array([-1.0, 0.0]), 1000, rng).mean()   # Monte Carlo
exact = sr.exact_value([-1.0, 0.0])                                     # no sampling



using ADM
@assert regulator_exact_value([-1.0, 0.0]) ≈ -(0.1 + 0.01 * sum(0.9^t for t in 1:9))



Where it’s used. Ch 10: every policy search method is scored by the exact value of the policy it finds. Ch 11: the exact gradient (exact_gradient, from differentiating the same recursion) scores every gradient estimator’s bias and variance. Ch 12: the policy’s log_policy and policy_kl drive TRPO and PPO, and exact values score every update rule. Ch 13: actor-critic with a quadratic critic, and the deterministic policy gradient.

title: F · Problems
text:
Aircraft collision avoidance
The story. Our aircraft flies head on toward an intruder and will meet it in 40 seconds. Each second, a collision avoidance system can advise the pilot to climb, to descend, or nothing. Gusts nudge the vertical rate, and the pilot can change it only gradually. The system must avoid passing within 50 m of the intruder vertically, without issuing needless or frequently changing advisories. It is a highly simplified version of the problem behind airborne collision avoidance systems.



Table 6: Aircraft collision avoidance.









Part
Definition




State
altitude relative to the intruder \(h\) (m), vertical rate \(\dot h\) (m/s), previous advisory, time to collision \(t_{\text{col}}\) (s)


Actions
no advisory; descend at 5 m/s; climb at 5 m/s


Transition, each second
\(h \leftarrow h + \dot h\), \(\ \dot h \leftarrow \dot h + \ddot h + \nu\), \(\ t_{\text{col}} \leftarrow t_{\text{col}} - 1\)


Pilot response \(\ddot h\)
toward the advised rate, at most 1 m/s² (so \(\ddot h = \operatorname{clip}(\text{rate} - \dot h, -1, 1)\)); 0 with no advisory


Gusts \(\nu\)
−2, 0, +2 m/s with probabilities ¼, ½, ¼


Costs
1 if \(|h| < 50\) m at \(t_{\text{col}} = 0\) (collision); 0.01 for each change of advisory


Start (this site)
\(t_{\text{col}} = 40\), no advisory; \(h\) and \(\dot h\) uniform on the integers in ±200 m and ±10 m/s






Two choices are this site’s. The book’s formula for \(\ddot h\) reads \(a/\Delta t\) when the advised rate is within reach; we take the step that reaches the advised rate, \((\text{rate} - \dot h)/\Delta t\). And starts are integers: then \(h\) and \(\dot h\) stay integers forever (every change is a whole number), so the problem is an exact finite MDP on an integer lattice. optimal_policy solves it by backward induction on that lattice in about 0.1 s, with no interpolation. That gives exact answers for every metric, which Ch 14 uses to check its sampling methods. The lattice is clamped at ±500 m and ±30 m/s; a lattice of ±800 m and ±50 m/s changes the collision probabilities by less than \(10^{-10}\) (tested).
The Model settings (noise, p_noise, accel_limit, compliance, the two costs) describe variants for robustness checks. For instance, compliance = 0.8 is a pilot who follows each advisory only 80% of the time. simple_policy is a threshold policy for comparison: climb or descend away from the intruder when it is within 50 m vertically and less than 30 s away.

PythonJulia



from adm.problems import collision_avoidance as ca
m = ca.Model()
policy, cost = ca.optimal_policy(m)                          # policy[t][a_prev, i_h, i_hdot]
p_collision = ca.start_average(m, ca.evaluate(m, policy))    # exact, by policy evaluation
p_simple = ca.start_average(m, ca.evaluate(m, ca.simple_policy(m)))



collision probability: optimal 6.42e-04, simple 0.072




using ADM
m = CAModel()
policy, cost = ca_optimal_policy(m)                          # policy[t][a_prev, i_h, i_ḣ]
p_collision = ca_start_average(m, ca_evaluate(m, policy))
p_simple = ca_start_average(m, ca_evaluate(m, ca_simple_policy(m)))
@assert 6e-4 < p_collision < 7e-4 && 0.07 < p_simple < 0.075



Where it’s used. Ch 14: exact evaluation of collision risk and advisory changes, Monte Carlo and importance sampling checked against it, robustness to pilot compliance and gusts, robust dynamic programming, trade-off curves, and the most likely failure found by an adversary.

title: F · Problems
text:
Crying baby
The story. A caregiver can’t tell whether a baby is hungry; it only hears whether the baby cries. Each hour it can feed the baby (effective but costly), sing to it (cheap, and more informative about hunger), or ignore it. It is the standard small POMDP: two hidden states, three actions and two observations. It is small enough to solve exactly and to draw every belief on a single axis, \(P(\text{hungry})\).



Table 7: The crying baby.









Part
Definition




States
sated, hungry


Actions
feed, sing, ignore


Observations
crying, quiet


Transitions
feeding always sates; otherwise a sated baby becomes hungry w.p. 0.1, and a hungry one stays hungry


Observations
\(P(\text{cry} \mid \text{hungry})\) = 0.8 (feed, ignore), 0.9 (sing); \(P(\text{cry} \mid \text{sated})\) = 0.1 (feed, ignore), 0 (sing); both depend on the state after the action


Rewards
−10 while hungry, −5 more to feed, −0.5 more to sing; discount 0.9







PythonJulia



from adm.problems.crying_baby import belief_update, crying_baby
pomdp = crying_baby()                    # T[s, a, s2], R[s, a], O[a, s2, o]; 0 = sated / feed / crying
b = belief_update(pomdp, np.array([0.8, 0.2]), 2, 0)   # ignore, then hear crying



using ADM
p = crying_baby()                        # 1-based: 1 = sated / feed / crying
b = update_discrete([0.8, 0.2], p.T, p.O, 3, 1)       # ignore, then hear crying
@assert b[2] ≈ 0.224 / 0.296



Where it’s used. Ch 20: conditional plans, alpha vectors, pruning and exact value iteration. The long-horizon policy ignores the baby until \(P(\text{hungry})\) reaches about 0.28, then feeds; with the problem as defined here, singing is never optimal. Ch 21: every offline bound is compared with the exact value. Ch 22: forward search, branch and bound, sparse sampling, determinized search, Monte Carlo tree search and gap heuristic search, all scored against the exact solution. Ch 23: a 2-node controller (“feed on crying, but not twice in a row”) is exactly optimal; policy iteration and gradient ascent find it.

title: F · Problems
text:
Simple games
The story. Three one-round games for two agents, who choose at the same time. In the prisoner’s dilemma (F.10), each prisoner can stay silent (cooperate) or blame the other (defect); rewards are minus the years served. In rock-paper-scissors (F.11), the winner gets 1 and the loser −1. In the traveler’s dilemma (F.12; K. Basu, 1994), two travelers claim between $2 and $100 for identical lost suitcases; equal claims are paid, otherwise both are paid the lower claim, plus $2 for the lower claimant and minus $2 for the higher. All three store \(R[i, a^1, a^2]\), agent \(i\)’s reward, with discount 0.9 when repeated.



Table 8: The simple games.










Game
Actions
Rewards (agent 1, agent 2)




Prisoner’s dilemma
cooperate, defect
(C, C) −1, −1; (C, D) −4, 0; (D, C) 0, −4; (D, D) −3, −3


Rock-paper-scissors
rock, paper, scissors
winner 1, loser −1, draw 0


Traveler’s dilemma
claims $2–$100 (99 actions)
equal: both get the claim; else lower + 2 and lower − 2







PythonJulia



from adm.problems.simple_games import prisoners_dilemma, rock_paper_scissors, travelers_dilemma
game = travelers_dilemma()               # R[i, a1, a2]; action 0 = $2
print(game.R[:, 97, 98])                 # claims $99 and $100: [101.  97.]

[101.  97.]




using ADM
g = travelers_dilemma()                  # R[i, a1, a2]; action 1 = $2
@assert g.R[:, 98, 99] == [101.0, 97.0]  # claims $99 and $100



Where it’s used. Ch 24: defecting is a dominant strategy in the prisoner’s dilemma; rock-paper-scissors has only a mixed Nash equilibrium, and iterated best response cycles in it; in the traveler’s dilemma best responses unravel to $2, while a hierarchical softmax model predicts claims near $90.

title: F · Problems
text:
Predator-prey hex world
The story. A predator chases a prey across a small map of hexagonal tiles. Both move at once, as in Hex World: in the chosen direction with probability 0.7, or veering to a neighboring direction with probability 0.15 each; a move off the map stays put. When they share a tile, the prey is caught and reappears on a random tile. The predator pays 1 per move and gains 1 per capture; the prey loses 100 when caught. The map is the 12-tile one of the book’s figure F.16, transcribed as three rows (row 1: columns 0–2; row 2: columns 0, 2, 4, 5; row 3: columns 0–4, odd rows shifted right). The predator starts at (1, 2) and the prey at (3, 2).



Table 9: The predator-prey hex world.





Part
Definition




Agents
predator (agent 1), prey (agent 2)


States
(predator’s tile, prey’s tile): 144 pairs


Actions
six hex directions each: E, NE, NW, W, SW, SE


Rewards
predator −1 per step, +1 on capture; prey −100 on capture


Discount
0.9







PythonJulia



from adm.problems.markov_games import predator_prey
game = predator_prey()                     # T[s, a1, a2, s2], R[i, s, a1, a2]; s = pred * 12 + prey



using ADM
g = predator_prey()                        # 1-based; s = (pred - 1) * 12 + prey
@assert size(g.T) == (144, 6, 6, 144) && all(sum(g.T; dims = 4) .≈ 1)



Where it’s used. Ch 25: a predator’s best response to a random prey and the prey’s reply; iterated best response cycles without settling; fictitious play’s exploitability falls from about 67 after 1,000 steps to about 19 after 50,000.

title: F · Problems
text:
Multicaregiver crying baby
The story. Two caregivers look after one baby. Each hour, each can feed, sing to or ignore it. Either caregiver feeding sates the baby; otherwise a hungry baby stays hungry and a sated one stays sated with probability 0.5. Both hear the same thing: a hungry baby cries 90% of the time, a sated one never. Both pay 10 per hour while the baby is hungry; feeding costs caregiver 1 an extra 2.5 and caregiver 2 an extra 5; singing costs 0.5 and 0.25. It’s implemented exactly as Appendix F.14 defines it. Two consequences of that definition: singing is no more informative than ignoring, and there is no discount for both doing the same thing (the book’s Example 26.1 describes a variant where the cost is halved).



Table 10: The multicaregiver crying baby.









Part
Definition




States
sated, hungry


Actions (each)
feed, sing, ignore


Observations (each)
crying, quiet; always the same for both


Transitions
a feed by either sates; else hungry stays hungry, sated stays sated w.p. 0.5


Rewards (each)
−10 while hungry; feeding −2.5 (caregiver 1) or −5 (caregiver 2); singing −0.5 or −0.25


Discount
0.9







PythonJulia



from adm.problems.multicaregiver import multicaregiver
game = multicaregiver()                    # T[s, a1, a2, s2], O[a1, a2, s2, o1, o2], R[i, s, a1, a2]



using ADM
g = multicaregiver()                       # 1-based: 1 = sated / feed / crying
@assert g.O[3, 3, 2, 1, 1] == 0.9 && g.R[2, 2, 3, 1] == -15.0



Where it’s used. Ch 26: evaluation of joint conditional plans and controllers; the two-step game over plans (27 × 27) and dynamic programming with pruning (32 of 48 four-step candidates survive); equilibria where one caregiver feeds and the other free-rides.

Problems made for this site
The chapters also use small original problems, built to make one idea easy to see. The ones reused across pages get a full entry here, in both languages; the rest are listed in Table 21.

Morning commute
The story. Five yes/no facts about a morning: was there a storm, roadwork, a traffic jam; were you late; did the radio warn of a storm. Storms and roadwork cause jams, jams make you late, and storms trigger radio alerts. It is small enough to check every answer by hand, yet it contains all three d-separation patterns: a chain, a fork and a collider.

Ch 4: its tables are learned back from simulated mornings, including with the storm value missing (EM). Ch 5: its graph is learned back from data, and the radio alert’s near-copy of the storm shows why small samples can mislead. Ch 6: extended into a decision network.


Commute decision
The story. The morning commute becomes a choice: leave on time, leave 30 minutes early, or stay home and work remotely. Leaving early makes lateness unlikely even in a jam, and staying home rules it out, but both have a cost of their own. It is the smallest decision network with a real trade-off, and its observations have clearly different values of information: the traffic app, which shows the jam, is worth over five times as much as the radio.

Coffee machine
The story. An espresso machine is fine, has scale buildup, or has a worn pump. You can’t see which, but you can notice three symptoms: slow flow, a loud noise, and weak-tasting coffee. Each symptom depends only on the machine’s condition, which makes this a naive Bayes model. It shows how a rare cause can become the most likely one once the evidence fits it well.

Where it’s used. Ch 3: naive Bayes inference.


Commute times
The story. Morning and evening commute times, in minutes, are jointly Gaussian: morning \(\mathcal{N}(35, 8^2)\) and evening \(\mathcal{N}(40, 10^2)\), with correlation \(\rho = 0.6\), because a bad traffic day tends to be bad all day. It is the smallest example of conditioning a Gaussian: one observation shifts the other’s mean and shrinks its spread.



Table 14: Commute times as a bivariate Gaussian.

from adm.problems.commute import COMMUTE_TIMES_COV, COMMUTE_TIMES_MEAN   # index 0 = morning, 1 = evening



using ADM

@assert COMMUTE_TIMES_COV[1, 2] == 0.6 * 8 * 10



Where it’s used. Ch 3: Gaussian conditioning.


Mountain trail
The story. A hiker is somewhere on a six-position trail, from the trailhead (0) to the summit (5). Resting at the trailhead earns a small, sure reward: a snack from the car. The view at the summit is worth twenty times as much, but the climb is unreliable. Each attempt to climb gains ground only 35% of the time, and occasionally slips back. It is a small test of exploration. An agent that grabs the nearby reward and trusts its early experience never learns that the long climb pays. The structure follows the RiverSwim benchmark (A. L. Strehl and M. L. Littman, J. Comput. Syst. Sci., 2008), with this site’s own numbers.

Ch 17: Q-learning with ε-greedy exploration gets stuck too; optimistic initial values and potential-based shaping fix it, while a naive “+5 per step up” bonus makes walking back down optimal.


The park
The story. Walkers cross an 8 × 8 park from its left edge to the gate in the top-right corner. Paths are pleasant, grass is slower, and mud is miserable; the ground is slippery, so a step sometimes goes sideways or back. The reward is a weighted sum of terrain features, which makes the park a clean test for imitation learning. An expert’s walks can be copied cell by cell, or explained by the weights they imply. Two layouts share the terrain types, so a learned reward can be tried in a park it has never seen.

The fork
The story. A hiker reaches a fork and doesn’t know which trail leads home. Taking the right trail is worth 10; the wrong one costs 50; either way a new hike then starts at a fresh fork. A passerby can be asked (cost 1), and answers correctly 85% of the time; or the hiker can wait, which is free and teaches nothing. The problem is built to show when information has to be paid for: methods that treat information as free (QMDP) conclude that waiting is best, forever. Its structure follows the classic tiger problem (L. P. Kaelbling, M. L. Littman and A. R. Cassandra, Artificial Intelligence, 1998), with the free wait action added.

The intersection
The story. Two drivers reach an empty intersection at the same moment, and each chooses to go or stop. If one goes and the other stops, the one who goes saves time (+3) and the other gets 0. If both go they nearly crash (−10 each); if both stop they both waste time (−1 each). It is a game of chicken: there’s no dominant strategy, there are two pure Nash equilibria that each favor one driver, and a mixed one that is bad for both. A traffic light, a correlated equilibrium, gives each driver 1.5.

The lake
The story. Two fishing boats share a lake whose fish stock is low, medium or high. Each day, each boat fishes lightly or heavily. Heavy fishing catches more today but depletes the stock, and a depleted lake pays both boats less for years: a sequential tragedy of the commons. It has exactly two deterministic stationary Nash equilibria: both fish lightly unless the stock is high (which is also what a single owner of both boats would do), or both always fish heavily.

Two rescuers at separate lookouts can each listen for a radio report (cost 1; right 80% of the time, and private to that rescuer), search the left valley or search the right one. Any search ends the episode, and a new hiker is lost in a random valley. The team shares one reward: a Dec-POMDP. The structure is similar to the decentralized tiger problem of the Dec-POMDP literature, with this site’s own story and numbers.

title: D · Neural Representations
text:
Executed in: Python · Book: ADM Appendix D
A neural network is a flexible function with many adjustable parameters. Fed enough examples, gradient descent tunes the parameters until the function matches the data. On this site, neural networks are one option wherever a chapter needs a function it can’t write down: a value function (Chapter 8), a policy (Chapters 10–13), a critic (Chapter 13) or a discriminator (Chapter 18). This appendix follows ADM Appendix D. All code runs in plain NumPy, with the gradient computed by hand, so every step is visible.

title: D · Neural Representations
text:
Feedforward networks
A feedforward network, or multilayer perceptron, is a chain of layers. Each layer mixes its inputs linearly and then bends the result with a fixed nonlinear function:

\[
\mathbf{x}' = \phi\big(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}\big)
\tag{1}\]

In words. Each output unit takes a weighted sum of all inputs, adds a bias, and passes it through an activation function.
Term by term.

\(\mathbf{x}\): the layer’s input, a vector of length \(m\); \(\mathbf{x}'\): its output, of length \(n\).
\(\mathbf{W}\): an \(n \times m\) weight matrix; row \(i\) holds the weights of output unit \(i\). \(\mathbf{b}\): a bias vector of length \(n\).
\(\phi\): the activation function, applied to each element separately (Figure 1).

Why it holds. It is a design choice, and the nonlinearity is essential. Without it, two layers collapse into one: \(\mathbf{W}_2(\mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1) + \mathbf{b}_2 = (\mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{W}_1)\mathbf{x} + (\mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{b}_1 + \mathbf{b}_2)\), still an affine map, so any depth of linear layers can only draw straight lines. With a nonlinear \(\phi\), a network with one wide enough hidden layer can approximate any continuous function on a bounded region to any accuracy (the universal approximation theorem; Cybenko 1989, Hornik 1991).
The code on this page stores samples as rows, so a layer computes X @ W + b with W of shape \(m \times n\): the transpose of Equation 1, applied to a whole batch at once. Hidden layers apply \(\phi\); the output layer is left linear so it can produce any real number.








Figure 1: The four activation functions in adm.neural. Each changes slowly or not at all for very negative inputs and grows with the input.





When the output must be a probability distribution, for example a stochastic policy over actions, the last layer is followed by a softmax:

\[
\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_i = \frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j)}
\tag{2}\]

In words. Exponentiate every score so it is positive, then divide by the total so the results add up to 1.
Term by term.

\(z_i\): the score (logit) of option \(i\); larger scores get larger probabilities.
\(\exp\): keeps the order of the scores and makes them positive; a gap of 1 between scores means a ratio of \(e \approx 2.72\) between probabilities.
The denominator: normalizes the results to sum to 1.

Why it holds. Adding the same constant to every score cancels between numerator and denominator, so only differences between scores matter; the code subtracts the largest score before exponentiating to avoid overflow. Example: scores \((2, 1, -1)\) give probabilities 0.705, 0.259, 0.035.

title: D · Neural Representations
text:
Backpropagation
Training needs the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight. Backpropagation (reverse-mode differentiation) gets all of them in one backward sweep, at about the cost of one extra forward pass:

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mathbf{x}'}\,\frac{\partial \mathbf{x}'}{\partial \mathbf{x}}
\tag{3}\]

In words. The gradient with respect to a layer’s input is the gradient with respect to its output, times how much the output moves when the input moves.
Term by term.

\(\ell\): the loss, a single number.
\(\partial \ell / \partial \mathbf{x}'\): arrives from the layer above (from the loss itself, at the top).
\(\partial \mathbf{x}' / \partial \mathbf{x}\): local to the layer. For Equation 1 it is \(\phi'(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b})\) times \(\mathbf{W}\), and the weight gradient is the incoming gradient (after \(\phi'\)) times the layer input.

Why it holds. It is the chain rule of calculus, applied once per layer. Going from the output backward means each layer multiplies a gradient vector by its local derivative, so no large Jacobian matrix is ever formed. That is why the backward pass costs about as much as the forward pass, however many parameters there are.

Worked example
Take a network with one hidden ReLU unit: \(\hat{y} = w_2\,\max(0, w_1 x + b_1) + b_2\) with \(w_1 = 0.8\), \(b_1 = -0.2\), \(w_2 = 1.5\), \(b_2 = 0.1\), one sample \(x = 1.5\), \(y = 1\), and loss \(\ell = (\hat{y} - y)^2\).
Forward. \(z = 0.8 \cdot 1.5 - 0.2 =\) 1.00, \(h = \max(0, z) =\) 1.00, \(\hat{y} = 1.5 h + 0.1 =\) 1.60, \(\ell =\) 0.36.
Backward.

\(\partial\ell/\partial\hat{y} = 2(\hat{y} - y) =\) 1.20. Since \(\hat{y} = w_2 h + b_2\): \(\partial\ell/\partial w_2 =\) 1.20 \(\times h =\) 1.20 and \(\partial\ell/\partial b_2 =\) 1.20.
Into the hidden unit: \(\partial\ell/\partial h =\) 1.20 \(\times w_2 =\) 1.80. The ReLU is in its active region (\(z > 0\)), so its slope is 1 and \(\partial\ell/\partial z\) is the same.
Since \(z = w_1 x + b_1\): \(\partial\ell/\partial w_1 =\) 1.80 \(\times x =\) 2.70 and \(\partial\ell/\partial b_1 =\) 1.80.

Fitting a curve
Figure 3 fits 60 noisy samples of \(f(x) = \sin(2x)\,e^{-x^2/4}\) with three networks of the same 1-16-16-1 shape, trained for 3,000 steps of Adam (a gradient method that scales each parameter’s step by its recent gradient size). Only the activation differs.








Figure 3: Left: three 1-16-16-1 networks fitted to 60 noisy samples (dots) of the gray target curve. Right: training loss (mean squared error) per step on a log scale; the dashed line is the noise variance, 0.0025.





The test error on a fine grid, measured against the true \(f\), is 0.209 for the linear network, which can only draw a straight line, against 0.0017 for ReLU and 0.0012 for tanh. Both nonlinear networks settle slightly below the noise variance of 0.0025; driving the training loss much lower would mean fitting the noise itself. The spikes in the tanh curve are Adam steps that overshoot; after step 500 the loss is back below the noise level within about 15 steps each time.

title: D · Neural Representations
text:
Regularization
A large network fitted to few points can pass through every point, noise included, and swing wildly between them. Weight regularization adds a penalty on large weights to the training loss:

\[
\min_{\theta}\ \frac{1}{\lvert \mathcal{D} \rvert}\sum_{(x, y) \in \mathcal{D}} \big(f_\theta(x) - y\big)^2 + \beta \lVert \mathbf{W} \rVert_2^2
\tag{4}\]

In words. Fit the data, but pay a price for every large weight.
Term by term.

\(\mathcal{D}\): the training data; \(f_\theta\): the network with parameters \(\theta\).
\(\lVert \mathbf{W} \rVert_2^2\): the sum of all squared weights (the code leaves biases unpenalized).
\(\beta \ge 0\): the strength. \(\beta = 0\) is plain fitting; a large \(\beta\) flattens the network toward a constant.

Why it holds. The penalty’s gradient, \(2\beta\mathbf{W}\), pulls every weight toward zero at each step, so a weight survives only if the data keep pushing it. Small weights keep each \(\tanh\) unit near its linear region, which gives smoother functions. In Bayesian terms it is a Gaussian prior on the weights (Appendix B), and the minimizer is the most probable network given the data.








Figure 4: A 1-64-64-1 tanh network fitted to 12 noisy points (dataset 1 of 8) with three regularization strengths β. The gray curve is the true function.

title: D · Neural Representations
text:
Other architectures
Convolutional networks. Instead of connecting every input to every unit, a convolutional layer slides one small filter along the input, computing \(y_i = \sum_j w_j\,x_{i+j}\) at each position. The same few weights are reused everywhere, so a pattern is detected wherever it appears. With the filter \((-1, 0, 1)\), the signal 0 0 0 1 1 1 1 0 0 becomes 0 1 1 0 0 −1 −1: the filter responds \(+1\) around the step up, \(-1\) around the step down, and 0 on flat stretches. Stacks of such layers, learned from data, find edges, then shapes, then objects in images.
Recurrent networks. A recurrent network reads a sequence one element at a time and carries a hidden state forward, \(\mathbf{h}_t = \phi(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}_t + \mathbf{b})\), with the same weights at every step. The hidden state is a learned summary of everything seen so far, which makes recurrent networks a natural way to turn a POMDP’s action-observation history into something a policy can use, in place of an exact belief (Chapter 19). Training unrolls the network over time and backpropagates through the unrolled chain; gradients that shrink or grow at each step make long memories hard to learn, which gated designs such as the LSTM (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997) address.
Autoencoders. An autoencoder is trained to reproduce its input through a narrow middle layer, the code. Because the input must pass through the bottleneck, the code has to capture what matters about it. Figure 5 squeezes 200 noisy points on three quarters of a circle through a single number. A linear autoencoder can only project onto a line (it recovers principal component analysis), with reconstruction error 0.137. A 2-32-1-32-2 tanh network bends its code around the arc, with error 0.0006, and its code is almost a monotone function of the angle (rank correlation 0.999): it has discovered that the data are one-dimensional.








Figure 5: Left: 200 points near three quarters of a circle (gray) and their reconstructions through a one-number code, by a linear autoencoder (orange) and a tanh autoencoder (blue). Right: the tanh autoencoder’s code against each point’s angle.





Adversarial networks. A generative adversarial network (Goodfellow et al. 2014) trains two networks against each other. A generator turns random noise into samples; a discriminator tries to tell those samples from real data. The generator improves by fooling the discriminator, and at the balance point its samples are indistinguishable from the data. Chapter 18’s GAIL uses the same game with a policy as the generator: the discriminator tries to tell the policy’s state-action pairs from an expert’s, and the policy is rewarded for fooling it.
References. G. Cybenko, “Approximation by superpositions of a sigmoidal function,” Mathematics of Control, Signals and Systems 2, 1989. K. Hornik, “Approximation capabilities of multilayer feedforward networks,” Neural Networks 4, 1991. S. Hochreiter and J. Schmidhuber, “Long short-term memory,” Neural Computation 9, 1997. I. Goodfellow et al., “Generative adversarial nets,” NeurIPS, 2014.

title: D · Neural Representations
text:
Code
The forward pass caches each layer’s input and pre-activation; the backward pass walks the layers in reverse, applying Equation 3. Chapter 8’s NeuralNetValue is the one-hidden-layer case of the same computation.

PythonJulia


def forward(params, X, act="tanh"):
    """Returns the output and a cache of (layer input, pre-activation)
    per layer, which the backward pass needs."""
    phi = ACTIVATIONS[act][0]
    A, cache = X, []
    for k, (W, b) in enumerate(params):
        Z = A @ W + b                   # (n, d_in) @ (d_in, d_out)
        cache.append((A, Z))
        A = Z if k == len(params) - 1 else phi(Z)   # linear output layer
    return A, cache

def backward(params, cache, dA, act="tanh") -> list:
    """Chain rule from the output back: dA is dLoss/dOutput, (n, d_out).
    Returns [(dW, db)] matching params."""
    dphi = ACTIVATIONS[act][1]
    grads = [None] * len(params)
    for k in reversed(range(len(params))):
        A_prev, Z = cache[k]
        # Through the activation (skipped at the linear output layer)
        dZ = dA if k == len(params) - 1 else dA * dphi(Z)
        W = params[k][0]
        # Z = A_prev @ W + b: each weight's gradient sums over the batch
        grads[k] = (A_prev.T @ dZ, dZ.sum(axis=0))
        dA = dZ @ W.T                   # hand the gradient to layer k - 1
    return grads

def mse_loss(params, X, Y, act="tanh", beta=0.0):
    """Mean squared error plus beta * (sum of squared weights), and its
    gradient. Biases are not penalized."""
    Yhat, cache = forward(params, X, act)
    err = Yhat - Y
    loss = (err ** 2).sum() / len(X) + beta * sum((W ** 2).sum()
                                                  for W, _ in params)
    grads = backward(params, cache, 2 * err / len(X), act)
    grads = [(dW + 2 * beta * W, db) for (dW, db), (W, _) in
             zip(grads, params)]
    return loss, grads


using Random

# Layers are (W, b) with W of size (d_out, d_in): Julia keeps one sample
# per COLUMN, so a layer computes W * X .+ b (the transpose of the Python
# layout, which is natural for Julia's column-major arrays).
function forward(params, X)
    A, cache = X, []
    for (k, (W, b)) in enumerate(params)
        Z = W * A .+ b
        push!(cache, (A, Z))
        A = k == length(params) ? Z : tanh.(Z)   # linear output layer
    end
    return A, cache
end

function mse_loss(params, X, Y)
    Yhat, cache = forward(params, X)
    n = size(X, 2)
    dA = 2 .* (Yhat .- Y) ./ n
    grads = Vector{Any}(undef, length(params))
    for k in length(params):-1:1
        A_prev, Z = cache[k]
        dZ = k == length(params) ? dA : dA .* (1 .- tanh.(Z) .^ 2)
        W = params[k][1]
        # sum over the batch (dims = 2), then drop that axis
        grads[k] = (dZ * A_prev', vec(sum(dZ; dims = 2)))
        dA = W' * dZ
    end
    return sum(abs2, Yhat .- Y) / n, grads
end

function demo()
    rng = MersenneTwister(0)
    f(x) = sin(2x) * exp(-x^2 / 4)
    X = 6 .* rand(rng, 1, 60) .- 3              # 1 × 60: one sample per column
    Y = f.(X)
    params = [(randn(rng, 16, 1), zeros(16)), (randn(rng, 16, 16) ./ 4, zeros(16)),
              (randn(rng, 1, 16) ./ 4, zeros(1))]
    # Finite-difference check of one weight
    loss0, grads = mse_loss(params, X, Y)
    h = 1e-6
    params[2][1][3, 5] += h; up = mse_loss(params, X, Y)[1]
    params[2][1][3, 5] -= 2h; down = mse_loss(params, X, Y)[1]
    params[2][1][3, 5] += h
    @assert isapprox((up - down) / 2h, grads[2][1][3, 5]; atol = 1e-6)
    # Plain gradient descent (Python's train() uses Adam)
    for _ in 1:3000
        _, grads = mse_loss(params, X, Y)
        for ((W, b), (dW, db)) in zip(params, grads)
            W .-= 0.05 .* dW; b .-= 0.05 .* db
        end
    end
    loss = mse_loss(params, X, Y)[1]
    println("loss ", round(loss0; digits = 4), " -> ", round(loss; digits = 4))
    @assert loss < loss0 / 5
end
demo()

title: B · Probability Distributions
text:
Discrete distributions
A Bernoulli variable is a single yes/no outcome, like a coin toss or whether a click happens (the bandits of Chapter 15). A categorical variable takes one of \(n\) values with given probabilities: every discrete variable in a Bayesian network (Chapter 2), every row of a transition model \(T(s' \mid s, a)\), and every stochastic policy is one.

title: B · Probability Distributions
text:
Uniform
\(\mathcal{U}(a, b)\) spreads probability evenly over an interval: every point in \([a, b]\) is equally likely. It is the natural “know nothing but the range” distribution, used for random initial conditions and, as \(\text{Beta}(1, 1)\), as the uninformative prior of Chapter 4.

title: B · Probability Distributions
text:
Gaussian

\[
\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\Big(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)
\tag{1}\]

In words. A bell curve centered at \(\mu\), whose width is set by \(\sigma\).
Term by term.

\(\mu\): the mean, center and peak of the curve.
\(\sigma\): the standard deviation; about 68% of the probability lies within \(\mu \pm \sigma\) and 95% within \(\mu \pm 1.96\sigma\).
\(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\): the constant that makes the area 1.

Why it holds. \(\int e^{-z^2/2}\,dz = \sqrt{2\pi}\) (square the integral and switch to polar coordinates), and substituting \(z = (x - \mu)/\sigma\) gives the constant. The central limit theorem explains why the Gaussian is everywhere: sums of many small independent effects are approximately Gaussian. Used for continuous Bayesian networks (Chapter 2), exploration noise (Chapter 10–12) and Kalman filters (Chapter 19).

title: B · Probability Distributions
text:
Beta
The Beta distribution describes an unknown probability, a number in \((0, 1)\). Its main use is as the conjugate prior for a Bernoulli probability:

\[
p \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta),\ \ \text{observe } k \text{ successes in } n \text{ trials}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
p \mid \text{data} \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha + k,\ \beta + n - k)
\tag{2}\]

In words. Start with pseudo-counts \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\); add the observed successes and failures.
Term by term.

\(\text{Beta}(1, 1)\) is uniform: no prior preference.
The posterior mean \((\alpha + k)/(\alpha + \beta + n)\) moves from the prior mean toward the observed fraction \(k/n\) as \(n\) grows.
Example: from a uniform prior, 7 successes in 10 trials give \(\text{Beta}(8, 4)\): mean 0.667, 95% interval 0.390 to 0.891.

Why it holds. By Bayes’ rule, the posterior is proportional to prior times likelihood: \(p^{\alpha - 1}(1 - p)^{\beta - 1} \cdot p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}\), which is the Beta form with exponents increased by \(k\) and \(n - k\). Used for parameter learning (Chapter 4), Bayesian bandits (Chapter 15) and failure-probability intervals (Chapter 14).

title: B · Probability Distributions
text:
Multivariate Gaussian

\[
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2} |\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}} \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\Big)
\tag{3}\]

In words. A bell-shaped hill in \(n\) dimensions, centered at \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), stretched and tilted by \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\).
Term by term.

\(\boldsymbol{\mu}\): the mean vector. \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\): the covariance matrix, symmetric and positive definite (Appendix A); its off-diagonal entries tilt the hill when variables are correlated.
\((\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\): the squared Mahalanobis distance; its level sets are the elliptical contours.
\(|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|\): the determinant, which normalizes for the ellipses’ volume.

Why it holds. Changing variables to \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{L}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\), with \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^\top\), turns it into a product of \(n\) standard Gaussians; the Jacobian contributes \(|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}\). Numerically, the example in Figure 1 integrates to 1.0000. Used for commute times (Chapter 3), the cross-entropy method (Chapter 10) and Kalman filters (Chapter 19).

title: B · Probability Distributions
text:
Dirichlet
The Dirichlet generalizes the Beta to a whole probability vector, and is the conjugate prior for categorical variables:

\[
\text{Dir}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\alpha}) = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} \Gamma(\alpha_i)} \prod_{i=1}^{n} x_i^{\alpha_i - 1}, \qquad x_i > 0,\ \sum_i x_i = 1,\ \ \alpha_0 = \sum_i \alpha_i
\tag{4}\]

In words. A distribution over probability vectors: the \(\alpha_i\) act as pseudo-counts for each category.
Term by term.

With all \(\alpha_i = 1\), every probability vector is equally likely.
Larger \(\alpha_0\) concentrates the vectors near the mean \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}/\alpha_0\).
Updating on counts \(m_i\) gives \(\text{Dir}(\boldsymbol{\alpha} + \mathbf{m})\), exactly as for the Beta.
Example: \(\boldsymbol{\alpha} = (2, 3, 5)\) has mean \((0.2, 0.3, 0.5)\); 100,000 samples averaged 0.200, 0.300, 0.500.

Why it holds. The normalizing constant is the multivariate Beta function; with \(n = 2\) it reduces to the Beta distribution. Used for learning conditional probability tables (Chapter 4), Bayesian structure scores (Chapter 5) and posterior sampling of transition models (Chapter 16).

title: 27 · Collaborative Agents
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 26’s agents each had their own reward, so the question was which joint policies were stable. Here all agents share one reward: a team. The model, a decentralized POMDP (Dec-POMDP), is a POMG with identical rewards. Now there is a single best joint policy, and the question is how to find it when each agent acts on its own observations. This is the last chapter of the book’s main text; it ties together plans and controllers (Chapters 20 and 23), equilibria (Chapter 24) and multiagent dynamics.
The question: how should a team act when its members can’t share what they observe?
The short answer: plan all members’ policies together, offline, knowing that each will act on its own observations; exact methods are hopeless beyond tiny problems, so use search that improves one member at a time or keeps a bounded set of plans.

A shared reward removes the conflict of Part V’s earlier chapters, but not the coordination problem: each agent must guess what the others have seen.
Exact planning (dynamic programming, or brute force on tiny problems) is NEXP-complete in general.
Iterated best response (JESP) improves one agent at a time and can stop at a poor joint policy.
Memory-bounded search (MBDP) keeps a few plans per agent, chosen at sampled beliefs.
Controllers of fixed size can be optimized directly, if the optimizer doesn’t get stuck.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. A Dec-POMDP is a POMG with one shared reward. Exact planning optimizes all agents’ plans together; approximate methods improve one agent at a time, keep a bounded set of plans, or optimize fixed-size controllers. Sharing observations would turn it into a single POMDP, which bounds what the team can achieve.







The key ideas at a glance

A Dec-POMDP has a hidden state, joint actions, private observations and one reward \(R(s, \boldsymbol{a})\) that every agent maximizes. It is a POMG whose agents all have that same reward.
Cooperation doesn’t remove the hard part. Each agent acts on its own observation history, without knowing the others’. Policies are again conditional plans or controllers. Finding the optimal joint policy is NEXP-complete (D. S. Bernstein et al., 2002), harder than POMDPs.
Structure helps. Subclasses make it easier: if the joint observations reveal the state (Dec-MDP); if the state, transitions, observations and rewards factor per agent; or if observations can be shared freely (an MPOMDP, which is just a big POMDP). Sharing observations gives an upper bound on what the team can do.
Search. Dynamic programming with pruning (Chapter 26) is exact but can prune little when rewards are shared. Iterated best response (JESP) improves one agent at a time; it converges to a joint policy no single agent can improve, which may be far from the best. Memory-bounded search (MBDP) keeps a fixed number of plans per agent, chosen at beliefs sampled by simulation.
Controllers of fixed size handle infinite horizons. They can be optimized by nonlinear programming, which can also stop at a poor local optimum.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Dec-POMDP
A team problem: shared reward, private observations


Dec-MDP
A Dec-POMDP whose agents’ observations, pooled, would reveal the state


MMDP / MPOMDP
Multiagent MDP / POMDP: the team shares everything, so it’s one big MDP / POMDP


Factored model
State split into one part per agent (plus the environment)


JESP
Joint equilibrium-based search for policies: iterated best response for teams


MBDP
Memory-bounded dynamic programming: keep a few plans per agent


Value of communication
How much more the team could earn by sharing observations








After this chapter you can

Write down a Dec-POMDP, and place a problem among its subclasses.
Compute a team’s optimal joint plan for small problems, and an upper bound by pooling observations.
Run iterated best response and memory-bounded search, and recognize the local optima they reach.
Evaluate and search over joint controllers.
Explain why a shared reward doesn’t make decentralized planning easy.

title: 27 · Collaborative Agents
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Two rescuers at separate lookouts are looking for a lost hiker in one of two valleys. Each hears a crackly, private radio report about which valley. Carrying the hiker out takes both of them, in the same valley. They agreed on a plan before setting out, but now they can’t talk. Should a rescuer who heard “left” go left, trusting that the other heard the same? Or listen again?


We use the lost hiker, this site’s problem (problem gallery). Each rescuer can listen (cost 1; the report is right 80% of the time), search the left valley, or search the right. Both searching the right valley earns 20; one alone earns 5; each wrong search costs 10. Any search starts a new episode with a new hiker in a random valley. We also revisit Chapter 26’s caregivers, now scored by their total reward.

Coordinate on what each will hear
Over three steps, the best joint plan is worth 7.36: both listen once, then each searches the valley their own report names. Their reports agree 0.68 of the time; when they disagree, the two search different valleys. Listening a second time wouldn’t help: the benefit of better information doesn’t outweigh the cost and the delay. See Equation 1.


Talking would be worth a lot
If the rescuers could pool their reports, the team could earn 11.33 over three steps instead of 7.36: they would search only when the pooled evidence is strong, and always together. That gap, 3.97, is the value of communication. See Equation 2.


Improving one at a time gets stuck
Iterated best response starts from random plans and lets each rescuer improve given the other’s plan. In 9 of 20 runs it ended with both rescuers searching the left valley blindly every step, worth 0. A rescuer who listens instead pays 1 and learns nothing, since the other’s search keeps resetting the hiker; one who searches the other valley splits the team. Only 1 run found the optimum. See Equation 3.


Small controllers need the right memory
Over an infinite horizon, each rescuer can follow a small controller. With 3 nodes, “listen; search where told; listen again”, a pair is worth 38.74. With 2 nodes, no deterministic controller pair beats 0: a rescuer can’t remember both “go left” and “go right”. An optimizer started at random 3-node controllers found only 0.00.

title: 27 · Collaborative Agents
text:
Formalism

Dec-POMDPs
A Dec-POMDP (ADM §27.1; D. S. Bernstein, R. Givan, N. Immerman and S. Zilberstein, Mathematics of Operations Research, 2002) is a POMG (Chapter 26) with a single reward \(R(s, \boldsymbol{a})\) shared by all agents. A joint policy \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\) of conditional plans or controllers is scored by its common value, and the goal is the best one:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\pi}^* &= \arg\max_{\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi^1, \dots, \pi^k)} U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(b), \\
U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) &= R(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}()) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{\pi}()) \sum_{\boldsymbol{o}} O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{\pi}(), s')\, U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{o})}(s')
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

In words. Choose every agent’s plan together to maximize the team’s expected reward, evaluating joint plans exactly as in Chapter 26.
Term by term.

\(U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(b) = \sum_s b(s) U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)\), one number for the whole team.
Each \(\pi^i\) still branches only on agent \(i\)’s own observations.
The search space is every combination of plans: \(\prod_i |\Pi^i_h|\), doubly exponential in the horizon \(h\).

Why it holds. It’s the POMG evaluation with every \(R^i = R\); with identical rewards, the best joint policy is also a Nash equilibrium (nobody can gain by deviating from the optimum), but not every equilibrium is optimal.


Subclasses
The general problem is NEXP-complete for finite horizons (Bernstein et al.). Structure changes that (ADM §27.2):

Dec-MDP: pooled observations would reveal the state. Still NEXP-complete: the pooling can’t happen during execution.
Factored, with independence: each agent has its own state factor, and transitions, observations and rewards split per agent. With all three independent, each agent solves its own MDP (P-complete). With transitions and observations independent only, NP-complete. Otherwise NEXP-complete (ADM Table 27.1).
ND-POMDP: rewards are sums over small groups of agents (a coordination graph), which scales to many agents.
MMDP / MPOMDP: agents share all observations instantly, so the team is a single agent with joint actions: an MDP or a POMDP.

Figure 2: How the models of this book relate. An arrow points from a more general model to a special case, labeled with what’s assumed.







The value of communication
If the agents could share every observation, they would act as one agent with joint actions and joint observations: a POMDP over the same states (an MPOMDP). Its optimal value bounds the team’s:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\boldsymbol{\pi}} U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(b) &\;\le\; U^*_{\text{MPOMDP}}(b), \\
U^*_{\text{MPOMDP}}(b) &= \max_{\boldsymbol{a}} \Big[ R(b, \boldsymbol{a}) + \gamma \sum_{\boldsymbol{o}} P(\boldsymbol{o} \mid b, \boldsymbol{a})\, U^*_{\text{MPOMDP}}\big(\text{Update}(b, \boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{o})\big) \Big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]

In words. A team that shares everything can do at least as well as one that can’t.
Term by term.

The right side is the Chapter 20 lookahead, with joint actions and joint observations; here it is computed by forward search to the horizon.
Every decentralized policy is also a policy of the shared team (one that ignores the others’ observations), so the maximum over the larger set is at least as large.
The difference is the value of communication: the most the team would pay for a perfect, free radio.

Why it holds. Decentralized policies are a subset of centralized ones.


Iterated best response (JESP)
Pick an agent and replace its plan with its best response to the others’ current plans, keeping the current plan in a tie (ADM §27.4; R. Nair, M. Tambe, M. Yokoo, D. Pynadath and S. Marsella, IJCAI, 2003):

\[
\pi^i \leftarrow \arg\max_{\pi^{i\prime} \in \Pi^i} U^{\pi^{i\prime}, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}}(b)
\tag{3}\]

In words. Holding everyone else’s plan fixed, give one agent the plan that’s best for the team.
Term by term.

Each step searches only one agent’s plans, \(|\Pi^i|\) of them, instead of all joint plans.
The team value never decreases, so the process stops, at a joint plan that no single agent can improve.

Why it holds. With a shared reward, an improvement for one agent is an improvement for the team. But a joint plan that no single agent can improve can still be improved by several agents changing together: the process can stop at a poor local optimum, as the blind searchers show.


Memory-bounded search (MBDP) and controllers
MBDP (ADM §27.5; S. Seuken and S. Zilberstein, IJCAI, 2007) builds plans from the last step backward, like dynamic programming, but keeps only a fixed number per agent. To choose them, it simulates random actions from \(b\) to reach a belief a few steps into the future, and keeps the best joint plan for that belief. Its memory is fixed, so it scales to long horizons, but the plans it keeps depend on which beliefs it samples.
For infinite horizons, fixed-size controllers (ADM §27.6; C. Amato, D. S. Bernstein and S. Zilberstein, 2010) are evaluated by Chapter 26’s linear solve (eq. 26.3) and optimized over all agents’ \(\psi\) and \(\eta\) together, a nonlinear program (as in Chapter 23). The page solves it with SciPy’s SLSQP from random starts.

title: 27 · Collaborative Agents
text:
Worked example

The best two-step plan
Both listen, then each searches the valley their own report names. Step 1 costs 2 (two listeners). The two reports are independent given the valley, each right with probability 0.8:

both right (0.64): both search the right valley, +20;
one right, one wrong (2 × 0.16 = 0.32): one finds the hiker alone (+5) and the other searches the wrong valley (−10): −5;
both wrong (0.04): both search the wrong valley, −20.

So step 2 is worth \(0.64 \times 20 + 0.32 \times (-5) + 0.04 \times (-20) = 10.4\), and the plan \(-2 + 0.9 \times 10.4 = 7.36\).
Brute force over all 729 pairs of two-step plans agrees: 7.36, for L[A | B] (both rescuers), where L = listen, A = search left, B = search right, and the brackets give the next action after hearing “left” | “right”.


What pooled reports would add
With both reports shared after one round of listening, the team could search together and only when it makes sense. If the reports agree (probability 0.68), the valley they name is right with probability \(0.64/0.68 = 0.94\): searching together there is worth \(0.94 \times 20 + 0.06 \times (-20) = 17.6\). If they disagree, the valley is a coin flip, and searching blind is worth 0, no better than doing nothing useful. Two steps are then worth \(-2 + 0.9 \times 0.68 \times 17.6 = 8.8\):
The code’s forward search over shared beliefs: 8.800 for two steps, 11.334 for three (decentralized optimum 7.360).

title: 27 · Collaborative Agents
text:
Algorithms & code

Exact planning, search and controllers for teams

PythonJulia


def shared(game):
    """A POMG with both reward rows set to the team's total reward."""
    total = game.R.sum(axis=0)
    return game.__class__(game.T, game.O, np.stack([total, total]), game.gamma,
                          game.states, game.actions, game.observations,
                          game.name + " (team)")

def best_joint_plan(game, b, plans, U=None):
    """The joint plan with the highest shared value from b, among
    plans[0] x plans[1], by checking every pair. Returns (p1, p2, value)."""
    U = pomg.plan_evaluator(game) if U is None else U
    best = max(((p1, p2, pomg.utility(U, b, p1, p2)[0])
                for p1, p2 in product(*plans)), key=lambda t: t[2])
    return best

def exact_best_plans(game, b, horizon, U=None):
    """Brute force over every joint plan of the given horizon, for two
    agents with two observations each. A plan is (a, (p_obs0, p_obs1)), so
    a joint plan's value is its first reward plus four lookups in the table
    W of (horizon - 1)-step joint values, one per joint observation: all
    |A|^2 |P|^4 of them can be scored at once with NumPy broadcasting."""
    U = pomg.plan_evaluator(game) if U is None else U
    nS, nA = game.T.shape[0], game.T.shape[1]
    if horizon == 1:                   # one step: the best joint action
        v, a1, a2 = max((b @ game.R[0, :, a1, a2], a1, a2)
                        for a1, a2 in product(range(nA), repeat=2))
        return (a1,), (a2,), float(v)
    subs = pomg.all_plans(nA, 2, horizon - 1)
    n = len(subs)
    # W[k1, k2, s2]: shared value of subplans k1 and k2 from next state s2.
    W = np.array([[[U(p, q, s)[0] for s in range(nS)] for q in subs]
                  for p in subs])
    best = (-np.inf, None)
    for a1, a2 in product(range(nA), repeat=2):
        first = b @ game.R[0, :, a1, a2]
        # w[s2, o1, o2]: probability of next state s2 and joint observation.
        w = np.einsum("s,st,tuv->tuv", b, game.T[:, a1, a2], game.O[a1, a2])
        # M[o1][o2][k1, k2] = gamma sum_s2 w W: the value of subplan pair
        # (k1 after o1, k2 after o2), weighted by that observation pair.
        M = game.gamma * np.einsum("tuv,ijt->uvij", w, W)
        # Axes: agent 1's subplans after obs 0 and 1, agent 2's after 0, 1.
        V = (first + M[0, 0][:, None, :, None] + M[0, 1][:, None, None, :]
             + M[1, 0][None, :, :, None] + M[1, 1][None, :, None, :])
        k = np.unravel_index(np.argmax(V), V.shape)
        if V[k] > best[0]:
            p1 = (a1, (subs[k[0]], subs[k[1]]))
            p2 = (a2, (subs[k[2]], subs[k[3]]))
            best = (float(V[k]), (p1, p2))
    return best[1][0], best[1][1], best[0]

def iterated_best_response(game, b, plans, rng, k_max=50, U=None):
    """§27.4 (JESP): start from random plans; in random agent order, switch
    each agent to its best plan against the other's (ties keep the current
    plan) until nobody changes. Returns the joint plan and its value."""
    U = pomg.plan_evaluator(game) if U is None else U
    joint = [plans[0][rng.integers(len(plans[0]))],
             plans[1][rng.integers(len(plans[1]))]]
    value = lambda p1, p2: pomg.utility(U, b, p1, p2)[0]
    for _ in range(k_max):
        changed = False
        for i in rng.permutation(2):
            def v(p):
                return value(p, joint[1]) if i == 0 else value(joint[0], p)
            best = max(plans[i], key=v)
            if v(best) > v(joint[i]) + 1e-9:        # ties keep the current plan
                joint[i], changed = best, True
        if not changed:
            break
    return joint[0], joint[1], value(*joint)

def explore_belief(game, b, steps, rng) -> Array:
    """Belief after `steps` random joint actions and sampled joint
    observations from b (the heuristic of memory-bounded search)."""
    nS, n1, n2 = game.T.shape[:3]
    s = rng.choice(nS, p=b)
    for _ in range(steps):
        a1, a2 = rng.integers(n1), rng.integers(n2)
        s2 = rng.choice(nS, p=game.T[s, a1, a2])
        flat = game.O[a1, a2, s2].ravel()
        o1, o2 = divmod(rng.choice(len(flat), p=flat), game.O.shape[4])
        # Filter with the joint action and joint observation (Ch. 19).
        b = game.O[a1, a2, :, o1, o2] * (b @ game.T[:, a1, a2, :])
        b, s = b / b.sum(), s2
    return b

def memory_bounded_search(game, b, horizon, max_plans, rng, U=None):
    """§27.5 (MBDP): keep at most max_plans plans per agent. At each step,
    expand every kept plan by one step; then, max_plans times, sample a
    belief that many steps from the end and keep the best joint plan there.
    Returns the best kept joint plan from b and its value."""
    U = pomg.plan_evaluator(game) if U is None else U
    nA, nO = game.T.shape[1:3], game.O.shape[3:]
    kept = [[(a,) for a in range(nA[i])] for i in range(2)]
    for t in range(1, horizon):
        grown = [pomg.expand(kept[i], nA[i], nO[i]) for i in range(2)]
        kept = [[], []]
        for _ in range(max_plans):
            bt = explore_belief(game, b, horizon - t - 1, rng)
            p1, p2, _ = best_joint_plan(game, bt, grown, U)
            for i, p in enumerate((p1, p2)):
                if p not in kept[i]:
                    kept[i].append(p)
    return best_joint_plan(game, b, kept, U)

def centralized_value(game, b, horizon) -> float:
    """The team's optimal value if the agents could share observations
    (an MPOMDP): forward search over beliefs, joint actions and joint
    observations. An upper bound on any Dec-POMDP policy's value."""
    nS, n1, n2 = game.T.shape[:3]
    R = game.R[0]

    def value(b, h):
        best = -np.inf
        for a1, a2 in product(range(n1), range(n2)):
            q = b @ R[:, a1, a2]
            if h > 1:
                pred = b @ game.T[:, a1, a2, :]          # predicted next state
                for o1, o2 in product(*map(range, game.O.shape[3:])):
                    joint = game.O[a1, a2, :, o1, o2] * pred
                    p = joint.sum()
                    if p > 0:
                        q += game.gamma * p * value(joint / p, h - 1)
            best = max(best, q)
        return best

    return value(np.asarray(b, dtype=float), horizon)

def optimize_controllers(game, b, n_nodes, rng, starts=5):
    """§27.6: the best pair of n-node stochastic controllers for the shared
    reward, by SLSQP over psi and eta (values from the linear solve of
    eq. 26.3, starting both controllers at node 0). Returns the value."""
    nA, nO = game.T.shape[1], game.O.shape[3]
    size = n_nodes * nA + n_nodes * nA * nO * n_nodes

    def unpack(z):
        psi = z[:n_nodes * nA].reshape(n_nodes, nA)
        eta = z[n_nodes * nA:].reshape(n_nodes, nA, nO, n_nodes)
        return psi, eta

    def negative_value(z):
        c1, c2 = unpack(z[:size]), unpack(z[size:])
        return -pomg.evaluate_controllers(game, c1, c2)[0, 0, 0] @ b

    # Every psi row (over actions) and eta row (over next nodes) sums to 1.
    rows = [(k * nA, nA) for k in range(n_nodes)]
    rows += [(n_nodes * nA + k * n_nodes, n_nodes)
             for k in range(n_nodes * nA * nO)]
    def row_sum(o, w):                 # constraint: z[o:o+w] sums to 1
        return {"type": "eq", "fun": lambda z: z[o:o + w].sum() - 1}
    cons = [row_sum(off + a, w) for off in (0, size) for a, w in rows]
    best = -np.inf
    for _ in range(starts):
        z0 = np.concatenate([rng.dirichlet(np.ones(w)) for _ in range(2)
                             for _, w in rows])
        res = minimize(negative_value, z0, method="SLSQP",
                       bounds=[(0, 1)] * (2 * size), constraints=cons,
                       options={"maxiter": 300})
        best = max(best, -res.fun)
    return best


using ADM

g = lost_hiker()            # POMG with identical reward rows; 1 = listen / left
b = [0.5, 0.5]

# A plan is (a,) at the last step, or (a, (plan after "left", plan after "right")).
plans(h) = h == 1 ? [(a,) for a in 1:3] :
           [(a, (p, q)) for a in 1:3 for p in plans(h - 1) for q in plans(h - 1)]

# Shared value of joint plans (p1, p2) from state s (eq. 27 as in eq. 26.1).
function value(p1, p2, s)
    a1, a2 = p1[1], p2[1]
    u = g.R[1, s, a1, a2]
    length(p1) == 1 && return u
    for s′ in 1:2, o1 in 1:2, o2 in 1:2
        w = g.T[s, a1, a2, s′] * g.O[a1, a2, s′, o1, o2]
        w > 0 && (u += g.γ * w * value(p1[2][o1], p2[2][o2], s′))   # own branches
    end
    return u
end

# Brute force over all 27 × 27 two-step joint plans (in a function, so the
# loop's assignments are local: Julia's soft-scope rule).
function brute_force(h)
    best, arg = -Inf, nothing
    for p1 in plans(h), p2 in plans(h)
        v = sum(b[s] * value(p1, p2, s) for s in 1:2)
        v > best && ((best, arg) = (v, (p1, p2)))
    end
    return best, arg
end
best, arg = brute_force(2)
println("best two-step team value: ", round(best; digits = 3), ", plans ", arg)
@assert isapprox(best, 7.36; atol = 1e-9) && arg[1] == (1, ((2,), (3,)))









NoteReading the Python code






D.shared turns a POMG into a team problem by giving every agent the sum of the rewards; for the lost hiker, both rows are already equal.
exact_best_plans uses broadcasting: M[0, 0][:, None, :, None] has axes (agent 1’s subplan after “left”, agent 1’s after “right”, agent 2’s after “left”, agent 2’s after “right”), and adding the four such terms scores all \(27^4\) subplan combinations for one pair of first actions at once.
iterated_best_response uses max(plans[i], key=v): the plan with the highest team value, holding the other agent’s plan fixed.
centralized_value is the Chapter 20 lookahead, written recursively over joint actions and joint observations.

b = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
p1, p2, v = D.exact_best_plans(game, b, 3)
print(f"exact, 3 steps: {v:.3f}; with shared reports: {D.centralized_value(game, b, 3):.3f}")
full = P.all_plans(3, 2, 3)
for seed in range(3):
    print("JESP:", round(D.iterated_best_response(game, b, [full, full],
                                                  np.random.default_rng(seed))[2], 3))

title: 27 · Collaborative Agents
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: why isn’t a Dec-MDP just an MDP? In a Dec-MDP, the agents’ observations together reveal the state. Why can’t each agent just act on the state?






TipSolution





Because no agent has all the observations while acting. Each sees only its own part, so it must plan for what the others might have seen. The state is known “jointly” only at planning time, not during execution; that’s why Dec-MDPs remain NEXP-complete.



Problem 2: fully independent agents. A factored Dec-MDP has transition, observation and reward independence. How would you solve it?






TipSolution





Solve one MDP per agent: agent \(i\)’s own states, actions, transitions and reward component. Because nothing couples the agents (not their dynamics, their observations or their rewards), the sum of the individually optimal values is the team’s optimum, and the total cost is linear in the number of agents.



Problem 3: a two-step value by hand. In the lost hiker, suppose rescuer 1 listens then searches where told, while rescuer 2 searches the left valley both steps. What is the team’s two-step value from 50–50?






TipSolution





Step 1: rescuer 1 listens (−1); rescuer 2 searches left alone: right valley half the time (+5), else wrong (−10): −2.5. Total step 1: −3.5. Because rescuer 2 searched, the hiker resets, and the report rescuer 1 hears is uninformative, so its step-2 search is a coin flip. Step 2 (both search): same valley with probability 0.5, and then right half the time: \(0.5 \times 0.5 \times 20 + 0.5 \times 0.5 \times (-20) = 0\); different valleys (0.5): one finds the hiker (+5), one is wrong (−10): −5 × 0.5 = −2.5. Value: \(-3.5 + 0.9 \times (-2.5) = -5.75\). A mixed team is worse than either coordinated one.



Problem 4: a JESP trap. Show that “both always search left” is a point iterated best response can’t leave, even though it’s worth only 0.






TipSolution





Hold rescuer 2 at “always search left”. Every step, rescuer 2’s search resets the hiker, so rescuer 1’s reports are uninformative, and listening costs 1 for nothing. Searching right while rescuer 2 searches left splits the team: one wrong search every time (−5 per step). Searching left with rescuer 2 earns 0 on average. So rescuer 1’s best response is to keep searching left; by symmetry the same for rescuer 2. Both agents would have to switch to listening together to escape.



Problem 5: the price of silence. Using the page’s numbers, how much would the rescuers pay per three-step mission for a perfect radio, and why is it so large here?






TipSolution





Up to 3.97, the value of communication: the pooled-reports value minus the decentralized optimum. It’s large because the reward demands coordination: +20 needs both rescuers in the right valley at once. Without sharing, they must act on reports that disagree 32% of the time, splitting up; with sharing, they search only when the pooled evidence is strong, and always together.

title: 27 · Collaborative Agents
text:
Recap

A Dec-POMDP is a team version of a POMG: one shared reward, private observations (Equation 1). Why it matters: it models robot teams, sensor networks and rescuers, and it is the hardest model in the book (NEXP-complete).
Structure makes it tractable (subclasses). Why it matters: independence between agents, or free communication, can turn it into separate MDPs or one POMDP; model a problem with its structure.
Communication has a computable value (Equation 2). Why it matters: the lost hiker’s team would gain 3.97 per three-step mission by sharing reports; that’s the case for spending on a radio.
Improving one agent at a time finds local optima (Equation 3). Why it matters: JESP, and nonlinear programming over controllers, both stopped at “both search blindly”, a joint policy no single agent can improve. Coordinated changes require search over several agents at once.
Bounded memory trades optimality for scale. Why it matters: MBDP and small controllers handle long horizons with fixed resources; how good they are depends on the beliefs sampled and the nodes allowed.

title: 27 · Collaborative Agents
text:
Cheat sheet & connections



Table 4: Key equations from this page.










Name
Formula
Ref




Dec-POMDP objective
\(\max_{\boldsymbol{\pi}} U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(b)\), plans branching on own observations
Equation 1


Communication bound
\(\max_{\boldsymbol{\pi}} U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(b) \le U^*_{\text{MPOMDP}}(b)\)
Equation 2


JESP step
\(\pi^i \leftarrow \arg\max_{\pi^{i\prime}} U^{\pi^{i\prime}, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}}(b)\)
Equation 3


MBDP
keep \(m\) plans per agent, chosen at sampled beliefs
§27.5


Controllers
maximize \(\sum_s b(s) U(\boldsymbol{x}_1, s)\) over all \(\psi^i, \eta^i\) (eq. 26.3 constraints)
§27.6






Common pitfalls

Assuming cooperation makes it easy. Shared goals remove conflict, not the need to coordinate on private information.
Letting plans use others’ observations. That’s the MPOMDP, an upper bound, not an executable decentralized policy.
Trusting one run of a local method. JESP and nonlinear programming need many starts; compare against an exact answer or a bound when you can.
Too little controller memory. If the best controller does nothing useful, it may not have enough nodes to represent a sensible policy.

title: 25 · Sequential Problems
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 24 had agents meet once, with no state. Here they interact over time in a changing world: a Markov game (also called a stochastic game) is an MDP (Chapter 7) with several agents, each with its own reward, whose joint action moves a shared state. The ideas of Chapter 24 carry over, with values in place of one-shot rewards: best responses become MDPs, and equilibria become joint policies over states. Chapter 26 removes the assumption that everyone sees the state.
The question: when several agents act repeatedly in a shared, changing world, what are sensible joint policies, and how do agents find them?
The short answer: fix the others and you have an MDP; ask everyone to be at a best response at once and you have a Nash equilibrium; let them learn from play and they may reach one, or not.

Policy evaluation of a joint policy is a linear solve, one value function per agent.
Best response: with the others’ policies fixed, an agent faces an MDP.
Nash equilibria exist for every finite discounted game, can be found by nonlinear programming, and there may be several.
Learning: fictitious play, gradient ascent and Nash Q-learning adapt policies from experience.
