Figure 1: Map of this chapter. A Markov game gives each agent a value for any joint policy. Fixing the others turns an agent’s problem into an MDP; equilibria make every agent’s problem solved at once; learning rules adapt toward them from experience.







The key ideas at a glance

A Markov game has states \(\mathcal{S}\), agents with action sets \(\mathcal{A}^i\), a transition model \(T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a})\) driven by the joint action, and a reward \(R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})\) for each agent. Each agent’s policy \(\pi^i(a^i \mid s)\) depends on the current state.
Evaluation is an MDP calculation. With every policy fixed, the state moves as a Markov chain, and each agent’s value \(U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(s)\) solves its own linear Bellman equation.
A best response is an MDP. Hold the others’ policies fixed: they become part of the environment. Solving that MDP (Chapter 7) gives agent \(i\)’s best response.
Nash equilibria. A joint policy where every agent’s policy is a best response, in every state. Every finite discounted Markov game has one (A. M. Fink, 1964), possibly several, with very different values: our lake has a sustainable one and a tragic one.
Learning. Agents can adapt from experience: fictitious play best-responds to the others’ observed frequencies in each state; gradient ascent nudges policies along learned action values; Nash Q-learning learns joint action values and plays the equilibrium of each state’s “stage game”. Which equilibrium they reach, if any, depends on chance and on how they explore.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Markov game (stochastic game)
An MDP with several agents, each with its own reward


Joint policy \(\boldsymbol{\pi}\)
Every agent’s state-dependent policy


Best response
An agent’s optimal policy when the others’ policies are fixed


Exploitability
The most any agent could gain, in any state, by switching to its best response


Stationary Nash equilibrium
A joint policy with zero exploitability


Stage game
The simple game played in one state, with values in place of rewards


Fictitious play
Best-respond to the others’ observed action frequencies in each state


Nash Q-learning
Q-learning on joint actions, valuing next states by stage-game equilibria








After this chapter you can

Write down a Markov game, and evaluate any joint policy by solving linear equations.
Compute a best response by building and solving the MDP the other agents induce.
Check whether a joint policy is a Nash equilibrium, and find equilibria by nonlinear programming or enumeration.
Run fictitious play, gradient ascent and Nash Q-learning, and judge the result by its exploitability.
Explain why several equilibria can exist, and why learning may land on the worse one.

title: 25 · Sequential Problems
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Two fishing boats share a lake. Each day each can fish lightly or heavily. Fishing heavily fills today’s hold, but if both do it every day the fish population collapses and both are poorer for years. It’s the prisoner’s dilemma of Chapter 24, except that today’s choices change tomorrow’s lake. That’s what makes the sequential version interesting: a boat that overfishes today pays for it later, so the long view can make restraint pay.


We use two games. The lake is this site’s problem (problem gallery): the stock is low, medium or high; light fishing catches 1, 2 or 3 and heavy fishing 2, 3.5 or 5; the stock grows if both fish lightly and shrinks if both fish heavily. The predator-prey hex world (Appendix F.13, gallery) has a predator chasing a prey across 12 hexagonal tiles.

Every agent has its own value
If both boats always fish lightly, the lake stays full and each boat earns 30.0 from a high stock. If both always fish heavily, each earns only 25.9. These values come from the same linear equations as MDP policy evaluation, one set per boat. See Equation 1.


Fix the others, and it’s an MDP
If boat 2 always fishes lightly, boat 1’s best response is to fish heavily at a high stock and lightly otherwise, worth 41.9 from high. The other boat’s restraint is just part of boat 1’s environment. See Equation 2.


Several equilibria, one tragic
Trying all 64 deterministic joint policies finds exactly two Nash equilibria. In one, both fish lightly unless the stock is high, worth 36.1 each from high: this is also the best the two could do as a team. In the other, both always fish heavily, worth 25.9. Neither boat can do better alone in either one. See Equation 3.


Learning finds one, or none
Two boats learning by fictitious play reached the sustainable equilibrium in 12 of 20 runs and the tragic one in 7. In the predator-prey game, best responses chase each other in circles, while fictitious play slowly settles: the most either agent could gain by switching fell from 67 after 1,000 steps to 19 after 50,000. See Equation 4 and Equation 5.

title: 25 · Sequential Problems
text:
Formalism

Markov games and policy evaluation
A Markov game (ADM §25.1; L. S. Shapley, PNAS, 1953) has states \(\mathcal{S}\), agents \(\mathcal{I}\) with actions \(\mathcal{A}^i\), transitions \(T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a})\) and rewards \(R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})\). Under a joint policy with \(\pi^j(a^j \mid s)\), the expected reward and transitions are averages over joint actions, \(R^i(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}(s)) = \sum_{\boldsymbol{a}} R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a}) \prod_j \pi^j(a^j \mid s)\) and likewise for \(T\), and agent \(i\)’s value satisfies

\[
U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(s) = R^i\big(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}(s)\big) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T\big(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{\pi}(s)\big)\, U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(s')
\tag{1}\]

In words. Each agent’s value is its expected reward now plus the discounted value of where the joint policy takes the state.
Term by term.

\(R^i(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}(s))\) and \(T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{\pi}(s))\) average over joint actions, weighting each by \(\prod_j \pi^j(a^j \mid s)\): the agents choose independently in each state.
The equation is linear in \(U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}\): \(U = (I - \gamma T_{\boldsymbol{\pi}})^{-1} R^i_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\), one solve per agent.
The agents share the state dynamics \(T_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\) but not the rewards.

Why it holds. With every policy fixed, the state alone evolves as a Markov chain with rewards for each agent, and Equation 1 is that chain’s Bellman expectation equation (Chapter 7).


Best and softmax responses
With the others’ policies \(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}\) fixed, agent \(i\) faces an MDP (ADM §25.2):

\[
T'(s' \mid s, a^i) = T\big(s' \mid s, a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}(s)\big), \qquad R'(s, a^i) = R^i\big(s, a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}(s)\big)
\tag{2}\]

In words. Average the others’ actions into the environment, and solve the single-agent MDP that is left.
Term by term.

\(T(s' \mid s, a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}(s))\) averages the transition over the others’ actions in state \(s\).
Only agent \(i\)’s own reward \(R^i\) appears.
Solving the MDP exactly (policy iteration) gives a deterministic best response.
A softmax response takes this MDP’s optimal \(Q(s, a^i)\) and plays \(\pi^i(a^i \mid s) \propto \exp(\lambda Q(s, a^i))\).

Why it holds. When the others’ policies depend only on the current state, the rest of the world, including them, is Markov from agent \(i\)’s point of view.


Nash equilibrium

\[
U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(s) \ge U^{(\pi^{i\prime}, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}), i}(s) \quad \text{for every agent } i, \text{ policy } \pi^{i\prime} \text{ and state } s
\tag{3}\]

In words. In every state, no agent can do better by changing its own policy.
Term by term.

The deviation \(\pi^{i\prime}\) can be any policy, but it’s enough to check the best response of Equation 2.
Exploitability \(= \max_{i, s}\big(U^{*, i}(s) - U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(s)\big)\), where \(U^{*, i}\) is the value of agent \(i\)’s best response. It is 0 exactly at an equilibrium; the page uses it to check every result.
Because policies here depend only on the state, these are stationary Markov perfect equilibria: no agent wants to deviate from any state, even ones the equilibrium rarely visits.

Why it holds. Every finite discounted Markov game has a stationary Nash equilibrium (A. M. Fink, 1964). As a computation, the book (ADM eq. 25.7, after J. A. Filar et al., 1991) minimizes \(\sum_{i,s} \big(U^i(s) - Q^i(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}(s))\big)\) subject to \(U^i(s) \ge Q^i(s, a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}(s))\), with \(Q^i(s, \cdot) = R^i(s, \cdot) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \cdot) U^i(s')\); the minimum, 0, is attained exactly at equilibria. The page solves it with SciPy’s SLSQP, and checks the answer’s exploitability.


Learning in Markov games
Fictitious play (ADM §25.4) counts, in each state, how often each agent played each action, \(N(j, a^j, s)\), and best-responds to those frequencies:

\[
\hat{\pi}^j(a^j \mid s) \propto N(j, a^j, s), \qquad a^i = \arg\max_{a^i} Q^i\big(s, a^i, \hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-i}(s)\big)
\tag{4}\]

In words. In each state, assume the others play as often as you’ve seen them play there, and act to maximize your action value against that.
Term by term.

\(N(j, a^j, s)\) starts at 1 and grows each time \(j\) plays \(a^j\) in \(s\).
\(Q^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})\) is agent \(i\)’s value of the joint action, computed from the known model: \(R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a}) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a}) U^i(s')\), with \(U^i(s')\) the value of \(s'\) when everyone plays their frequencies.
Only the state just visited is updated, as in asynchronous value iteration.

Why it holds. If the frequencies settle, each agent is best-responding to the others’ limiting policy in every visited state: an equilibrium on the states the play visits. There’s no general guarantee that they settle.
Gradient ascent (ADM §25.5) has each agent learn \(Q^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})\) by Q-learning, treating the others as if they will repeat their last actions, and step its policy at the visited state along \(Q^i(s, \cdot, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i})\), projected back onto the simplex.
Nash Q-learning (ADM §25.6; J. Hu and M. P. Wellman, JMLR, 2003) learns joint-action values for every agent. After a transition from \(s\) to \(s'\), it solves the stage game at \(s'\), the simple game with rewards \(Q^j(s', \cdot)\), for a Nash equilibrium \(\boldsymbol{\pi}'\), and updates

\[
Q^i(s, \boldsymbol{a}) \leftarrow Q^i(s, \boldsymbol{a}) + \alpha \Big( R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a}) + \gamma \sum_{\boldsymbol{a}'} Q^i(s', \boldsymbol{a}') \prod_j \pi^{j\prime}(a^{j\prime}) - Q^i(s, \boldsymbol{a}) \Big)
\tag{5}\]

In words. Like Q-learning, but the next state is valued by the equilibrium of its stage game instead of by a maximum.
Term by term.

\(\alpha = 1/\sqrt{N(s, \boldsymbol{a})}\) shrinks with the number of visits to the state and joint action.
The sum is agent \(i\)’s value of the stage game at \(s'\) under its equilibrium \(\boldsymbol{\pi}'\).
The agents act on the stage equilibrium at the current state, choosing a random action with probability \(\varepsilon\). The book uses \(\varepsilon = 1/\sum_{\boldsymbol{a}} N(s, \boldsymbol{a})\).
When a stage game has several equilibria, all agents must pick the same one; the page takes the first one support enumeration finds.

Why it holds. If every agent’s \(Q\) were the equilibrium’s joint-action values, the stage equilibria would reproduce the equilibrium, and the update would leave \(Q\) unchanged. Convergence is proved only under strong conditions on the stage games (Hu and Wellman), which the lake does not guarantee.

title: 25 · Sequential Problems
text:
Worked example

Why “both always light” isn’t an equilibrium
If both boats always fish lightly from a high stock, the stock stays high (it grows or stays, and can’t exceed high), so each boat earns 3 per day forever: \(3/(1 - 0.9) = 30\). Now let boat 1 deviate once, at a high stock, and fish heavily, then go back to light fishing. Today it catches 5. With one heavy boat, the stock rises or stays with probability \(0.2 + 0.5 = 0.7\) (still high), and falls to medium with probability 0.3:
\[
5 + 0.9\,\big(0.7 \times 30 + 0.3 \times U(\text{medium})\big), \qquad U(\text{medium}) = 28.63
\]
That’s 31.63, more than 30. One day of heavy fishing pays, so restraint everywhere is not an equilibrium. Boat 1’s full best response, heavy only at a high stock, earns 41.90: the exploitability of “both always light” is 11.90.


Why “light unless high” is
Now both boats fish heavily at a high stock and lightly otherwise. From high, both fish heavily; the stock falls to medium with probability 0.7, where both fish lightly and it regrows. Could boat 1 gain by fishing lightly at high instead? Then only one boat fishes heavily, and the stock falls less often, but boat 1 catches 3 instead of 5. And by fishing heavily at medium? It would catch 3.5 instead of 2, but push the stock down. The code checks every deviation in every state at once:
Values (low, medium, high) for each boat: 30.62, 33.90, 36.10. Exploitability: 0.0e+00. Both always heavy: 20.00, 22.05, 25.88, exploitability 0.0e+00.
Both are equilibria. The first is worth more than half again as much from a low stock.

title: 25 · Sequential Problems
25 · Sequential Problems
text:
Algorithms & code

Evaluation, responses, equilibria and learning

PythonJulia


def joint_matrices(game, policies):
    """eqs. 25.1-25.2: the rewards R^i(s, pi(s)) and transitions
    T(s2 | s, pi(s)) when both agents follow their policies."""
    p1, p2 = policies
    # w[s, a1, a2]: probability of the joint action in state s.
    w = p1[:, :, None] * p2[:, None, :]
    R = np.einsum("sab,isab->is", w, game.R)
    T = np.einsum("sab,sabt->st", w, game.T)
    return R, T

def policy_evaluation(game, policies) -> Array:
    """eq. 25.3 for both agents by one linear solve: U[i, s]."""
    R, T = joint_matrices(game, policies)
    n = len(T)
    return np.linalg.solve(np.eye(n) - game.gamma * T, R.T).T

def response_mdp(game, policies, i):
    """eqs. 25.4-25.5: with the other agent's policy fixed, agent i faces an
    MDP with T'[s, ai, s2] and R'[s, ai]."""
    other = policies[1 - i]
    if i == 0:          # sum out agent 2's action a2
        T = np.einsum("sb,sabt->sat", other, game.T)
        R = np.einsum("sb,sab->sa", other, game.R[0])
    else:               # sum out agent 1's action a1
        T = np.einsum("sa,sabt->sbt", other, game.T)
        R = np.einsum("sa,sab->sb", other, game.R[1])
    return T, R

def best_response(game, policies, i):
    """Agent i's optimal policy against the other's fixed policy, by exact
    policy iteration on the response MDP. Returns (policy matrix, values)."""
    T, R = response_mdp(game, policies, i)
    pi, U = policy_iteration(T, R, game.gamma, np.zeros(len(R), int))[:2]
    return np.eye(R.shape[1])[pi], U

def softmax_response(game, policies, i, lam) -> Array:
    """eq. 25.6: pi^i(a | s) proportional to exp(lam Q(s, a)), with Q from
    the response MDP's optimal values."""
    T, R = response_mdp(game, policies, i)
    _, U = best_response(game, policies, i)
    Q = lam * (R + game.gamma * T @ U)
    P = np.exp(Q - Q.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return P / P.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

def exploitability(game, policies) -> float:
    """The most either agent could gain, in any state, by switching to its
    best response: 0 exactly at a (stationary) Nash equilibrium."""
    U = policy_evaluation(game, policies)
    return max((best_response(game, policies, i)[1] - U[i]).max()
               for i in range(2))

def nash_equilibrium(game, rng, starts=10):
    """eq. 25.7 by SLSQP: minimize sum_{i,s} U_i(s) - Q_i(s, pi(s)) subject
    to U_i(s) >= Q_i(s, a_i, pi^-i(s)) for every agent, state and action.
    Returns the best run's policies and its exploitability."""
    nS, n1, n2 = game.T.shape[:3]
    sizes = (nS * n1, nS * n2, 2 * nS)

    def unpack(z):
        p1 = z[:sizes[0]].reshape(nS, n1)
        p2 = z[sizes[0]:sizes[0] + sizes[1]].reshape(nS, n2)
        return p1, p2, z[-sizes[2]:].reshape(2, nS)

    def action_q(p1, p2, U):
        """Q^i(s, a_i, pi^-i(s)) for each agent, using the value guess U."""
        # q[i, s, a1, a2] = R^i(s, a1, a2)
        #                   + gamma sum_s2 T(s2 | s, a1, a2) U_i(s2)
        q = game.R + game.gamma * np.einsum("sabt,it->isab", game.T, U)
        q1 = np.einsum("sab,sb->sa", q[0], p2)   # average out agent 2
        q2 = np.einsum("sab,sa->sb", q[1], p1)   # average out agent 1
        return q1, q2

    def objective(z):
        p1, p2, U = unpack(z)
        q1, q2 = action_q(p1, p2, U)
        return (U[0] - (q1 * p1).sum(1)).sum() + (U[1] - (q2 * p2).sum(1)).sum()

    def gaps(z):                          # >= 0: no action beats U_i(s)
        p1, p2, U = unpack(z)
        q1, q2 = action_q(p1, p2, U)
        return np.concatenate([(U[0][:, None] - q1).ravel(),
                               (U[1][:, None] - q2).ravel()])

    def sums(z):                          # every policy row sums to 1
        p1, p2, _ = unpack(z)
        return np.concatenate([p1.sum(1) - 1, p2.sum(1) - 1])

    cons = [{"type": "ineq", "fun": gaps}, {"type": "eq", "fun": sums}]
    bounds = [(0, 1)] * (sizes[0] + sizes[1]) + [(None, None)] * sizes[2]
    best = None
    for _ in range(starts):
        p1 = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(n1), nS)
        p2 = rng.dirichlet(np.ones(n2), nS)
        U0 = policy_evaluation(game, [p1, p2])
        z0 = np.concatenate([p1.ravel(), p2.ravel(), U0.ravel()])
        res = minimize(objective, z0, method="SLSQP", bounds=bounds,
                       constraints=cons,
                       options={"maxiter": 1000, "ftol": 1e-12})
        p1, p2, _ = unpack(res.x)
        pols = [np.clip(p, 0, None) for p in (p1, p2)]
        pols = [p / p.sum(1, keepdims=True) for p in pols]
        e = exploitability(game, pols)
        if best is None or e < best[1]:
            best = (pols, e)
    return best

def fictitious_play(game, steps, rng, s0=0, reset=None, counts=1.0):
    """§25.4: each agent keeps counts N(j, a_j, s) of both agents' actions
    (eq. 25.9) and joint-action values Q_i(s, a) from the known model. It
    acts greedily on Q_i against the others' frequencies in s (eq. 25.11),
    then refreshes Q_i(s, .) at the state just visited. `reset` restarts
    every so many steps at s0. Returns the visited states, joint actions and
    each agent's frequency model after every step."""
    nS, n1, n2 = game.T.shape[:3]
    N = [np.full((nS, n1), counts), np.full((nS, n2), counts)]
    Q = [game.R[0].copy(), game.R[1].copy()]   # Q[i][s, a1, a2]
    s, trace = s0, []
    for t in range(steps):
        if reset and t % reset == 0:
            s = s0
        freq = [N[0][s] / N[0][s].sum(), N[1][s] / N[1][s].sum()]
        a1 = int(np.argmax(Q[0][s] @ freq[1]))       # sum over agent 2's action
        a2 = int(np.argmax(freq[0] @ Q[1][s]))       # sum over agent 1's action
        N[0][s, a1] += 1
        N[1][s, a2] += 1
        # Refresh Q_i(s, .): reward plus the discounted value of the next
        # state, where both agents play their frequencies there.
        pol = [Ni / Ni.sum(1, keepdims=True) for Ni in N]
        w = pol[0][:, :, None] * pol[1][:, None, :]
        for i in range(2):
            U = (Q[i] * w).sum(axis=(1, 2))           # U_i(s2) for every s2
            Q[i][s] = game.R[i, s] + game.gamma * game.T[s] @ U
        trace.append((s, a1, a2))
        s = step(game, s, (a1, a2), rng)
    return {"trace": trace, "N": N}

def gradient_ascent_play(game, steps, rng, s0=0):
    """§25.5: each agent learns Q_i(s, a1, a2) by Q-learning, treating the
    other's last action as its policy (eq. 25.15), and moves its policy at
    the visited state along Q_i(s, ., a^-i) (eqs. 25.13-25.14), projected
    onto the simplex. Step sizes and exploration are 1 / sqrt(t).
    Returns the final policies."""
    nS, n1, n2 = game.T.shape[:3]
    Q = np.zeros((2, nS, n1, n2))
    pol = [np.full((nS, n1), 1 / n1), np.full((nS, n2), 1 / n2)]
    s = s0
    for t in range(1, steps + 1):
        rate = 1 / np.sqrt(t)
        # Act: epsilon-greedy mixing with the uniform policy, epsilon = rate.
        a = [rng.choice(n, p=rate / n + (1 - rate) * p[s])
             for n, p in zip((n1, n2), pol)]
        s2 = step(game, s, a, rng)
        for i in range(2):
            # The other agent's action is held at what it just did.
            q_next = Q[i, s2, :, a[1]] if i == 0 else Q[i, s2, a[0], :]
            idx = (i, s) + tuple(a)
            Q[idx] += rate * (game.R[idx] + game.gamma * q_next.max() - Q[idx])
            grad = Q[i, s, :, a[1]] if i == 0 else Q[i, s, a[0], :]
            pol[i][s] = games.project_simplex(pol[i][s] + rate * grad)
        s = s2
    return pol

def nash_q_learning(game, steps, rng, s0=0, eps=None):
    """§25.6 (J. Hu and M. P. Wellman, 2003): learn joint-action values
    Q[i, s, a1, a2] for both agents. After each transition, solve the stage
    game Q[:, s2] for a Nash equilibrium (support enumeration; the first
    one found) and move Q toward reward + gamma times its value, with
    rate 1 / sqrt(N(s, a)). Acts on the stage equilibrium at the current
    state, exploring (a uniform action) with probability eps, or by default
    1 / sum_a N(s, a) as in the book."""
    nS, n1, n2 = game.T.shape[:3]
    Q = np.zeros((2, nS, n1, n2))
    N = np.ones((nS, n1, n2))
    s = s0

    def stage(s):
        g = SimpleGame(Q[:, s], (tuple(range(n1)), tuple(range(n2))))
        eqs = games.support_enumeration(g)
        if not eqs:                         # degenerate stage game: fall back
            return games.nash_equilibrium(g, rng, starts=3)[0]
        return list(eqs[0])

    for _ in range(steps):
        pols = stage(s)
        e = 1 / N[s].sum() if eps is None else eps
        a = [rng.integers(n) if rng.random() < e else rng.choice(n, p=p)
             for n, p in zip((n1, n2), pols)]
        s2 = step(game, s, a, rng)
        nxt = stage(s2)
        N[(s,) + tuple(a)] += 1
        alpha = 1 / np.sqrt(N[(s,) + tuple(a)])
        for i in range(2):
            u2 = nxt[0] @ Q[i, s2] @ nxt[1]           # stage value at s2
            target = game.R[(i, s) + tuple(a)] + game.gamma * u2
            Q[(i, s) + tuple(a)] += alpha * (target - Q[(i, s) + tuple(a)])
        s = s2
    policies = [np.zeros((nS, n1)), np.zeros((nS, n2))]
    for s in range(nS):
        p1, p2 = stage(s)
        policies[0][s], policies[1][s] = p1, p2
    return Q, policies, N                    # N - 1 = visits of (s, a1, a2)


using ADM, LinearAlgebra

g = lake()                        # T[s, a1, a2, s′], R[i, s, a1, a2]; 1-based
nS = size(g.T, 1)

# eq. 25.3 for agent i: average rewards and transitions over the joint action,
# weighting each by p1[s, a1] * p2[s, a2], then one linear solve.
function evaluate(g, p1, p2, i)
    w(s, a1, a2) = p1[s, a1] * p2[s, a2]
    R = [sum(w(s, a1, a2) * g.R[i, s, a1, a2] for a1 in 1:2, a2 in 1:2) for s in 1:nS]
    T = [sum(w(s, a1, a2) * g.T[s, a1, a2, t] for a1 in 1:2, a2 in 1:2)
         for s in 1:nS, t in 1:nS]
    return (I - g.γ * T) \ R
end

# eqs. 25.4-25.5: agent 1's MDP when agent 2 plays p2, solved by value iteration.
function best_response_value(g, p2; iters = 2000)
    U = zeros(nS)
    for _ in 1:iters
        U = [maximum(sum(p2[s, a2] * (g.R[1, s, a1, a2] + g.γ * (g.T[s, a1, a2, :] ⋅ U))
                         for a2 in 1:2) for a1 in 1:2) for s in 1:nS]
    end
    return U
end

good = [1.0 0.0; 1.0 0.0; 0.0 1.0]            # light unless the stock is high
U = evaluate(g, good, good, 1)
gain = maximum(best_response_value(g, good) .- U)
println("light unless high: ", round.(U; digits = 3), "; best deviation gains ", round(gain; digits = 6))
@assert gain < 1e-6 && isapprox(U[3], 36.103; atol = 1e-3)

light = [1.0 0.0; 1.0 0.0; 1.0 0.0]
gain = maximum(best_response_value(g, light) .- evaluate(g, light, light, 1))
println("both always light: best deviation gains ", round(gain; digits = 3))
@assert isapprox(gain, 11.9; atol = 1e-2)









NoteReading the Python code






np.einsum("sab,sabt->st", w, game.T) sums over both agents’ actions (a, b) at once: for each state s and next state t, the transition probability averaged over the joint action. The letters name the axes; any letter missing from the output is summed over.
T.reshape(3, 4, 3) (in the team-optimum check) merges the two action axes into one axis of four joint actions, turning the game into a single-agent MDP.
M.step samples the next state with rng.choice from the row T[s, a1, a2].
Fictitious play stores counts N[i][s, a], and turns them into policies by dividing each row by its sum.






Run them

game = lake()
good = np.eye(2)[[0, 0, 1]]                  # light unless the stock is high
print("values:", M.policy_evaluation(game, [good, good]).round(2))
print("exploitability:", M.exploitability(game, [good, good]))
br, U = M.best_response(game, [np.eye(2)[[0, 0, 0]]] * 2, 0)
print("best response to 'always light':", br.argmax(1), U.round(2))

values: [[30.62 33.9  36.1 ]
 [30.62 33.9  36.1 ]]
exploitability: 0.0
best response to 'always light': [0 0 1] [34.94 38.9  41.9 ]




Results

The lake: values of four joint policies








Figure 3: The lake. Left: each boat’s value from each stock level under four joint policies (for the mixed pair, the light boat’s value). Right: how much a boat could gain by switching to its best response (exploitability); the two equilibria are at 0.






The sustainable equilibrium is also the team optimum. Maximizing the two boats’ total catch as one MDP gives exactly “light unless high”. Unlike the prisoner’s dilemma, here the best outcome needs no enforcement: once both play it, neither wants to deviate.
Restraint everywhere is exploitable. “Both always light” is worth less than the equilibrium (30.0 against 36.1 from high), because it never harvests the surplus of a full lake, and a boat can gain 11.9 by switching.
The nonlinear program found a third equilibrium. SLSQP from random starts returned policies with exploitability below \(10^{-9}\): heavy at low and high, but light with probability 0.047 at a medium stock, where the two actions are worth exactly the same. It’s worth 25.96 from high: a mixed equilibrium next to the tragic one, which the enumeration of deterministic policies could not find.
Softmax responses soften the rule. Against a partner playing the sustainable equilibrium, a boat with precision 0.1 fishes heavily at high with probability 0.53; with precision 10, 1.00.



Learning in the lake








Figure 4: Where learning ends in the lake, over 20 runs of each method from a high stock: the sustainable equilibrium, the tragic one (both always heavy), or a joint policy that is not an equilibrium (exploitability above 10⁻⁶).






Fictitious play reached the sustainable equilibrium in 12 runs and the tragedy in 7. Early bad luck (both fish heavily and the stock crashes) teaches each boat that the other fishes heavily, and the belief sustains itself.
Nash Q-learning needs exploration. With a constant exploration rate of 0.2, it found an equilibrium in 16 of 20 runs. With the book’s rate, \(1/\sum_{\boldsymbol{a}} N(s, \boldsymbol{a})\), which falls to 0.01 after 96 visits to a state, it found one in 0. Each run left between 3 and 8 of the 12 joint actions never tried (median 5), and their values stayed at their initial 0. With the constant rate, every joint action was tried in every run.
Gradient ascent didn’t settle in 20,000 steps. No run ended at an equilibrium; the median exploitability was 8.2. Treating the other boat as “will repeat its last action” gives noisy targets in a game where the value of an action depends on what the other does in future states.



The chase: best responses cycle, fictitious play settles








Figure 5: Predator-prey hex world, from the starting position. Left: both agents’ values under iterated best response, round by round. Right: exploitability of fictitious play’s frequency policies after 1,000 to 50,000 steps (three runs each, resets every 10 steps).






A predator that knows the prey wanders at random earns −8.12 from the start (it pays 1 per step and gains 1 per capture), and the random prey loses 188. A prey that best-responds to that predator cuts its loss to 49.
Best responses chase each other. Each round, the predator adapts to the last prey and the prey to the last predator. After 12 rounds the prey’s value was still swinging between −24 and −102, and the final pair was exploitable by 82.6.
Fictitious play averages the chase. Best-responding to frequencies instead of the last policy damps the cycle: exploitability fell from 67.3 after 1,000 steps to 18.7 after 50,000, still well away from 0.

title: 25 · Sequential Problems
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: special cases. Show that an MDP and a repeated simple game are both Markov games.






TipSolution





An MDP is a Markov game with one agent: \(\mathcal{I} = \{1\}\), the same states, actions, transitions and reward. A simple game played repeatedly is a Markov game with a single state \(s\) that always returns to itself, \(T(s \mid s, \boldsymbol{a}) = 1\), and \(R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})\) equal to the game’s rewards. Everything on this page then reduces to Chapter 7 or Chapter 24.



Problem 2: evaluate a joint policy. A Markov game has two states. In state 1 both agents’ only sensible actions lead to state 2 with probability 0.5 and back to state 1 otherwise, paying agent 1 a reward of 2; in state 2 they return to state 1 with certainty, paying agent 1 a reward of 0. With \(\gamma = 0.9\), what is agent 1’s value in each state?






TipSolution





\(U(2) = 0 + 0.9\,U(1)\) and \(U(1) = 2 + 0.9\,(0.5\,U(1) + 0.5\,U(2))\). Substituting: \(U(1) = 2 + 0.45\,U(1) + 0.405\,U(1)\), so \(U(1)(1 - 0.855) = 2\) and \(U(1) \approx 13.79\), \(U(2) \approx 12.41\). It’s policy evaluation (Equation 1) with the joint policy already folded in.



Problem 3: the stage game. In Nash Q-learning, the agents reach a state \(s'\) whose current joint-action values are, for (agent 1, agent 2): (light, light) (30, 30); (light, heavy) (25, 34); (heavy, light) (34, 25); (heavy, heavy) (22, 22). Find the stage game’s pure Nash equilibria and the value used in the update.






TipSolution





Against light, heavy is better (34 > 30); against heavy, light is better (25 > 22). So the pure equilibria are (light, heavy) and (heavy, light), like the intersection of Chapter 24. The update uses the value of whichever equilibrium is selected, 25 for one agent and 34 for the other. Both agents must pick the same one, or their updates are inconsistent; that selection problem is one reason Nash Q-learning’s guarantees are limited.



Problem 4: why can’t the predator best-respond once and be done? In the predator-prey game, the predator computes a best response to a random prey. Why isn’t that the end of the story?






TipSolution





Because the prey will respond too. The predator’s best response exploits the random prey’s habits, and the prey’s best response to that predator avoids exactly those habits, which makes the predator’s policy wrong again. A best response is only optimal against fixed opponents; an equilibrium needs every agent’s policy to be a best response to the others simultaneously. Iterated best response looks for that fixed point by alternating, and on this page it circled instead of finding it.



Problem 5: design a sustainable lake. In the lake, suppose heavy fishing at a high stock caught 4 instead of 5. Would “light unless high” still be an equilibrium? How would you check?






TipSolution





Build the game with the new catch and compute the exploitability of the joint policy: evaluate it (Equation 1), solve each boat’s best-response MDP against it (Equation 2), and compare the values in every state. With a smaller reward for heavy fishing at high, “light unless high” may stop being a best response to itself (light might be better at high too), so the equilibrium could change to “always light”. The only reliable way to know is to compute; intuition about which deviations pay is easy to get wrong in sequential games.

title: 25 · Sequential Problems
text:
Recap

A Markov game is an MDP with several agents and several rewards (Equation 1). Why it matters: every joint policy has a value per agent, computed exactly like MDP policy evaluation; the rest of Part V builds on this.
Fixing the others turns a Markov game into an MDP (Equation 2). Why it matters: best responses, exploitability and equilibrium checks all reduce to Chapter 7’s solvers.
Nash equilibria can be several, and very different (Equation 3). Why it matters: the lake has a sustainable equilibrium that is also the team optimum, and a tragic one; which one agents end up in is not settled by the game alone.
Learning can reach an equilibrium, the wrong one, or none (Equation 4, Equation 5). Why it matters: fictitious play split between the two equilibria; Nash Q-learning worked only with enough exploration; best responses in the chase cycled. Always measure exploitability.
Exploration matters even more with several learners. Why it matters: joint actions that are never tried keep their initial values, and every agent’s plan is built on them.

Common pitfalls

Checking equilibrium only on the path of play. A stationary equilibrium must hold in every state, including rarely visited ones.
Reporting what a learner converged to without checking it. Compute the exploitability.
Starving exploration. Fast-decaying exploration leaves joint actions untried, and their values stay wrong.
Assuming one equilibrium. Enumerate small games, or run from several starts.
Confusing the team optimum with an equilibrium. They coincide in the lake; in the prisoner’s dilemma they don’t.

title: 23 · Controller Abstractions
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapters 20–22 planned over beliefs: to act, the agent kept a probability distribution over states and updated it after every observation. This chapter represents a policy differently, as a finite state controller: a small graph whose nodes each prescribe an action, and whose edges say which node to move to after each observation. The node is the agent’s entire memory. There’s no belief to update, and a controller with a handful of nodes can run forever.
The question: how much memory does a good policy need, and how do we find the best policy with a fixed amount of it?
The short answer: evaluate a controller by solving linear equations, then improve it by adding nodes or by climbing a gradient.

Evaluation is exact and cheap: a controller and a POMDP together form a Markov chain on (node, state) pairs.
Policy iteration adds nodes that improve on the current ones, and prunes nodes that are no better than others.
Nonlinear programming and gradient ascent fix the number of nodes and optimize the action and transition probabilities directly.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. A controller is evaluated exactly on the chain of (node, state) pairs; its nodes’ values are alpha vectors. Policy iteration grows the controller; nonlinear programming and gradient ascent optimize one of fixed size.







The key ideas at a glance

A controller is a policy with a finite memory. Each node \(x\) has an action distribution \(\psi(a \mid x)\) and, for each action and observation, a successor distribution \(\eta(x' \mid x, a, o)\). Conditional plans (Chapter 20) are controllers shaped like trees; a controller can loop back, so it can act forever with a few nodes.
Evaluation is a linear system. Pair the controller’s node with the hidden state. The pair \((x, s)\) moves as a Markov chain, so the value \(U(x, s)\) solves one set of linear equations. Each node’s values over states form an alpha vector, so a controller’s value over beliefs is piecewise linear and convex, just as in Chapter 20.
Policy iteration grows the controller. Try every deterministic node “take \(a\), then go to these nodes”: keep the ones that are better somewhere, and let a new node replace any old node it beats in every state. Replacing a node reroutes every link into it, which is how loops form.
Or fix the size and optimize. With \(n\) nodes, the best controller solves a nonlinear program over \(\psi\) and \(\eta\). Gradient ascent climbs the same objective, projecting back onto probability distributions after each step. Both can stop at local optima.
Memory is the limiting resource. How many nodes a good policy needs depends on the problem. For the crying baby, 2 nodes are optimal. For the fork, anything under 4 nodes can do no better than waiting.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Finite state controller
A policy given by a graph of nodes, with actions at nodes and observation-labeled edges


Node \(x\)
The controller’s memory state (not the environment’s state)


Action distribution \(\psi(a \mid x)\)
How the controller chooses its action at node \(x\)


Successor distribution \(\eta(x' \mid x, a, o)\)
Which node comes next, after action \(a\) and observation \(o\)


Deterministic controller
One action per node and one successor per observation


Dominated node
A node whose value is no better than another node’s in every state


Projection onto the simplex
The closest probability distribution to a vector








After this chapter you can

Read a controller as a policy, run it, and evaluate it exactly by solving linear equations.
Explain how each node’s value is an alpha vector, and choose the best starting node for a belief.
Run policy iteration for controllers, and explain why pruning with pointwise dominance can leave many nodes.
Set up the fixed-size problem as a nonlinear program, and optimize it by projected gradient ascent.
Recognize when a controller needs more memory, and when an optimizer is stuck at a local optimum.

title: 23 · Controller Abstractions
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



A night nurse doesn’t compute the probability that the baby is hungry. They follow a rule on a card: “If the baby cries, feed it. After a feed, ignore the next cry, it’s probably just fussing.” The card has two states of mind, watching and just fed, and a rule for moving between them. That card is a finite state controller. It’s easy to follow, needs no arithmetic, and, for this problem, it is exactly optimal.


We use the two problems of Chapter 21. The crying baby has an exact solution to compare against. The fork (problem gallery) asks a hiker to pay for directions: its optimal value from 50–50 is 27.115.

A policy that remembers just enough
The two-node rule above, “feed on crying, but not right after a feed”, is worth -24.675 from the 50–50 belief, starting with a feed: the exact optimum. The simpler rule “feed whenever the baby cries” is worth -25.423, 0.75 less. It wastes feeds on the false cries that follow a feed, since a sated baby still cries 10% of the time. See Figure 3.


Values are alpha vectors again
Each node’s values in each state form an alpha vector. A controller started at the best node for a belief earns the upper surface of these lines, as in Chapter 20. For the two-node rule, that surface is the optimal value, to within \(10^{-6}\) at every belief: the exact solution of Chapter 20 has two alpha vectors, and they are this rule’s two nodes. See Equation 1.


Count what you’ve heard
At the fork, the optimal policy asks until the answers lead by two, then goes. A controller does that by counting: 3 asking nodes (even, one ahead “right”, one ahead “left”) and 2 going nodes. With fewer than 4 nodes, no deterministic controller does better than waiting forever, because it can’t remember enough answers to act on them safely. The best 4-node controller, found by trying all 16,777,216 of them, earns 15.33; 5 nodes reach the optimum. See Figure 4.


Growing a controller
Policy iteration starts with one node and keeps adding nodes that improve on the current ones. For the crying baby, it reached the optimal value at 50–50 after 2 iterations. For the fork, after 3. See Equation 3.


Climbing, and getting stuck
Gradient ascent adjusts the probabilities of a fixed-size controller. For the crying baby with 2 nodes, 23 of 30 random starts reached the optimum. At the fork it failed every time: all 30 five-node starts ended by waiting forever. Asking only pays if a later node goes the right way, and a small step can’t change both at once. See Equation 5.

title: 23 · Controller Abstractions
text:
Formalism

Controllers and their value
A controller has nodes \(X\), an action distribution \(\psi(a \mid x)\) and a successor distribution \(\eta(x' \mid x, a, o)\) (ADM §23.1). At node \(x\) it draws \(a \sim \psi(\cdot \mid x)\); the world moves to \(s'\) and emits \(o\); the controller moves to \(x' \sim \eta(\cdot \mid x, a, o)\). The value of being at node \(x\) in state \(s\) is

\[
\begin{aligned}
U(x, s) = \sum_a \psi(a \mid x)\Big[ R(s, a) &+ \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \\
&\times \sum_o O(o \mid a, s') \sum_{x'} \eta(x' \mid x, a, o)\, U(x', s') \Big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]

In words. A node’s value in a state is the expected reward of its action, plus the discounted value of wherever the world and the controller go next.
Term by term.

\(\psi(a \mid x)\) averages over the node’s actions; \(R(s, a)\) is the reward.
\(T(s' \mid s, a)\,O(o \mid a, s')\) is the chance of the next state and observation.
\(\eta(x' \mid x, a, o)\) is the chance of the next node, which depends on what was observed, never on the hidden state.
There are \(|X||\mathcal{S}|\) equations and unknowns: 4 for a 2-node crying baby controller.

Why it holds. The pair (node, state) evolves as a Markov chain: its next value depends only on the current pair. Equation 1 is that chain’s Bellman expectation equation, the same as MDP policy evaluation (Chapter 7) on \(|X||\mathcal{S}|\) states. So it has a unique solution for \(\gamma < 1\), found by one linear solve.
From a belief \(b\), the value of starting at node \(x\), and the best starting node, are (ADM eqs. 23.2–23.3)

\[
U(x, b) = \sum_s b(s)\, U(x, s) = \alpha_x^\top b, \qquad x^* = \arg\max_x \alpha_x^\top b
\tag{2}\]

In words. Each node is an alpha vector; start at the one that is best for your belief.
Term by term.

\(\alpha_x(s) = U(x, s)\) is node \(x\)’s alpha vector.
\(\max_x \alpha_x^\top b\) is piecewise linear and convex in \(b\), like Chapter 20’s value functions.

Why it holds. The controller’s future doesn’t depend on the belief, only on the hidden state, so the value from a belief is the belief-weighted average over states.


Policy iteration
Policy iteration (ADM §23.2; E. A. Hansen, UAI, 1998) alternates evaluation with improvement. Improvement considers every deterministic node “take \(a\), then after \(o\) go to node \(\nu(o)\)”, whose alpha vector is a one-step backup of the current ones:
\[
\alpha_{a,\nu}(s) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \sum_o O(o \mid a, s')\, U(\nu(o), s')
\]
There are \(|\mathcal{A}||X|^{|\mathcal{O}|}\) such nodes. Pruning compares nodes state by state:

\[
x \text{ is dominated by } x' \quad\text{if}\quad U(x, s) \le U(x', s) \text{ for every state } s
\tag{3}\]

In words. A node that is never better than another, whatever the state, can be removed.
Term by term.

A new node dominated by an existing node (or by another new one) is dropped.
A new node that dominates an existing node replaces it in place: every link into the old node now reaches the new one. That can create loops.
New nodes that are neither dominated nor dominating are added.

Why it holds. Replacing a node by one that is at least as good in every state can’t lower any node’s value, since every path through it does at least as well. The candidates are exactly the alpha vectors of a Bellman backup of the current value function. If every one of them is dominated by an existing node, the backup can’t raise the value at any belief, so the controller’s value already satisfies the Bellman optimality equation: it is optimal. The catch: pointwise dominance is weaker than Chapter 20’s belief-space pruning, so nodes that are never best at any belief can survive. For the crying baby, the controller grew to 58 nodes in 10 iterations, although only 2 are reachable from the best starting node.


Nonlinear programming
Fix the number of nodes and optimize everything at once (ADM §23.3; C. Amato, D. S. Bernstein and S. Zilberstein, Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems, 2010). Starting at node \(x_1\) from belief \(b\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max_{U,\,\psi,\,\eta}\quad & \textstyle\sum_s b(s)\, U(x_1, s) \\
\text{subject to}\quad & U \text{ satisfies @eq-eval for every } x, s \\
& \psi(\cdot \mid x) \text{ and } \eta(\cdot \mid x, a, o) \text{ are probability distributions}
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]

In words. Choose the controller’s probabilities, and the values that go with them, to maximize the value at the start.
Term by term.

The unknowns are \(U\) (\(|X||\mathcal{S}|\) numbers), \(\psi\) and \(\eta\).
The evaluation constraints multiply \(\psi\) and \(\eta\) by \(U\), so they are quadratic: a quadratically constrained linear program.
The remaining constraints say each row is nonnegative and sums to 1.

Why it holds. Any feasible point is a real controller and its exact value, so the program’s optimum is the best \(n\)-node controller. But the constraints are not convex, so a local solver can stop at a local optimum. The Python tab solves it with SciPy’s SLSQP after substituting \(U\) from the linear solve.


Gradient ascent
Write the evaluation as a matrix equation on (node, state) pairs (ADM §23.4; N. Meuleau, K.-E. Kim, L. P. Kaelbling and A. R. Cassandra, UAI, 1999):
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_\theta &= r_\theta + \gamma T_\theta u_\theta, \qquad r_\theta(x, s) = \sum_a \psi(a \mid x) R(s, a), \\
T_\theta\big((x, s), (x', s')\big) &= \sum_a \psi(a \mid x)\, T(s' \mid s, a) \sum_o O(o \mid a, s')\, \eta(x' \mid x, a, o)
\end{aligned}
\]
The objective is \(J(\theta) = \beta^\top u_\theta\), where \(\beta\) puts belief \(b\) on node \(x_1\) and zero elsewhere. Its gradient is

\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial \theta} = v^\top \Big( \frac{\partial r_\theta}{\partial \theta} + \gamma \frac{\partial T_\theta}{\partial \theta}\, u_\theta \Big),
\qquad u_\theta = (I - \gamma T_\theta)^{-1} r_\theta, \quad v = (I - \gamma T_\theta)^{-\top} \beta
\tag{5}\]

In words. Changing a probability matters in proportion to how often the controller is at that node (the weights \(v\)), times how much the change alters the reward and the value of what comes next.
Term by term.

\(u_\theta\) is the value of every (node, state) pair; \(v\) is the expected discounted time spent in each pair, starting from \(\beta\).
For \(\psi(a \mid x)\): the derivative of \(r_\theta\) is \(R(s, a)\) in node \(x\)’s rows; the derivative of \(T_\theta\) is the transition that action \(a\) would make from node \(x\).
For \(\eta(x' \mid x, a, o)\): only \(T_\theta\) depends on it, through \(\psi(a \mid x)\,T(s' \mid s, a)\,O(o \mid a, s')\).
A node that is never visited (\(v = 0\) in its rows) gets no gradient.

Why it holds. Differentiate \((I - \gamma T_\theta)u_\theta = r_\theta\): \((I - \gamma T_\theta)\,\partial u = \partial r + \gamma\,(\partial T)\,u\). Multiply by \(\beta^\top (I - \gamma T_\theta)^{-1} = v^\top\). This is the book’s eq. 23.18 multiplied by \(\beta\), arranged so that one linear solve gives \(v\) for every parameter at once. The code checks it against finite differences.
After each step, every distribution is projected back onto the probability simplex:

\[
\text{proj}(y) = \arg\min_{z \ge 0,\ \mathbf{1}^\top z = 1} \|y - z\|_2 = \max(y - \tau, 0)
\tag{6}\]

with the shift \(\tau\) chosen so that the result sums to 1.
In words. Shift every entry down by the same amount, clip at zero, and choose the shift so the result is a distribution.
Term by term.

\(\tau\): sort \(y\) in decreasing order, find the largest \(k\) with \(y_{(k)} > (\sum_{i \le k} y_{(i)} - 1)/k\), and set \(\tau = (\sum_{i \le k} y_{(i)} - 1)/k\) (J. Duchi, S. Shalev-Shwartz, Y. Singer and T. Chandra, ICML, 2008).
Entries below \(\tau\) become exactly 0: projection can switch actions off completely.

Why it holds. The optimality conditions for the least-squares problem give \(z_i = \max(y_i - \tau, 0)\) with one multiplier \(\tau\) for the sum constraint; the sort finds which entries stay positive.

title: 23 · Controller Abstractions
text:
Worked example

Evaluating the two-node rule
The rule “feed on crying, but not right after a feed” has nodes I (ignore; crying → F, quiet → I) and F (feed; then → I). Feeding always sates the baby, so a feed’s value is its reward plus the value of ignoring a sated baby:

\(U(F, \text{sated}) = -5 + 0.9\,U(I, \text{sated})\) and \(U(F, \text{hungry}) = -15 + 0.9\,U(I, \text{sated})\).

Ignoring a sated baby: it stays sated with probability 0.9 (then cries with probability 0.1) or turns hungry (then cries with probability 0.8):

\(U(I, \text{sated}) = 0 + 0.9\,\big[0.9\,(0.1\,U(F, \text{sated}) + 0.9\,U(I, \text{sated})) + 0.1\,(0.8\,U(F, \text{hungry}) + 0.2\,U(I, \text{hungry}))\big]\).
\(U(I, \text{hungry}) = -10 + 0.9\,\big[0.8\,U(F, \text{hungry}) + 0.2\,U(I, \text{hungry})\big]\), since a hungry baby stays hungry.

Four linear equations, four unknowns. The solution:



Table 2: The two-node rule’s values (alpha vectors).





Node
Sated
Hungry




I (ignore)
-16.31
-38.25


F (feed)
-19.67
-29.67






At 50–50, starting at I gives the average of its two values, -27.28, and starting at F gives -24.67. Feed first: that’s the exact optimal value, -24.67.


A projection by hand
A gradient step turns an action distribution into \(y = (0.7, 0.5, -0.1)\), which isn’t a distribution. Sorted, it’s the same order; the running sums are 0.7, 1.2, 1.1.

\(k = 1\): \(0.7 > (0.7 - 1)/1 = -0.3\). Yes.
\(k = 2\): \(0.5 > (1.2 - 1)/2 = 0.1\). Yes.
\(k = 3\): \(-0.1 > (1.1 - 1)/3 = 0.033\)? No.

So \(\tau = 0.1\), and the projection is \((0.6, 0.4, 0)\): the third action is switched off.
The code: project_simplex([0.7, 0.5, -0.1]) = [0.6, 0.4, 0.0].

title: 23 · Controller Abstractions
23 · Controller Abstractions
text:
Algorithms & code

Controllers: evaluation, policy iteration, brute force, gradient ascent

JuliaPython


# Finite state controllers for POMDPs (ADM Ch. 23).
# A POMDP p has p.T[s, a, s′], p.R[s, a], p.O[a, s′, o] and p.γ (as in Ch. 20-22).
# A controller has nodes x = 1..n. At node x it takes action a with probability
# ψ[x, a]; after taking a and observing o it moves to node x′ with probability
# η[x, a, o, x′]. It keeps no belief: the node is its whole memory.
struct Controller
    ψ::Matrix{Float64}            # ψ[x, a]
    η::Array{Float64,4}           # η[x, a, o, x′]
end
nnodes(c::Controller) = size(c.ψ, 1)

# A deterministic controller: action acts[x] at node x, then node next[x][o]
# after observation o (whatever the action, since only one action is ever taken).
function deterministic_controller(p, acts, next)
    n, nA, nO = length(acts), size(p.T, 2), size(p.O, 3)
    ψ, η = zeros(n, nA), zeros(n, nA, nO, n)
    for x in 1:n
        ψ[x, acts[x]] = 1
        for a in 1:nA, o in 1:nO
            η[x, a, o, next[x][o]] = 1
        end
    end
    return Controller(ψ, η)
end

# The controller and the POMDP together form a Markov chain on pairs (x, s),
# stored as index (x - 1) * |S| + s. Returns its transition matrix and reward
# vector (eqs. 23.8-23.9):
#   Tθ[(x,s), (x′,s′)] = Σ_a ψ[x,a] T[s,a,s′] Σ_o O[a,s′,o] η[x,a,o,x′]
#   rθ[(x,s)]          = Σ_a ψ[x,a] R[s,a]
function controller_chain(p, c::Controller)
    nS, nA, nO, n = size(p.T, 1), size(p.T, 2), size(p.O, 3), nnodes(c)
    idx(x, s) = (x - 1) * nS + s
    Tθ, rθ = zeros(n * nS, n * nS), zeros(n * nS)
    for x in 1:n, s in 1:nS, a in 1:nA
        c.ψ[x, a] == 0 && continue
        rθ[idx(x, s)] += c.ψ[x, a] * p.R[s, a]
        for s′ in 1:nS, o in 1:nO, x′ in 1:n
            Tθ[idx(x, s), idx(x′, s′)] += c.ψ[x, a] * p.T[s, a, s′] * p.O[a, s′, o] * c.η[x, a, o, x′]
        end
    end
    return Tθ, rθ
end

# Policy evaluation (eq. 23.1) by one linear solve: u = (I - γ Tθ)⁻¹ rθ.
# Returns U[x, s]; row x is node x's alpha vector (eq. 23.2: U(x, b) = U[x, :] ⋅ b).
function evaluate_controller(p, c::Controller)
    Tθ, rθ = controller_chain(p, c)
    u = (I - p.γ * Tθ) \ rθ
    return permutedims(reshape(u, size(p.T, 1), nnodes(c)))   # reshape fills s fastest
end

# Value at belief b from the best starting node (eq. 23.3), and that node.
function controller_value(p, c::Controller, b; U = evaluate_controller(p, c))
    vals = [U[x, :] ⋅ b for x in 1:nnodes(c)]
    return (u = maximum(vals), x = argmax(vals))
end

# Nodes the controller can ever reach from node x: follow every successor that
# has positive probability after an action that has positive probability.
function reachable_nodes(c::Controller, x)
    seen, stack = Set([x]), [x]
    while !isempty(stack)
        y = pop!(stack)
        for a in axes(c.ψ, 2), o in axes(c.η, 3), y′ in axes(c.η, 4)
            if c.ψ[y, a] > 0 && c.η[y, a, o, y′] > 0 && !(y′ in seen)
                push!(seen, y′); push!(stack, y′)
            end
        end
    end
    return sort(collect(seen))
end

# Run the controller on the true POMDP from node x and state s for `steps`
# steps; returns the discounted return and the (node, action, observation) trace.
function run_controller(p, c::Controller, x, s, steps, rng)
    ret, trace = 0.0, Tuple{Int,Int,Int,Int}[]
    for t in 0:steps-1
        a = rand(rng, Categorical(c.ψ[x, :]))
        s′, r, o = pomdp_step(p, s, a, rng)
        push!(trace, (x, s, a, o))
        ret += p.γ^t * r
        x, s = rand(rng, Categorical(c.η[x, a, o, :])), s′
    end
    return ret, trace
end

# Policy iteration for controllers (§23.2; E. A. Hansen, 1998). Improvement
# adds every deterministic node "take a, then go to next[o]" whose alpha vector
# is not dominated state by state (eq. 23.4). A new node that dominates an old
# node replaces it in place, so every link into the old node now reaches the
# new one: that is how loops form. Stops when no node survives, or at k_max.
# Returns the controller and, per iteration, (nodes, value at b).
function controller_policy_iteration(p, b; k_max = 20, c = nothing, tol = 1e-9, max_nodes = 500)
    nS, nA, nO = size(p.T, 1), size(p.T, 2), size(p.O, 3)
    c === nothing && (c = Controller(fill(1 / nA, 1, nA), ones(1, nA, nO, 1)))   # one uniform node
    history = [(nnodes(c), controller_value(p, c, b).u)]
    for _ in 1:k_max
        U = evaluate_controller(p, c)
        n = nnodes(c)
        # Every candidate: an action and a successor for each observation.
        cands = Tuple{Int,Vector{Int},Vector{Float64}}[]
        for a in 1:nA, next in Iterators.product(fill(1:n, nO)...)
            α = [p.R[s, a] + p.γ * sum(p.T[s, a, s′] * p.O[a, s′, o] * U[next[o], s′]
                                       for s′ in 1:nS, o in 1:nO) for s in 1:nS]
            push!(cands, (a, collect(next), α))
        end
        dominated(α, β) = all(α .<= β .+ tol)                  # α ≤ β in every state
        # Drop candidates no better than an old node, or than an earlier survivor.
        keep = Int[]
        for (i, (_, _, α)) in enumerate(cands)
            any(dominated(α, U[x, :]) for x in 1:n) && continue
            any(dominated(α, cands[j][3]) for j in keep) && continue
            filter!(j -> !dominated(cands[j][3], α), keep)       # α beats earlier survivors
            push!(keep, i)
        end
        isempty(keep) && break                                   # no improvement anywhere
        ψ, η = copy(c.ψ), copy(c.η)
        added = Tuple{Int,Vector{Int}}[]
        for i in keep
            a, next, α = cands[i]
            olds = [x for x in 1:n if dominated(U[x, :], α)]
            if isempty(olds)
                push!(added, (a, next))                          # a genuinely new node
            else
                for x in olds                                    # overwrite dominated nodes
                    ψ[x, :] .= 0; ψ[x, a] = 1
                    η[x, :, :, :] .= 0
                    for a′ in 1:nA, o in 1:nO
                        η[x, a′, o, next[o]] = 1
                    end
                end
            end
        end
        n + length(added) > max_nodes && break
        # Grow the arrays; new nodes point only to old nodes.
        m = n + length(added)
        ψ2, η2 = zeros(m, nA), zeros(m, nA, nO, m)
        ψ2[1:n, :], η2[1:n, :, :, 1:n] = ψ, η
        for (k, (a, next)) in enumerate(added)
            ψ2[n + k, a] = 1
            for a′ in 1:nA, o in 1:nO
                η2[n + k, a′, o, next[o]] = 1
            end
        end
        c = Controller(ψ2, η2)
        push!(history, (nnodes(c), controller_value(p, c, b).u))
    end
    return c, history
end

# Solve M u = r in place by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting; r
# becomes u. Used by the brute-force search below, which solves millions of
# tiny systems: avoiding allocation makes it about ten times faster.
function solve_inplace!(M, r)
    m = length(r)
    for k in 1:m
        piv = k
        for i in k+1:m
            abs(M[i, k]) > abs(M[piv, k]) && (piv = i)
        end
        if piv != k                                  # swap rows k and piv
            for j in 1:m
                M[k, j], M[piv, j] = M[piv, j], M[k, j]
            end
            r[k], r[piv] = r[piv], r[k]
        end
        for i in k+1:m                               # eliminate below the pivot
            f = M[i, k] / M[k, k]
            f == 0 && continue
            for j in k:m
                M[i, j] -= f * M[k, j]
            end
            r[i] -= f * r[k]
        end
    end
    for k in m:-1:1                                  # back substitution
        t = r[k]
        for j in k+1:m
            t -= M[k, j] * r[j]
        end
        r[k] = t / M[k, k]
    end
    return r
end

# Brute force, for validation: evaluate every deterministic n-node controller
# (|A|^n action choices times n^(n|O|) successor tables) and return the best
# value at belief b (from its best start node), with its actions and successors.
# acts and next are counted like the digits of a mixed-radix number.
function best_deterministic_controller(p, n, b)
    nS, nA, nO = size(p.T, 1), size(p.T, 2), size(p.O, 3)
    m = n * nS
    M, r = zeros(m, m), zeros(m)
    acts, next = ones(Int, n), ones(Int, n * nO)       # next[(x - 1) * nO + o]
    best = (u = -Inf, acts = copy(acts), next = copy(next))
    # Increment a digit vector with base `base`; false once it wraps to all ones.
    function increment!(v, base)
        for i in eachindex(v)
            v[i] < base && (v[i] += 1; return true)
            v[i] = 1
        end
        return false
    end
    while true
        while true
            fill!(M, 0.0)                              # build I - γTθ and rθ
            for x in 1:n, s in 1:nS
                a, i = acts[x], (x - 1) * nS + s
                r[i] = p.R[s, a]
                M[i, i] += 1
                for s′ in 1:nS, o in 1:nO
                    M[i, (next[(x - 1) * nO + o] - 1) * nS + s′] -= p.γ * p.T[s, a, s′] * p.O[a, s′, o]
                end
            end
            solve_inplace!(M, r)                       # r now holds u
            for x in 1:n
                v = 0.0
                for s in 1:nS
                    v += r[(x - 1) * nS + s] * b[s]
                end
                v > best.u + 1e-12 && (best = (u = v, acts = copy(acts), next = copy(next)))
            end
            increment!(next, n) || break
        end
        increment!(acts, nA) || break
    end
    return best
end

# Gradient of J(θ) = β ⋅ u_θ, the value of starting in node 1 with belief b
# (β holds b in node 1's block, zeros elsewhere; eq. 23.11). With Z = I - γTθ,
# u = Z⁻¹rθ and v = Z⁻ᵀβ (how much discounted time is spent in each (x, s)),
#   ∂J/∂θ = v ⋅ (∂rθ/∂θ + γ (∂Tθ/∂θ) u),
# which is eq. 23.18 multiplied by β, arranged to need only two linear solves.
function controller_gradient(p, c::Controller, b)
    nS, nA, nO, n = size(p.T, 1), size(p.T, 2), size(p.O, 3), nnodes(c)
    Tθ, rθ = controller_chain(p, c)
    Z = I - p.γ * Tθ
    β = [x == 1 ? b[s] : 0.0 for s in 1:nS, x in 1:n][:]     # column-major: s fastest
    u, v = Z \ rθ, Z' \ β
    U, V = permutedims(reshape(u, nS, n)), permutedims(reshape(v, nS, n))
    gψ, gη = zeros(n, nA), zeros(n, nA, nO, n)
    for x in 1:n, a in 1:nA, s in 1:nS
        V[x, s] == 0 && continue
        gψ[x, a] += V[x, s] * p.R[s, a]
        for s′ in 1:nS, o in 1:nO
            w = p.γ * V[x, s] * p.T[s, a, s′] * p.O[a, s′, o]
            w == 0 && continue
            for x′ in 1:n
                gψ[x, a] += w * c.η[x, a, o, x′] * U[x′, s′]
                gη[x, a, o, x′] += w * c.ψ[x, a] * U[x′, s′]
            end
        end
    end
    return (J = β ⋅ u, ψ = gψ, η = gη)
end

# Euclidean projection onto the probability simplex (J. Duchi et al., 2008):
# sort, find how many entries stay positive, and shift them all by one amount.
function project_simplex(y)
    μ = sort(y, rev = true)
    cs = cumsum(μ)
    ρ = findlast(j -> μ[j] - (cs[j] - 1) / j > 0, 1:length(μ))
    θ = (cs[ρ] - 1) / ρ
    return max.(y .- θ, 0.0)
end

# A random n-node controller: each distribution drawn uniformly from its simplex
# (normalized exponential draws are uniform on the simplex).
function random_controller(p, n, rng)
    nA, nO = size(p.T, 2), size(p.O, 3)
    unif(k) = (e = -log.(rand(rng, k)); e ./ sum(e))
    ψ = permutedims(reduce(hcat, [unif(nA) for _ in 1:n]))
    η = zeros(n, nA, nO, n)
    for x in 1:n, a in 1:nA, o in 1:nO
        η[x, a, o, :] = unif(n)
    end
    return Controller(ψ, η)
end

# Controller gradient ascent (§23.4): step along the gradient, then project
# each distribution back onto the simplex. Starts from `c` (default: random).
# Returns the controller and J after each step.
function controller_gradient_ascent(p, b, n, rng; α = 0.01, k_max = 2000, c = random_controller(p, n, rng))
    nA, nO, Js = size(p.T, 2), size(p.O, 3), Float64[]
    for _ in 1:k_max
        g = controller_gradient(p, c, b)
        push!(Js, g.J)
        ψ = reduce(vcat, [project_simplex(c.ψ[x, :] .+ α .* g.ψ[x, :])' for x in 1:n])
        η = copy(c.η)
        for x in 1:n, a in 1:nA, o in 1:nO
            η[x, a, o, :] = project_simplex(c.η[x, a, o, :] .+ α .* g.η[x, a, o, :])
        end
        c = Controller(ψ, η)
    end
    push!(Js, controller_gradient(p, c, b).J)
    return c, Js
end


import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

from adm.problems.crying_baby import crying_baby

p = crying_baby()                     # 0 = sated / feed / crying
nS, nA, nO = p.T.shape[0], p.T.shape[1], p.O.shape[2]
n = 2                                 # controller nodes
b0 = np.array([0.5, 0.5])


def unpack(theta):
    """Split the parameters into psi[x, a] and eta[x, a, o, x2]."""
    psi = theta[: n * nA].reshape(n, nA)
    eta = theta[n * nA:].reshape(n, nA, nO, n)
    return psi, eta


def evaluate(psi, eta):
    """eq. 23.1 as one linear system on (node, state) pairs; returns U[x, s]."""
    # Tt[x, s, y, t] = sum over a, o of psi[x,a] T[s,a,t] O[a,t,o] eta[x,a,o,y]
    Tt = np.einsum("xa,sat,ato,xaoy->xsyt", psi, p.T, p.O, eta)
    Tt = Tt.reshape(n * nS, n * nS)       # row x*nS + s, column y*nS + t
    r = np.einsum("xa,sa->xs", psi, p.R).reshape(n * nS)
    U = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(n * nS) - p.gamma * Tt, r)
    return U.reshape(n, nS)


def negative_value(theta):
    psi, eta = unpack(theta)
    return -evaluate(psi, eta)[0] @ b0    # start in node 0


# eq. 23.5 with U substituted: every psi and eta row must sum to 1.
rows = [slice(x * nA, (x + 1) * nA) for x in range(n)]
rows += [slice(n * nA + k * n, n * nA + (k + 1) * n) for k in range(n * nA * nO)]
cons = [{"type": "eq", "fun": lambda th, sl=sl: th[sl].sum() - 1} for sl in rows]

best = None
for seed in range(5):                 # a local solver: try several starts
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    theta0 = np.concatenate([rng.dirichlet(np.ones(nA), n).ravel(),
                             rng.dirichlet(np.ones(n), n * nA * nO).ravel()])
    res = minimize(negative_value, theta0, method="SLSQP",
                   bounds=[(0, 1)] * len(theta0), constraints=cons)
    if best is None or res.fun < best.fun:
        best = res

psi, eta = unpack(best.x)
print(f"best 2-node value at b0: {-best.fun:.3f}")
print("most likely action per node:", [p.actions[a] for a in psi.argmax(axis=1)])
assert abs(-best.fun - (-24.6749)) < 0.01             # the exact optimum









NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






Array{Float64,4} is a 4-dimensional array; η[x, a, o, :] is a view of its last axis, like eta[x, a, o, :] in NumPy (but 1-based).
permutedims(reshape(u, nS, n)): Julia reshapes column-major, filling the first index fastest, so the vector indexed (x - 1) * nS + s becomes an nS × n matrix whose columns are nodes; permutedims transposes it to U[x, s].
Z' \ β solves the transposed system \(Z^\top v = \beta\); \ is np.linalg.solve.
Iterators.product(fill(1:n, nO)...) is itertools.product(range(n), repeat=nO): every successor table.
increment!(v, base) counts through all digit vectors, like an odometer, without building the whole list.
v[i] < base && (v[i] += 1; return true) runs the parenthesized block only if the test is true: a one-line if.






Run it

p = crying_baby()
# Node 1 ignores (crying → node 2, quiet → node 1); node 2 feeds (then → node 1).
c = deterministic_controller(p, [3, 1], [[2, 1], [1, 1]])
U = evaluate_controller(p, c)          # U[x, s]: rows are alpha vectors
controller_value(p, c, [0.5, 0.5])     # best starting node and its value

(u = -24.674934966510335, x = 2)




Results

Controllers for the crying baby







Figure 3: Crying baby. Left: the alpha vectors of two 2-node controllers (dashed: feed whenever crying; solid: never feed twice in a row), against the exact value (black). Right: the value of the controller built by policy iteration, from its best starting node, after 0, 1 and 2 iterations.





Two nodes are enough. The rule that never feeds twice in a row is optimal at 50–50 (starting at F), and from its best node at every belief. Brute force over all 2-node and 3-node deterministic controllers agrees: the best value at 50–50 is -24.675 with 2 nodes and -24.675 with 3. The best 1-node controller always feeds: -55.
Randomness helps a tiny controller. A 1-node controller that feeds with probability 0.396 and otherwise ignores (found by gradient ascent from all 30 starts) earns -40.23. It can’t remember when it last fed, so it spreads its feeds out at random.
Policy iteration finds the optimum, then keeps growing. It reached the optimal value at 50–50 after 2 iterations, with 3 nodes. After 10 iterations it had 58 nodes, of which 2 are reachable from the best starting node. Pointwise pruning can’t remove nodes that are better in some state but never best at any belief.



How much memory does the fork need?







Figure 4: The fork: the best value at 50–50 achievable by a deterministic controller with 1 to 5 nodes (brute force for 1 to 4; the counting controller for 5), against the optimal value (dashed). Left of the dashed line’s reach, the controller can only wait.





Below 4 nodes, waiting is best. With 3 nodes, the natural policy “ask once, then go where told” is worth -0.51: an 85%-reliable answer isn’t worth acting on at these stakes, so it loses a little each hike.
4 nodes get part of the way. The best 4-node controller asks, goes left after a single “left”, but asks again after a “right” and goes right only after two in a row. It earns 15.33, from its best starting node.
5 nodes are optimal. The counting controller earns 27.115, which matches Chapter 21’s bounds on the optimum (27.115 from below).
Policy iteration finds it too. Starting from one node, it reached the optimum after 3 iterations, with 23 nodes. It stopped after 6 iterations with 242 nodes, of which 5 are reachable from its best starting node.



Gradient ascent: local optima







Figure 5: Controller gradient ascent (step size 0.003, 3000 steps). Left: crying baby, 2 nodes, 30 random starts; the exact optimum is dashed. Right: fork, 5 nodes, 30 random starts (gray) and 10 starts blended 50/50 with the counting controller (blue); the optimum is dashed.





The crying baby is easy. With 2 nodes, 23 of 30 starts reached the optimum (within 0.01); with 3 nodes, 16. The others stopped at local optima.
The fork has a trap. From random 5-node starts, all 30 of 30 runs ended by waiting forever, with value 0. In the first run’s final controller, 3 nodes are ever visited, and each waits. At those nodes the gradient for waiting is 0, for asking at most -6.7, and for going at most -125.8. Asking alone only costs; it pays only together with a later node that goes the right way.
A good start escapes it. Blending the counting controller 50/50 with a random one, 10 of 10 runs climbed to the optimum; at 70/30, 10; at 30/70, 1.

title: 23 · Controller Abstractions
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: counting controllers. For the fork (\(|\mathcal{A}| = 4\), \(|\mathcal{O}| = 2\)), how many candidate nodes does one policy-iteration step try on a 5-node controller? How many deterministic 4-node controllers are there?






TipSolution





Each candidate is an action and a successor for each observation: \(|\mathcal{A}||X|^{|\mathcal{O}|} = 4 \times 5^2 = 100\). A deterministic \(n\)-node controller chooses an action per node (\(4^n\)) and a successor per node and observation (\(n^{2n}\)): for \(n = 4\), \(256 \times 65{,}536 = 16{,}777{,}216\). That is why brute force stops at 4 nodes here; for \(n = 5\) it would be about \(10^{10}\).



Problem 2: a 1-node controller by hand. A crying baby controller has one node, which always feeds. Find its values and its value at 50–50.






TipSolution





Feeding always leads to a sated baby, and the controller stays in its one node: \(U(\text{sated}) = -5 + 0.9\,U(\text{sated})\), so \(U(\text{sated}) = -50\). \(U(\text{hungry}) = -15 + 0.9\,U(\text{sated}) = -60\). At 50–50: \(-55\), the brute-force result for one node above. Always ignoring is far worse, since the baby stays hungry forever: \(U(\text{hungry}) = -10/(1 - 0.9) = -100\).



Problem 3: why randomize? Why can a 1-node controller that feeds at random beat both “always feed” and “always ignore”? Would randomness help a controller with enough nodes?






TipSolution





With one node, the controller can’t tell a quiet baby from a crying one, or remember its last feed; a deterministic node must do the same thing forever. Random feeding with a moderate probability feeds roughly as often as the baby gets hungry, without paying for a feed every step. It’s a substitute for memory. With enough nodes, a deterministic controller can match the optimal belief-based policy, which is itself deterministic; here 2 nodes did. Randomness helps when memory is scarce.



Problem 4: project a distribution. Project \(y = (0.9, 0.4, -0.2)\) onto the simplex.






TipSolution





Running sums: 0.9, 1.3, 1.1. \(k = 1\): \(0.9 > -0.1\); \(k = 2\): \(0.4 > 0.15\); \(k = 3\): \(-0.2 > 0.033\)? No. So \(\tau = (1.3 - 1)/2 = 0.15\) and the projection is \((0.75, 0.25, 0)\).



Problem 5: why does “ask once, then go” lose? Compute the value of the 3-node fork controller that asks once and goes where told, and explain the result.






TipSolution





Let \(V\) be the value at the asking node. Going after one answer is right with probability 0.85: expected reward \(0.85 \times 10 + 0.15 \times (-50) = 1\), then a new hike starts at the asking node. So \(V = -1 + 0.95\,(1 + 0.95\,V)\), which gives \(V(1 - 0.9025) = -0.05\) and \(V \approx -0.513\). Each hike costs 1 to ask and earns only 1 on average, a step later, so the controller loses slowly and waiting (0) is better. A second answer that agrees raises the chance of being right to about 0.97, which is worth the extra cost: that’s why the optimal controller counts to two.

title: 23 · Controller Abstractions
text:
Recap

A controller is a policy with a finite memory (Equation 1). Why it matters: it runs without belief updates, which is useful when the model is too big to filter, or when the policy must run on simple hardware.
Evaluation is exact: one linear solve on (node, state) pairs, giving an alpha vector per node (Equation 2). Why it matters: controllers slot into the value-function picture of Chapters 20–21; their value over beliefs is a lower bound on the optimal one.
Policy iteration adds and replaces nodes, and reaches the optimum on small problems (Equation 3). Why it matters: replacing dominated nodes creates the loops that make controllers compact, but pointwise pruning can leave many useless nodes.
Fixed-size controllers can be optimized as a nonlinear program or by gradient ascent (Equation 4, Equation 5, Equation 6). Why it matters: the objective is not concave, and at the fork every random start fell into the same trap. Information-gathering behavior needs coordinated changes that local search can’t make one step at a time.
The number of nodes is the real design decision. Why it matters: the crying baby needs 2, the fork needs 5 (with fewer than 4 it can only wait). Too few nodes caps the value; too many makes optimization harder.

title: 23 · Controller Abstractions
text:
Cheat sheet & connections



Table 3: Key equations from this page.










Name
Formula
Ref




Controller evaluation
\(U(x, s) = \sum_a \psi(a \mid x)[R(s, a) + \gamma\sum_{s'} T \sum_o O \sum_{x'} \eta\, U(x', s')]\)
Equation 1


Node values over beliefs
\(U(x, b) = \alpha_x^\top b\); start at \(\arg\max_x \alpha_x^\top b\)
Equation 2


Pointwise dominance
\(U(x, s) \le U(x', s)\) for all \(s\)
Equation 3


Fixed-size program
\(\max \sum_s b(s) U(x_1, s)\) s.t. Equation 1, \(\psi\) and \(\eta\) distributions
Equation 4


Controller gradient
\(v^\top(\partial r_\theta + \gamma\,\partial T_\theta\, u_\theta)\), \(v = (I - \gamma T_\theta)^{-\top}\beta\)
Equation 5


Simplex projection
\(\max(y - \tau, 0)\), \(\tau\) so it sums to 1
Equation 6






Common pitfalls

Confusing nodes with states. A node is the controller’s memory; the environment’s state stays hidden. \(\eta\) may depend on the observation, never on the state.
Starting at the wrong node. A controller’s value at a belief depends on the starting node; choose it with Equation 2.
Trusting a local optimum. Gradient ascent and local nonlinear solvers need several starts, or a start from a known good controller.
Too few nodes. If the value plateaus at something simple (like waiting), the controller may lack the memory to do better. Brute force on small sizes, or policy iteration, can tell you.
Counting nodes that are never used. Report the nodes reachable from the starting node, not the total.

Connections

Ch 20 · Exact Belief State Planning: conditional plans are tree-shaped controllers, and alpha vectors come from there.
Ch 7 · Exact Solution Methods: policy evaluation by a linear solve, and policy iteration, for MDPs.
Ch 11 · Policy Gradient Estimation: gradients of a policy’s value; here computed exactly from the model.
Ch 21 · Offline Belief State Planning: the fork’s optimal value, which the counting controller reaches.
Ch 22 · Online Belief State Planning: the opposite trade-off: no stored policy, a search at every step.

title: 21 · Offline Belief State Planning
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 20 solved POMDPs exactly by value iteration over conditional plans. That works for toy problems only. Exact solution of a finite-horizon POMDP is PSPACE-complete in the worst case, and the sets of alpha vectors can grow without bound. This chapter keeps Chapter 20’s representation, a value function over beliefs, but computes it approximately and offline, before the agent acts. Many methods here produce bounds: an upper bound that the true value never exceeds, or a lower bound it never falls below. Bounds let us say how good an approximation is, and they guide the search for better ones. Chapter 22 plans online instead, from the current belief only.
The question: how can we get a good value function over beliefs, with a guarantee on its quality, without solving the POMDP exactly?
The short answer: bound it from both sides, and refine where it matters.

Cheap upper bounds pretend the agent will soon know more than it will: QMDP assumes the state becomes known after one step; the fast informed bound also uses the observations.
Cheap lower bounds assume it can’t adapt at all.
Point-based value iteration computes alpha vectors only at a chosen set of beliefs, giving a lower bound. Sawtooth and triangulated value functions interpolate between beliefs, giving an upper bound.
Heuristic search tightens both bounds along the beliefs reachable from the start, until they meet.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Offline methods bound the optimal value over beliefs from above and below; point-based methods and interpolation refine the bounds at chosen beliefs.







The key ideas at a glance

Bounds make approximations checkable. If \(U_{\text{lo}}(b) \le U^*(b) \le U_{\text{hi}}(b)\), then either bound’s policy is within the gap \(U_{\text{hi}}(b) - U_{\text{lo}}(b)\) of optimal, in the sense of the value it guarantees. A gap near zero certifies near-optimality.
Upper bounds assume too much information. QMDP solves the fully observed MDP and averages its action values over the belief, as if the state would be revealed after one step. The fast informed bound lets the next action depend on the observation, which is tighter. Both give one alpha vector per action.
Lower bounds assume too little flexibility. The best-action worst-state bound takes the best action’s worst reward forever. The blind bound commits to a single action forever, ignoring observations.
Point-based value iteration. Instead of all beliefs, back up alpha vectors only at a finite set of beliefs \(B\), one per belief. Starting from a lower bound, it stays a lower bound and is exact at the chosen beliefs when they are well placed. Perseus backs up random beliefs until all have improved, often with fewer vectors.
Interpolating upper bounds. The sawtooth bound stores values at a few beliefs and interpolates with teeth that dip to each stored value. Triangulation interpolates over a regular grid of beliefs. Both remain upper bounds because the true value is convex.
Search where it matters. Sawtooth heuristic search starts from the initial belief, follows the upper bound’s actions and the observations with the largest gap, and tightens both bounds on the way back, until the gap at the start closes.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.

Perseus

Triangulated value function

Gap
