After this chapter you can

Compute QMDP and fast informed upper bounds, and blind and best-action worst-state lower bounds.
Explain why QMDP undervalues information-gathering actions, and recognize problems where that matters.
Run point-based value iteration and Perseus on a set of beliefs, and choose those beliefs.
Evaluate sawtooth and triangulated upper bounds at any belief.
Use heuristic search to close the gap between the bounds from a starting belief.

title: 21 · Offline Belief State Planning
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



You’re estimating how long a trip across an unfamiliar city will take.

An optimistic estimate: “if I knew exactly where every traffic jam was, it would take 30 minutes”. That’s QMDP: pretend you’ll know everything. It can’t be beaten, so it’s an upper bound on how well you’ll do.
A pessimistic estimate: “if I just drive my usual route and ignore the radio, it takes 55 minutes”. That’s the blind bound: a plan you can certainly carry out.
Refining both: check the estimates at a few key intersections and interpolate. The truth lies between the bounds, and when they meet, you know it.



We use two problems. The crying baby of Chapter 20 has an exact solution to compare against. The fork is a small problem built for this chapter, in the problem gallery. A hiker at a fork doesn’t know which trail leads home. Choosing right earns 10, choosing wrong costs 50, and then a new hike starts. The hiker can ask a passerby for 1, and the answer is right 85% of the time; or wait, which costs nothing and teaches nothing.

Pretend you’ll know: QMDP
QMDP assumes the state will be revealed after one step. For the crying baby that’s a mild fiction, and its bound is at most 4.14 above the true value. At the fork, it’s a disaster. If you’ll know the right trail for free next step anyway, why pay to ask? QMDP waits, the belief never changes, and it waits forever: a return of 0, where the best policy earns about 27. See Equation 1.


Use what you’ll observe: the fast informed bound
The fast informed bound lets the next action depend on the observation, which tightens the crying baby’s bound to within 0.65. At the fork it still fails: after waiting, the state is unchanged and certain in its per-state calculation, so waiting still looks like it reveals the trail. Its value at the fork’s start is 97.4, compared with QMDP’s 190.0 and the true 27.11. See Equation 2.


Plan at a few beliefs: point-based value iteration
Back up alpha vectors only at a handful of beliefs. For the crying baby, 5 beliefs spaced 0.25 apart give a lower bound within 0.002 of the true value everywhere. At the fork, 21 beliefs give a policy that asks until fairly sure (below \(P(\text{home right}) =\) 0.08 go left, above 0.92 go right). It earns 27.28 ± 0.17 in simulation, asking 2.7 times per hike. See Equation 4.


Interpolate from above: sawtooth and triangulation
Store upper-bound values at a few beliefs and interpolate. Because the true value is convex, straight-line interpolation between true values stays above it. Six beliefs and three sawtooth iterations bring the crying baby’s upper bound to within 1.1. A triangulation with 11 grid beliefs gets within 0.17. See Equation 5 and Equation 7.


Close the gap where you’ll go
Starting from a sated baby, sawtooth heuristic search follows the most uncertain branch, tightening both bounds. The gap at the start fell from 83.9 to 0.009 in 24 explorations (Figure 6). See Equation 6.

title: 21 · Offline Belief State Planning
text:
Formalism

QMDP
Compute one alpha vector per action by value iteration on the fully observed MDP (ADM §21.1; M. L. Littman, A. R. Cassandra and L. P. Kaelbling, ICML, 1995):

\[
\alpha_a^{(k+1)}(s) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \max_{a'} \alpha_{a'}^{(k)}(s'),
\qquad
U_{\text{QMDP}}(b) = \max_a \alpha_a^\top b
\tag{1}\]

In words. Solve the problem as if the state were visible, then average each action’s value over the belief.
Term by term.

At convergence, \(\alpha_a(s) = Q^*_{\text{MDP}}(s, a)\), the fully observed action value.
The \(\max_{a'}\) inside the sum picks the best next action for each next state, as if the next state were known.
Each iteration costs \(O(|\mathcal{A}|^2|\mathcal{S}|^2)\).
For any problem, \(U_{\text{QMDP}}(b) \ge U^*(b)\) (when run to convergence or started from an upper bound).

Why it holds. An agent that will be told the state after one step can do everything the real agent can, and more. So its value is an upper bound. The flip side: QMDP treats information as free, so it never pays for it. Actions whose only purpose is to learn look no better than doing nothing.


Fast informed bound
Let the next alpha vector depend on the observation (ADM §21.2; M. Hauskrecht, JAIR, 2000):

\[
\alpha_a^{(k+1)}(s) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_o \max_{a'} \sum_{s'} O(o \mid a, s')\, T(s' \mid s, a)\, \alpha_{a'}^{(k)}(s')
\tag{2}\]

In words. After acting from \(s\), the agent sees an observation and may choose its next alpha vector accordingly, but still knows where it started.
Term by term.

The max over \(a'\) now sits outside the sum over \(s'\) but inside the sum over \(o\). The choice may depend on the observation, not on the unobserved next state.
It is never looser than QMDP, and it costs \(O(|\mathcal{A}|^2|\mathcal{S}|^2|\mathcal{O}|)\) per iteration.
It still knows the current state \(s\) exactly. When an action doesn’t change the state, as waiting at the fork doesn’t, that knowledge carries over, and the bound again treats the state as known.

Why it holds. Knowing the current state, and choosing the next plan after seeing the observation, is more information than the real agent has. So the value is still an upper bound, but it credits the information carried by observations rather than assuming the next state is revealed.


Fast lower bounds
The best-action worst-state bound and the blind bound (ADM §21.3):

\[
r_{\text{baws}} = \frac{1}{1 - \gamma}\max_a \min_s R(s, a),
\qquad
\alpha_a^{(k+1)}(s) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a)\, \alpha_a^{(k)}(s')
\tag{3}\]

In words. The first is the reward of the best action in its worst state, received forever. The second is the value of repeating one action forever, whatever is observed.
Term by term.

The BAWS bound is one flat alpha vector: very loose, but safe.
The blind iteration has no max over next actions: each vector follows a single action. It is started from the BAWS bound.

Why it holds. Both describe policies the agent could actually follow (always do \(a\)). An achievable policy’s value can’t exceed the optimum, so both are lower bounds.


Point-based value iteration
Keep a set of beliefs \(B\) and one alpha vector per belief. The backup at a belief \(b\) (ADM §21.4; J. Pineau, G. Gordon and S. Thrun, IJCAI, 2003):

\[
\alpha_{a,o} = \arg\max_{\alpha \in \Gamma} \alpha^\top \text{Update}(b, a, o),
\qquad
\alpha_a(s) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s', o} O(o \mid a, s')\, T(s' \mid s, a)\, \alpha_{a,o}(s'),
\qquad
\alpha = \arg\max_{\alpha_a} \alpha_a^\top b
\tag{4}\]

In words. For each action, find the best existing plan to follow after each possible observation. Combine them into a new plan, as in Chapter 20, and keep the action whose plan is best at \(b\).
Term by term.

\(\alpha_{a,o}\) is chosen at the belief that would actually follow, \(\text{Update}(b, a, o)\), not over all beliefs. That’s what makes it cheap.
The combination is Chapter 20’s backup (eq. 20.17) with the chosen subplans.
Each backup costs \(O(|\mathcal{A}||\mathcal{O}||\Gamma||\mathcal{S}|^2)\), and there are \(|B|\) of them per iteration: polynomial, not exponential.

Why it holds. Each new vector is the value of a real conditional plan: act, then follow an existing plan chosen by the observation. If every vector in \(\Gamma\) is the value of a real plan (a lower bound), so is the new one. At the beliefs in \(B\), it is exactly the Bellman backup restricted to those plans, so values rise toward the optimum there.
Perseus (M. T. J. Spaan and N. Vlassis, JAIR, 2005; ADM §21.5) backs up beliefs chosen at random and skips any belief whose value an earlier backup in the same round already improved. It often needs far fewer backups and vectors.


Sawtooth upper bound
Store belief-utility pairs \(V\), including every corner belief \(e_i\) (the states themselves). Each non-corner pair \((b', u')\) defines a tooth (ADM §21.6):

\[
U^{(b', u')}(b) = u_E^\top b + \rho(b, b')\big(u' - u_E^\top b'\big),
\qquad
\rho(b, b') = \min_{i:\, b'_i > 0} \frac{b_i}{b'_i},
\qquad
U^V(b) = \min_{(b', u') \in V} U^{(b', u')}(b)
\tag{5}\]

In words. Start from the plane through the corners’ values. Near each stored belief, the bound dips down to the stored value, like a tooth, and the overall bound is the lowest of the teeth.
Term by term.

\(u_E\) is the vector of corner values.
\(\rho(b, b')\) is the largest multiple of \(b'\) that fits inside \(b\): 1 at \(b = b'\), and 0 at the corners that \(b'\) doesn’t use.
With two states, each tooth is two line segments from the corners down to \((b', u')\).
The result is piecewise linear but not convex.

Why it holds. Write \(b = \rho b' + (1 - \rho)c\), where \(c\) is some other belief. The true value is convex, so \(U^*(b) \le \rho U^*(b') + (1 - \rho)U^*(c)\). Bounding \(U^*(b')\) by \(u'\) and \(U^*(c)\) by the corners’ plane gives exactly the tooth.
Sawtooth iteration replaces each stored value by its one-step lookahead (Chapter 20, eq. 20.13) on the current bound. Since the lookahead of an upper bound is again an upper bound, it stays one.


Heuristic search on the gap
From the initial belief, repeatedly explore (ADM §21.8; T. Smith and R. Simmons, UAI, 2004):

\[
a = \pi_{\text{hi}}(b),
\qquad
o = \arg\max_o \Big[U_{\text{hi}}\big(\text{Update}(b, a, o)\big) - U_{\text{lo}}\big(\text{Update}(b, a, o)\big)\Big],
\qquad
\text{stop when } U_{\text{hi}}(b) - U_{\text{lo}}(b) \le \delta/\gamma^d
\tag{6}\]

In words. Follow the optimistic policy’s action, and go wherever the bounds disagree most. On the way back, back up both bounds at every belief visited.
Term by term.

\(U_{\text{hi}}\) is a sawtooth bound, started from the fast informed bound; \(U_{\text{lo}}\) is a set of alpha vectors, started from the BAWS bound.
At depth \(d\), a gap of \(\delta/\gamma^d\) contributes at most \(\delta\) to the gap at the start, so exploration stops there.
The algorithm stops when the gap at the start belief is below \(\delta\).

Why it holds. The gap at a belief after a backup is at most \(\gamma\) times the average gap at its successors. Tightening the successors with the largest gaps shrinks the start’s gap fastest. Following the upper bound’s action is optimism under uncertainty (Chapter 15): either that action really is good, or exploring it lowers its upper bound.


Triangulated value functions
Place beliefs on a regular grid of granularity \(m\) over the simplex, the Freudenthal triangulation (ADM §21.9; W. S. Lovejoy, Operations Research, 1991), and interpolate within the small simplex that contains \(b\):

\[
U(b) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i\, U\big(b^{(i)}\big),
\qquad
\sum_i \lambda_i = 1,\quad \sum_i \lambda_i b^{(i)} = b,\quad \lambda_i \ge 0
\tag{7}\]

In words. A belief’s value is a weighted average of the values at the nearby grid beliefs that surround it.
Term by term.

The grid has \(\binom{m + n - 1}{n - 1}\) beliefs: for two states, \(m + 1\) evenly spaced beliefs.
The \(b^{(i)}\) are the corners of the grid simplex containing \(b\), and the \(\lambda_i\) its barycentric weights. The code finds them in \(O(n \log n)\) by sorting the fractional parts of cumulative coordinates.
Value iteration updates the grid values by one-step lookahead on the interpolated function.

Why it holds. Linear interpolation of a convex function between points on the function lies on or above it. Value iteration on the interpolated function therefore converges to an upper bound (Lovejoy’s lemma 4).

title: 21 · Offline Belief State Planning
text:
Worked example

QMDP’s first step for the crying baby
Start from zero vectors. After one iteration, \(\alpha_a = R(\cdot, a)\): feed \((-5, -15)\), sing \((-0.5, -10.5)\), ignore \((0, -10)\) over (sated, hungry). After two, with \(\max_{a'}\alpha_{a'}(\text{sated}) = 0\) (ignore) and \(\max_{a'}\alpha_{a'}(\text{hungry}) = -10\) (ignore):

feed, from hungry: \(-15 + 0.9 \times 0 = -15\), since feeding always sates;
ignore, from sated: \(0 + 0.9\,(0.9 \times 0 + 0.1 \times -10) = -0.9\);
ignore, from hungry: \(-10 + 0.9 \times -10 = -19\).

The code’s two-step QMDP vectors: feed (-5.0, -15.0); sing (-1.4, -19.5); ignore (-0.9, -19.0).


A tooth by hand
Suppose the corners have upper-bound values \(u_E = (-2, -20)\) for (sated, hungry), and one stored belief \(b' = (0.6, 0.4)\) has upper-bound value \(-10\). Evaluate the bound at \(b = (0.8, 0.2)\):

The corners’ plane: \(u_E^\top b = 0.8(-2) + 0.2(-20) = -5.6\) at \(b\), and \(u_E^\top b' = -9.2\) at \(b'\). The stored value, \(-10\), is 0.8 below the plane there.
The ratio: \(\rho = \min(0.8/0.6,\ 0.2/0.4) = 0.5\): half of \(b'\) fits inside \(b\).
The tooth: the plane plus half the dip, \(-5.6 + 0.5\,(-10 - (-9.2)) = -6.0\).
The bound: the smaller of the plane and the tooth, \(-6.0\).

A stored value above the plane (say \(-8\)) would make a tooth above the plane, and the bound would stay at the plane. Only stored values below the corners’ plane tighten the bound.
The code gives -6.0 with the stored −10, and -5.6 with −8.


Why QMDP waits at the fork
With the trail known, the hiker would always go home: \(+10\) per hike, worth \(10/(1 - 0.95) = 200\). QMDP’s value of waiting in either state is \(0 + 0.95 \times 200 = 190\), since it pretends it will then know the trail. Asking is worth \(-1 + 0.95 \times 200 = 189\), less than waiting. Going left at \(P(\text{home right}) = 0.5\) is worth \(0.5\,(10 + 190) + 0.5\,(-50 + 190) = 170\). So QMDP waits, the belief stays at 0.5, and it waits again, forever.
The policies on this page act by one-step lookahead on QMDP’s value, which takes one real step first. Waiting then scores \(0 + 0.95 \times 190 = 180.5\). Asking scores \(-1 + 0.95 \times 190 = 180.45\), because either answer (0.15 or 0.85) lands where QMDP’s value is still flat at 190. The ranking is the same:
QMDP’s one-step lookahead values at the start: wait 180.5, ask 180.4, go left 160.5, go right 160.5.

title: 21 · Offline Belief State Planning
21 · Offline Belief State Planning
text:
Algorithms & code

Bounds, point-based methods, interpolation and search

JuliaPython


# Offline belief state planning (ADM Ch. 21): bounds and approximate value functions.
# A POMDP p has p.T[s, a, s′], p.R[s, a], p.O[a, s′, o] and p.γ; alpha vectors
# are plain vectors over states, and U(b) = max α ⋅ b over a set Γ (utility).

nstates(p) = size(p.T, 1)
nactions(p) = size(p.T, 2)
nobs(p) = size(p.O, 3)

# QMDP (eq. 21.1): one alpha vector per action, by value iteration on the fully
# observed MDP. It assumes the state will be known after one step: an upper bound.
function qmdp(p; k_max = 100)
    Γ = [zeros(nstates(p)) for _ in 1:nactions(p)]
    for _ in 1:k_max
        U = [maximum(α[s′] for α in Γ) for s′ in 1:nstates(p)]  # best action per state
        Γ = [[p.R[s, a] + p.γ * (p.T[s, a, :] ⋅ U) for s in 1:nstates(p)]
             for a in 1:nactions(p)]
    end
    return Γ
end

# Fast informed bound (eq. 21.4): like QMDP, but the next alpha vector may be
# chosen per observation, so information that arrives is partly credited.
function fast_informed_bound(p; k_max = 100)
    Γ = [zeros(nstates(p)) for _ in 1:nactions(p)]
    for _ in 1:k_max
        Γ = [[p.R[s, a] + p.γ * sum(maximum(
                  sum(p.O[a, s′, o] * p.T[s, a, s′] * α[s′] for s′ in 1:nstates(p))
                  for α in Γ) for o in 1:nobs(p))
              for s in 1:nstates(p)] for a in 1:nactions(p)]
    end
    return Γ
end

# Best-action worst-state lower bound (eq. 21.5): the best action's worst
# reward, received forever.
baws_lowerbound(p) = fill(maximum(minimum(p.R[:, a]) for a in 1:nactions(p)) /
                          (1 - p.γ), nstates(p))

# Blind lower bound (eq. 21.6): commit to one action forever, ignoring
# observations; one alpha vector per action, iterated from the BAWS bound.
function blind_lowerbound(p; k_max = 100)
    Γ = [baws_lowerbound(p) for _ in 1:nactions(p)]
    for _ in 1:k_max
        Γ = [[p.R[s, a] + p.γ * (p.T[s, a, :] ⋅ Γ[a]) for s in 1:nstates(p)]
             for a in 1:nactions(p)]
    end
    return Γ
end

# Point-based backup at belief b (eqs. 21.8-21.10): for each action, pick the
# best alpha vector at each updated belief, combine them (as in eq. 20.17),
# and keep the action whose new vector is best at b.
function belief_backup(p, Γ, b)
    best, best_val = Float64[], -Inf
    for a in 1:nactions(p)
        αo = map(1:nobs(p)) do o
            po = observation_probability(p, b, a, o)
            # An impossible observation's subplan never matters; any vector works.
            po > 0 || return Γ[1]
            b′ = update_discrete(b, p.T, p.O, a, o)
            Γ[argmax([α ⋅ b′ for α in Γ])]
        end
        α = combine_alpha(p, a, αo)
        if α ⋅ b > best_val
            best, best_val = α, α ⋅ b
        end
    end
    return best
end

# Point-based value iteration (algorithm 21.7): one backup per belief in B.
function pbvi(p, B; k_max = 50, Γ = [baws_lowerbound(p)])
    for _ in 1:k_max
        Γ = [belief_backup(p, Γ, b) for b in B]
    end
    return Γ
end

# Randomized point-based value iteration (Perseus, algorithm 21.8): back up
# random beliefs until every belief in B has improved (or kept its value).
function perseus(p, B, rng; k_max = 50, Γ = [baws_lowerbound(p)])
    for _ in 1:k_max
        Γ′, todo = Vector{Float64}[], collect(B)
        while !isempty(todo)
            b = rand(rng, todo)
            α_old = Γ[argmax([α ⋅ b for α in Γ])]
            α_new = belief_backup(p, Γ, b)
            push!(Γ′, α_new ⋅ b ≥ α_old ⋅ b ? α_new : α_old)
            # Keep only beliefs whose value Γ′ has not yet matched.
            filter!(b -> utility(Γ′, b) < utility(Γ, b), todo)
        end
        Γ = Γ′
    end
    return Γ
end

# Sawtooth upper bound (eqs. 21.14-21.16). V maps beliefs to upper-bound
# utilities and must contain every corner belief e_i. Each non-corner pair
# (b′, u′) is a "tooth": the corners' plane, dipping down to u′ at b′.
function sawtooth(V, b)
    haskey(V, b) && return V[b]
    n = length(b)
    corners = [[i == j ? 1.0 : 0.0 for j in 1:n] for i in 1:n]
    uE = [V[e] for e in corners]
    best = uE ⋅ b                          # the corners' plane alone
    for (b′, u′) in V
        b′ in corners && continue
        # ρ: how much of b′ fits inside b (the minimum ratio, eq. 21.14).
        ρ = minimum(b[i] / b′[i] for i in 1:n if b′[i] > 0)
        best = min(best, uE ⋅ b + ρ * (u′ - uE ⋅ b′))
    end
    return best
end

# Sawtooth iteration (algorithm 21.10): replace each non-corner value in B by
# its one-step lookahead on the current sawtooth bound.
function sawtooth_iteration(p, V, B; k_max = 10)
    corners = [[i == j ? 1.0 : 0.0 for j in 1:nstates(p)] for i in 1:nstates(p)]
    for _ in 1:k_max
        U = b -> sawtooth(V, b)
        V = Dict(b => (b in corners ? V[b] : greedy_belief(p, U, b).u) for b in B)
    end
    return V
end

# One random step in belief space (algorithm 21.11): sample a state from b,
# move and observe with the model, and update the belief.
function randstep(p, b, a, rng)
    s = rand(rng, Categorical(b))                    # Distributions.Categorical
    s′ = rand(rng, Categorical(p.T[s, a, :]))
    o = rand(rng, Categorical(p.O[a, s′, :]))
    return update_discrete(b, p.T, p.O, a, o), p.R[s, a]
end

# Exploratory belief expansion (algorithm 21.13): from each belief, try every
# action once and keep the new belief farthest (in L1) from the set so far.
function exploratory_belief_expansion(p, B, rng)
    B′ = copy(B)
    for b in B
        cands = [randstep(p, b, a, rng)[1] for a in 1:nactions(p)]
        dist(c) = minimum(sum(abs.(c .- x)) for x in B′)
        c = cands[argmax(dist.(cands))]
        dist(c) > 0 && push!(B′, c)
    end
    return B′
end

# Sawtooth heuristic search (algorithm 21.14): from b0, repeatedly follow the
# upper bound's greedy action and the observation with the largest gap,
# then tighten both bounds on the way back. Returns (V, Γ, gaps at b0).
function sawtooth_heuristic_search(p, b0; depth = 10, k_max = 30, δ = 0.01)
    fib = fast_informed_bound(p)
    corners = [[i == j ? 1.0 : 0.0 for j in 1:nstates(p)] for i in 1:nstates(p)]
    V = Dict(e => utility(fib, e) for e in corners)          # upper bound
    Γ = [baws_lowerbound(p)]                                   # lower bound
    gap(b) = sawtooth(V, b) - utility(Γ, b)
    function explore(b, d)
        (d >= depth || gap(b) <= δ / p.γ^d) && return
        a = greedy_belief(p, b -> sawtooth(V, b), b).a
        # The observation leading to the belief with the widest gap.
        obs = [o for o in 1:nobs(p) if observation_probability(p, b, a, o) > 0]
        next = [update_discrete(b, p.T, p.O, a, o) for o in obs]
        b′ = next[argmax(gap.(next))]
        explore(b′, d + 1)
        b′ in corners || (V[b′] = greedy_belief(p, b -> sawtooth(V, b), b′).u)
        push!(Γ, belief_backup(p, Γ, b′))
        return
    end
    gaps = [gap(b0)]
    for _ in 1:k_max
        explore(b0, 0)
        V[b0] = min(sawtooth(V, b0), greedy_belief(p, b -> sawtooth(V, b), b0).u)
        push!(Γ, belief_backup(p, Γ, b0))
        push!(gaps, gap(b0))
        gaps[end] < δ && break
    end
    return V, Γ, gaps
end

# Freudenthal interpolation (Lovejoy, 1991) on the belief simplex with
# granularity m. Returns the vertices (beliefs whose entries are multiples of
# 1/m) of the sub-simplex containing b, and weights λ with Σλ = 1, Σλ v = b.
function freudenthal(b, m)
    n = length(b)
    # Cumulative coordinates: x_i = m (b_i + ... + b_n). x_1 = m exactly; set it
    # directly, since a sum a hair below 1 would floor to m - 1.
    x = [i == 1 ? float(m) : m * sum(b[i:n]) for i in 1:n]
    base = floor.(x)
    d = x .- base                                      # fractional parts
    # Visit coordinates by decreasing fraction; coordinate 1 (fraction 0) last.
    order = sortperm(1:n, by = i -> (i == 1, -d[i]))
    to_belief(v) = [(v[i] - (i < n ? v[i+1] : 0.0)) / m for i in 1:n]
    # Vertices: the base, then the base stepped up along order[1], order[2], ...
    verts, v = [to_belief(base)], copy(base)
    for k in 1:n-1
        v[order[k]] += 1
        push!(verts, to_belief(v))
    end
    # Weights: 1 - d_(1), then successive differences of the sorted fractions.
    λ = [1 - d[order[1]]; [d[order[k]] - d[order[k+1]] for k in 1:n-1]]
    return verts, λ
end

# Triangulated value iteration (algorithm 21.16): values at the grid beliefs,
# interpolated elsewhere; each sweep replaces them by one-step lookahead.
# Starting from 0 gives an upper bound when rewards are never positive.
function triangulated_iteration(p, m; k_max = 50)
    n = nstates(p)
    key(b) = round.(b; digits = 10)                    # grid beliefs as keys
    grid = [key(collect(c) ./ m)
            for c in Iterators.product(fill(0:m, n)...) if sum(c) == m]
    V = Dict(b => 0.0 for b in grid)
    function U(b)
        verts, λ = freudenthal(b, m)
        # Skip zero weights: on a tie their vertex may lie off the grid.
        return sum(l * V[key(v)] for (v, l) in zip(verts, λ) if l > 1e-12)
    end
    for _ in 1:k_max
        V = Dict(b => greedy_belief(p, U, b).u for b in grid)   # U sees the old V
    end
    return V, U
end


import numpy as np

from adm.problems.crying_baby import belief_update
from adm.problems.fork import fork

p = fork()                       # states: home left, home right; actions: wait, ask, go left, go right
nS, nA, nO = p.T.shape[0], p.T.shape[1], p.O.shape[2]


def qmdp(p, k_max=300):
    """eq. 21.1: one alpha vector per action; the max over next actions is per next state."""
    G = np.zeros((nA, nS))
    for _ in range(k_max):
        G = p.R.T + p.gamma * np.einsum("sat,t->as", p.T, G.max(axis=0))
    return G


def backup(p, G, b):
    """eq. 21.8-21.10: the best new alpha vector at belief b from the vectors G."""
    best = None
    for a in range(nA):
        alpha = p.R[:, a].copy()
        for o in range(nO):
            po = (b @ p.T[:, a, :]) @ p.O[a, :, o]
            sub = G[np.argmax(G @ belief_update(p, b, a, o))] if po > 0 else G[0]
            alpha += p.gamma * p.T[:, a, :] @ (p.O[a, :, o] * sub)
        if best is None or alpha @ b > best @ b:
            best = alpha
    return best


def lookahead_action(p, G, b):
    """eq. 20.13 with U(b) = max over G of alpha . b."""
    q = []
    for a in range(nA):
        v = p.R[:, a] @ b
        for o in range(nO):
            po = (b @ p.T[:, a, :]) @ p.O[a, :, o]
            if po > 0:
                v += p.gamma * po * (G @ belief_update(p, b, a, o)).max()
        q.append(v)
    return int(np.argmax(q))


B = [np.array([1 - x, x]) for x in np.linspace(0, 1, 21)]
G = np.full((1, nS), p.R.min(axis=0).max() / (1 - p.gamma))    # best-action worst-state bound
for _ in range(300):
    G = np.array([backup(p, G, b) for b in B])

b0 = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
print("QMDP at the start:", p.actions[lookahead_action(p, qmdp(p), b0)],
      "| point-based:", p.actions[lookahead_action(p, G, b0)], f"(value {(G @ b0).max():.3f})")
assert lookahead_action(p, qmdp(p), b0) == 0 and lookahead_action(p, G, b0) == 1
assert abs((G @ b0).max() - 27.1149) < 1e-3









NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






map(1:nobs(p)) do o ... end applies the block to each observation, like a list comprehension with a multi-line body; return inside the block returns from the block only.
filter!(b -> ..., todo) removes, in place, every belief for which the condition fails.
Dict(e => utility(fib, e) for e in corners) builds a dictionary from pairs, like a dict comprehension.
function explore(b, d) ... end inside another function is a closure that sees and changes V and Γ, like a nested def using nonlocal.
sortperm(1:n, by = i -> (i == 1, -d[i])) sorts indices by a tuple key: false sorts before true, so index 1 goes last, and ties within each group are ordered by decreasing d.
Iterators.product(fill(0:m, n)...) is itertools.product(range(m + 1), repeat=n).






Run them

p = crying_baby()
upper = fast_informed_bound(p; k_max = 300)
beliefs = [[1 - x, x] for x in 0:0.25:1]
lower = pbvi(p, beliefs; k_max = 100)
gap(b) = utility(upper, b) - utility(lower, b)

gap (generic function with 1 method)




gap between the fast informed bound and point-based VI: 0.0: 0.236, 0.25: 0.611, 0.5: 0.213, 0.75: 0.213, 1.0: 0.213




Results

Upper and lower bounds for the crying baby







Figure 3: Fast bounds for the crying baby. Left: QMDP (dashed) and the fast informed bound (solid) after 1, 2, 3 and 300 iterations, above the exact value (black). Right: the best-action worst-state and blind lower bounds, far below it.




At convergence, QMDP overestimates by up to 4.14 and the fast informed bound by up to 0.65. The blind bound, one action forever, falls up to 32.9 below. Always feeding and always ignoring are both far from adaptive care.


Point-based value iteration and Perseus







Figure 4: Lower bounds from point-based value iteration (left) and Perseus (right) on five beliefs (P(hungry) = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1; ticks), after 0, 5, 10, 20 and 40 iterations, rising toward the exact value (black).




After 40 iterations, point-based value iteration is within 1.197 of the exact value everywhere, using 2 distinct alpha vectors. Perseus is within 1.918 with 2. Five well-spread beliefs suffice here because the exact value has only 2 pieces (Chapter 20).


Sawtooth and triangulated upper bounds







Figure 5: Interpolating upper bounds for the crying baby. Left: the sawtooth bound on six beliefs (ticks) after 1, 2, 3 and 20 iterations, started from the fast informed bound’s corner values. Right: triangulated value iteration with grids of 3, 6 and 11 beliefs. The exact value is black.




The sawtooth bound is within 1.07 after 20 iterations; its remaining error sits between the stored beliefs, where the teeth interpolate. The triangulated bound with 3, 6 and 11 grid beliefs exceeds the exact value by at most 2.45, 0.56 and 0.17.


Closing the gap from a starting belief







Figure 6: Sawtooth heuristic search from a sated baby: the gap between the upper (sawtooth) and lower (alpha vector) bounds at the start belief, after each exploration (log scale).




The search only visits beliefs reachable from a sated baby, under the upper bound’s policy. It closes the gap there without making either bound tight elsewhere.


The fork: when information has to be paid for







Figure 7: The fork. Left: value over P(home right) according to QMDP and the fast informed bound (upper bounds), point-based value iteration on 21 beliefs (lower bound) and triangulated value iteration (upper bound); the last two nearly coincide. Right: each method’s one-step lookahead action at every belief.





QMDP waits in a band around 50–50, from \(P(\text{home right}) =\) 0.47 to 0.53, and asks outside it. Its value is flat at 190.0 across the middle and rises only near the ends. So asking looks worthwhile only if a likely answer would land near an end. Starting from 50–50, the hiker waits, the belief never moves, and the return is exactly 0.
The fast informed bound waits over a wider band, from 0.27 to 0.73, with a value near 97.0 there. It too never leaves the fork from 50–50. Both values assume the trail will somehow become known.
The point-based policy asks until \(P(\text{home right})\) is below 0.08 or above 0.92, then goes. In simulation it asked 2.7 times per hike, chose wrong 3.0% of the time, and earned 27.28 ± 0.17.
The bounds pinch. Point-based value iteration (a lower bound) and triangulation (an upper bound) agree at the start to within 5.9e-6. So the optimal value is 27.115, and the point-based policy is essentially optimal.
Exact value iteration struggles here. Chapter 20’s method still keeps 23 alpha vectors after 10 steps, and has to build 2116 candidate plans to get there, a number that grows with the square of the kept set. Its 10-step value at the start is only 9.73, far from the infinite-horizon 27.11: many hikes lie beyond 10 steps.

title: 21 · Offline Belief State Planning
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: a QMDP value. A two-state POMDP has fully observed action values \(Q(s_1, a_1) = 10\), \(Q(s_1, a_2) = 4\), \(Q(s_2, a_1) = 0\), \(Q(s_2, a_2) = 6\). What does QMDP choose at \(b = (0.4, 0.6)\), and what value does it claim?






TipSolution





\(\alpha_{a_1} = (10, 0)\) and \(\alpha_{a_2} = (4, 6)\). At \(b\): \(a_1 \to 4\) and \(a_2 \to 1.6 + 3.6 = 5.2\). QMDP chooses \(a_2\) and claims 5.2. That’s an upper bound on the true value: a real agent at \(b\) can’t do better than one who will learn the state immediately.



Problem 2: why the fast informed bound is tighter. In Equation 2 the max over \(a'\) sits inside the sum over \(o\); in QMDP it sits inside the sum over \(s'\). Explain why moving the max outward can only lower the bound.






TipSolution





QMDP computes \(\sum_{s'} T(s')\max_{a'}\alpha_{a'}(s')\), choosing the best vector separately for every next state. That is the same as \(\sum_o \sum_{s'} O(o \mid s')T(s')\max_{a'}\alpha_{a'}(s')\), since the observation probabilities sum to 1. The fast informed bound instead computes \(\sum_o \max_{a'}\sum_{s'} O\,T\,\alpha_{a'}(s')\), one vector per observation. For every \(o\), a maximum of a sum is at most the sum of maxima, so the fast informed value is at most QMDP’s. It knows less at choice time: the observation, not the next state.



Problem 3: a point-based backup’s guarantee. Your alpha vectors are all lower bounds. After a point-based backup at belief \(b\), why is the new vector also a lower bound everywhere, not just at \(b\)?






TipSolution





The new vector is the exact value of a concrete conditional plan: take action \(a\), then after each observation \(o\) follow the plan behind \(\alpha_{a,o}\). That plan’s value at any belief is at most the optimal value there. Its value is at least what the new vector says, because each \(\alpha_{a,o}\) is itself a lower bound on its plan. Choosing the subplans using \(b\) only affects how good the plan is, not whether its vector is achievable.



Problem 4: triangulation weights. With two states and granularity \(m = 4\), which grid beliefs surround \(b = (0.3, 0.7)\), with what weights, and what is the interpolated value if the grid values are \(U(0.25, 0.75) = -20\) and \(U(0.5, 0.5) = -16\)?






TipSolution





The grid beliefs are \((1, 0), (0.75, 0.25), (0.5, 0.5), (0.25, 0.75), (0, 1)\). \(b\) lies between \((0.25, 0.75)\) and \((0.5, 0.5)\): \(0.3 = 0.8 \times 0.25 + 0.2 \times 0.5\), so the weights are 0.8 and 0.2. \(U(b) \approx 0.8(-20) + 0.2(-16) = -19.2\). If the grid values are upper bounds and the true value is convex, this interpolation is also an upper bound.



Problem 5: design a problem that breaks QMDP. The fork breaks QMDP because a free action teaches nothing. Would QMDP still wait if waiting cost 2 per step? What does that suggest?






TipSolution





QMDP would value waiting at \(-2 + 0.95 \times 200 = 188\) and asking at \(189\), so it would ask. Then it would ask again and again: at any belief short of certainty, QMDP compares asking (189) with going under uncertainty, and only goes when it’s nearly sure. It would behave reasonably, by accident: its preference would be right only because asking happens to be cheaper than waiting. QMDP’s rankings of information-gathering actions are driven by their costs, never by their information. Any problem where the informative action is not the cheapest safe action will fool it.

title: 21 · Offline Belief State Planning
text:
Recap

Offline approximations come with bounds; the gap measures their quality (Equation 6). Why it matters: for the fork, the lower and upper bounds pinched to within a thousandth at the start, certifying the point-based policy as essentially optimal without solving exactly.
QMDP and the fast informed bound are cheap upper bounds that overvalue information (Equation 1, Equation 2). Why it matters: they are often good enough, within 0.65 for the crying baby. But in problems like the fork, where information must be bought, both wait forever from an even start. Online methods (Chapter 22) often use them as optimistic heuristics instead.
Point-based value iteration gives lower bounds at polynomial cost (Equation 4). Why it matters: backing up only at chosen beliefs sidesteps Chapter 20’s explosion of alpha vectors; this is the idea behind modern solvers such as SARSOP.
Convexity turns interpolation into upper bounds (Equation 5, Equation 7). Why it matters: sawtooth and triangulated values bound from above, giving the other side of the gap.
Heuristic search focuses on beliefs that matter from the start (Equation 6). Why it matters: reachable beliefs are usually a tiny part of the belief space, and closing the gap only there is what makes large POMDPs solvable offline.

text:
Cheat sheet & connections



Table 2: Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name).

Equation 7






Common pitfalls

Using QMDP where information costs something. It will never pay for information, and may do nothing at all.
Stopping QMDP early. Before convergence, it’s an upper bound only if started from one (for example, the best-action best-state value).
Belief points that miss the reachable beliefs. Point-based bounds are only tight near the chosen beliefs; choose them by simulating from the start belief.
Comparing against a finite-horizon “exact” value. A 60-step solution is not the infinite-horizon value; with rewards of −10 per step it can be off by tenths.
Reading a lower bound as the value of its policy. A lower bound is guaranteed, but the policy acting greedily on it may do better; simulate to find out.

Ch 15 · Exploration and Exploitation: the value of information, which QMDP ignores.

title: 19 · Beliefs
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
In Parts II and III, the agent always knew which state it was in: the rover knew its cell, even when it didn’t know where its wheels would take it next. Part IV (Chapters 19–23) drops that assumption. A robot has noisy sensors, a doctor sees symptoms rather than the disease, and a tracker sees radar blips rather than the aircraft. The agent can’t act on the state, because it doesn’t know it. So it acts on a belief: a probability distribution over the states it might be in.
This chapter is about keeping that belief up to date. It is Chapter 3’s inference, repeated at every time step, with Chapter 2’s building blocks as the models. Chapters 20–23 then decide what to do given a belief, treating the belief itself as the state of a new, larger decision problem.
The question: as an agent acts and receives noisy observations, how should it keep track of where it probably is?
The short answer: by repeating two moves forever. Predict: push the belief through what the action does, so it spreads out. Correct: reweight it by how well each possible state explains what you just observed, so it sharpens. The rest of the chapter is about storing the belief so that these two moves stay cheap.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Every filter runs the same predict–correct loop; they differ in how they store the belief. The book also covers belief initialization, the extended and unscented Kalman filters for nonlinear models, and particle injection (ADM §19.1, §19.4–19.5, §19.7).







The key ideas at a glance

A belief replaces the state. A belief gives each possible state a probability, given everything done and observed so far. It needs one extra piece of model beyond an MDP: an observation model, the probability of each possible observation in each state. For example, the chance the window looks dark when the tram is in a tunnel.
Every update is predict, then correct. Predict: for each possible new state, add up all the ways of getting there from where you might have been. The belief spreads out. Correct: multiply each state’s probability by how likely the actual observation is in that state, then normalize. The belief sharpens. This is Bayes’ rule applied over and over, and it’s called the Bayes filter.
With few states, store the whole table: the discrete filter. Keep one probability per state and apply predict and correct exactly. It’s simple and exact, and it costs about (number of states)² per step.
With linear motion and Gaussian noise, store a mean and a covariance: the Kalman filter. If the belief starts as a bell curve and everything is linear with Gaussian noise, it stays a bell curve. So only its center and spread need updating. The key quantity is the Kalman gain, how far to move from the prediction toward the observation. A noisy sensor gives a small gain; a shaky prediction gives a large one. For nonlinear models, the extended and unscented Kalman filters approximate the same idea.
Otherwise, store samples: the particle filter. Represent the belief by a cloud of guesses (particles). Move each guess with a random draw from the dynamics, weight it by how well it explains the observation, then resample: copy the heavy ones and drop the light ones. The cloud can take any shape, including a ring or two separate clumps. It only needs a simulator of the world, and more particles give more accuracy.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Belief \(b(s)\)
Probability that the current state is \(s\), given the history


Observation model \(O(o \mid a, s')\)
Probability of seeing \(o\) after action \(a\) lands you in \(s'\)


Predict / correct
Push the belief through the dynamics / reweight it by the observation


Bayes filter
Predict-then-correct, repeated every step


Kalman gain \(K\)
Fraction of the gap between prediction and observation to move by


Innovation
The observation minus what you expected to observe


Particle
One sampled guess of the state


Resampling
Copying high-weight particles and dropping low-weight ones


Particle degeneracy
Nearly all weight falling on one or two particles








After this chapter you can

Update a belief over a handful of states by hand, and in code for many.
Run a Kalman filter, and explain its gain in terms of trust in the prediction versus the sensor.
Track a state with a particle filter when the belief has several peaks or odd shapes.
Choose between the three representations for a given problem.

title: 19 · Beliefs
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



A ship’s navigator before GPS works in two alternating moves.
Dead reckoning (predict). “We sailed north at 10 knots for an hour, so we’re about 10 miles north of where we were.” But currents and wind add error, so every hour of dead reckoning makes the navigator less sure. The circle of possible positions on the chart grows.
A sighting (correct). A lighthouse comes into view at a known bearing. Positions that fit that sighting become more likely, and positions that don’t become less likely. The circle shrinks.
Uncertainty grows when you move and shrinks when you look. A filter is that routine written as math, run at every step.


What the belief looks like depends on the problem. In Figure 2, a tram rider on a 12-stop loop can’t see the stop signs, only whether the window is dark (tunnel) or light. At first every stop is equally likely. As the pattern of tunnels and open track goes by, the belief concentrates on the right stop, and it never becomes perfectly sure, because the tram sometimes lingers or skips a stop.







Figure 2: Discrete filter on the tram. Each column is the belief over the 12 stops after that step’s observation; darker blue is more probable. Diamonds mark the true stop. The top strip shows what the sensor read.





Predict spreads, correct sharpens
The tram starts with every stop equally likely, \(1/12\) each. The window goes dark. Five stops are in tunnels, where “dark” is 0.9 likely, against 0.2 elsewhere. So each tunnel stop’s share becomes \(0.9/5.9 = 0.153\) and each open stop’s \(0.2/5.9 = 0.034\): the belief has sharpened toward the tunnels. Then the tram drives. Each stop’s probability flows mostly one stop forward, with some staying put and some skipping ahead, so the peaks blur and shift. Every step repeats these two moves. See Equation 3.


Kalman: blending two noisy guesses
A kayaker’s predicted position is 2 m, uncertain with variance 10; the GPS says 3.5 m, with variance 4. Neither is trustworthy alone. The Kalman filter trusts each in proportion to the other’s uncertainty. The gain is \(10/(10+4) = 0.71\), so it moves 71% of the way from the prediction toward the GPS, to 3.07 m. The combined variance, 2.86, is smaller than both sources: two independent opinions beat either one. See Equation 6.


Particles: a crowd of guesses
A rover can only measure its distance to one beacon. After the first reading, every point on a ring around the beacon is equally plausible. No bell curve can represent a ring, but a cloud of 2,000 random guesses, reweighted by the reading, forms one on its own. Driving straight east leaves the rover’s side of the beacon ambiguous, so the cloud splits into two mirror-image clumps. After a turn north, the wrong clump’s predictions stop matching the readings, and it dies out. See Equation 7 and Figure 6.


Choosing how to store the belief
A table is exact but grows with the number of states. A mean and covariance are tiny and exact, but only for linear-Gaussian worlds. Particles fit any shape but need many samples when the sensor is precise. The three filters make exactly this trade-off, and the cheat sheet summarizes when to use each.

title: 19 · Beliefs
text:
Formalism

Beliefs

\[
b(s) = P(s_t = s \mid a_{1:t},\ o_{1:t})
\tag{1}\]

In words. \(b(s)\) is how probable it is that the current state is \(s\), given every action taken and every observation received so far.
Term by term.

\(s_t\) is the (hidden) state at time \(t\).
\(a_{1:t}\) and \(o_{1:t}\) are the whole history of actions and observations.
\(b\) is a probability distribution: \(b(s) \ge 0\) and it sums (or integrates) to 1.

Keeping the whole history would grow without bound. The point of a filter is that the belief summarizes the history: to update it, you need only the old belief, the latest action, and the latest observation.
The model now has one more piece than an MDP. Besides \(T(s' \mid s, a)\), there is an observation model \(O(o \mid a, s')\): the probability of observing \(o\) when you took action \(a\) and landed in \(s'\).


The belief update
Updating a belief rests on one famous rule:

\[
P(s \mid o) = \frac{P(o \mid s)\, P(s)}{P(o)} \;\propto\; P(o \mid s)\, P(s)
\tag{2}\]

In words. After seeing \(o\), a state’s probability is its old probability times how well it explains \(o\), rescaled so everything sums to 1.
Term by term. \(P(s)\) is the prior, what you believed before looking. \(P(o \mid s)\) is the likelihood, how expected \(o\) is if \(s\) is true. \(P(s \mid o)\) is the posterior, what you believe after looking. \(P(o)\) doesn’t depend on \(s\), so it only rescales. That is why “\(\propto\)” (proportional to) plus normalizing is enough.
Combining Bayes’ rule with the transition model gives the update for one step:

\[
b'(s') \;\propto\; \underbrace{O(o \mid a, s')}_{\text{correct}} \;\underbrace{\sum_{s} T(s' \mid s, a)\, b(s)}_{\text{predict}}
\tag{3}\]

In words. First predict where you probably are after acting. Then reweight each candidate by how well it explains what you saw, and normalize.
Term by term.

\(\sum_{s} T(s' \mid s, a)\, b(s)\) is the prediction. Add up every way of reaching \(s'\): start in \(s\) (probability \(b(s)\)), then move to \(s'\) (probability \(T(s' \mid s, a)\)). This is the law of total probability, and it spreads the belief out.
\(O(o \mid a, s')\) is the correction, the likelihood from Equation 2. It sharpens the belief toward states consistent with \(o\).
\(\propto\): divide by the sum over \(s'\) so that \(b'\) sums to 1.

Why it holds. It is Equation 2 with the prediction as the prior. That works because of two Markov assumptions: the next state depends only on the current state and action, and the observation depends only on the action and the state you land in. So the old belief carries everything the past can tell you.
For a finite set of states, Equation 3 is the algorithm: the discrete state filter (ADM §19.2). It costs \(O(|\mathcal{S}|^2)\) per step for the prediction.
Try it. On the tram, start uniform (\(b = 1/12\)) and read “dark”. Tunnel stops explain that with probability 0.9 and open stops with 0.2. Five stops are tunnels, so the normalizer is \(5(0.9) + 7(0.2) = 5.9\). Each tunnel stop gets \(0.9 / 5.9 \approx 0.153\) and each open stop gets \(0.2 / 5.9 \approx 0.034\).


Kalman filter: when everything is Gaussian
Continuous states make the sum an integral, which in general has no closed form. One important case does: linear dynamics with Gaussian noise (ADM §19.3).

\[
T(s' \mid s, a) = \mathcal{N}(s' \mid \mathbf{T}_s s + \mathbf{T}_a a,\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s)
\qquad
O(o \mid s') = \mathcal{N}(o \mid \mathbf{O}_s s',\ \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_o)
\tag{4}\]

In words. The next state is a linear function of the state and action, plus Gaussian noise. The observation is a linear function of the state, plus Gaussian noise.
Term by term.

\(\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \Sigma)\) is the Gaussian density at \(x\), with mean \(\mu\) and covariance \(\Sigma\).
\(\mathbf{T}_s\) and \(\mathbf{T}_a\) say how the state and the action move the state. For a buoy drifting at constant velocity, \(\mathbf{T}_s\) adds the velocity to the position at each step.
\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s\) is the process noise: currents, gusts, anything the model leaves out.
\(\mathbf{O}_s\) picks out what the sensor sees, such as position but not velocity. \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_o\) is the sensor noise.

If the belief starts Gaussian, \(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_b, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b)\), it stays Gaussian forever. So the whole belief is just a mean and a covariance, and Equation 3 becomes a few matrix formulas.

\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}_p = \mathbf{T}_s \boldsymbol{\mu}_b + \mathbf{T}_a a
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_p = \mathbf{T}_s \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b \mathbf{T}_s^\top + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s
\tag{5}\]

In words. Move the best guess through the dynamics. The uncertainty is carried along (and stretched or rotated) by the dynamics, then grows by the process noise.
Term by term.

\(\boldsymbol{\mu}_p\) is the predicted mean: where the physics says you should be.
\(\mathbf{T}_s \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b \mathbf{T}_s^\top\) is how a linear map transforms a covariance. In 1D with \(\mathbf{T}_s = t\), it is \(t^2 \sigma^2\).
\(+\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_s\) is the new uncertainty added by the step. This is dead reckoning’s growing circle.


\[
\mathbf{K} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_p \mathbf{O}_s^\top \big(\mathbf{O}_s \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_p \mathbf{O}_s^\top + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_o\big)^{-1}
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\mu}_b' = \boldsymbol{\mu}_p + \mathbf{K}\big(o - \mathbf{O}_s \boldsymbol{\mu}_p\big)
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_b' = (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K} \mathbf{O}_s)\, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_p
\tag{6}\]

In words. Compare what you observed with what you expected to observe. Move the estimate part of the way toward the observation, by a fraction \(\mathbf{K}\) set by how much you trust the prediction versus the sensor. The uncertainty always shrinks.
Term by term.

\(o - \mathbf{O}_s \boldsymbol{\mu}_p\) is the innovation, or surprise: the observation minus the observation you predicted.
\(\mathbf{K}\) is the Kalman gain. In 1D with \(\mathbf{O}_s = 1\), it is \(K = \sigma_p^2 / (\sigma_p^2 + \sigma_o^2)\), a number between 0 and 1. A noisy sensor (\(\sigma_o^2\) large) gives \(K \approx 0\): ignore it. A shaky prediction (\(\sigma_p^2\) large) gives \(K \approx 1\): trust the sensor.
\((\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}\mathbf{O}_s)\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_p\): in 1D, \((1 - K)\sigma_p^2 = \frac{\sigma_p^2 \sigma_o^2}{\sigma_p^2 + \sigma_o^2}\), which is smaller than both \(\sigma_p^2\) and \(\sigma_o^2\).

Why it holds (1D). The corrected belief is proportional to the prior times the likelihood, \(\mathcal{N}(s \mid \mu_p, \sigma_p^2)\, \mathcal{N}(o \mid s, \sigma_o^2)\). A product of two Gaussians in \(s\) is a Gaussian whose precision (inverse variance) is the sum of the two precisions, \(1/\sigma_b^2 = 1/\sigma_p^2 + 1/\sigma_o^2\). Its mean is the precision-weighted average of \(\mu_p\) and \(o\). Rearranging that average gives \(\mu_p + K(o - \mu_p)\) with \(K = \sigma_p^2 / (\sigma_p^2 + \sigma_o^2)\).
When the dynamics or sensor are nonlinear, two variants keep the Gaussian shape by approximation. The extended Kalman filter linearizes the model around the current mean (ADM §19.4). The unscented Kalman filter pushes a few carefully chosen “sigma points” through the true nonlinear model (ADM §19.5).


Particle filter: any shape at all
A Gaussian has one peak. Some beliefs have two (“I’m either north or south of the lighthouse”), and some have odd shapes. A particle filter (ADM §19.6) stores the belief as a cloud of sampled states, or particles, and lets the cloud take any shape:

\[
b(s) \approx \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \delta\big(s - s^{(i)}\big)
\qquad
w^{(i)} \propto O\big(o \mid a, s'^{(i)}\big), \quad s'^{(i)} \sim T\big(\cdot \mid s^{(i)}, a\big)
\tag{7}\]

In words. The belief is “wherever the particles are”: a region holding 30% of the particles has probability about 0.3. To update, move every particle with a random draw from the dynamics (predict), score it by how well it explains the observation (the weight \(w\)), then draw a fresh set of \(N\) particles in proportion to those weights (resample).
Term by term.

\(\delta(s - s^{(i)})\) is a spike of probability at particle \(s^{(i)}\).
\(s'^{(i)} \sim T(\cdot \mid s^{(i)}, a)\) is the predict step, done by simulation. You only need to be able to sample from the model, not to write down its probabilities.
\(w^{(i)}\) is the correct step. It is Equation 3’s likelihood, applied to each particle.
Resampling copies high-weight particles and drops low-weight ones, so effort goes where the probability is.

The cost is \(O(N)\) per step whatever the shape, but accuracy improves only like \(1/\sqrt{N}\). When the sensor is very precise, almost no particle lands where the likelihood is high. Particle injection adds fresh random particles to recover (ADM §19.7).

title: 19 · Beliefs
text:
Worked example

The tram by hand
The tram is a discrete filter with 12 states and one action (drive). The transition and observation models are two arrays:

PythonJulia


import numpy as np

# 12 stops on a loop (0-based here); stops 2, 3, 4, 8 and 10 are in tunnels.
n, tunnels = 12, {2, 3, 4, 8, 10}
# One action (0 = drive): advance 1 stop w.p. 0.8, stay w.p. 0.1, skip ahead 2 w.p. 0.1.
# The % n wraps around the loop: after stop 11 comes stop 0.
T = np.zeros((n, 1, n))
for s in range(n):
    for step, p in ((0, 0.1), (1, 0.8), (2, 0.1)):
        T[s, 0, (s + step) % n] += p
# Light sensor: o = 0 "light", o = 1 "dark". Reads dark 90% of the time in a tunnel, 20% outside.
O = np.zeros((1, n, 2))
for s in range(n):
    p_dark = 0.9 if s in tunnels else 0.2
    O[0, s] = [1 - p_dark, p_dark]



# 12 stops on a loop; stops 3, 4, 5, 9 and 11 are in tunnels.
n, tunnels = 12, [3, 4, 5, 9, 11]
# One action (1 = drive): advance 1 stop w.p. 0.8, stay w.p. 0.1, skip ahead 2 w.p. 0.1.
# mod1 wraps around the loop with 1-based numbering: after stop 12 comes stop 1.
T = zeros(n, 1, n)
for s in 1:n, (step, p) in ((0, 0.1), (1, 0.8), (2, 0.1))
    T[s, 1, mod1(s + step, n)] += p
end
# Light sensor: o = 1 "light", o = 2 "dark". Reads dark 90% of the time in a tunnel, 20% outside.
# O[a, s′, o]: the last axis is the observation, so each O[1, s, :] sums to 1.
O = zeros(1, n, 2)
for s in 1:n
    p_dark = s in tunnels ? 0.9 : 0.2
    O[1, s, :] = [1 - p_dark, p_dark]
end




Step 0: read “dark”. The prior is uniform. As in the “Try it” above, each tunnel stop gets \(0.9/5.9 = 0.153\) and each open stop gets \(0.2/5.9 = 0.034\).
Step 1: predict. The tram drives one step. Take stop 6, which is open and just past the tunnel run 3–5. It can be reached from stop 5 (advance 1, probability 0.8), from stop 6 (stay, 0.1), or from stop 4 (skip 2, 0.1):
\[
b_p(6) = 0.8\,(0.153) + 0.1\,(0.034) + 0.1\,(0.153) = 0.141
\]
So stop 6 is now fairly likely, because the tunnel belief shifted forward by one stop.
Step 1: correct. Suppose the sensor now reads “light”. Every open stop is multiplied by 0.8 and every tunnel stop by 0.1, and then the belief is normalized. Table 2 shows all 12 stops.

A Kalman step by hand
A kayaker paddles downriver about 2 m per step. The position after one step is \(s' = s + 2 + \text{noise}\), with noise variance \(\Sigma_s = 1\). A GPS reads the position with noise variance \(\Sigma_o = 4\). The starting belief is \(\mathcal{N}(0, 9)\). Everything is 1D, so every matrix is a number: \(T_s = T_a = O_s = 1\).

Predict (Equation 5): \(\mu_p = 0 + 2 = 2\) and \(\Sigma_p = 9 + 1 = 10\).
Gain: \(K = 10 / (10 + 4) = 0.714\). The prediction is shakier than the GPS, so the filter leans toward the GPS.
Correct (Equation 6) with a GPS reading \(o = 3.5\). The innovation is \(3.5 - 2 = 1.5\), so \(\mu_b = 2 + 0.714 \times 1.5 = 3.07\) and \(\Sigma_b = (1 - 0.714) \times 10 = 2.86\).

The new variance, 2.86, is smaller than both the prediction’s (10) and the GPS’s (4). Combining two independent sources of information beats either one alone.

PythonJulia


# Arrays are 1×1 so the matrix formulas work unchanged.
kayak = dict(Ts=np.eye(1), Ta=np.eye(1), Sigma_s=np.eye(1), Os=np.eye(1), Sigma_o=4 * np.eye(1))



# Fields in order: Ts, Ta, Σs, Os, Σo. In 1D they can be plain numbers.
kayak = LinearGaussianModel(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 4.0)

title: 19 · Beliefs
19 · Beliefs
text:
Algorithms & code
Each tab shows the complete implementation. The Julia code is exactly what produced this page’s figures.

Discrete state filter
This implements Equation 3, split into its predict and correct halves.

PythonJulia


# b[s] is the belief; T[s, a, s2] = T(s2 | s, a); O[a, s2, o] = O(o | a, s2).
def predict_discrete(b, T, a):
    return b @ T[:, a, :]    # sum over s of b(s) T(s2 | s, a)

def correct_discrete(b_pred, O, a, o):
    b_new = O[a, :, o] * b_pred
    total = b_new.sum()
    if total == 0:
        raise ValueError(f"observation {o} is impossible under this belief")
    return b_new / total

def update_discrete(b, T, O, a, o):
    return correct_discrete(predict_discrete(b, T, a), O, a, o)


# Discrete state filter (ADM §19.2).
# b[s] is the belief; T[s, a, s′] = T(s′ | s, a); O[a, s′, o] = O(o | a, s′).

# Predict: push the belief through the transition model.
# b_pred(s′) adds up every way of reaching s′: start in s (prob b[s]), then move (prob T[s, a, s′]).
predict_discrete(b, T, a) = [sum(T[s, a, s′] * b[s] for s in eachindex(b)) for s′ in axes(T, 3)]

# Correct: weight each state by how well it explains the observation, then normalize.
function correct_discrete(b_pred, O, a, o)
    b′ = [O[a, s′, o] * b_pred[s′] for s′ in eachindex(b_pred)]
    total = sum(b′)
    total > 0 || throw(ArgumentError("observation $o is impossible under this belief"))
    return b′ ./ total
end

update_discrete(b, T, O, a, o) = correct_discrete(predict_discrete(b, T, a), O, a, o)





Kalman filter
This implements Equation 5 and Equation 6.

PythonJulia


def kalman_predict(mu_b, Sigma_b, a, m):
    mu_p = m["Ts"] @ mu_b + m["Ta"] @ a
    Sigma_p = m["Ts"] @ Sigma_b @ m["Ts"].T + m["Sigma_s"]
    return mu_p, Sigma_p

def kalman_correct(mu_p, Sigma_p, o, m):
    Os = m["Os"]
    # (Os Sigma_p Os^T + Sigma_o) is the covariance of the predicted observation.
    # inv() is fine for these small matrices; np.linalg.solve is more stable for big ones.
    K = Sigma_p @ Os.T @ np.linalg.inv(Os @ Sigma_p @ Os.T + m["Sigma_o"])
    mu_b = mu_p + K @ (o - Os @ mu_p)       # move toward the observation by the innovation
    Sigma_b = Sigma_p - K @ Os @ Sigma_p    # the uncertainty always shrinks
    return mu_b, Sigma_b, K

def kalman_update(mu_b, Sigma_b, a, o, m):
    mu_p, Sigma_p = kalman_predict(mu_b, Sigma_b, a, m)
    mu_b, Sigma_b, _ = kalman_correct(mu_p, Sigma_p, o, m)
    return mu_b, Sigma_b


# Kalman filter (ADM §19.3) for a linear-Gaussian model:
#   T(s′ | s, a) = N(s′ | Ts s + Ta a, Σs)     O(o | s′) = N(o | Os s′, Σo)
# The belief is a Gaussian N(μb, Σb). Works with matrices, or with plain numbers in 1D.
struct LinearGaussianModel
    Ts; Ta; Σs; Os; Σo
end

# Predict: move the mean through the dynamics; the covariance grows by Σs.
function kalman_predict(μb, Σb, a, m::LinearGaussianModel)
    μp = m.Ts * μb + m.Ta * a
    Σp = m.Ts * Σb * m.Ts' + m.Σs
    return μp, Σp
end

# Correct: blend prediction and observation using the Kalman gain K.
function kalman_correct(μp, Σp, o, m::LinearGaussianModel)
    # A / B means A * inv(B), computed without forming the inverse.
    # (Os Σp Os' + Σo) is the covariance of the predicted observation.
    K = Σp * m.Os' / (m.Os * Σp * m.Os' + m.Σo)
    μb = μp + K * (o - m.Os * μp)     # move toward the observation by the innovation
    Σb = Σp - K * m.Os * Σp           # same as (I - K Os) Σp, but also works with plain numbers
    return μb, Σb, K
end

function kalman_update(μb, Σb, a, o, m::LinearGaussianModel)
    μp, Σp = kalman_predict(μb, Σb, a, m)
    μb′, Σb′, _ = kalman_correct(μp, Σp, o, m)
    return μb′, Σb′
end





Particle filter
This implements Equation 7. The model enters only through two functions you supply: one that samples a next state, and one that scores an observation.

PythonJulia


# sample_next(rng, s, a) draws s2 ~ T(. | s, a); likelihood(o, a, s2) returns O(o | a, s2).
def update_particles(particles, a, o, sample_next, likelihood, rng):
    moved = np.array([sample_next(rng, s, a) for s in particles])   # predict
    w = np.array([likelihood(o, a, s2) for s2 in moved])            # weight
    if w.sum() == 0:
        raise ValueError("every particle has zero weight")
    # Resample: draw N indices with probability proportional to weight. Heavy
    # particles get copied, light ones tend to vanish, and all weights reset to equal.
    keep = rng.choice(len(moved), size=len(moved), p=w / w.sum())
    return moved[keep]


# Particle filter (ADM §19.6). The belief is a vector of sampled states.
#   sample_next(rng, s, a) draws s′ ~ T(· | s, a)
#   likelihood(o, a, s′)   returns O(o | a, s′)

function update_particles(particles, a, o, sample_next, likelihood, rng)
    moved = [sample_next(rng, s, a) for s in particles]    # predict
    w = [likelihood(o, a, s′) for s′ in moved]             # weight
    sum(w) > 0 || error("every particle has zero weight: the observation is impossible under this belief")
    # Resample: draw N particle indices with probability proportional to weight.
    # Heavy particles get copied, light ones tend to vanish; all weights reset to equal.
    keep = rand(rng, Categorical(w ./ sum(w)), length(moved))
    return moved[keep]
end





Run them on the worked examples

PythonJulia


b0 = correct_discrete(np.full(n, 1 / n), O, 0, 1)             # uniform prior, read "dark"
b1 = update_discrete(b0, T, O, 0, 0)                           # drive, read "light"
mu_p, Sigma_p = kalman_predict(np.zeros(1), 9 * np.eye(1), np.full(1, 2.0), kayak)
mu_b, Sigma_b, K = kalman_correct(mu_p, Sigma_p, np.full(1, 3.5), kayak)
assert np.isclose(b0[2], 0.9 / 5.9) and b1.argmax() == 5       # stop 6 in 1-based numbering
assert np.allclose([K[0, 0], mu_b[0], Sigma_b[0, 0]], [10 / 14, 2 + 15 / 14, 20 / 7])



b0 = correct_discrete(fill(1 / n, n), O, 1, 2)                 # uniform prior, read "dark"
b1 = update_discrete(b0, T, O, 1, 1)                           # drive, read "light"
μp, Σp = kalman_predict(0.0, 9.0, 2.0, kayak)
μb, Σb, K = kalman_correct(μp, Σp, 3.5, kayak)






Tram: after 'dark' then 'light', the most likely stop is 6 (b = 0.23).
Kayak: K = 0.714, posterior mean = 3.071, variance = 2.857.








NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






mod1(s + step, n) wraps around a loop with 1-based numbering: it returns a value in 1:n, where mod would return 0:n-1.
struct LinearGaussianModel is like a Python dataclass. Fields without type annotations accept anything, which is why the same code works with numbers in 1D and with matrices in 2D.
Σp * m.Os' / (…): ' is the transpose, and A / B means \(A B^{-1}\), computed without forming the inverse.
rand(rng, Categorical(w), N) draws \(N\) indices with probabilities w, like rng.choice(len(w), N, p=w) in NumPy.
[f(x) for x in xs] comprehensions read just like Python’s. for s in 1:n, (step, p) in pairs is a nested loop on one line.






Results

Kalman filter: tracking a drifting buoy
A buoy drifts on the sea with a roughly constant velocity. Its state is position and velocity, \(s = (x, y, \dot x, \dot y)\), and GPS reports only the position, with 2 m of noise in each direction. The filter never measures velocity directly, yet it learns it from how the positions change. As the velocity estimate improves, each prediction gets better and the uncertainty shrinks (Figure 5). By step 30 the position’s standard deviation is 0.9 m, less than half the GPS noise.







Figure 5: Kalman filter tracking a buoy from noisy GPS fixes. Shaded ellipses are 95% regions of the position belief, drawn every third step; they start large and shrink as the filter learns the buoy’s velocity.






Particle filter: a range-only sensor
A rover can measure only its distance to a single beacon, with 0.5 m of noise, and it knows how it drove. One distance reading puts the rover anywhere on a ring around the beacon. No Gaussian can represent a ring, but a particle cloud can (Figure 6).
While the rover drives straight east, the readings can’t tell north of the beacon from south: both would produce the same sequence of distances. So the cloud splits into two mirror-image clusters. At step 7 the rover turns north. The mirror-image cluster now predicts distances that don’t match, so it dies out.







Figure 6: Particle filter with a range-only sensor. The star is the beacon, gray dots are particles, and the orange diamond is the true position. After one reading the belief is a ring. Driving east leaves two mirror-image clusters; the turn north at step 7 removes the wrong one.

title: 19 · Beliefs
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: a discrete update by hand. A cat is in one of three rooms, A, B or C. Your belief is \((0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\). Each minute the cat stays put with probability 0.6, or moves to the next room in the cycle A → B → C → A with probability 0.4. You then hear a meow, which you would hear with probability 0.9 if the cat is in A, 0.5 if in B, and 0.1 if in C. What is your new belief?






TipSolution





Predict. Each room can be reached by staying, or by moving from the previous room in the cycle:

\(b_p(A) = 0.6(0.5) + 0.4(0.2) = 0.38\) (stay in A, or move C → A)
\(b_p(B) = 0.6(0.3) + 0.4(0.5) = 0.38\)
\(b_p(C) = 0.6(0.2) + 0.4(0.3) = 0.24\)

Correct. Multiply by the meow likelihoods: \(0.9(0.38) = 0.342\), \(0.5(0.38) = 0.190\), \(0.1(0.24) = 0.024\). These sum to \(0.556\), so
\[
b' = (0.615,\ 0.342,\ 0.043).
\]
The prediction made A and B equally likely. The meow, much likelier near A, broke the tie.



Problem 2: the Kalman gain at the extremes. In 1D with \(O_s = 1\), the prediction is \(\mathcal{N}(10, 4)\) and the sensor variance is \(\Sigma_o = 1\). You observe \(o = 12\). Find \(K\), the new mean and the new variance. Then describe what happens as \(\Sigma_o \to 0\) and as \(\Sigma_o \to \infty\).






TipSolution





\(K = 4 / (4 + 1) = 0.8\), so the mean is \(10 + 0.8(12 - 10) = 11.6\) and the variance is \((1 - 0.8) \times 4 = 0.8\).

\(\Sigma_o \to 0\) (perfect sensor): \(K \to 1\), the mean jumps to \(o\), and the variance goes to 0. You believe the sensor completely.
\(\Sigma_o \to \infty\) (useless sensor): \(K \to 0\), and the mean and variance stay at the prediction. The observation is ignored.

The filter is always a compromise between these two extremes, and \(K\) says where on that line it sits.



Problem 3: steady state. Keep running the kayak’s filter from the worked example, with \(\Sigma_s = 1\) and \(\Sigma_o = 4\). The posterior variance settles to a fixed value \(\Sigma_\infty\). Find it.






TipSolution





At steady state, one predict-and-correct cycle returns the same variance. Predicting gives \(\Sigma_\infty + 1\). Correcting gives
\[
\Sigma_\infty = \frac{(\Sigma_\infty + 1) \cdot 4}{(\Sigma_\infty + 1) + 4}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\Sigma_\infty^2 + \Sigma_\infty - 4 = 0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\Sigma_\infty = \frac{\sqrt{17} - 1}{2} \approx 1.56.
\]
The steady-state gain is \(K_\infty = 2.56 / 6.56 \approx 0.39\), the value the kayak slider settles to at the true noise levels. The variance doesn’t depend on the observations at all, only on the noise levels. That’s a special property of linear-Gaussian models: you can compute a Kalman filter’s accuracy before collecting any data.



Problem 4: when particles fail. A robot on a 20 m track uses 500 particles spread evenly over the track. Its position sensor is very precise, with noise standard deviation 1 cm. About how many particles land within ±3 cm (three standard deviations) of the true position? What goes wrong, and what are two fixes?






TipSolution





The ±3 cm window covers \(0.06 / 20 = 0.3\%\) of the track, so about \(500 \times 0.003 = 1.5\) particles land in it. Nearly all the weight goes to one or two particles, and resampling fills the cloud with copies of them. This is particle degeneracy: the cloud has collapsed, so it can no longer represent uncertainty, and a single bad draw loses track of the robot.
Some fixes:

Use many more particles, which works but is costly.
Inflate the likelihood’s variance when computing weights. This throws away some precision to keep the cloud diverse.
Add random new particles each step (particle injection, ADM §19.7), so the filter can recover when it loses track.

title: 19 · Beliefs
text:
Recap

When the state is hidden, the agent acts on a belief: a probability distribution over states (Equation 1). Why it matters: this turns a problem with a hidden state into one with a fully known “state” (the belief), which is the key move for all of Part IV.
Every filter repeats predict (Equation 3‘s sum, where uncertainty grows) then correct (Bayes’ rule, where uncertainty shrinks). Why it matters: the same two moves appear in robot localization, object tracking, speech recognition and medical monitoring. Recognizing them makes the variants easy to learn.
The discrete filter stores the full table. It is exact, costs \(O(|\mathcal{S}|^2)\) per step, and suits small state spaces. Why it matters: it is the reference answer that the approximations try to match, and the belief update used by the exact planners in Ch 20.
The Kalman filter is exact for linear-Gaussian models, where the belief is just a mean and covariance (Equation 5, Equation 6). The gain \(K\) trades off trust in the prediction against trust in the sensor. Why it matters: it is cheap and optimal, which is why it runs inside nearly every navigation system. Its variants (EKF, UKF) stretch it to mild nonlinearity.
The particle filter represents any belief shape with samples (Equation 7), including rings and multiple peaks. It needs only a simulator, not a formula, for the dynamics. Why it matters: it is the workhorse when models are nonlinear or multimodal, and it is how online POMDP planners represent beliefs (Ch 22).

Which filter? Use the discrete filter for small, finite state spaces. Use the Kalman filter when the dynamics and sensor are (close to) linear with Gaussian noise. Use the particle filter when the belief can have several peaks or odd shapes, or when you can simulate the model but not write it down.
Common pitfalls

Forgetting to normalize after the correct step. The unnormalized numbers look plausible but aren’t probabilities.
An observation the model says is impossible. The normalizer becomes 0 and the belief is undefined. The code on this page raises an error instead of silently returning NaNs. Real systems avoid it with a small floor on every likelihood.
Assuming the wrong noise levels. Too little assumed noise makes a Kalman filter overconfident and slow to react. Try it in the kayak slider by making \(\Sigma_s\) tiny.
Too few particles for a sharp sensor. See Problem 4.

title: 17 · Model-Free Methods
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 16 learned a model of the world and planned on it. That works well when the state space is small enough to count transitions in. Model-free methods skip the model entirely: they learn the action value function \(Q(s, a)\), how good each action is in each state, straight from experience. There’s no transition table to fill in and no planning step, just a small correction to \(Q\) after every step. This is the core of practical reinforcement learning, from classic Q-learning to the deep Q-networks that learned to play Atari games. Chapter 18 turns to learning from an expert’s demonstrations instead of from rewards.
The question: how can an agent learn good action values from its own experience, one step at a time, without ever writing down the dynamics?
The short answer: nudge each estimate toward a one-step target. An average can be learned incrementally: move the estimate a fraction \(\alpha\) of the way toward each new sample. Q-learning uses the sample \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\), the reward plus the best value available next, and learns the optimal action values even while exploring. Sarsa uses the action actually taken next, and learns the values of the policy it follows, exploration included. Eligibility traces pass each update back along the recent path, so a distant reward is learned quickly. Reward shaping adds hints, safely if they take a potential-based form. With function approximation, the same updates become gradient steps on parameters, and experience replay reuses past experience to make them efficient and stable.
