Figure 1: Map of this chapter. One idea, incremental estimation toward a sampled target, gives Q-learning and Sarsa; the rest speed them up or scale them up.







The key ideas at a glance

Incremental estimation. To learn an average from a stream of samples, keep an estimate and move it a fraction \(\alpha\) of the way toward each new sample. With \(\alpha = 1/m\) it is exactly the running average. With a constant \(\alpha\) it tracks recent samples and never quite settles. The gap between the sample and the estimate is a temporal difference error.
Q-learning. The value of taking \(a\) in \(s\) is, on average, the reward plus the discounted value of the best action from wherever you land. Each experience \((s, a, r, s')\) gives one sample of that, \(r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\); move \(Q(s, a)\) toward it. Q-learning is off-policy: it learns the values of the greedy policy while behaving differently, for example exploring with ε-greedy.
Sarsa. Use the action \(a'\) actually taken next instead of the best one: the target is \(r + \gamma Q(s', a')\). Sarsa is on-policy: it learns the values of the policy it follows, exploration included. Near a cliff, that makes it cautious, because it knows it sometimes stumbles.
Eligibility traces. One-step updates pass news of a reward back only one state per visit. Traces keep a fading memory of recently visited state-action pairs, and apply each update to all of them in proportion. A reward found at the end of a long path is credited to the whole path at once.
Reward shaping. Sparse rewards make learning slow; adding intermediate rewards can speed it up, but can also change what is optimal. Shaping of the form \(F = \gamma\beta(s') - \beta(s)\), a difference of potentials, never changes the optimal policy.
Function approximation and experience replay. With too many states for a table, represent \(Q_\theta(s, a)\) with parameters and turn the update into a gradient step. Experience replay stores recent experience and learns from random batches of it, which reuses data and breaks up the correlations between consecutive steps.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Model-free learning
Learning values or policies directly, without estimating \(T\) and \(R\)


Learning rate \(\alpha\)
How far each update moves an estimate toward its new sample


Temporal difference (TD) error
Sampled target minus current estimate


Q-learning
TD learning of \(Q\) with target \(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\)


Sarsa
TD learning of \(Q\) with target \(r + \gamma Q(s', a')\), using the next action taken


On-policy / off-policy
Learning the values of the policy being followed / of a different policy


Eligibility trace \(N(s, a)\)
A decaying record of how recently and often a pair was visited


Reward shaping \(F(s, a, s')\)
Extra reward added during training to guide learning


Potential function \(\beta(s)\)
A score of states whose differences define safe shaping


Experience replay
Storing past transitions and learning from random batches of them








After this chapter you can

Estimate a mean incrementally, and choose a learning rate schedule.
Implement Q-learning and Sarsa, and explain when they learn different policies.
Speed up learning with eligibility traces, optimistic initialization, and potential-based reward shaping, and recognize shaping that changes the optimal policy.
Apply Q-learning with linear function approximation, and use experience replay.

title: 17 · Model-Free Methods
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



You’re learning how long each route to work takes, without a map.

Incremental averaging: every trip, you adjust your estimate for the route you took a little toward that day’s time.
Q-learning: you judge the first leg of a trip by the time it took plus the best time you know from where it left you, even if today you took a detour from there.
Sarsa: you judge it by what you actually did next, detours included. If you often take detours, Sarsa’s estimates include them.
Traces: when a trip turns out great, you credit the whole route, not just the last turn.
Shaping: a friend’s hint (“the closer to the river, the faster”) helps you learn, as long as it can’t lure you into driving in circles.




Moving averages
Bus waits average 8 minutes but vary a lot. With \(\alpha = 1/m\) the estimate is the exact running average; after 300 waits its typical error is 0.46 minutes. A constant \(\alpha = 0.3\) keeps chasing the latest waits, with an error of 3.3 minutes that never shrinks. A schedule that decays too fast, \(\alpha = 1/m^{1.5}\), stops learning before it has enough data: error 2.1 (Figure 4). See Equation 1.


One step of truth, then trust your estimates
Q-learning never sees the rules of Hex World. It moves each \(Q(s, a)\) toward the reward just received plus the best \(Q\) at the next tile. After 1,432 steps of ε-greedy experience, its greedy policy is worth 3.16 on average; after 30,000, 4.29 (the optimum is 4.53). See Equation 2.


Learning the policy you follow
On a towpath beside a canal, the shortest route runs right along the edge. Q-learning learns that route (9 steps), because it values the best next move. But while it still explores 10% of the time, it keeps stumbling into the water: it averaged -31.1 per episode late in training. Sarsa learns the value of its own stumbling policy, so it prefers a path that stays at least 2 rows from the water, 13 steps long, and averaged -20.6 (Figure 6). See Equation 3.


Pass the credit back
When Sarsa reaches a reward, only the last step’s value changes. Eligibility traces also update the steps before it, fading with distance. On Hex World, after 1,432 steps, Sarsa’s greedy policy was worth 3.48, and Sarsa(λ) with λ = 0.5 3.78 (Figure 5). See Equation 4.


Hints that don’t mislead
On the mountain trail of Chapter 16, Q-learning with ε-greedy exploration learned to climb in 0% of 20 runs. Adding a potential-based hint, “being higher is worth 1 per position”, it learned in 85%. A naive hint, “+5 for every step up”, backfires: the policy that is optimal for the hinted rewards walks down from the summit so it can earn the bonus again, and never enjoys the view. See Equation 5.


Scale up with parameters, reuse with replay
For the mountain car, a table won’t do: position and speed are continuous. Q-learning with a linear function of 49 Fourier features needed 178 steps per episode after 100 episodes. Replaying random batches of stored experience, it needed 123 (Figure 7). See Equation 6 and Equation 7.

title: 17 · Model-Free Methods
text:
Formalism

Incremental estimation of the mean
The average of \(m\) samples can be updated one sample at a time (ADM §17.1):

\[
\hat x_m = \hat x_{m-1} + \alpha(m)\big(x^{(m)} - \hat x_{m-1}\big),
\qquad
\sum_{m=1}^\infty \alpha(m) = \infty,\quad \sum_{m=1}^\infty \alpha(m)^2 < \infty
\tag{1}\]

In words. Move the estimate a fraction of the way toward each new sample. For the estimate to converge, the steps must shrink, but not too fast.
Term by term.

\(x^{(m)} - \hat x_{m-1}\) is the temporal difference error: how much the new sample surprised the old estimate.
With \(\alpha(m) = 1/m\), \(\hat x_m\) is exactly the sample mean.
The first condition keeps the steps large enough to reach the answer from any start. The second keeps them small enough for the noise to average out. \(1/m\) and \(1/m^{0.6}\) satisfy both. \(1/m^{1.5}\) fails the first: its steps shrink so fast that the estimate stops early. A constant \(\alpha\) fails the second: it keeps fluctuating, but it tracks a mean that drifts.
With a constant \(\alpha\), the estimate is a weighted average in which a sample \(k\) updates old has weight \(\alpha(1 - \alpha)^k\): an exponential moving average.

Why it holds. \(\hat x_m = \frac1m \sum_{i \le m} x^{(i)} = \frac1m\big(x^{(m)} + (m - 1)\hat x_{m-1}\big) = \hat x_{m-1} + \frac1m\big(x^{(m)} - \hat x_{m-1}\big)\). The conditions on \(\alpha\) are the Robbins–Monro conditions for stochastic approximation (H. Robbins and S. Monro, Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 1951).


Q-learning
The action value satisfies the Bellman equation \(Q(s, a) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \max_{a'} Q(s', a')\), which is an expectation over the next state. Replace the expectation with one sample, and use the incremental update (ADM §17.2; C. J. C. H. Watkins, 1989):

\[
Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\Big(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\Big)
\tag{2}\]

In words. After each step, move the value of what you just did toward what you got plus the best you believe you can do from where you landed.
Term by term.

\(r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\) is the target: a one-sample estimate of the right side of the Bellman optimality equation, using the current \(Q\) for the future.
The target doesn’t depend on which action the agent takes next, so the agent may explore freely while learning the greedy policy’s values. That is what off-policy means.
The max over noisy estimates tends to overestimate, a bias that double Q-learning reduces.
If every pair is tried infinitely often and \(\alpha\) meets the conditions of Equation 1 for each pair, \(Q\) converges to \(Q^*\).

Why it holds. In expectation over \((r, s')\) the target equals the Bellman backup of \(Q\), and that backup is a contraction (Chapter 7). So Q-learning is a noisy, sample-by-sample version of value iteration on \(Q\), and stochastic approximation theory handles the noise.


Sarsa
Sarsa uses the quintuple \((s, a, r, s', a')\), where \(a'\) is the action the agent actually takes next (ADM §17.3; G. A. Rummery and M. Niranjan, 1994):

\[
Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \alpha\Big(r + \gamma\, Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\Big)
\tag{3}\]

In words. Move the value of what you did toward what you got plus the value of what you actually do next.
Term by term.

The target uses \(Q(s', a')\) for the action chosen by the behavior policy (for example ε-greedy), not the maximum.
So Sarsa estimates \(Q^\pi\) for the policy \(\pi\) it follows, exploration included: it is on-policy.
If exploration is reduced over time, so that the policy becomes greedy in the limit, Sarsa too converges to \(Q^*\).

Why it holds. In expectation, the target is the Bellman expectation backup for the behavior policy, \(R + \gamma \sum_{s'} T \sum_{a'} \pi(a' \mid s') Q(s', a')\). Sarsa is a sampled version of policy evaluation for the policy it follows, and it improves as that policy improves.


Eligibility traces
Keep a trace \(N(s, a)\) for every pair. With the Sarsa TD error \(\delta = r + \gamma Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)\), each step does (ADM §17.4):

\[
N(s, a) \leftarrow N(s, a) + 1;
\qquad
Q(\tilde s, \tilde a) \leftarrow Q(\tilde s, \tilde a) + \alpha\,\delta\, N(\tilde s, \tilde a)\ \ \text{and}\ \ N(\tilde s, \tilde a) \leftarrow \gamma\lambda N(\tilde s, \tilde a)\ \ \text{for all } (\tilde s, \tilde a)
\tag{4}\]

In words. Every pair visited recently gets a share of the current surprise, a smaller share the longer ago it was visited.
Term by term.

\(N(\tilde s, \tilde a)\) counts visits, decaying by \(\gamma\lambda\) per step: a pair visited \(k\) steps ago has trace \((\gamma\lambda)^k\) (if visited once).
\(\lambda = 0\) is plain Sarsa. \(\lambda \to 1\) credits the whole episode, like a Monte Carlo return.
Traces are reset at the start of each episode.
With Q-learning, traces must be cut whenever an exploratory action is taken, or they credit the greedy policy with the explorer’s outcomes (Watkins’s \(Q(\lambda)\)).

Why it holds. Summing the trace-weighted updates over an episode gives approximately the update toward a λ-return, an average of \(n\)-step returns with weights \((1 - \lambda)\lambda^{n-1}\). It is the same blend of short and long lookaheads as generalized advantage estimation in Chapter 13 (R. S. Sutton, Machine Learning, 1988).


Reward shaping
During training, add \(F(s, a, s')\) to the reward. In general this changes the optimal policy, but not if \(F\) is a difference of potentials (ADM §17.5; A. Y. Ng, D. Harada and S. Russell, ICML, 1999):

\[
F(s, a, s') = \gamma\, \beta(s') - \beta(s)
\tag{5}\]

In words. Reward progress in a “potential” score, discounting the new state’s score as the future is discounted.
Term by term.

\(\beta(s)\) is any function of the state, for example minus the distance to a goal. On the trail we use \(\beta(s) = s\), the position.
Along any trajectory, the shaping terms telescope: \(\sum_t \gamma^t F_t = \gamma^T\beta(s_T) - \beta(s_0)\). So every policy’s value shifts by \(-\beta(s_0)\) (plus a vanishing term), which is the same for every policy starting from \(s_0\).
A bonus that isn’t of this form, like “+5 for every step up”, can be collected in loops, creating new optima that the designer never intended.

Why it holds. With shaping, the optimal action values become \(Q'^*(s, a) = Q^*(s, a) - \beta(s)\). Subtracting a function of the state alone doesn’t change which action is best. Ng, Harada and Russell also showed the converse: shaping that preserves the optimal policy for every MDP must have this form.


Action value function approximation
With a parameterized \(Q_\theta\), minimize \(\frac12\mathbb{E}[(Q^*(s, a) - Q_\theta(s, a))^2]\) by stochastic gradient descent, replacing the unknown \(Q^*(s, a)\) by the one-step target (ADM §17.6):

\[
\theta \leftarrow \theta + \alpha\Big(r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q_\theta(s', a') - Q_\theta(s, a)\Big)\nabla_\theta Q_\theta(s, a)
\tag{6}\]

In words. Move the parameters so that \(Q_\theta(s, a)\) comes closer to the target, in proportion to the TD error.
Term by term.

For a linear \(Q_\theta(s, a) = \theta_a^\top \phi(s)\), the gradient is the feature vector \(\phi(s)\) in the block of \(\theta\) for action \(a\).
The target also depends on \(\theta\), but the update treats it as fixed: a “semi-gradient”. That is one reason such methods can diverge. Scaling each step to a bounded norm (Chapter 12), as here, helps.
Every update changes \(Q_\theta\) everywhere the features overlap, which generalizes across states, but can also overwrite what was learned elsewhere (“catastrophic forgetting”).

Why it holds. With the true \(Q^*\) in place of the target, it is exactly stochastic gradient descent on the squared error: the gradient of \(\frac12(Q^* - Q_\theta)^2\) is \(-(Q^* - Q_\theta)\nabla_\theta Q_\theta\). The one-step target is Q-learning’s estimate of \(Q^*\).


Experience replay
Store the most recent transitions in a buffer. Periodically sample a random batch of \(m_{\text{grad}}\) of them and step along their average gradient (ADM §17.7; L.-J. Lin, 1992; V. Mnih et al., 2013):

\[
\theta \leftarrow \theta + \frac{\alpha}{m_{\text{grad}}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{\text{grad}}}\Big(r^{(i)} + \gamma\max_{a'} Q_\theta(s'^{(i)}, a') - Q_\theta(s^{(i)}, a^{(i)})\Big)\nabla_\theta Q_\theta(s^{(i)}, a^{(i)})
\tag{7}\]

In words. Learn from a random handful of past experiences at once, not just the latest one.
Term by term.

Each tuple \((s^{(i)}, a^{(i)}, r^{(i)}, s'^{(i)})\) comes from the buffer, which holds recent experience from older versions of the policy. Because Q-learning is off-policy, that’s fine.
Averaging over a batch reduces the variance of the step, and sampling at random breaks the correlation between consecutive steps.
Each experience is used many times, which improves data efficiency.
In this page’s code the step is taken every step (the book takes one every \(m\) steps, discarding the \(m\) oldest tuples), and scaled to norm at most 1.

Why it holds. It is minibatch stochastic gradient descent on the same objective as Equation 6. The data are drawn from the recent experience distribution instead of the current state alone.

title: 17 · Model-Free Methods
text:
Worked example

A running average by hand
Four bus waits: 12, 6, 9 and 3 minutes, starting from \(\hat x_0 = 0\).



Table 2: Incremental estimates of the mean wait.











Wait \(m\)

\(6 + 0.5(6 - 6) = 6\)

\(6 + 0.5(9 - 6) = 7.5\)

\(9 + \tfrac14(3 - 9) = 7.5\)
\(7.5 + 0.5(3 - 7.5) = 5.25\)






With \(\alpha = 1/m\), the last estimate is the exact average, \(30/4 = 7.5\). With \(\alpha = 0.5\), the most recent wait counts half, and the first one only \(0.5^4 = 1/16\). Starting from 0 also drags that estimate down.


Q-learning and Sarsa disagree by the canal
On the towpath, the agent walks east along the row right next to the canal (reward −1 per step, \(\gamma = 1\), \(\alpha = 0.5\)). Suppose its current estimates at the new cell are: \(Q(\text{east}) = -8\), the best, along the edge; \(Q(\text{north}) = -10\); \(Q(\text{south}) = -101\), into the canal. It currently estimates \(Q(\text{east})\) at its old cell as \(-10\).

Q-learning uses the best next value: target \(-1 + (-8) = -9\), so \(Q \leftarrow -10 + 0.5(-9 - (-10)) = -9.5\).
Sarsa uses the action actually taken next. If ε-greedy happened to pick “south” (probability \(0.1 / 4 = 0.025\)), the target is \(-1 + (-101) = -102\), and \(Q \leftarrow -10 + 0.5(-102 + 10) = -56\).

Sarsa’s value of standing by the water absorbs the occasional stumble; Q-learning’s doesn’t. Averaged over many visits, Sarsa learns that edge cells are worth less for an agent that explores. So it routes further from the water, where a stumble costs only a step.


A trace in three steps
Sarsa(λ) with \(\gamma = 0.9\), \(\lambda = 0.8\), so traces decay by 0.72 per step. The agent visits \((s_1, a_1)\), then \((s_2, a_2)\), then \((s_3, a_3)\), and at the third step receives a surprise \(\delta = 5\). The traces are then \(0.72^2 = 0.518\), \(0.72\) and \(1\). With \(\alpha = 0.1\) the three values change by \(0.1 \times 5 \times (0.518, 0.72, 1) = (0.26, 0.36, 0.5)\). Plain Sarsa would change only the last, by 0.5.

title: 17 · Model-Free Methods
17 · Model-Free Methods
text:
Algorithms & code

Tabular learners

PythonJulia


def incremental_mean(xs, alpha):
    """Running estimates x_hat_m = x_hat_{m-1} + alpha(m) (x_m - x_hat_{m-1})
    (eq. 17.5), starting from 0. alpha(m) = 1/m gives the sample mean."""
    est, out = 0.0, []
    for m, x in enumerate(xs, start=1):
        est += alpha(m) * (x - est)
        out.append(est)
    return np.array(out)

def epsilon_greedy(q, epsilon, rng):
    """A random action w.p. epsilon, else a greedy one (ties at random)."""
    if rng.random() < epsilon:
        return int(rng.integers(len(q)))
    return int(rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(q == q.max())))

class QLearning:
    """Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha (r + gamma max_a' Q(s', a') - Q(s, a))
    (eq. 17.10): off-policy, it learns the greedy policy's values while
    following an exploring one."""

    def __init__(self, n_states, n_actions, gamma, alpha, q0=0.0):
        self.Q = np.full((n_states, n_actions), float(q0))
        self.gamma, self.alpha = gamma, alpha

    def start(self):
        """Called at the start of each episode (nothing to reset here)."""

    def update(self, s, a, r, s2, a2):
        target = r + self.gamma * self.Q[s2].max()
        self.Q[s, a] += self.alpha * (target - self.Q[s, a])

class Sarsa(QLearning):
    """Q(s, a) <- Q(s, a) + alpha (r + gamma Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)) (eq. 17.11),
    with a' the action actually taken next: on-policy, it learns the
    values of the exploring policy itself."""

    def update(self, s, a, r, s2, a2):
        target = r + self.gamma * self.Q[s2, a2]
        self.Q[s, a] += self.alpha * (target - self.Q[s, a])

class SarsaLambda(QLearning):
    """Sarsa with eligibility traces (eqs. 17.12-17.14). N[s, a] is a
    decaying visit count; each TD error delta updates every pair in
    proportion to it, so reward flows back along the recent path."""

    def __init__(self, n_states, n_actions, gamma, alpha, lam, q0=0.0):
        super().__init__(n_states, n_actions, gamma, alpha, q0)
        self.lam = lam
        self.N = np.zeros_like(self.Q)

    def start(self):
        self.N[:] = 0.0                               # traces don't cross episodes

    def update(self, s, a, r, s2, a2):
        self.N[s, a] += 1
        delta = r + self.gamma * self.Q[s2, a2] - self.Q[s, a]
        self.Q += self.alpha * delta * self.N         # every pair, by its trace
        self.N *= self.gamma * self.lam

def run_tabular(env, learner, steps, s0, rng, epsilon=0.1, reset=None,
                shaping=None, on_step=None):
    """Learn on a DiscreteMDP env for `steps` steps with epsilon-greedy
    actions on learner.Q.

    reset(s2, rng) returns a new start state when an episode ends (and
    None otherwise). shaping(s, s2) is added to the reward the learner
    sees (not to the reward recorded). on_step(t, learner) is called after
    every step. Returns the rewards received.
    """
    n_s = env.R.shape[0]
    rewards = np.zeros(steps)
    s = s0
    learner.start()
    a = epsilon_greedy(learner.Q[s], epsilon, rng)
    for t in range(steps):
        s2 = rng.choice(n_s, p=env.T[s, a])
        r = env.R[s, a]
        a2 = epsilon_greedy(learner.Q[s2], epsilon, rng)   # Sarsa needs a'
        bonus = 0.0 if shaping is None else shaping(s, s2)
        learner.update(s, a, r + bonus, s2, a2)
        rewards[t] = r
        s, a = s2, a2
        start = None if reset is None else reset(s, rng)
        if start is not None:                              # new episode
            s = start
            learner.start()
            a = epsilon_greedy(learner.Q[s], epsilon, rng)
        if on_step is not None:
            on_step(t, learner)
    return rewards

def potential_shaping(beta, gamma):
    """F(s, s') = gamma beta(s') - beta(s) (eq. 17.15): shaping that
    provably leaves the optimal policy unchanged."""
    return lambda s, s2: gamma * beta[s2] - beta[s]


using ADM, Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra
import Distributions

hw = hex_world()                                  # states 1..27; the last one is the terminal
nS, nA, γ = size(hw.R, 1), size(hw.R, 2), hw.γ
decision = [s for s in 1:nS-1 if hw.T[s, 1, nS] < 1]   # tiles that don't end the episode

ε_greedy(q, ε, rng) = rand(rng) < ε ? rand(rng, 1:length(q)) : rand(rng, findall(==(maximum(q)), q))

# One learner = a function update!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′); N holds eligibility traces.
q_learning!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′; α = 0.1) = (Q[s, a] += α * (r + γ * maximum(Q[s′, :]) - Q[s, a]))
sarsa!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′; α = 0.1) = (Q[s, a] += α * (r + γ * Q[s′, a′] - Q[s, a]))
function sarsa_λ!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′; α = 0.1, λ = 0.5)
    N[s, a] += 1
    δ = r + γ * Q[s′, a′] - Q[s, a]
    Q .+= α * δ .* N                               # every pair, in proportion to its trace
    N .*= γ * λ
end

function learn(update!, steps, rng; ε = 0.1)
    Q, N = zeros(nS, nA), zeros(nS, nA)
    s = rand(rng, decision)
    a = ε_greedy(Q[s, :], ε, rng)
    for t in 1:steps
        s′ = rand(rng, Distributions.Categorical(hw.T[s, a, :]))
        a′ = ε_greedy(Q[s′, :], ε, rng)
        update!(Q, N, s, a, hw.R[s, a], s′, a′)
        s, a = s′, a′
        if s == nS                                 # terminal: start a new episode
            s = rand(rng, decision)
            N .= 0.0                               # traces don't cross episodes
            a = ε_greedy(Q[s, :], ε, rng)
        end
    end
    return Q
end

# True value of the greedy policy, by exact policy evaluation.
function greedy_value(Q)
    π = [argmax(Q[s, :]) for s in 1:nS]
    Tπ = [hw.T[s, π[s], s′] for s in 1:nS, s′ in 1:nS]
    Rπ = [hw.R[s, π[s]] for s in 1:nS]
    return mean(((I - γ * Tπ) \ Rπ)[decision])
end

for (name, f) in (("Q-learning", q_learning!), ("Sarsa", sarsa!), ("Sarsa(λ)", sarsa_λ!))
    v = mean(greedy_value(learn(f, 1000, MersenneTwister(seed))) for seed in 1:10)
    println(rpad(name, 12), "after 1,000 steps: ", round(v; digits = 2))
end
@assert mean(greedy_value(learn(q_learning!, 30_000, MersenneTwister(seed))) for seed in 1:5) > 4.0





Function approximation and replay

PythonJulia


class GradientQLearning:
    """Q-learning with a linear action value function
    Q_theta(s, a) = theta[a] @ features(s) (eq. 17.21), with the step's
    gradient scaled to norm at most 1.

    With replay > 0, experience tuples go into a buffer of that size and,
    every `every` steps, one step is taken along the average gradient of
    a random batch of `batch` tuples (eq. 17.22) instead.
    """

    def __init__(self, features, n_features, n_actions, gamma, alpha,
                 replay=0, batch=32, every=1):
        self.features, self.gamma, self.alpha = features, gamma, alpha
        self.theta = np.zeros((n_actions, n_features))
        self.buffer = deque(maxlen=replay) if replay else None
        self.batch, self.every, self.t = batch, every, 0

    def q(self, f):
        """Q values of all actions, for one feature vector f."""
        return self.theta @ f

    def update(self, f, a, r, f2, done, rng):
        self.t += 1
        if self.buffer is None:
            # One tuple: TD error times grad_theta Q = the features f.
            target = r + (0.0 if done else self.gamma * self.q(f2).max())
            g = np.zeros_like(self.theta)
            g[a] = (target - self.q(f)[a]) * f
        else:
            self.buffer.append((f, a, r, f2, done))
            if len(self.buffer) < self.batch or self.t % self.every:
                return
            pick = rng.integers(len(self.buffer), size=self.batch)
            F, A, R, F2, D = (np.array(x) for x in
                              zip(*(self.buffer[i] for i in pick)))
            # Batched targets: (batch, n_actions) values of the next states.
            targets = R + np.where(D, 0.0,
                                   self.gamma * (F2 @ self.theta.T).max(1))
            td = targets - (F * self.theta[A]).sum(axis=1)
            g = np.zeros_like(self.theta)
            np.add.at(g, A, td[:, None] * F)          # sum rows per action
            g /= self.batch
        self.theta += self.alpha * scale_gradient(g, 1.0)

def run_episode(learner, env_step, s0, rng, epsilon=0.0, max_steps=1000):
    """One episode of gradient Q-learning from state s0.

    env_step(s, a) returns (s2, r, done) for action index a. Actions are
    epsilon-greedy on the current Q. Returns the number of steps taken.
    """
    s, f = s0, learner.features(s0)
    for t in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        a = epsilon_greedy(learner.q(f), epsilon, rng)
        s2, r, done = env_step(s, a)
        f2 = learner.features(s2)
        learner.update(f, a, r, f2, done, rng)
        if done:
            return t
        s, f = s2, f2
    return max_steps


using ADM, Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra

# Fourier features over (position, speed): cos/sin up to order 3 per axis, all products.
lo, hi = [MOUNTAIN_CAR_X[1], MOUNTAIN_CAR_V[1]], [MOUNTAIN_CAR_X[2], MOUNTAIN_CAR_V[2]]
function φ(s)
    z = (s .- lo) ./ (hi .- lo)                    # 0 to 1 across each axis
    axis(t) = [0.5; [sin(2π * i * t) for i in 1:3]; [cos(2π * i * t) for i in 1:3]]
    return vec(axis(z[1]) * axis(z[2])')           # all pairwise products (outer product)
end
scaled(g) = norm(g) > 1 ? g ./ norm(g) : g        # cap the step's length at 1

# One episode of gradient Q-learning; θ has one row of weights per action.
# With a replay buffer, each step learns from a random batch of 32 stored tuples.
function episode!(θ, rng; α = 0.3, buffer = nothing, cap = 1000)
    s = [-0.6 + 0.2rand(rng), 0.0]
    for t in 1:cap
        f = φ(s)
        q = θ * f
        a = rand(rng, findall(==(maximum(q)), q))
        s′ = mountain_car_step(s, MOUNTAIN_CAR_ACTIONS[a])
        done = mountain_car_goal(s′)
        batch = buffer === nothing ? [(f, a, φ(s′), done)] : (push!(buffer, (f, a, φ(s′), done));
                                                               length(buffer) < 32 ? [] : rand(rng, buffer, 32))
        if !isempty(batch)
            g = zero(θ)
            for (fb, ab, f2, d) in batch           # TD error × features, in action ab's row
                target = -1 + (d ? 0.0 : maximum(θ * f2))
                g[ab, :] .+= (target - dot(θ[ab, :], fb)) .* fb
            end
            θ .+= α .* scaled(g ./ length(batch))
        end
        done && return t
        s = s′
    end
    return cap
end

nf = length(φ([0.0, 0.0]))
for (name, buf) in (("gradient Q-learning", () -> nothing), ("with replay", () -> Any[]))
    late = mean(begin
        rng, θ, b = MersenneTwister(seed), zeros(3, nf), buf()
        lengths = [episode!(θ, rng; buffer = b) for _ in 1:60]
        mean(lengths[41:60])
    end for seed in 1:3)
    println(rpad(name, 21), "steps per episode, episodes 41-60: ", round(late))
end









NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






q_learning!(Q, N, s, a, r, s′, a′; α = 0.1) = (...) is a one-line function; keyword arguments come after the ;. All three learners share one signature, so learn can take any of them.
Q .+= α * δ .* N updates the whole table in place, like Q += alpha * delta * N on NumPy arrays.
(I - γ * Tπ) \ Rπ solves the linear system for the policy’s values: I is the identity from LinearAlgebra, \ is NumPy’s np.linalg.solve.
vec(axis(z[1]) * axis(z[2])'): a column times a row (' transposes) gives the outer product, a 7 × 7 matrix of all products, flattened to 49 features.
(push!(...); expr) runs two expressions and returns the second, a compact way to append and then decide.
rand(rng, buffer, 32) draws 32 elements with replacement, like rng.choice(len(buffer), 32).






Run them

env = hex_world()
learner = mf.QLearning(len(env.R), 6, env.gamma, alpha=0.1)
terminal = len(env.R) - 1
decision = [s for s in range(terminal) if env.T[s, 0, terminal] < 1]
mf.run_tabular(env, learner, 30_000, decision[0], np.random.default_rng(0), epsilon=0.1,
               reset=lambda s, rng: rng.choice(decision) if s == terminal else None)
greedy_value = policy_evaluation_exact(env.T, env.R, env.gamma, learner.Q.argmax(axis=1))[decision].mean()

Results

Learning rates








Figure 4: Incremental estimates of a mean wait of 8 minutes. Left: one stream of 300 waits, for five learning rate schedules. Right: root-mean-square error over 500 streams (log scales).







Tabular learning on Hex World








Figure 5: The true value of the greedy policy (averaged over Hex World’s 21 decision tiles) against steps of ε-greedy experience (ε = 0.1, α = 0.1; 10 runs; log scale across).





After 1,432 steps, the greedy policies were worth 3.16 (Q-learning), 3.48 (Sarsa), 3.78 (Sarsa(λ), λ = 0.5), 3.65 (Sarsa(λ), λ = 0.9). After 30,000 steps: 4.29, 4.31, 4.31, 4.34. Traces help most early, when rewards have only been reached a few times. Later all four converge toward the optimum, 4.53. None gets there exactly, because a constant \(\alpha = 0.1\) keeps the estimates noisy (Equation 1).


On-policy versus off-policy








Figure 6: The towpath, 20 runs of 500 episodes each (α = 0.5, ε = 0.1). Left: return per episode while learning (average of 20 runs, smoothed over 10 episodes). Right: the greedy path each method learned most often.





In 100% of runs, Q-learning’s greedy path was the 9-step route along the edge, the optimal one. In 90% of runs, Sarsa’s was a 13-step route further from the water. Yet during training, Sarsa collected more reward: -20.6 per episode over the last 100 episodes, against -31.1 for Q-learning. Both are right about different questions. Q-learning answers “what is the best path if I stop exploring?” Sarsa answers “what is the best path given that I keep exploring?”

Plain ε-greedy exploration fails, as it did with a model in Chapter 16. Eligibility traces don’t help, because the problem is getting to the summit at all, not propagating its reward.
Optimistic initial values (\(Q_0 = 20\), the most any action could be worth) are the model-free version of R-MAX: every untried action looks excellent until tried, so the agent keeps climbing to find out.
Potential-based shaping with \(\beta(s) = s\) rewards each step up by about \(\gamma(s + 1) - s\) and charges the same for each step down. The optimal policy for the shaped rewards is climb everywhere (true value 8.13), the same as for the real rewards, and the hint makes it easy to find.
A naive “+5 per step up” bonus changes what is optimal. For the shaped rewards, the best policy at the summit is back: step back down, then climb again to collect the bonus. Its true value from the trailhead is 0.00, because the view is never enjoyed.



Function approximation on the mountain car








Figure 7: Q-learning with a linear action value function (49 Fourier features per action, α = 0.3, steps scaled to norm 1) on the mountain car, with and without experience replay (buffer 10,000, batches of 32). Left: steps per episode (average of 10 runs, smoothed over 5 episodes). Right: the learned value function max_a Q(s, a) from one replay run.





Over the first 10 episodes, plain gradient Q-learning needed 555 steps per episode and replay 374. Over the last 50: 178 and 123. From the ten standard starts of Chapter 10, the final greedy policies needed 156 and 119 steps on average. Replay does 32 gradient evaluations per step instead of 1, so it trades computation for data: it gets more out of every step of experience.
The value map is right where the car travels: lowest at rest in the valley, where the most steps remain. With every reward −1 and \(\gamma = 1\), no true value can be positive, yet the fit reaches 51 in corners of the state space the car never visits. A linear function is fitted only where there is data, and extrapolates freely elsewhere. That is harmless here, because the policy never goes there. There’s no explicit exploration here. Every step costs −1 and the values start at 0, so untried actions look better than tried ones, which is optimistic initialization again.

title: 17 · Model-Free Methods
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: incremental averages. Temperatures 20, 22, 18 and 24 arrive. Compute the incremental estimates with \(\alpha = 0.25\), starting from \(\hat x_0 = 20\). What weight does each sample have in the final estimate?






TipSolution





\(\hat x_1 = 20 + 0.25(20 - 20) = 20\); \(\hat x_2 = 20 + 0.25(2) = 20.5\); \(\hat x_3 = 20.5 + 0.25(-2.5) = 19.875\); \(\hat x_4 = 19.875 + 0.25(4.125) \approx 20.91\). Sample \(k\) steps before the last has weight \(0.25 \times 0.75^k\): 0.25 for 24, 0.1875 for 18, 0.141 for 22, 0.105 for 20. The initial value keeps weight \(0.75^4 \approx 0.32\). With a constant rate, the start is never fully forgotten, only exponentially discounted.



Problem 2: one Q-learning step. \(\gamma = 0.9\), \(\alpha = 0.2\). The agent takes \(a\) in \(s\), receives \(r = 2\) and lands in \(s'\) where \(Q(s', \cdot) = (1, 4, 3)\). The current \(Q(s, a) = 5\). What is the new \(Q(s, a)\)? What would Sarsa give if the next action were the third?






TipSolution





Q-learning: target \(2 + 0.9 \times 4 = 5.6\), TD error \(0.6\), new \(Q(s, a) = 5 + 0.2 \times 0.6 = 5.12\). Sarsa with \(a' = 3\): target \(2 + 0.9 \times 3 = 4.7\), TD error \(-0.3\), new \(Q = 5 - 0.06 = 4.94\). The two updates even go in opposite directions, because Sarsa’s target reflects the non-greedy action actually taken.



Problem 3: shaping that loops. A robot gets +1 when it reaches its charger. To help, a designer adds +0.5 every time the robot moves closer to the charger (by distance), and nothing for moving away. With \(\gamma = 0.9\), why can this change the optimal policy? Fix it with a potential.






TipSolution





Moving away costs nothing, and moving back earns 0.5, so a two-step loop earns 0.5 every other step, worth about \(0.5/(1 - 0.81) \approx 2.6\) discounted, forever. That beats reaching the charger for +1 once. Use \(\beta(s) = -0.5 \times \text{distance}(s)\) and \(F = \gamma\beta(s') - \beta(s)\). Moving closer by one then earns about \(+0.5\) and moving away costs about \(-0.5\), so any loop nets roughly nothing (exactly a discount term), and the optimal policy is unchanged.



Problem 4: how far back does a trace reach? With \(\gamma = 0.95\) and \(\lambda = 0.9\), after how many steps does a pair’s trace fall below 0.1 of its value when visited? What happens with \(\lambda = 0\)?






TipSolution





The trace decays by \(\gamma\lambda = 0.855\) per step. \(0.855^k < 0.1\) when \(k > \ln 0.1 / \ln 0.855 \approx 14.7\), so after 15 steps. A reward found 15 steps after a decision still moves that decision’s value by at least a tenth of the full amount. With \(\lambda = 0\), traces vanish after one step: plain Sarsa, which updates only the most recent pair.



Problem 5: why replay needs an off-policy learner. The replay buffer holds transitions collected by older, worse policies. Why is that acceptable for Q-learning but not for Sarsa?






TipSolution





Q-learning’s target, \(r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q(s', a')\), uses only \((s, a, r, s')\) and the current \(Q\). It doesn’t matter which policy chose \(a\), because the target is about the greedy policy. Sarsa’s target uses \(a'\), the action the behavior policy took next. With old transitions, that is an old policy’s action, so Sarsa would learn a mixture of outdated policies’ values rather than the current one’s. Replay pairs naturally with off-policy methods.

title: 17 · Model-Free Methods
text:
Recap

Model-free learning is incremental averaging toward sampled targets (Equation 1). Why it matters: the learning rate decides whether estimates converge (decaying) or track change (constant). That choice reappears in every method on this page and in deep reinforcement learning.
Q-learning learns optimal values while exploring (Equation 2). Why it matters: it needs no model and converges to \(Q^*\) under mild conditions. It is the ancestor of deep Q-networks.
Sarsa learns the values of the policy it actually follows (Equation 3). Why it matters: when exploration is risky, on-policy learning is safer while training. On the towpath, Sarsa collected -21 per episode against Q-learning’s -31, by choosing a longer, safer route.
Eligibility traces and shaping speed up learning; only potential-based shaping is safe (Equation 4, Equation 5). Why it matters: sparse rewards are the norm in real problems. A careless bonus on the trail created a policy that never reaches the summit: reward hacking in miniature.
Function approximation and experience replay scale Q-learning up (Equation 6, Equation 7). Why it matters: this pair, with a neural network in place of our linear features, is DQN. On the mountain car, replay cut the steps per episode from 178 to 123.

title: 17 · Model-Free Methods
text:
Cheat sheet & connections



Table 4: Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name).










Name
Formula

Equation 3

\(Q \mathrel{+}= \alpha\delta N\), \(N \leftarrow \gamma\lambda N\)

★ Potential-based shaping
\(F(s, a, s') = \gamma\beta(s') - \beta(s)\)
Equation 5


Gradient Q-learning
\(\theta \mathrel{+}= \alpha(r + \gamma\max_{a'}Q_\theta(s', a') - Q_\theta(s, a))\nabla_\theta Q_\theta(s, a)\)
Equation 6


Experience replay
average the gradient over a random batch from a buffer
Equation 7






Common pitfalls

A learning rate that decays too fast. \(\alpha = 1/m^{1.5}\) stops learning while the estimate is still wrong; constant rates never settle.
Judging Q-learning by its training rewards. It learns the greedy policy’s values, but earns the exploring policy’s rewards. Evaluate the greedy policy separately.
Reward bonuses that can be farmed. Any shaping reward that isn’t a difference of potentials can create loops that pay more than the real goal.
Eligibility traces with off-policy learning. Cut the traces when an exploratory action is taken, or the greedy policy is credited with the explorer’s luck.
Divergence with function approximation. Bootstrapping, off-policy learning and function approximation together can make the parameters blow up. Small or scaled steps, replay and target networks help.

Connections

Ch 15 · Exploration and Exploitation: ε-greedy and optimism, now at every state.
Ch 16 · Model-Based Methods: the same trail learned with a model; optimistic initial values mirror R-MAX.
Ch 8 · Approximate Value Functions: the Fourier features and the mountain car.
Ch 13 · Actor-Critic Methods: TD errors and λ-weighted returns (GAE) for training a critic.
Ch 18 · Imitation Learning: learning from demonstrations when rewards are hard to specify.
Appendix D · Neural Representations: the networks that replace linear features in deep Q-learning.

title: 15 · Exploration and Exploitation
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Parts I and II assumed we know the model: the transition probabilities and the rewards. Part III drops that assumption. The agent must learn from its own experience, and this is reinforcement learning. Learning by acting raises a problem that planning never had. Every action both earns reward and produces information, and the two goals pull apart. This chapter studies that tension in its purest form, a problem with a single state: the multi-armed bandit. Chapters 16 and 17 carry the same ideas to problems with many states.
The question: when you don’t know which option is best, how much should you try options that look worse, to find out whether they really are?
The short answer: keep a belief about each option, and let its uncertainty drive exploration. Trying options at random (undirected exploration) is simple but keeps wasting pulls forever unless it is switched off on a schedule. Favoring options that might be best (directed exploration: optimism, upper confidence bounds, posterior sampling) spends exploration where it can pay off. With a finite number of pulls, the Bayes-optimal strategy can be computed exactly by dynamic programming over beliefs. It shows that how much to explore depends on how many pulls remain.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. A belief about each arm feeds an exploration strategy; the strategies differ in how they use it.







The key ideas at a glance

Bandits. Several slot machines (“arms”) pay 1 with unknown probabilities \(\theta_a\) and 0 otherwise. You have \(h\) pulls. Every pull earns a reward and teaches you about one arm. A/B tests, clinical trials, and ad placement all have this shape.
A belief per arm. Starting from a uniform prior, \(w\) wins and \(\ell\) losses give a \(\text{Beta}(w + 1, \ell + 1)\) posterior for an arm’s payoff probability (Chapter 4). Its mean, \((w + 1)/(w + \ell + 2)\), is the probability that the next pull wins. Its width says how much you still don’t know.
Exploitation versus exploration. The greedy choice pulls the arm with the highest posterior mean. It can lock onto a worse arm after an unlucky start and never find out. Exploration means sometimes pulling an arm that looks worse, to learn about it.
Undirected exploration ignores what you know: ε-greedy pulls a random arm with probability \(\varepsilon\); explore-then-commit pulls randomly for \(k\) steps, then goes greedy. With a fixed \(\varepsilon\), the wasted pulls never stop, so the loss (regret) grows in proportion to the number of pulls.
Directed exploration uses the uncertainty. Optimism under uncertainty scores each arm by an optimistic estimate: a high quantile of its posterior, or UCB1’s mean-plus-bonus. Thompson sampling draws a plausible payoff for each arm from its posterior and pulls the best draw. Arms that could plausibly be best get tried; arms that are clearly worse stop being tried.
Bayes-optimal exploration. The counts are a belief state, and a finite-horizon bandit is an MDP over those beliefs. Dynamic programming solves it exactly, but the number of belief states grows like \(h^{2n}\). It shows that the right amount of exploration depends on the pulls remaining: with one pull left, greedy is optimal.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.

Posterior \(\text{Beta}(w_a + 1, \ell_a + 1)\)
The belief about \(\theta_a\) after those counts, from a uniform prior


\(\rho_a\)
Posterior probability that the next pull of arm \(a\) wins


Greedy arm
An arm with the highest \(\rho_a\)


Regret

Undirected / directed exploration

Acting as if each arm were as good as the data plausibly allow


Thompson (posterior) sampling
Pull the arm whose sampled payoff probability is highest


Bayes-optimal policy
The best possible strategy for a given prior and horizon








After this chapter you can

Maintain Beta beliefs for a Bernoulli bandit and compute each arm’s win probability.
Implement ε-greedy, explore-then-commit, softmax, quantile, UCB1 and Thompson sampling, and tune them.
Explain why fixed undirected exploration has regret that grows linearly, and why directed methods do much better over long horizons.
Compute the Bayes-optimal strategy for a small bandit by dynamic programming over belief states, and explain why it depends on the pulls remaining.

title: 15 · Exploration and Exploitation
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



You’ve moved to a new town with three coffee shops. One visit tells you little: even a good shop has off days.

Pure exploitation: after one great latte at shop A, you go there forever and never learn that shop C is better.
Pure exploration: you rotate among all three forever, drinking plenty of mediocre coffee long after you could have known better.
Sensible: try each a few times. Keep going back to a shop that might be the best, and stop visiting one that clearly isn’t.
How long you’ll live there matters. If you’re leaving next week, stick with what’s good now; if you’re staying ten years, explore more.



Our running example is a newsletter testing three headlines. Each reader who sees a headline clicks (1) or doesn’t (0). The click rates are A: 0.35, B: 0.50, C: 0.55, but the editor doesn’t know them. Every reader is one pull of a three-armed bandit.

Counting wins is a belief
After 5 clicks from 8 readers, a headline’s click rate could be anything from about 0.3 to 0.9. The Beta posterior summarizes exactly that: \(\text{Beta}(6, 4)\), with mean \(6/10 = 0.6\). After 50 clicks from 80 readers, the mean is similar, but the posterior is much narrower. The mean says which headline looks best; the width says how much to trust that (Figure 4). See Equation 2.


Greedy gets stuck
The greedy editor always shows the headline with the best mean so far. If the best headline has a couple of unlucky first readers, its mean drops. Greedy then never shows it again, and never finds out. Over 1,000 readers of randomly chosen three-headline tests, greedy loses 33.3 clicks on average compared with always showing the best headline. That loss is its regret. See Equation 1.


Random exploration never stops paying
ε-greedy shows a random headline to 10% of readers. That rescues it from getting stuck, but it keeps showing bad headlines to 10% of readers forever. Its regret after 1,000 readers is 32.4, still growing in a straight line. Decaying \(\varepsilon\) over time helps: 15.5. See Equation 3.


Be optimistic about what you haven’t seen
Score each headline by how good it could plausibly be: a high quantile of its posterior, or its mean plus a bonus that shrinks as it gets shown more. A rarely shown headline has a wide posterior and a high optimistic score, so it gets tried. A headline that has been shown often and is clearly worse has a narrow posterior and a low score, so it stops being tried. With the 99% quantile, regret after 1,000 readers is 7.0. See Equation 5 and Equation 6.


Sample a plausible world
Thompson sampling draws one plausible click rate for each headline from its posterior, and shows the headline with the highest draw. A headline is shown as often as it is likely to be the best. There is nothing to tune. Its regret is 10.0 after 1,000 readers (Figure 5). See Equation 7.


How long is the game?
With only a few readers left, exploring is pointless: there’s no time to use what you’d learn. Take headline A with 5 clicks from 8 readers and headline B with 1 click from 2. A looks better (mean 0.60 against 0.50). The Bayes-optimal choice is A while fewer than 19 readers remain, and B, to learn about it, when 19 or more remain. In short tests, even plain greedy is close to optimal. Over 10 pulls of a two-armed bandit it loses 0.66, against the optimum’s 0.64. See Equation 8.

title: 15 · Exploration and Exploitation
text:
Formalism

Bandit problems and regret
A Bernoulli bandit has \(n\) arms. Pulling arm \(a\) pays 1 with probability \(\theta_a\) and 0 otherwise, independently each time; we have \(h\) pulls (ADM §15.1). It is an \(h\)-step MDP with one state, \(n\) actions and an unknown reward function. How well a strategy does is measured against an oracle that knows the best arm:

\[
\text{regret}(h) = h\,\theta^* - \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^h r_t\Big] = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^h \big(\theta^* - \theta_{a_t}\big)\Big],
\qquad \theta^* = \max_a \theta_a
\tag{1}\]

In words. Regret is the reward you gave up by not knowing which arm is best: each pull of a worse arm costs the gap between its payoff probability and the best one.
Term by term.

\(a_t\) is the arm pulled at step \(t\), and \(r_t\) the reward it paid.
The second form counts only the gaps, which removes the luck of the individual wins and losses. The simulations on this page use it.
Bayes regret also averages over bandits drawn from a prior. With \(\theta_a \sim U(0, 1)\) for two arms, \(\mathbb{E}[\theta^*] = 2/3\), so the oracle earns \(2h/3\).

Why it holds. \(\mathbb{E}[r_t \mid a_t] = \theta_{a_t}\), so the expected total reward is \(\mathbb{E}[\sum_t \theta_{a_t}]\). Subtracting it from \(h\theta^*\) gives the sum of gaps.
This book’s chapter doesn’t define regret, but it is the standard yardstick for bandit algorithms (T. Lattimore and C. Szepesvári, Bandit Algorithms, 2020).


Bayesian model estimation
With a uniform prior \(\text{Beta}(1, 1)\), arm \(a\)’s posterior after \(w_a\) wins and \(\ell_a\) losses is \(\text{Beta}(w_a + 1, \ell_a + 1)\) (ADM §15.2; Chapter 4). The probability that its next pull wins is

\[
\rho_a = P(\text{win}_a \mid w_a, \ell_a) = \int_0^1 \theta\, \text{Beta}(\theta \mid w_a + 1, \ell_a + 1)\, d\theta = \frac{w_a + 1}{w_a + \ell_a + 2}
\tag{2}\]

In words. Add one imaginary win and one imaginary loss to the counts, then take the win fraction.
Term by term.

The integral averages the win probability \(\theta\) over everything we believe about it.
The mean of \(\text{Beta}(\alpha, \beta)\) is \(\alpha/(\alpha + \beta)\), which gives the fraction.
The “+1” and “+2” come from the prior. With no data, \(\rho_a = 1/2\). This is Laplace’s rule of succession.

Why it holds. By Bayes’ rule, the posterior is proportional to prior × likelihood \(= 1 \times \theta^{w}(1 - \theta)^{\ell}\), which is a \(\text{Beta}(w + 1, \ell + 1)\) density.
Updating is counting: a win adds 1 to \(w_a\), a loss adds 1 to \(\ell_a\).


Undirected exploration
ε-greedy pulls a uniformly random arm with probability \(\varepsilon\) and a greedy arm, \(\arg\max_a \rho_a\), otherwise. Explore-then-commit pulls random arms for the first \(k\) steps, then greedy ones (ADM §15.3). Because a constant \(\varepsilon\) explores as much at the end as at the start, it is often decayed:

\[
P(a) = \frac{\varepsilon_t}{n} + (1 - \varepsilon_t)\, \mathbb{1}\big[a = \arg\max_{a'} \rho_{a'}\big],
\qquad \varepsilon_{t+1} = \alpha\, \varepsilon_t
\tag{3}\]

In words. Usually take the best-looking arm; occasionally take any arm at random, and do that less and less as time goes on.
Term by term.

The random choice may land on the greedy arm too, so the greedy arm’s probability is \(1 - \varepsilon_t + \varepsilon_t/n\).
\(\alpha \in (0, 1)\), close to 1, is the decay factor.
Ties for the greedy arm are split evenly.

Why it holds. With a fixed \(\varepsilon\), a worse arm with gap \(\Delta\) is pulled at least \(\varepsilon/n\) of the time, so regret grows at least as \(h\,\varepsilon\,\bar\Delta\), where \(\bar\Delta\) is the average gap over the arms: linearly in \(h\). Decaying \(\varepsilon\) removes that floor.


Directed exploration
Softmax pulls arm \(a\) with probability proportional to \(\exp(\lambda \rho_a)\) (ADM §15.4):

\[
P(a) = \frac{\exp(\lambda \rho_a)}{\sum_{a'} \exp(\lambda \rho_{a'})}
\tag{4}\]

In words. Better-looking arms are pulled more often, but every arm keeps some chance, graded by how good it looks.
Term by term. The precision \(\lambda \ge 0\) runs from uniform (\(\lambda = 0\)) to greedy (\(\lambda \to \infty\)). Multiplying \(\lambda\) by a factor slightly above 1 after each pull reduces exploration over time. Softmax uses only the means, not the uncertainty: two arms with equal means get equal probability, however many times each was pulled.
Quantile exploration is optimistic in proportion to the uncertainty:

\[
a = \arg\max_a\ F^{-1}_{\text{Beta}(w_a + 1,\, \ell_a + 1)}(\alpha)
\tag{5}\]

In words. Score each arm by the payoff probability it exceeds only with probability \(1 - \alpha\): an optimistic but plausible value.
Term by term. \(F^{-1}(\alpha)\) is the posterior’s \(\alpha\)-quantile. For \(\alpha > 0.5\) it lies above the median, and further above for wider posteriors, so rarely tried arms get a boost. Larger \(\alpha\) means more optimism.
UCB1 uses a simple bonus instead of the exact quantile:

\[
a = \arg\max_a\ \rho_a + c \sqrt{\frac{\log N}{N(a)}}
\tag{6}\]

In words. Mean plus a bonus that is large for arms pulled rarely compared with the total.
Term by term.

\(N(a)\) counts arm \(a\)’s pulls and \(N = \sum_a N(a)\). Here we use the Beta pseudocounts, \(N(a) = w_a + \ell_a + 2\), so untried arms need no special case.
\(c \ge 0\) sets the strength of exploration; \(c = 0\) is greedy.
\(\log N\) grows slowly, so an arm that is not pulled sees its bonus creep up until it is tried again: every arm is revisited, but ever more rarely.

Why it holds. The bonus is the width of a confidence interval (from Hoeffding’s inequality) around the observed mean. An arm is pulled only if its interval reaches above the best arm’s mean, which a worse arm’s interval stops doing after about \(\log h / \Delta^2\) pulls. This keeps the regret growing only logarithmically (P. Auer et al., Machine Learning, 2002). UCB1 appeared as the exploration rule of Monte Carlo tree search in Chapter 9.
Thompson sampling (posterior sampling) needs no parameter:

\[
\tilde\theta_a \sim \text{Beta}(w_a + 1, \ell_a + 1),\quad a = \arg\max_a \tilde\theta_a;
\qquad
P(a) = P\big(\theta_a = \max_{a'} \theta_{a'} \mid \text{data}\big)
\tag{7}\]

In words. Imagine one plausible world by sampling each arm’s payoff probability from its posterior, then act optimally in that world. Each arm is pulled with exactly the probability that it is the best one.
Term by term.

Each \(\tilde\theta_a\) is one draw from arm \(a\)’s posterior.
The probability of choosing \(a\) is \(\int_0^1 p_a(x) \prod_{a' \neq a} F_{a'}(x)\, dx\): arm \(a\)’s draw is \(x\) and every other draw is below it. The code computes it this way for exact evaluation. The integrand is a polynomial, so Gauss–Legendre quadrature gets it exactly.

Why it holds. The second form follows from the first: since the draws are from the posterior, the arm with the largest draw is distributed like the arm that is actually best, given the data (W. R. Thompson, Biometrika, 1933).


Bayes-optimal exploration
The counts \((w_1, \ell_1, \ldots, w_n, \ell_n)\) are a belief state, and each pull moves it to one of two next beliefs. With \(r\) pulls remaining, the optimal expected reward satisfies (ADM §15.5)

\[
Q^*_r(w, \ell, a) = \rho_a\big(1 + U^*_{r-1}(\ldots, w_a + 1, \ell_a, \ldots)\big) + (1 - \rho_a)\, U^*_{r-1}(\ldots, w_a, \ell_a + 1, \ldots),
\qquad U^*_r = \max_a Q^*_r,\quad U^*_0 = 0
\tag{8}\]

In words. Pulling arm \(a\) wins with probability \(\rho_a\), earning 1 and a belief with one more win; otherwise it earns nothing and a belief with one more loss. Either way, continue optimally.
Term by term.

\(\rho_a\) from Equation 2 is both the chance of the reward and the chance of that belief update.
The first \(U^*\) holds the value after a win, the second after a loss. Their difference is what the pull teaches: the value of information.
With \(r = 1\), both \(U^*_0\) terms are 0, and \(Q^*_1 = \rho_a\): the last pull is greedy.
Backward induction from \(r = 0\) solves it exactly. With \(n\) arms and horizon \(h\) there are \(\binom{h + 2n}{2n}\) belief states, \(O(h^{2n})\): fine for two arms and dozens of pulls, hopeless for many arms. For the infinite-horizon discounted version, the Gittins index gives an optimal policy from a per-arm lookup table (J. C. Gittins, JRSS B, 1979).

Why it holds. It is the Bellman optimality equation (Chapter 7) for the MDP whose states are beliefs, whose transitions are Bayesian updates, and whose rewards are the expected payoffs. The same code, with the \(\max\) replaced by an average over a strategy’s action probabilities, evaluates any strategy exactly.


Exploration with many states
In a general MDP with unknown dynamics, the loop is the same (ADM §15.6). The agent chooses \(a\) from its current model and state, the environment returns \(s'\) and \(r\), the model is updated with \((s, a, r, s')\), and the agent moves on to \(s'\). What changes is the model: counts of transitions and rewards per state and action (Chapter 16), or action values learned directly (Chapter 17). The exploration strategies of this chapter apply per state, and so does the tension between exploring and exploiting. In addition, a state may have to be reached before it can be explored.

title: 15 · Exploration and Exploitation
text:
Worked example

Six strategies, one belief
Headline A has 5 clicks from 8 readers; headline B has 1 click from 2. What does each strategy do next?

Posteriors: A is \(\text{Beta}(6, 4)\) with \(\rho_A = 6/10 = 0.6\); B is \(\text{Beta}(2, 2)\) with \(\rho_B = 2/4 = 0.5\).
90% quantiles: A 0.790, B 0.804. B’s wider posterior reaches higher.
UCB1 scores with \(c = 0.5\), \(N = 10 + 4 = 14\) pseudocounts: A \(0.6 + 0.5\sqrt{\log 14 / 10} =\) 0.857, B \(0.5 + 0.5\sqrt{\log 14 / 4} =\) 0.906.

Thompson sampling pulls A with the posterior probability that A is the better headline.



The value of looking
What would the Bayes-optimal editor do? With one reader left, \(Q^*_1 = \rho\): 0.60 for A, 0.50 for B. Pick A. With two readers left, work out B by hand. After a click on B, B’s mean becomes \(3/5 = 0.6\), tied with A, so the last reader is worth 0.6. After no click, B’s mean drops to \(2/5\) and A is best at 0.6. So
\[Q^*_2(B) = 0.5\,(1 + 0.6) + 0.5\,(0.6) = 1.1,\]

title: 15 · Exploration and Exploitation
15 · Exploration and Exploitation
text:
Algorithms & code

Beliefs and strategies

PythonJulia


def posterior_mean(w: Array, l: Array) -> Array:
    """rho_a = P(win | w_a, l_a) = (w_a + 1) / (w_a + l_a + 2) (eq. 15.1)."""
    return (w + 1) / (w + l + 2)

class EpsilonGreedy(Strategy):
    """A random arm with probability eps (decayed as eps * decay^t,
    eq. 15.2), otherwise a greedy one."""

    def __init__(self, eps, decay=1.0):
        self.eps, self.decay = eps, decay

    def probs(self, w, l, t):
        eps = self.eps * self.decay**t
        n = w.shape[-1]
        return eps / n + (1 - eps) * argmax_split(posterior_mean(w, l))

class ExploreThenCommit(Strategy):
    """Uniformly random arms for the first k pulls, then greedy."""

    def __init__(self, k):
        self.k = k

    def probs(self, w, l, t):
        if t < self.k:
            return np.full(w.shape, 1 / w.shape[-1])
        return argmax_split(posterior_mean(w, l))

class Softmax(Strategy):
    """P(a) proportional to exp(lam * rho_a), with the precision growing
    as lam * factor^t."""

    def __init__(self, lam, factor=1.0):
        self.lam, self.factor = lam, factor

    def probs(self, w, l, t):
        z = self.lam * self.factor**t * posterior_mean(w, l)
        z = np.exp(z - z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))  # subtract max: no overflow
        return z / z.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

class Quantile(Strategy):
    """The arm whose posterior has the highest alpha-quantile: optimism
    under uncertainty when alpha > 0.5."""

    def __init__(self, alpha):
        self.alpha = alpha

    def probs(self, w, l, t):
        return argmax_split(stats.beta.ppf(self.alpha, w + 1, l + 1))

class UCB1(Strategy):
    """The arm maximizing rho_a + c sqrt(log N / N_a) (eq. 15.3), with
    the Beta pseudocounts N_a = w_a + l_a + 2 and N = sum_a N_a."""

    def __init__(self, c):
        self.c = c

    def probs(self, w, l, t):
        Na = w + l + 2
        N = Na.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
        return argmax_split(posterior_mean(w, l) + self.c * np.sqrt(np.log(N) / Na))

class Thompson(Strategy):
    """Posterior (Thompson) sampling: draw theta_a from each posterior and
    pull the arm with the largest draw. Its probabilities are
    P(a) = integral of pdf_a(x) prod_{b != a} cdf_b(x) dx."""

    def probs(self, w, l, t):
        x = _X[:, None]                                # (nodes, 1): broadcasts over arms
        pdf = stats.beta.pdf(x, w[..., None, :] + 1, l[..., None, :] + 1)
        cdf = stats.beta.cdf(x, w[..., None, :] + 1, l[..., None, :] + 1)
        # prod over the other arms = prod over all arms / own cdf, done in
        # logs; an arm's own cdf can be 0 only where its pdf is also 0.
        with np.errstate(divide="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
            others = np.exp(np.log(cdf).sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) - np.log(cdf))
        others = np.nan_to_num(others)
        p = (_WX[:, None] * pdf * others).sum(axis=-2)
        return p / p.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

    def act(self, w, l, t, rng):
        return rng.beta(w + 1, l + 1).argmax(axis=-1)

def simulate(theta: Array, strategy: Strategy, h: int, rng):
    """Run a strategy on bandits side by side for h pulls.

    theta has shape (m, n_arms): row i is bandit i's win probabilities.
    Returns (actions, rewards), each of shape (m, h), and the final
    counts (w, l).
    """
    m, n = theta.shape
    w, l = np.zeros((m, n), dtype=int), np.zeros((m, n), dtype=int)
    rows = np.arange(m)
    A, R = np.zeros((m, h), dtype=int), np.zeros((m, h), dtype=int)
    for t in range(h):
        a = strategy.act(w, l, t, rng)
        r = (rng.random(m) < theta[rows, a]).astype(int)
        w[rows, a] += r                      # paired indexing: one arm per row
        l[rows, a] += 1 - r
        A[:, t], R[:, t] = a, r
    return A, R, (w, l)


using Random, Statistics
import Distributions

# Belief: wins w[a] and losses l[a]; posterior Beta(w + 1, l + 1); ρ = (w + 1)/(w + l + 2).
posterior_mean(w, l) = (w .+ 1) ./ (w .+ l .+ 2)
greedy(w, l, rng) = rand(rng, findall(==(maximum(posterior_mean(w, l))), posterior_mean(w, l)))  # random tie-break

# Each strategy maps (w, l, t, rng) to an arm (1-based).
epsilon_greedy(ε; decay = 1.0) = (w, l, t, rng) -> rand(rng) < ε * decay^t ? rand(rng, eachindex(w)) : greedy(w, l, rng)
quantile_rule(α) = (w, l, t, rng) -> argmax([Distributions.quantile(Distributions.Beta(w[a] + 1, l[a] + 1), α) for a in eachindex(w)])
function ucb1(c)
    return function (w, l, t, rng)
        Na = w .+ l .+ 2                       # Beta pseudocounts per arm
        argmax(posterior_mean(w, l) .+ c .* sqrt.(log(sum(Na)) ./ Na))
    end
end
thompson() = (w, l, t, rng) -> argmax([rand(rng, Distributions.Beta(w[a] + 1, l[a] + 1)) for a in eachindex(w)])

# Run one strategy on one bandit for h pulls; return the regret (sum of gaps).
function run_bandit(θ, strategy, h, rng)
    w, l, regret = zeros(Int, length(θ)), zeros(Int, length(θ)), 0.0
    for t in 0:h-1
        a = strategy(w, l, t, rng)
        rand(rng) < θ[a] ? (w[a] += 1) : (l[a] += 1)   # update the belief by counting
        regret += maximum(θ) - θ[a]
    end
    return regret
end

# Average regret over 300 random three-armed bandits, 1,000 pulls each.
rng = MersenneTwister(0)
bandits = [rand(rng, 3) for _ in 1:300]
for (name, s) in (("ε-greedy 0.1", epsilon_greedy(0.1)), ("quantile 0.99", quantile_rule(0.99)),
                  ("UCB1 0.5", ucb1(0.5)), ("Thompson", thompson()))
    println(rpad(name, 14), round(mean(run_bandit(θ, s, 1000, rng) for θ in bandits); digits = 1))
end
@assert mean(run_bandit(θ, thompson(), 1000, rng) for θ in bandits) <
        mean(run_bandit(θ, epsilon_greedy(0.1), 1000, rng) for θ in bandits)





Exact evaluation and the Bayes-optimal strategy

PythonJulia


def evaluate(strategy, n: int, h: int, optimal=False):
    """Exact expected total reward of a strategy over h pulls, averaged
    over bandits drawn from the uniform prior (theta_a ~ U(0, 1)).

    Backward induction over belief states (the counts), one layer of
    total t at a time. With optimal=True it computes the Bayes-optimal
    value instead (eq. 15.6), ignoring `strategy`. Returns the value at
    the start (all counts 0).
    """
    V = np.zeros((h + 1,) * (2 * n))           # V[w_1, l_1, ..., w_n, l_n]
    for t in range(h - 1, -1, -1):
        S = _layer(t, n)                       # (m, 2n)
        w, l = S[:, 0::2], S[:, 1::2]          # wins and losses, (m, n)
        rho = posterior_mean(w, l)
        Q = np.zeros(w.shape)
        for a in range(n):
            win, loss = S.copy(), S.copy()
            win[:, 2 * a] += 1
            loss[:, 2 * a + 1] += 1
            # V[tuple(columns)] looks up one value per row of counts.
            Q[:, a] = (rho[:, a] * (1 + V[tuple(win.T)])
                       + (1 - rho[:, a]) * V[tuple(loss.T)])
        if optimal:
            V[tuple(S.T)] = Q.max(axis=1)
        else:
            V[tuple(S.T)] = (strategy.probs(w, l, t) * Q).sum(axis=1)
    return V[(0,) * (2 * n)]

def optimal_values(r_max: int, k_max: int):
    """Bayes-optimal values of a two-armed bandit with r pulls left.

    Returns U with U[r, w1, l1, w2, l2] for r = 0..r_max and counts up
    to k_max (states whose next counts would exceed k_max are left 0,
    so keep k_max >= largest total count + r). Q values for the two arms
    are then q_values(U, r, ...). Recursion (eq. 15.6):
      U_r(c) = max_a [rho_a (1 + U_{r-1}(c + win_a))
                      + (1 - rho_a) U_{r-1}(c + loss_a)].
    """
    K = k_max + 1
    U = np.zeros((r_max + 1, K, K, K, K))
    for r in range(1, r_max + 1):
        U[r, :-1, :-1, :-1, :-1] = np.max(q_values(U, r), axis=0)
    return U

def q_values(U, r):
    """Q[a, w1, l1, w2, l2] with r pulls left, for counts below k_max
    (the arrays are one shorter on each axis than U's count axes)."""
    K = U.shape[1]
    w1, l1, w2, l2 = np.meshgrid(*(np.arange(K - 1),) * 4, indexing="ij")
    prev = U[r - 1]
    rho1, rho2 = posterior_mean(w1, l1), posterior_mean(w2, l2)
    # Slicing shifts one count by 1: prev[1:, :-1, :-1, :-1] is
    # U_{r-1} at (w1 + 1, l1, w2, l2), a win for arm 1.
    q1 = rho1 * (1 + prev[1:, :-1, :-1, :-1]) + (1 - rho1) * prev[:-1, 1:, :-1, :-1]
    q2 = rho2 * (1 + prev[:-1, :-1, 1:, :-1]) + (1 - rho2) * prev[:-1, :-1, :-1, 1:]
    return np.array([q1, q2])


# Bayes-optimal value of a two-armed Bernoulli bandit with r pulls left, from counts
# c = (w1, l1, w2, l2), by memoized recursion on eq. 15.6.
const memo = Dict{Tuple{Int,NTuple{4,Int}},Float64}()

function U(r, c)
    r == 0 && return 0.0
    get!(memo, (r, c)) do                     # compute once per (r, c), then reuse
        best = -Inf
        for a in 1:2
            w, l = c[2a-1], c[2a]
            ρ = (w + 1) / (w + l + 2)
            win = Base.setindex(c, w + 1, 2a - 1)    # a copy of the tuple with one count changed
            loss = Base.setindex(c, l + 1, 2a)
            best = max(best, ρ * (1 + U(r - 1, win)) + (1 - ρ) * U(r - 1, loss))
        end
        best
    end
end

@assert U(1, (5, 3, 1, 1)) ≈ 0.6                  # last pull: greedy
@assert U(2, (0, 0, 0, 0)) ≈ 13 / 12
v30 = U(30, (0, 0, 0, 0))
println("Bayes-optimal reward over 30 pulls: ", round(v30; digits = 4), " (oracle 20)")
@assert 18.9 < v30 < 18.95









NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






(w, l, t, rng) -> ... is an anonymous function, like lambda. epsilon_greedy(0.1) returns one, so strategies are just functions.
findall(==(m), v) returns the indices where v equals m; ==(m) is a one-argument function (a curried comparison).
get!(memo, key) do ... end returns the cached value, or runs the block, stores its result and returns it. It is the idiom for memoization, like functools.cache.
Base.setindex(c, v, i) (no !) returns a new tuple with element i replaced: tuples are immutable, like Python’s.
c[2a-1]: 2a means 2 * a, and indices start at 1, so arm a’s wins and losses sit at positions 2a - 1 and 2a.






Run them

theta = np.random.default_rng(3).random((500, 3))       # 500 random three-armed bandits
A, R, (w, l) = simulate(theta, Thompson(), 1000, np.random.default_rng(4))
regret_ts = (theta.max(axis=1)[:, None] - np.take_along_axis(theta, A, axis=1)).sum(axis=1)

exact_greedy = evaluate(Greedy(), n=2, h=30)             # exact, over the uniform prior
exact_best = evaluate(None, n=2, h=30, optimal=True)



Thompson sampling, 1,000 pulls: regret 10.1 ± 0.4
30 pulls, two arms (exact): greedy 18.778, Bayes-optimal 18.920, oracle 20




Results

Beliefs narrow where the pulls go








Figure 4: One run of Thompson sampling on the headline test: each headline’s Beta posterior after 10, 50 and 300 readers, with the true click rates dotted. Counts give clicks / readers.





This run shows how luck steers exploration:

Early luck gets a headline shown. The weakest headline, A, drew 6 clicks from its first 10 readers, so its posterior looked promising, and Thompson sampling kept showing it until its mean came down.
Early bad luck gets a headline neglected. B, truly better than A, started with 0 clicks from 2 readers. After 300 readers it has been shown only 32 times, and its posterior is the widest. It is not written off, though: its wide posterior still gives it a chance of being sampled highest.
The best headline wins most readers. C was shown to 205 of the 300, and its posterior has narrowed around its true click rate.

A single run is noisy; Figure 5 averages over thousands.


Undirected versus directed exploration over 1,000 pulls








Figure 5: Average regret against the number of pulls, over 2,000 three-armed bandits with click rates drawn uniformly from 0 to 1. Left: greedy and undirected strategies. Right: directed strategies, with greedy repeated for reference.










Table 4: Average regret over 2,000 random three-armed bandits (± one standard error).





Strategy

Greedy and fixed ε-greedy grow almost in a straight line. Greedy gets stuck on a worse arm in a fraction of the bandits and pays the gap on every pull. ε-greedy pays for its random pulls forever.
Decaying ε and explore-then-commit stop exploring. They do better, but depend on a schedule that must be tuned to the horizon.
The directed strategies end between 7.0 and 10.0. Their curves bend over: each additional pull costs less and less, consistent with the logarithmic growth that theory predicts for UCB1 and Thompson sampling. Thompson sampling needed no tuning; the others’ parameters were picked from a handful of values.



Tuning, exactly, at short horizons








Figure 6: Exact Bayes regret of each tunable strategy against its parameter, for two-armed bandits with uniformly random payoff probabilities, over 10 pulls (light) and 50 pulls (dark). Horizontal lines: Bayes-optimal (solid), greedy (dashed) and Thompson sampling (dotted), each at the matching horizon.





These values are exact: dynamic programming over belief states averages over every possible bandit and every possible sequence of wins and losses, with no simulation noise.

Short horizons favor exploiting. Over 10 pulls, greedy’s regret is 0.661, against the Bayes-optimal 0.645. Over 50 pulls, greedy’s regret is 1.67 against 1.34.
Thompson sampling explores too much for short games: 0.962 over 10 pulls and 2.13 over 50, worse than greedy at both. It doesn’t know how many pulls are left, and learning is worth less when little time remains to use it. Over 1,000 pulls it was far better than greedy (10.0 against 33.3), though the tuned directed strategies did better still.
The best parameters over 50 pulls were ε = 0.0 (plain greedy), k = 2, λ = 30, α = 0.9 and c = 0.25. The best tuned strategy reached 1.36, close to the optimum.



The Bayes-optimal strategy explores more when more time remains








Figure 7: The Bayes-optimal choice when headline B has not been shown yet, for each count of A’s clicks (up) and non-clicks (across), with 1, 5 and 25 readers left. Blue: show B, to explore; orange: show A. The dashed line is where A’s posterior mean is 0.5, B’s prior mean: greedy explores only below it.





With one reader left, the optimal editor is greedy: it shows untried B only when A’s mean is below 0.5. With 25 readers left, it tries B even when A’s mean is as high as 0.73, as long as A’s record is short. Learning that B is excellent would pay for many readers. When A has a long, good record, trying B is not worth it at any horizon shown.

title: 15 · Exploration and Exploitation
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: a posterior by hand. A drug trial arm has 7 successes and 2 failures. With a uniform prior, what is the posterior, and the probability that the next patient succeeds? What would it be after 70 successes and 20 failures?






TipSolution





The posterior is \(\text{Beta}(8, 3)\), so \(\rho = 8/11 \approx 0.727\). After 70 and 20 it is \(\text{Beta}(71, 21)\) with \(\rho = 71/92 \approx 0.772\). The means approach the observed rate, 7/9 ≈ 0.778, as the prior’s two pseudo-observations matter less. The posterior’s standard deviation falls from about 0.13 to about 0.044, roughly by \(\sqrt{10}\).



Problem 2: ε-greedy’s choice. Four arms, one of which is greedy, and \(\varepsilon = 0.2\). What is the probability of pulling the greedy arm, and each other arm? If the greedy arm is best and the others’ gaps are 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3, what is the expected regret per pull, and over 10,000 pulls?






TipSolution





Greedy arm: \(0.8 + 0.2/4 = 0.85\); each other arm: \(0.2/4 = 0.05\). Expected regret per pull: \(0.05 \times (0.1 + 0.2 + 0.3) = 0.03\). Over 10,000 pulls that is 300, even if the best arm was identified long ago. That is the linear regret of fixed undirected exploration.



Problem 3: UCB1 bonuses. Two arms: arm 1 has 40 wins and 20 losses, arm 2 has 3 wins and 3 losses. With \(c = 1\) and Beta pseudocounts, which arm does UCB1 pull? And with \(c = 0.3\)?






TipSolution





\(\rho_1 = 41/62 \approx 0.661\) and \(\rho_2 = 4/8 = 0.5\). The pseudocounts are \(N(1) = 62\), \(N(2) = 8\) and \(N = 70\), with \(\log 70 \approx 4.25\). With \(c = 1\) the bonuses are \(\sqrt{4.25/62} \approx 0.262\) and \(\sqrt{4.25/8} \approx 0.729\), for scores 0.923 and 1.229: pull arm 2. With \(c = 0.3\) the bonuses are 0.079 and 0.219, for scores 0.740 and 0.719: pull arm 1. The exploration constant decides whether 8 observations are few enough to justify another look.



Problem 4: the last pull is greedy. Show from Equation 8 that with one pull left, the Bayes-optimal policy is greedy.






TipSolution





With \(r = 1\), both continuation values are \(U^*_0 = 0\), so \(Q^*_1(a) = \rho_a(1 + 0) + (1 - \rho_a) \cdot 0 = \rho_a\). Maximizing \(Q^*_1\) is maximizing \(\rho_a\): the greedy choice. Information has value only if there is a future in which to use it. With more pulls left, \(U^*_{r-1}\) after a win and after a loss can differ by more than the immediate reward, and that difference is what makes exploring worthwhile.



Problem 5: how big is the belief space? How many belief states (count vectors with total at most \(h\)) does exact dynamic programming visit for 2 arms and 50 pulls? For 3 arms and 100 pulls?






TipSolution





Count vectors of length \(2n\) with total at most \(h\) number \(\binom{h + 2n}{2n}\) (stars and bars, with one extra “slack” count). Two arms, 50 pulls: \(\binom{54}{4} = 316{,}251\), which this page solves in well under a second. Three arms, 100 pulls: \(\binom{106}{6} \approx 1.6 \times 10^9\), too many for a simple table. This is why index policies (Gittins) and heuristics (UCB1, Thompson sampling) matter.

title: 15 · Exploration and Exploitation
text:
Recap

A bandit’s belief is a set of win and loss counts; the Beta posterior turns them into a win probability and an uncertainty (Equation 2). Why it matters: every strategy on this page is a rule for turning that belief into an action. Beliefs return as the central object of Part IV.
Regret measures the price of not knowing the best arm (Equation 1). Why it matters: it separates strategies whose losses stop growing from those that keep paying forever. Over 1,000 pulls, fixed ε-greedy lost 32 against Thompson sampling’s 10.
Undirected exploration ignores the belief; fixed ε never stops paying (Equation 3). Why it matters: it is simple and widely used in reinforcement learning (Chapter 17), but needs a decay schedule matched to the horizon.
Directed exploration spends pulls where the uncertainty could matter (Equation 4, Equation 5, Equation 6, Equation 7). Why it matters: optimism and posterior sampling keep regret growing only slowly, and UCB-style bonuses reappear in tree search (Chapter 9) and in model-based reinforcement learning (Chapter 16).
The Bayes-optimal strategy comes from dynamic programming over beliefs, and explores more when more time remains (Equation 8). Why it matters: it is the gold standard for short horizons, and a preview of planning over belief states in POMDPs (Chapters 20–22). Its cost, \(O(h^{2n})\) states, is why heuristics matter.

Common pitfalls

Judging a strategy on one run. Bandit outcomes are very noisy; compare average regret over many bandits and seeds, as in Figure 5.
Tuning for the wrong horizon. Over 50 pulls the best ε was 0 (plain greedy) and the best UCB1 constant 0.25; over 1,000 pulls greedy was among the worst, and c = 0.5 beat c = 0.2. Thompson sampling explores too much for very short games.
Softmax on means only. Two arms with equal means get equal probability, whether one was pulled once or a thousand times; it has no notion of uncertainty.
Forgetting ties. At the start, all arms tie; always taking the first one biases the results. Break ties at random.
Nonstationary arms. If payoff probabilities drift over time, old counts mislead. Discount old observations or use a sliding window.
