title: 13 · Actor-Critic Methods
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapters 10–12 improved a policy directly, and Chapter 11 showed that the noise in the gradient comes mostly from judging actions by noisy returns. The fix hinted at there was a baseline, and the best baseline is the value function, which is exactly what Chapters 7–9 computed. Actor-critic methods bring the two families together. The actor is a parameterized policy, improved by policy gradients. The critic is a parameterized value function, learned at the same time, that tells the actor how much better or worse than expected each action turned out. This is the design behind most modern deep reinforcement learning (A2C, PPO with a value head, DDPG, SAC) and behind AlphaGo Zero, which trained a policy and a value network from Monte Carlo tree search. The model-free versions of these ideas return in Chapter 17.
The question: how can a learned value function make policy gradients less noisy, and what does it cost?
The short answer: use the critic to estimate each action’s advantage from a few observed rewards plus the critic’s opinion of where you ended up. Leaning on the critic cuts variance but adds bias whenever the critic is wrong. Generalized advantage estimation chooses a point on that trade-off with one number, \(\lambda\). For continuous actions, the critic’s slope with respect to the action points the way to a better action, and that gives the deterministic policy gradient. A search procedure can also play the critic’s teacher: Monte Carlo tree search produces better action choices and values than the current networks, and the networks learn to imitate it.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. An actor (policy) and a critic (value function) learn together; the variants differ in what the critic estimates and how it’s trained.







The key ideas at a glance

Two learners. The actor \(\pi_\theta\) is improved by policy gradients, as in Chapter 11. The critic \(U_\phi\) is fitted by regression, as in Chapter 8, to the returns the actor actually earns. Each needs the other: the actor needs the critic’s advantages, and the critic needs the actor’s data.
Advantages from one step. The temporal difference (TD) residual \(\delta = r + \gamma U_\phi(s') - U_\phi(s)\) compares what happened in one step, plus the critic’s view of the next state, with the critic’s view of the current state. It estimates the advantage \(A(s, a)\) with far less noise than a whole trajectory’s return. But if the critic is wrong, it is biased.
Generalized advantage estimation (GAE). Look ahead \(k\) steps of real rewards before trusting the critic, and average over all \(k\) with weights \(\lambda^{k-1}\). \(\lambda = 0\) is the TD residual (low variance, biased by the critic). \(\lambda = 1\) is the Monte Carlo return minus the critic’s value (no critic bias, high variance). The best \(\lambda\) depends on how good the critic is.
Deterministic policy gradient. For a deterministic policy with continuous actions, learn an action-value critic \(Q_\phi(s, a)\) and move the policy’s action in the direction that raises \(Q_\phi\), the slope \(\partial Q/\partial a\). Exploration must be added separately, for example with noise on the actions.
Tree search as the teacher. Run Monte Carlo tree search (Chapter 9), guided by the current policy (which actions to try) and critic (how good a new leaf is). The search’s visit counts are a better policy than the actor, and its action values a better value than the critic. Train both to match the search. This is the AlphaGo Zero idea.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning

Critic \(U_\phi(s)\), \(Q_\phi(s, a)\)
A learned value function that judges the actor’s actions

\(r + \gamma U(s') - U(s)\): one step of reality versus the critic’s expectation


\(k\)-step advantage \(\hat A^{(k)}\)
\(k\) real rewards, then the critic’s value, minus the critic’s value now


Generalized advantage estimation (GAE)
An exponentially weighted average of \(k\)-step advantages, with weight \(\lambda\)


Deterministic policy gradient (DPG)
Follow the critic’s slope in the action through the policy’s Jacobian


Exploration noise \(\sigma\)
Random noise added to a deterministic policy’s actions


Guided tree search
MCTS using the policy as a prior and the critic to value leaves


\(\pi_{\text{MCTS}}\), \(U_{\text{MCTS}}\)
Policy and value read off a finished search: visit shares, best action value








After this chapter you can

Compute TD residuals and generalized advantages from a trajectory and a critic.
Explain the bias–variance trade-off controlled by \(\lambda\), and how critic quality moves the best \(\lambda\).
Write the actor and critic updates, and diagnose an unstable critic.
Derive the deterministic policy gradient for a given policy and critic.
Describe how tree search can train a policy and a value function, as in AlphaGo Zero.

title: 13 · Actor-Critic Methods
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



A student (the actor) and a tutor (the critic) are learning together. After each practice problem, the tutor predicted how well the student would do, and the student then did better or worse.

Better than predicted: “whatever you did there, do more of it.” That surprise is the advantage.
The tutor improves too, by comparing predictions with actual scores.
A tutor who is still learning gives biased feedback. So early on, the student should wait for the final result (Monte Carlo). Later, the tutor’s quick verdict after each step (the TD residual) is both faster and steadier.
\(\lambda\) sets how long the student waits before trusting the tutor.



We use the simple regulator again: keep \(s\) near 0, with the stochastic policy \(a \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_1 s, \theta_2^2)\). The critic is \(U_\phi(s) = \phi_1 + \phi_2 s^2\): a constant plus a bowl, the natural shape for “how far from 0 are you”. At \(\theta = (-0.5, 0.5)\), a least-squares fit to many rollouts gives \(\phi \approx\) (-1.05, -1.13).

One step of reality, then trust the critic
A trajectory’s return is noisy because it adds up ten random steps. The TD residual adds up only one, the reward just received, and asks the critic about the rest. With the fitted critic and 10 rollouts, the gradient estimate built from TD residuals (\(\lambda = 0\)) has a spread of 2.9, against 4.9 using the full returns (\(\lambda = 1\)). See Equation 1.


When the critic is wrong
A critic that knows nothing (\(\phi = 0\), “every state is worth 0”) makes the TD residual just the immediate reward. That’s badly biased: the gradient estimate misses the truth by 7.3 on average, even with infinite data. With \(\lambda = 1\) the critic cancels out almost entirely, and the bias drops to 0.81, at the price of more noise. With this poor critic, the best compromise is \(\lambda =\) 0.75. With the fitted critic, it’s \(\lambda =\) 0.0 (Figure 4). See Equation 4.


Nudge the action uphill
A deterministic policy picks one action per state, so there’s no probability to push up or down. Instead, ask the critic: at this state, would a slightly larger action be better? If \(Q_\phi(s, a)\) increases with \(a\), move the policy so it outputs a larger action there. See Equation 5.


Learn from a better player
Tree search, guided by the current policy and critic, plays better than either one alone. It explores and looks ahead. So use it as a teacher: make the policy imitate the search’s choices and the critic match the search’s values. The next search starts from a better policy and critic and plays better still. On Hex World, starting from a uniformly random policy, this loop learns the optimal action on most tiles within a few dozen rounds (Figure 7). See Equation 7.

title: 13 · Actor-Critic Methods
text:
Formalism

Actor-critic
The actor follows the advantage form of the policy gradient (Chapter 11), with the advantage estimated from the critic by the TD residual (ADM §13.1):

\[
\delta_k = r_k + \gamma\, U_\phi(s_{k+1}) - U_\phi(s_k),
\qquad
\nabla U(\theta) \approx \mathbb{E}_\tau\left[\sum_{k} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_k \mid s_k)\, \gamma^{k-1} \delta_k\right]
\tag{1}\]

In words. Judge each action by one step of what actually happened (the reward, plus the critic’s value of where you landed), compared with what the critic expected beforehand.
Term by term.

If \(U_\phi\) equals the true value \(U^{\pi_\theta}\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\delta_k \mid s_k, a_k] = Q(s_k, a_k) - U(s_k) = A(s_k, a_k)\) exactly.
Otherwise \(\delta_k\) is a biased estimate of the advantage, with much less variance than the return, because it involves only one random reward.

The critic is trained to predict returns:

\[
\ell(\phi) = \tfrac12\, \mathbb{E}_s\Big[\big(U_\phi(s) - U^{\pi_\theta}(s)\big)^2\Big],
\qquad
\nabla \ell(\phi) \approx \mathbb{E}_\tau\left[\sum_k \big(U_\phi(s_k) - r_{\text{to-go}}^{(k)}\big)\, \nabla_\phi U_\phi(s_k)\right]
\tag{2}\]

In words. Pull the critic’s predictions toward the rewards-to-go that were actually observed.
Term by term. The unknown \(U^{\pi_\theta}(s_k)\) is replaced by its sample, the reward-to-go. For a linear critic, \(\nabla_\phi U_\phi(s)\) is the feature vector. The actor steps along its gradient and the critic against its own. Because each chases the other, step sizes matter. A common trick is to update the policy more often than the critic.


Generalized advantage estimation
Between one step and the whole trajectory lie \(k\)-step estimates (ADM §13.2; J. Schulman et al., ICLR, 2016):

\[
\hat A^{(k)}(s, a) = \sum_{\ell=1}^{k} \gamma^{\ell-1} r_\ell + \gamma^k U_\phi(s_{k+1}) - U_\phi(s)
= \sum_{\ell=1}^{k} \gamma^{\ell-1} \delta_\ell
\tag{3}\]

In words. Use \(k\) real rewards, then the critic’s opinion of where you are after \(k\) steps.
Term by term. The two forms are equal because the critic’s intermediate values cancel in the sum (it telescopes). Larger \(k\) means less reliance on the critic (less bias) and more random rewards (more variance).

\[
\hat A^{\text{GAE}}(s, a) = (1 - \lambda)\big(\hat A^{(1)} + \lambda \hat A^{(2)} + \lambda^2 \hat A^{(3)} + \cdots\big)
= \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (\gamma\lambda)^{k-1}\, \delta_k
\tag{4}\]

In words. Average all the \(k\)-step estimates, with geometrically decreasing weights. That turns out to equal a discounted sum of TD residuals with discount \(\gamma\lambda\).
Term by term.

\(\lambda = 0\) gives \(\delta_1\), the TD residual.
\(\lambda = 1\) gives \(\sum_k \gamma^{k-1} r_k - U_\phi(s)\): the Monte Carlo return with the critic as a baseline.
With a finite horizon, the sum stops at the last step. It’s computed with a backward sweep, \(\hat A_k = \delta_k + \gamma\lambda \hat A_{k+1}\).

Why it holds. Substitute Equation 3 into the weighted average. The residual \(\delta_k\) appears in every \(\hat A^{(j)}\) with \(j \ge k\), with total weight \((1-\lambda)\gamma^{k-1}(\lambda^{k-1} + \lambda^k + \cdots) = (\gamma\lambda)^{k-1}\).


Deterministic policy gradient
For a deterministic policy \(a = \pi_\theta(s)\) with continuous actions and a critic \(Q_\phi(s, a)\) (ADM §13.3; D. Silver et al., ICML, 2014):

\[
\nabla U(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{s}\Big[\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s)\ \nabla_a Q_\phi(s, a)\big|_{a = \pi_\theta(s)}\Big]
\tag{5}\]

In words. At each visited state, find which way to change the action to raise \(Q\), and change the parameters so the policy’s action moves that way.
Term by term.

\(\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s)\) is the policy’s Jacobian: how each parameter moves each action component.
\(\nabla_a Q_\phi\) is the critic’s slope in the action.
The critic is trained on the squared TD residual \(\tfrac12\big(r + \gamma Q_\phi(s', \pi_\theta(s')) - Q_\phi(s, a)\big)^2\).
Data comes from the policy plus exploration noise \(\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\), since a deterministic policy never tries anything else. Replay buffers and target networks (Chapter 17) stabilize it in practice.

Why it holds. \(U(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_s[Q(s, \pi_\theta(s))]\) with the state distribution held fixed. Differentiating through the action by the chain rule gives the product of the Jacobian and the action gradient.


Actor-critic with Monte Carlo tree search
Guide the tree search with the current policy as a prior and the critic as the leaf evaluation (ADM §13.4; D. Silver et al., Nature, 2017). Inside the tree, choose

\[
a = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_a\ Q(s, a) + c\, \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\, \frac{\sqrt{N(s)}}{1 + N(s, a)}
\tag{6}\]

In words. Like UCB1 (Chapter 9), but the exploration bonus is shared out in proportion to the policy’s own preferences, so promising actions are tried first.
Term by term. \(N(s, a)\) and \(Q(s, a)\) are the search’s visit counts and value estimates, and \(N(s) = \sum_a N(s, a)\). There’s no logarithm, and the 1 in the denominator follows AlphaGo Zero. After the search, the targets are:

\[
\pi_{\text{MCTS}}(a \mid s) \propto N(s, a)^\eta,
\qquad U_{\text{MCTS}}(s) = \max_a Q(s, a),
\qquad \ell(\theta) = -\sum_a \pi_{\text{MCTS}}(a \mid s) \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)
\tag{7}\]

In words. The policy should imitate how often the search chose each action (cross entropy), and the critic should match the search’s best value.
Term by term.

\(\eta\) sharpens (\(\eta > 1\)) or flattens the visit distribution.
For a softmax policy with one logit per action, \(\nabla_{\text{logits}}\,\ell = \pi_\theta - \pi_{\text{MCTS}}\), so each step moves the policy’s probabilities toward the search’s.
On this page, only the search’s root is trained, the state it spent all its simulations on, as AlphaGo Zero does. The book trains on every state the search visited. Here those deeper, rarely visited states gave noisy targets that stalled learning.

Worked example

TD residuals and GAE by hand
A 4-step episode with \(\gamma = 0.9\). The critic’s values at the visited states are \(U = (-2, -1.5, -1, -0.5)\), and the rewards are \(r = (-0.5, -0.3, -0.4, -0.2)\). The TD residuals exist for the first three steps:

With \(\lambda = 0.5\), so \(\gamma\lambda = 0.45\), the backward sweep gives:

\(\hat A_3 = 0.15\);
\(\hat A_2 = 0.30 + 0.45 \times 0.15 = 0.3675\);
\(\hat A_1 = 0.15 + 0.45 \times 0.3675 = 0.3154\).

With \(\lambda = 0\), the advantages are just the \(\delta\)s. All are positive: each step went slightly better than the critic predicted.


The deterministic policy gradient by hand
Policy \(a = \theta s\) with critic \(Q_\phi(s, a) = \phi_1 + \phi_2 s^2 + \phi_3 (s + a)^2\). Then \(\nabla_\theta \pi = s\) and \(\partial Q/\partial a = 2\phi_3(s + a)\). At \(\theta = 0\) with \(\phi_3 = -1\), a state \(s = 0.5\) contributes \(0.5 \times 2(-1)(0.5 + 0) = -0.5\): make \(\theta\) more negative, so the policy pushes back against \(s\). A state \(s = -0.2\) contributes \((-0.2) \times 2(-1)(-0.2) = -0.08\), the same direction. The critic says the next state \(s + a\) should be near 0, and the policy learns to cancel \(s\).

title: 13 · Actor-Critic Methods
13 · Actor-Critic Methods
text:
Algorithms & code

Advantages from the critic

PythonJulia


def td_residuals(values: Array, R: Array, gamma: float) -> Array:
    """delta_k = r_k + gamma U(s_(k+1)) - U(s_k) for steps 1..d-1, given
    the critic's values U(s_k) at every visited state (shape (m, d)).
    The last step has no next state in the data, so it is dropped."""
    return R[:, :-1] + gamma * values[:, 1:] - values[:, :-1]

def generalized_advantages(delta: Array, gamma: float,
                           lam: float) -> Array:
    """A_k = sum over l >= 0 of (gamma lam)^l delta_(k+l), computed by a
    backward sweep. lam = 0 gives the TD residual; lam = 1 the discounted
    reward-to-go minus the critic's value (Monte Carlo)."""
    adv = np.zeros_like(delta)
    running = np.zeros(delta.shape[0])
    for k in range(delta.shape[1] - 1, -1, -1):
        running = delta[:, k] + gamma * lam * running
        adv[:, k] = running
    return adv

def actor_gradient(scores: Array, adv: Array, gamma: float) -> Array:
    """Policy gradient sum_k grad log pi_k gamma^(k-1) A_k, averaged over
    trajectories. scores has shape (m, d', n) and adv (m, d')."""
    discount = gamma ** np.arange(adv.shape[1])
    return (scores * (discount * adv)[..., None]).sum(axis=1).mean(axis=0)

def critic_gradient(values: Array, features: Array, R: Array,
                    gamma: float) -> Array:
    """Gradient of (1/2) sum_k (U(s_k) - rtg_k)^2, averaged over
    trajectories: pull the critic toward the observed reward-to-go.
    features has shape (m, d, p): the gradient of U with respect to phi."""
    err = values - rewards_to_go(R, gamma)          # (m, d)
    return (err[..., None] * features).sum(axis=1).mean(axis=0)

def actor_critic_step(theta, phi, S, A, R, gamma, grad_logp, features,
                      lam: float, alpha_theta: float, alpha_phi: float):
    """One update of both: ascend the actor's policy gradient (with
    generalized advantages from the critic), scaled to length at most 1
    as in Chapter 12, and descend the critic's squared error. Returns the
    new (theta, phi)."""
    feats = features(S)                             # (m, d, p)
    values = feats @ phi                            # U_phi at every state
    adv = generalized_advantages(td_residuals(values, R, gamma), gamma,
                                 lam)
    scores = grad_logp(theta, S[:, :-1], A[:, :-1])
    grad = scale_gradient(actor_gradient(scores, adv, gamma), 1.0)
    theta = theta + alpha_theta * grad
    phi = phi - alpha_phi * critic_gradient(values, feats, R, gamma)
    return theta, phi


using ADM, LinearAlgebra, Random, Statistics

γ = REGULATOR_γ
# δ_k = r_k + γ U(s_{k+1}) - U(s_k) for steps 1..d-1; `values` holds U at every visited state.
td_residuals(values, R) = R[:, 1:end-1] .+ γ .* values[:, 2:end] .- values[:, 1:end-1]

# GAE by a backward sweep: A_k = δ_k + γλ A_{k+1}.
function generalized_advantages(δ, λ)
    A, running = zero(δ), zeros(size(δ, 1))
    for k in size(δ, 2):-1:1
        running = δ[:, k] .+ γ * λ .* running
        A[:, k] = running
    end
    return A
end

# The worked example: U = (-2, -1.5, -1, -0.5), r = (-0.5, -0.3, -0.4, -0.2).
δ = td_residuals([-2.0 -1.5 -1.0 -0.5], [-0.5 -0.3 -0.4 -0.2])
@assert δ ≈ [0.15 0.30 0.15]
@assert generalized_advantages(δ, 0.5) ≈ [0.15 + 0.45 * 0.3675 0.3675 0.15]





Deterministic policy gradient

PythonJulia


def deterministic_policy_gradients(theta, phi, S, A, R, gamma, policy,
                                   dpolicy, q_features, dq_da):
    """Deterministic policy gradient with a critic Q_phi(s, a) =
    phi . q_features(s, a). The actor ascends
      sum_k gamma^(k-1) (d pi / d theta)(s_k) (dQ/da)(s_k, pi(s_k)),
    and the critic descends the squared TD residual
      delta = r + gamma Q(s', pi(s')) - Q(s, a).
    Returns (actor gradient, critic gradient)."""
    discount = gamma ** np.arange(S.shape[1])
    pi_s = policy(theta, S)
    actor = (discount[None, :, None] * dpolicy(theta, S)
             * dq_da(phi, S, pi_s)[..., None]).sum(axis=1).mean(axis=0)
    f_sa = q_features(S[:, :-1], A[:, :-1])         # Q at taken actions
    s2 = S[:, 1:]
    f_next = q_features(s2, policy(theta, s2))       # Q at the next state
    delta = R[:, :-1] + gamma * f_next @ phi - f_sa @ phi
    critic = (delta[..., None] * (gamma * f_next - f_sa)).sum(axis=1)
    return actor, critic.mean(axis=0)


# Regulator: policy a = θ s, critic Q(s, a) = φ₁ + φ₂ s² + φ₃ (s + a)².
q_features(s, a) = [1.0, s^2, (s + a)^2]
dq_da(φ, s, a) = 2φ[3] * (s + a)

# Actor: Σ_k γ^(k-1) s_k ∂Q/∂a(s_k, θ s_k). Critic: TD residual times the gradient of the residual.
function dpg_gradients(θ, φ, S, A, R)
    m, d = size(S)
    actor = sum(γ^(k - 1) * S[i, k] * dq_da(φ, S[i, k], θ * S[i, k]) for i in 1:m, k in 1:d) / m
    critic = zeros(3)
    for i in 1:m, k in 1:d-1
        f, f′ = q_features(S[i, k], A[i, k]), q_features(S[i, k+1], θ * S[i, k+1])
        δ = R[i, k] + γ * (f′ ⋅ φ) - f ⋅ φ
        critic .+= δ .* (γ .* f′ .- f) ./ m
    end
    return actor, critic
end

function sample(θ, σ, m, rng)                         # the gain policy plus N(0, σ²) exploration
    S, A, R = zeros(m, 10), zeros(m, 10), zeros(m, 10)
    for i in 1:m
        s = REGULATOR_START[1] + REGULATOR_START[2] * randn(rng)
        for k in 1:10
            a = θ * s + σ * randn(rng)
            S[i, k], A[i, k] = s, a
            s, R[i, k] = regulator_step(s, a, rng)
        end
    end
    return S, A, R
end

rng, θ, φ = MersenneTwister(4), 0.0, [0.0, -1.0, -1.0]
for _ in 1:50
    S, A, R = sample(θ, 0.5, 5, rng)
    ga, gc = dpg_gradients(θ, φ, S, A, R)
    global θ += 0.05 * ga / max(1, abs(ga))           # capped actor step
    global φ -= 0.05 .* gc
end
@assert isapprox(θ, -1.0; atol = 0.15)





Tree search as the teacher

PythonJulia


def softmax(logits: Array) -> Array:
    z = np.exp(logits - logits.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return z / z.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

class GuidedTreeSearch:
    """Monte Carlo tree search guided by a policy prior and a value
    estimate (as in AlphaGo Zero): actions are chosen by
      Q(s, a) + c pi(a | s) sqrt(N(s)) / (1 + N(s, a)),
    and new leaves are valued by the critic instead of a rollout."""

    def __init__(self, mdp, prior: Array, values: Array, d: int, c: float,
                 rng):
        self.mdp, self.prior, self.values = mdp, prior, values
        self.d, self.c, self.rng = d, c, rng
        self.N, self.Q = {}, {}

    def simulate(self, s: int, d: int) -> float:
        if d <= 0:
            return self.values[s]
        if s not in self.N:                 # new leaf: the critic values it
            n_actions = self.mdp.T.shape[1]
            self.N[s], self.Q[s] = np.zeros(n_actions), np.zeros(n_actions)
            return self.values[s]
        N, Q = self.N[s], self.Q[s]
        score = Q + self.c * self.prior[s] * np.sqrt(N.sum()) / (1 + N)
        a = int(np.argmax(score))
        s2, r = sample_step(self.mdp, s, a, self.rng)
        q = r + self.mdp.gamma * self.simulate(s2, d - 1)
        N[a] += 1
        Q[a] += (q - Q[a]) / N[a]
        return q

def root_targets(tree: GuidedTreeSearch, s: int, eta: float = 1.0):
    """Training targets from a finished search at its root s:
    pi_MCTS(a | s) proportional to N(s, a)^eta, and U_MCTS(s) = the
    largest Q(s, a) among the actions tried."""
    N = tree.N[s]
    weights = N**eta
    return weights / weights.sum(), tree.Q[s][N > 0].max()

def tree_search_actor_critic_step(mdp, logits: Array, values: Array,
                                  starts, m: int, d: int, c: float,
                                  alpha_theta: float, alpha_phi: float,
                                  rng, eta: float = 1.0):
    """One round: search from each start state, then move the policy at
    that state toward the search's visit distribution (for softmax logits
    the cross-entropy gradient is pi_theta - pi_MCTS) and its value toward
    U_MCTS. Tabular: one logit per (state, action), one value per state.
    Only the roots are trained, where the search statistics are richest
    (as in AlphaGo Zero)."""
    logits, values = logits.copy(), values.copy()
    for s0 in starts:
        tree = GuidedTreeSearch(mdp, softmax(logits), values, d, c, rng)
        for _ in range(m):
            tree.simulate(s0, d)
        pi_target, u_target = root_targets(tree, s0, eta)
        logits[s0] -= alpha_theta * (softmax(logits[s0]) - pi_target)
        values[s0] -= alpha_phi * (values[s0] - u_target)
    return logits, values


softmax(x) = (z = exp.(x .- maximum(x)); z ./ sum(z))

hw = hex_world()
nS, nA = size(hw.R)
sample_next(s, a, rng) = findfirst(cumsum(hw.T[s, a, :]) .>= rand(rng))

# One search from s0: PUCT with prior π(·|s) and leaf values U; returns the root's N and Q.
function guided_search(s0, logits, U, m, d, c, rng)
    N, Q = Dict{Int, Vector{Float64}}(), Dict{Int, Vector{Float64}}()
    function simulate(s, depth)
        depth <= 0 && return U[s]
        if !haskey(N, s)                               # new leaf: the critic values it
            N[s], Q[s] = zeros(nA), zeros(nA)
            return U[s]
        end
        prior = softmax(logits[s, :])
        a = argmax(Q[s] .+ c .* prior .* sqrt(sum(N[s])) ./ (1 .+ N[s]))
        q = hw.R[s, a] + hw.γ * simulate(sample_next(s, a, rng), depth - 1)
        N[s][a] += 1
        Q[s][a] += (q - Q[s][a]) / N[s][a]
        return q
    end
    for _ in 1:m
        simulate(s0, d)
    end
    return N[s0], Q[s0]
end

# Rounds of: search from every decision tile, then move its logits and value toward the search.
decisions = [i for (i, t) in enumerate(ADM.HEX_STANDARD_TILES) if !haskey(ADM.HEX_STANDARD_REWARDS, t)]
rng = MersenneTwister(0)
logits, U = zeros(nS, nA), zeros(nS)
for _ in 1:30, s in decisions
    Ns, Qs = guided_search(s, logits, U, 100, 10, 5.0, rng)
    logits[s, :] .-= 1.0 .* (softmax(logits[s, :]) .- Ns ./ sum(Ns))   # cross-entropy gradient
    U[s] -= 0.5 * (U[s] - maximum(Qs[Ns .> 0]))
end
# Compare with the optimal policy (value iteration).
function optimal_policy()
    V = zeros(nS)
    for _ in 1:500
        V = [maximum(hw.R[s, a] + hw.γ * (hw.T[s, a, :] ⋅ V) for a in 1:nA) for s in 1:nS]
    end
    return [argmax([hw.R[s, a] + hw.γ * (hw.T[s, a, :] ⋅ V) for a in 1:nA]) for s in 1:nS]
end
@assert mean(argmax(logits[s, :]) == optimal_policy()[s] for s in decisions) >= 0.75









NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






global θ += ... is needed inside a top-level loop to update a variable defined outside it. Julia’s scoping rule differs from Python’s here.
function simulate(...) inside guided_search is a closure: it sees and changes N and Q, like a nested def with nonlocal.
R[:, 1:end-1] is all rows, every column but the last, like R[:, :-1].
for _ in 1:30, s in decisions is a nested loop in one line.
Ns ./ sum(Ns) normalizes the visit counts elementwise (the . means “for each element”).






Run them

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
theta, phi = np.array([0.0, 1.0]), np.zeros(2)
for _ in range(60):                               # 60 actor-critic updates, lambda = 0.5
    S, A, R = sr.sample_trajectories(theta, 10, rng)
    theta, phi = actor_critic_step(theta, phi, S, A, R, G, sr.grad_log_policy,
                                   features, lam=0.5, alpha_theta=0.1, alpha_phi=0.002)



actor theta = (-0.894, -0.024), exact value -0.160 (optimum -0.155); critic phi = (-0.47, -1.58)




Results

The bias–variance trade-off of λ








Figure 4: Bias (left) and spread (right) of the policy gradient estimate with generalized advantages, against λ, for three critics: none (φ = 0), halfway, and the least-squares fit. 300 estimates from 10 rollouts each, scored against the exact gradient. A poor critic makes small λ badly biased; larger λ trades that bias for spread.





The error that matters combines both, the root-mean-square error. It is smallest at \(\lambda =\) 0.75 without a critic, 0.5 with the halfway critic, and 0.0 with the fitted one.


Learning actor and critic together








Figure 5: Actor-critic on the regulator from θ = (0, 1) with a critic starting at zero: the exact value after each update (median of 20 runs), for several λ, and for Chapter 11’s estimator with a constant baseline and no critic. Early on the critic knows little, so λ = 0 (trusting it fully) climbs slowest. The other settings, with or without a critic, are close: on this 10-step problem the critic has little variance to remove.





After 60 updates, the share of runs within 0.05 of the optimum is 65% for λ = 0.0, 80% for λ = 0.5, 85% for λ = 0.9, 80% for λ = 1.0, and 85% without a critic. With only 10 steps per episode, returns aren’t very noisy, so the critic’s advantage is small here. It grows with the horizon, because the variance of a return adds up over every step. The critic’s step size matters as much as \(\lambda\). With a critic step of 0.02 instead of 0.002, 100% of runs end more than 1 below the optimum. Early states are large (the initial policy lets \(s\) grow), so the squared-state feature makes the critic’s gradient huge, and the critic’s values blow up and drag the actor with them.


Exploration in the deterministic policy gradient








Figure 6: Deterministic policy gradient on the regulator: the policy’s gain θ after each update (median of 20 runs; the optimum is −1), for four levels of exploration noise σ.





The median gain after 50 updates is -0.71 with σ = 0.05, -0.90 with σ = 0.2, -1.00 with σ = 0.5, -0.35 with σ = 1.0.

Too little noise teaches the critic little about how \(Q\) depends on the action, so progress is slow.
Too much noise pushes the state far from 0, where the quadratic critic’s TD updates become huge. The critic’s parameters blew up in 85% of the runs with \(\sigma = 1\), and the actor followed its wrong slopes.



Tree search as a teacher








Figure 7: Tree-search actor-critic on Hex World, from a uniform random policy and a zero critic (100 simulations per search, one search per tile per round). Left: average value over the 21 decision tiles of the learned stochastic policy and of its greedy version, against the optimum (dotted) and the uniform random policy (dashed). Middle: share of tiles where the policy’s favorite action is optimal. Right: the critic’s average error against the optimal values.





After 30 rounds, the greedy policy picks the optimal action on 20 of 21 tiles and averages 4.51, against the optimal 4.53. The critic’s values are off by 0.21 on average.

title: 13 · Actor-Critic Methods
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: the TD residual of a perfect critic. Show that if \(U_\phi = U^\pi\), then \(\mathbb{E}[\delta \mid s, a] = A^\pi(s, a)\).






TipSolution





\(\mathbb{E}[\delta \mid s, a] = \mathbb{E}[r + \gamma U^\pi(s') \mid s, a] - U^\pi(s) = Q^\pi(s, a) - U^\pi(s) = A^\pi(s, a)\). The first expectation is the definition of \(Q^\pi\): the expected reward plus the discounted value of the next state. The estimate is exact on average, and its noise comes from one step only.



Problem 2: GAE’s two extremes. Write out \(\hat A^{\text{GAE}}\) for a 3-step episode with \(\lambda = 0\) and \(\lambda = 1\), in terms of rewards and critic values.






TipSolution






\(\lambda = 0\): \(\hat A_1 = \delta_1 = r_1 + \gamma U(s_2) - U(s_1)\). Only the first reward is used.
\(\lambda = 1\): \(\hat A_1 = \delta_1 + \gamma\delta_2 + \gamma^2\delta_3 = r_1 + \gamma r_2 + \gamma^2 r_3 + \gamma^3 U(s_4) - U(s_1)\). The intermediate critic values cancel.

So \(\lambda = 1\) uses the critic only as a baseline at the start and a bootstrap at the very end. If the episode ends at step 3, it uses the critic only as a baseline.



Problem 3: a Jacobian for the deterministic policy gradient. A policy outputs two actions, \(\pi_\theta(s) = (\theta_1 s,\ \theta_2 + \theta_3 s^2)\). Write \(\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s)\), and the actor’s gradient if \(\nabla_a Q = (g_1, g_2)\).






TipSolution





Column \(j\) is the gradient of action \(j\): \[\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(s) = \begin{pmatrix} s & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 0 & s^2 \end{pmatrix}.\] The actor’s gradient is \(\nabla_\theta\pi\,\nabla_a Q = (s g_1,\ g_2,\ s^2 g_2)\). \(\theta_1\) follows the first action’s slope; \(\theta_2\) and \(\theta_3\) follow the second’s.



Problem 4: cross entropy for a softmax policy. A tile’s policy is \(\pi_\theta = \operatorname{softmax}(z)\) over three actions with logits \(z = (0, 0, 0)\). The search visited the actions 6, 3 and 1 times. With step size 1, what are the new logits and probabilities?






TipSolution





\(\pi_\theta = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)\) and \(\pi_{\text{MCTS}} = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1)\). The gradient of the cross entropy with respect to the logits is \(\pi_\theta - \pi_{\text{MCTS}} = (-0.267, 0.033, 0.233)\). Stepping against it, the new logits are \(z = (0.267, -0.033, -0.233)\), giving \(\operatorname{softmax}(z) \approx (0.42, 0.31, 0.26)\). That’s a step toward the search’s preferences.



Problem 5: which λ? Early in training the critic is poor; late in training it’s accurate. How should \(\lambda\) change, and why do practical systems often just fix \(\lambda \approx 0.95\)?






TipSolution





Early, a poor critic makes small \(\lambda\) badly biased (Figure 4), so a large \(\lambda\) is safer. Late, the critic’s bias is small, so a smaller \(\lambda\) cuts variance. A fixed \(\lambda \approx 0.95\) is a compromise that stays close to unbiased while still trimming the variance from rewards far in the future. Here the effective horizon is short (10 steps), so the benefit of small \(\lambda\) is modest. In long tasks, where \(\sum_k \gamma^k r_k\) is extremely noisy, it’s much larger.

title: 13 · Actor-Critic Methods
text:
Recap

An actor-critic learns a policy and a value function together; the critic supplies advantages for the actor’s gradient (Equation 1, Equation 2). Why it matters: it’s how policy gradients become practical: lower variance, and learning from every step instead of waiting for whole episodes.
GAE’s \(\lambda\) trades the critic’s bias against the returns’ variance (Equation 3, Equation 4). Why it matters: with no critic, \(\lambda = 0\) missed the gradient by 7.3; with a fitted critic, \(\lambda = 0\) gave the smallest error of all. The right \(\lambda\) depends on how good the critic is.
Two coupled learners need compatible step sizes. Why it matters: a critic that steps too fast can blow up and take the actor with it. This is the root of many practical tricks, such as target networks and slower critic updates.
The deterministic policy gradient follows the critic’s slope in the action (Equation 5). Why it matters: it handles continuous actions directly (DDPG, TD3), but it needs deliberate exploration noise, neither too little nor too much.
Tree search can teach the actor and critic (Equation 6, Equation 7). Why it matters: planning improves on the networks, and the networks make the next planning cheaper. This loop took AlphaGo Zero from random play to superhuman Go.

title: 13 · Actor-Critic Methods
text:
Cheat sheet & connections



Table 3: Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name).










Name
Formula
Ref




★ TD residual
\(\delta_k = r_k + \gamma U_\phi(s_{k+1}) - U_\phi(s_k)\)
Equation 1


Critic gradient
\(\sum_k (U_\phi(s_k) - r_{\text{to-go}}^{(k)}) \nabla_\phi U_\phi(s_k)\)
Equation 2


\(k\)-step advantage
\(\sum_{\ell \le k} \gamma^{\ell-1} r_\ell + \gamma^k U(s_{k+1}) - U(s) = \sum_{\ell \le k}\gamma^{\ell-1}\delta_\ell\)
Equation 3


★ GAE
\(\sum_k (\gamma\lambda)^{k-1} \delta_k\)
Equation 4


★ Deterministic policy gradient
\(\mathbb{E}_s[\nabla_\theta\pi_\theta(s)\, \nabla_a Q_\phi(s, a)]\)
Equation 5


PUCT
\(Q(s,a) + c\,\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\sqrt{N(s)}/(1 + N(s,a))\)
Equation 6


Tree search targets
\(\pi_{\text{MCTS}} \propto N^\eta\), \(U_{\text{MCTS}} = \max_a Q\)
Equation 7






Common pitfalls

Trusting a new critic. Small \(\lambda\) with an untrained critic gives confident but wrong advantages. Start with larger \(\lambda\), or pretrain the critic.
Critic step sizes tuned for small states. Features such as \(s^2\) can be huge early on. Scale features, cap the critic’s step, or step the critic more slowly.
No exploration with deterministic policies. Without action noise, the critic never learns \(\partial Q/\partial a\) away from the policy’s own actions.
Training on thin search statistics. Search targets from rarely visited states are noisy. Train where the search spent its simulations (here, the root).
Forgetting that the critic chases a moving target. As the actor changes, the true value changes. The critic always lags a little.

Connections

Ch 12 · Policy Gradient Optimization: TRPO and PPO typically use GAE advantages.
Ch 8 · Approximate Value Functions: the critic is a fitted value function.
Ch 9 · Online Planning: Monte Carlo tree search, here guided by a learned policy and value.

title: 11 · Policy Gradient Estimation
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 10 improved policies by trial and comparison: try parameters, keep the better ones. That ignores a valuable piece of information: the direction in which the expected return increases fastest, the gradient \(\nabla U(\theta)\). With a good estimate of it, you can climb steadily instead of searching blindly. This chapter is about estimating that gradient from simulated trajectories. The difficulty is that every estimate is noisy, and much of the chapter is about taming that noise. Chapter 12 then uses these estimates to optimize policies, and Chapter 13 adds a learned value function to make them far less noisy. The same estimators underlie modern reinforcement learning algorithms such as REINFORCE, PPO and actor-critic methods.
The question: how can you tell which way to change a policy’s parameters, when all you can do is run the policy and watch the rewards?
The short answer: either wiggle the parameters and see how the return changes (finite differences), or, for a stochastic policy, use the fact that the policy’s own probabilities tell you how to make good trajectories more likely (the likelihood ratio). Then cut the noise by crediting each action only with the rewards that come after it, and by comparing rewards with a baseline.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Two families estimate ∇U(θ): perturbation methods treat U as a black box; likelihood ratio methods use the policy’s log-probabilities. Reward-to-go and baseline subtraction then reduce the likelihood ratio’s variance without adding bias.







The key ideas at a glance

The gradient points uphill, but we can only estimate it. \(\nabla U(\theta)\) says how the expected return changes as each policy parameter changes. There’s rarely a formula, so we estimate it from rollouts. Every estimator trades bias (systematically wrong) against variance (noisy from run to run).
Finite differences: nudge and compare. Change one parameter by a small \(\delta\), estimate \(U\) again, and divide the change by \(\delta\). It’s simple and model-free, but noisy estimates of \(U\) are divided by a small number, which blows the noise up. The fix is common random numbers: run both evaluations with the same random seeds, so the noise mostly cancels. The regression gradient instead fits a plane to the results of many random nudges.
The likelihood ratio: make good trajectories more likely. For a stochastic policy, the gradient can be written as an average over trajectories of the return times \(\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)\), the direction that makes that particular trajectory more probable. The transition model cancels out of this term, leaving only the policy’s own \(\nabla \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\). You need no model and no parameter nudges.
Reward-to-go: an action can’t affect the past. The plain likelihood ratio credits every action with the whole trajectory’s return, including rewards collected before the action was taken. Those terms average to zero but add noise. Crediting each action only with the rewards that follow it removes them, with no bias.
Baseline subtraction: better than what? Subtracting a baseline from the reward-to-go, such as the typical return from that point, also leaves the average unchanged, because the policy’s probabilities sum to one. It can reduce the variance a lot. The variance-minimizing constant baseline has a simple formula. The best state-dependent choice leads to the advantage \(A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - U(s)\), which is the bridge to actor-critic methods.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning

How the expected return changes with each policy parameter


Bias, variance
Systematic error of an estimator, and its spread across repeated runs


Finite difference
Estimate a derivative from \(U(\theta + \delta e_i) - U(\theta)\)


Common random numbers
Reuse the same random seeds when comparing two policies


Regression gradient
Fit the gradient to the returns of many random perturbations


Score \(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\)
The direction that makes action \(a\) in state \(s\) more likely


Likelihood ratio (REINFORCE)
Gradient estimate: average of return × score of the trajectory


Reward-to-go
Discounted reward from a step onward


Baseline
A value subtracted from the reward-to-go to reduce variance


Advantage \(A(s, a)\)
How much better action \(a\) is than the policy’s average in \(s\)








After this chapter you can

Estimate a policy gradient with finite differences and regression, and use common random numbers.
Derive the likelihood ratio policy gradient, and compute it for a Gaussian policy.
Explain why reward-to-go and baselines reduce variance without introducing bias.
Compute the variance-minimizing constant baseline, and connect baselines to the advantage function.
Measure an estimator’s bias and variance, and choose an estimator for a problem.

title: 11 · Policy Gradient Estimation
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



You’re adjusting a thermostat schedule to cut your heating bill, and every month’s bill is noisy because the weather varies.

Finite differences: change one setting for a month and compare bills. Unless the two months had the same weather, the comparison is mostly noise. Comparing on matched weather (common random numbers) fixes that.
Likelihood ratio: you already vary your settings slightly from day to day (the policy is stochastic). Look at the days that turned out cheap and ask which way your settings leaned on those days. Lean further that way.
Reward-to-go: judge each day’s setting only by what happened after it, not by the heating costs of the days before.
Baseline: judge a day by whether it was cheaper than a typical day, not by its absolute cost.



We use the simple regulator from Chapter 10 (keep a number \(s\) near 0; reward \(-s^2\)) with the stochastic policy \(a \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_1 s, \theta_2^2)\). For this problem the exact gradient is available, so every estimator can be scored exactly. At \(\theta = (-0.5, 0.5)\) the gradient \(\nabla U\) is (-2.04, -6.96). The return improves by making the gain more negative (pushing \(s\) back harder) and by making the policy less random.

Finite differences and shared noise
Estimate \(U\) at \(\theta\) and at \(\theta + \delta e_1\) from 10 rollouts each, and divide the difference by \(\delta = 0.01\). Each estimate of \(U\) has a standard deviation of about 0.36, and the difference of two independent estimates about 0.51. Dividing by 0.01 turns that into gradient noise of about 51, many times larger than the gradient itself. Now run both evaluations with the same random numbers, so the same start states and the same disturbances. The noise that’s common to both cancels in the difference. At an equal budget of 30 simulated episodes, the error falls from 8.1 (with \(\delta = 0.1\), the least-bad step without shared noise) to 1.6 (Figure 4). See Equation 1.


Make good trajectories more likely
A stochastic policy sometimes pushes a bit harder than average and sometimes a bit softer. Episodes that went well tell you which way to lean. The likelihood ratio gradient adds up, for each episode, the return times the direction that makes that episode’s actions more likely. No parameter is ever nudged: the policy’s own randomness does the exploring. See Equation 3.


Don’t credit the past
In a 10-step episode, the plain likelihood ratio multiplies step 5’s action by the reward from steps 1–4 as well, even though that action couldn’t have affected them. On average those terms are exactly zero, but in any one episode they aren’t, so they add pure noise. Figure 5 shows it on the regulator: the terms in which the reward comes before the action average to zero but are just as noisy as the rest. Dropping them (reward-to-go) cuts the error at 30 episodes from 5.8 to 4.3. See Equation 4.


Better or worse than usual?
Here every reward is negative. So every action is “blamed” in proportion to how negative the rest of its episode was, even if it was a good action. Subtracting a baseline, a typical reward-to-go, turns this into a comparison: was this episode better or worse than usual? That doesn’t change the average gradient, and it cuts the error at 30 episodes to 2.3. See Equation 5 and Figure 6.

title: 11 · Policy Gradient Estimation
text:
Formalism

Finite differences
For a unit vector \(e_i\) along parameter \(i\) and a small step \(\delta > 0\) (ADM §11.1):

\[
\nabla U(\theta) \approx \left[\frac{U(\theta + \delta e_1) - U(\theta)}{\delta},\ \ldots,\ \frac{U(\theta + \delta e_n) - U(\theta)}{\delta}\right]
\tag{1}\]

In words. Nudge one parameter at a time and measure the slope.
Term by term.

Each \(U\) is itself a Monte Carlo estimate (Chapter 10), so \(n + 1\) evaluations with \(m\) rollouts each cost \(m(n+1)\) episodes.
A larger \(\delta\) adds bias (the function curves between the two points).
A smaller \(\delta\) multiplies the evaluation noise by \(1/\delta\).
With common random numbers, both evaluations use the same random seeds (A. Ng and M. Jordan’s PEGASUS, 2000). The difference then mostly reflects the parameter change, not luck.
The estimate depends on how the policy is parameterized: parameters on very different scales need different steps.



Regression gradient
Perturb \(\theta\) in \(m\) random directions \(\Delta\theta^{(i)}\) and record the changes \(\Delta U_i = U(\theta + \Delta\theta^{(i)}) - U(\theta)\) (ADM §11.2):

\[
\nabla U(\theta) \approx \Delta\Theta^+ \Delta U,
\qquad \Delta\Theta = \begin{bmatrix} (\Delta\theta^{(1)})^\top \\ \vdots \\ (\Delta\theta^{(m)})^\top \end{bmatrix}
\tag{2}\]

In words. Fit a linear model \(\Delta U \approx \Delta\theta^\top g\) to all the perturbations by least squares (Chapter 8), and take its slope \(g\) as the gradient.
Term by term. \(\Delta\Theta^+\) is the pseudoinverse. Using more perturbations than parameters (a rule of thumb is twice as many) averages out noise. This is also known as simultaneous perturbation.


The likelihood ratio
Write \(U\) as an expectation over trajectories and move the gradient inside (ADM §11.3; P. Glynn, Communications of the ACM, 1990):

\[
\nabla U(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\tau\big[\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)\ R(\tau)\big],
\qquad
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau) = \sum_{k=1}^{d} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta\big(a^{(k)} \mid s^{(k)}\big)
\tag{3}\]

In words. The gradient is the average, over trajectories, of the return times the direction that makes that trajectory more likely. That direction is the sum of the policy’s score at each step.
Term by term.

\(R(\tau) = \sum_k \gamma^{k-1} r^{(k)}\) is the discounted return.
\(\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) is the policy’s score. For \(a \sim \mathcal{N}(\theta_1 s, \theta_2^2)\) it is \(\big((a - \theta_1 s)s/\theta_2^2,\ ((a - \theta_1 s)^2 - \theta_2^2)/\theta_2^3\big)\).
Estimate the expectation by averaging over \(m\) rollouts.

Why it holds. \(U(\theta) = \int p_\theta(\tau) R(\tau)\,d\tau\). Differentiate under the integral, and use \(\nabla p = p \nabla \log p\) (the log-derivative trick of Chapter 10). That gives \(\int p_\theta(\tau)\,\nabla \log p_\theta(\tau)\,R(\tau)\,d\tau\), an expectation. The trajectory’s probability is \(p(s^{(1)}) \prod_k T(s^{(k+1)} \mid s^{(k)}, a^{(k)})\,\pi_\theta(a^{(k)} \mid s^{(k)})\). Its logarithm is a sum in which only the \(\pi_\theta\) terms depend on \(\theta\), so the transition model drops out. For a deterministic policy there is no \(\pi_\theta\) probability to differentiate. The gradient then has to flow through the transition model, which must be known.


Reward-to-go
Expanding Equation 3 gives products of each step’s score \(f^{(k)}\) with each step’s reward \(r^{(\ell)}\). The terms with \(\ell < k\), where the reward came before the action, have expectation zero. Removing them gives (ADM §11.4):

\[
\nabla U(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\tau\left[\sum_{k=1}^{d} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta\big(a^{(k)} \mid s^{(k)}\big)\ \gamma^{k-1}\, r_{\text{to-go}}^{(k)}\right],
\qquad r_{\text{to-go}}^{(k)} = \sum_{\ell=k}^{d} \gamma^{\ell-k} r^{(\ell)}
\tag{4}\]

In words. Credit each action only with the discounted rewards from its own step onward.
Term by term.

\(r_{\text{to-go}}^{(k)}\) is a one-sample estimate of the action value \(Q_\theta(s^{(k)}, a^{(k)})\), and replacing it by \(Q_\theta\) itself also gives the exact gradient.
\(\gamma^{k-1}\) discounts the whole credit back to the start.

Why it holds. For \(\ell < k\), condition on the history up to step \(k\). The reward \(r^{(\ell)}\) is then fixed, and \(\mathbb{E}_{a^{(k)}}[\nabla \log \pi_\theta(a^{(k)} \mid s^{(k)})] = \nabla \int \pi_\theta(a \mid s)\,da = \nabla 1 = 0\). So each such term averages to zero and can be dropped.


Baseline subtraction
Any function of the state alone can be subtracted from the reward-to-go without bias (ADM §11.5). The combination with reward-to-go is the classic REINFORCE algorithm (R. Williams, Machine Learning, 1992):

\[
\nabla U(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\tau\left[\sum_{k=1}^{d} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta\big(a^{(k)} \mid s^{(k)}\big)\ \gamma^{k-1} \Big(r_{\text{to-go}}^{(k)} - r_{\text{base}}\big(s^{(k)}\big)\Big)\right]
\tag{5}\]

In words. Judge each action by how much better its future rewards were than a typical level, not by their raw size.
Term by term.

\(r_{\text{base}}(s)\) can depend on the state but not on the action.
Its expected contribution is \(\mathbb{E}[\nabla \log \pi_\theta \cdot \gamma^{k-1} r_{\text{base}}(s^{(k)})]\). This is zero for the same reason as before: the score averages to zero over actions.

For a constant baseline per parameter \(i\), the variance is smallest when (ADM §11.5):

\[
r_{\text{base}, i} = \frac{\mathbb{E}\big[\ell_i^2\, r_{\text{to-go}}\big]}{\mathbb{E}\big[\ell_i^2\big]},
\qquad \ell_i = \gamma^{k-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_i} \log \pi_\theta\big(a^{(k)} \mid s^{(k)}\big)
\tag{6}\]

In words. The best constant baseline is an average of the reward-to-go, weighted by how strongly each step’s score counts.
Term by term. The expectations are over all steps of all trajectories. In practice they’re estimated from the same rollouts, which adds a small bias that fades as \(m\) grows.
Why it holds. The variance of the \(i\)-th component is \(\mathbb{E}[(\ell_i (r_{\text{to-go}} - b))^2] - (\text{gradient}_i)^2\), and the second term doesn’t depend on \(b\). Setting the derivative of the first term to zero, \(-2\,\mathbb{E}[\ell_i^2 r_{\text{to-go}}] + 2b\,\mathbb{E}[\ell_i^2] = 0\), gives the formula.
Using the state’s value \(U_\theta(s)\) as the baseline turns \(Q_\theta(s, a) - U_\theta(s)\) into the advantage:

\[
\nabla U(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_\tau\left[\sum_{k=1}^{d} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta\big(a^{(k)} \mid s^{(k)}\big)\ \gamma^{k-1} A_\theta\big(s^{(k)}, a^{(k)}\big)\right],
\qquad A_\theta(s, a) = Q_\theta(s, a) - U_\theta(s)
\tag{7}\]

In words. Push up actions that were better than the policy’s average in their state, and push down those that were worse.
Term by term. The advantage is usually unknown. Chapter 13’s actor-critic methods learn it alongside the policy.

Reward-to-go by hand
A 3-step episode with \(\gamma = 0.9\), scores \(f^{(1)}, f^{(2)}, f^{(3)} = 1, -1, 2\) (one parameter) and rewards \(r = (-1, -2, -1)\):

The return is \(R = -1 - 0.9 \times 2 - 0.81 \times 1 = -3.61\). The plain likelihood ratio term is \((1 - 1 + 2) \times (-3.61) = -7.22\).
The rewards-to-go are \(r_{\text{to-go}}^{(3)} = -1\), \(r_{\text{to-go}}^{(2)} = -2 + 0.9(-1) = -2.9\) and \(r_{\text{to-go}}^{(1)} = -1 + 0.9(-2.9) = -3.61\).
The reward-to-go term is \(1 \times 1 \times (-3.61) + (-1) \times 0.9 \times (-2.9) + 2 \times 0.81 \times (-1) = -3.61 + 2.61 - 1.62 = -2.62\).

The two terms differ by \(-4.60\). That’s exactly the “past reward” terms: \((-1) \times (-1) = 1\) for step 2’s score against the first reward, and \(2 \times (-1 + 0.9 \times (-2)) = -5.6\) for step 3’s score against the first two rewards. Averaged over many episodes such terms vanish, but in one episode they’re large.

title: 11 · Policy Gradient Estimation
11 · Policy Gradient Estimation
text:
Algorithms & code

Simulating the regulator

PythonJulia


def sample_trajectories(theta, m: int, rng, d: int = HORIZON):
    """m episodes of d steps under the Gaussian policy, as arrays of shape
    (m, d): states, actions and rewards (row i is episode i, column k is
    step k + 1)."""
    s = START_MEAN + START_SD * rng.standard_normal(m)
    S, A, R = np.zeros((m, d)), np.zeros((m, d)), np.zeros((m, d))
    for k in range(d):
        a = gaussian_policy(theta, s, rng)
        S[:, k], A[:, k] = s, a
        s, R[:, k] = step(s, a, rng)
    return S, A, R

def grad_log_policy(theta, s, a):
    """Gradient of log N(a | theta_1 s, sd^2) with sd = |theta_2| + 1e-5,
    for arrays s and a of the same shape. Returns shape s.shape + (2,):
      d/d theta_1 = (a - theta_1 s) s / sd^2
      d/d theta_2 = ((a - theta_1 s)^2 - sd^2) / sd^3 * sign(theta_2)"""
    sd = abs(theta[1]) + 1e-5
    z = a - theta[0] * s                     # deviation from the mean action
    g1 = z * s / sd**2
    g2 = (z**2 - sd**2) / sd**3 * np.sign(theta[1])
    return np.stack([g1, g2], axis=-1)

def exact_gradient(theta, d: int = HORIZON) -> np.ndarray:
    """Gradient of exact_value, by differentiating its recursion:
    ms' = gain^2 ms + noise_var, so
    d ms'/d theta_1 = 2 gain ms + gain^2 d ms/d theta_1,
    d ms'/d theta_2 = gain^2 d ms/d theta_2 + 2 sd sign(theta_2)."""
    gain, sd = 1 + theta[0], abs(theta[1]) + 1e-5
    noise_var = sd**2 + NOISE_SD**2
    ms, dms = START_MEAN**2 + START_SD**2, np.zeros(2)
    grad = np.zeros(2)
    for t in range(d):
        grad -= GAMMA**t * dms              # U = -sum_t gamma^t E[s_t^2]
        dms = np.array([2 * gain * ms + gain**2 * dms[0],
                        gain**2 * dms[1] + 2 * sd * np.sign(theta[1])])
        ms = gain**2 * ms + noise_var
    return grad


using ADM, LinearAlgebra, Random, Statistics

# m episodes of d steps: states, actions and rewards as m × d matrices.
function sample_trajectories(θ, m, rng; d = REGULATOR_HORIZON)
    S, A, R = zeros(m, d), zeros(m, d), zeros(m, d)
    for i in 1:m
        s = REGULATOR_START[1] + REGULATOR_START[2] * randn(rng)
        for k in 1:d
            a = regulator_policy(θ, s, rng)
            S[i, k], A[i, k] = s, a
            s, R[i, k] = regulator_step(s, a, rng)
        end
    end
    return S, A, R
end

# Score of the Gaussian policy: ∇θ log N(a | θ₁ s, sd²) with sd = |θ₂| + 1e-5.
function grad_log_policy(θ, s, a)
    sd, z = abs(θ[2]) + 1e-5, a - θ[1] * s
    return [z * s / sd^2, (z^2 - sd^2) / sd^3 * sign(θ[2])]
end

θ = [-0.5, 0.5]
∇U = regulator_exact_gradient(θ)





Finite differences and regression

PythonJulia


def finite_difference_gradient(U, theta, delta: float) -> Array:
    """Forward differences: (U(theta + delta e_i) - U(theta)) / delta for
    each coordinate i. U may be noisy; each call is a fresh estimate."""
    theta = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)
    u0 = U(theta)
    grad = np.zeros(len(theta))
    for i in range(len(theta)):
        step = np.zeros(len(theta))
        step[i] = delta
        grad[i] = (U(theta + step) - u0) / delta
    return grad

def regression_gradient(U, theta, delta: float, m: int, rng) -> Array:
    """Perturb theta in m random directions of length delta, record how U
    changes, and fit the gradient by least squares: grad ~ dTheta^+ dU."""
    theta = np.asarray(theta, dtype=float)
    directions = rng.standard_normal((m, len(theta)))
    dtheta = delta * directions / np.linalg.norm(directions, axis=1,
                                                 keepdims=True)
    u0 = U(theta)
    du = np.array([U(theta + dt) - u0 for dt in dtheta])
    return np.linalg.pinv(dtheta) @ du


# Forward differences, one parameter at a time.
function finite_difference_gradient(U, θ, δ)
    u0 = U(θ)
    return [(U(θ .+ δ .* (1:length(θ) .== i)) - u0) / δ for i in eachindex(θ)]
end

# Random perturbations of length δ; least-squares fit of the changes in U.
function regression_gradient(U, θ, δ, m, rng)
    ΔΘ = reduce(vcat, (δ .* normalize(randn(rng, length(θ)))' for _ in 1:m))   # m × n
    u0 = U(θ)
    ΔU = [U(θ .+ ΔΘ[i, :]) - u0 for i in 1:m]
    return pinv(ΔΘ) * ΔU
end

# Monte Carlo U with 10 rollouts; `shared` reuses one seed so both evaluations see the same noise.
function U_estimate(θ, rng; m = 10)
    total = 0.0
    for _ in 1:m
        s, ret = REGULATOR_START[1] + REGULATOR_START[2] * randn(rng), 0.0
        for t in 1:REGULATOR_HORIZON
            s, r = regulator_step(s, regulator_policy(θ, s, rng), rng)
            ret += REGULATOR_γ^(t - 1) * r
        end
        total += ret
    end
    return total / m
end
fd(seed; shared) = finite_difference_gradient(
    shared ? (t -> U_estimate(t, MersenneTwister(seed))) : (t -> U_estimate(t, MersenneTwister(rand(UInt32)))),
    θ, 0.01)
spread(v) = std(first.(v)) + std(last.(v))                # sum of the two components' spreads
fresh = [fd(s; shared = false) for s in 1:200]
common = [fd(s; shared = true) for s in 1:200]
@assert spread(common) < spread(fresh) / 10              # shared random numbers tame the noise





Likelihood ratio, reward-to-go and baseline

PythonJulia


def discounted_returns(r: Array, gamma: float) -> Array:
    """R(tau) = sum_k gamma^(k-1) r_k for each trajectory (row)."""
    return r @ gamma ** np.arange(r.shape[1])

def rewards_to_go(r: Array, gamma: float) -> Array:
    """rtg[i, k] = sum over l >= k of gamma^(l-k) r[i, l]: the discounted
    reward from step k on, discounted back to step k."""
    rtg = np.zeros_like(r)
    running = np.zeros(r.shape[0])
    for k in range(r.shape[1] - 1, -1, -1):      # sweep backward in time
        running = r[:, k] + gamma * running
        rtg[:, k] = running
    return rtg

def likelihood_ratio_gradient(g: Array, r: Array, gamma: float) -> Array:
    """Average over trajectories of (sum_k grad log pi_k) * R(tau)."""
    score = g.sum(axis=1)                        # (m, n): grad log p(tau)
    return (score * discounted_returns(r, gamma)[:, None]).mean(axis=0)

def reward_to_go_gradient(g: Array, r: Array, gamma: float) -> Array:
    """Like the likelihood ratio, but each action is credited only with
    rewards that come after it: sum_k grad log pi_k gamma^(k-1) rtg_k."""
    discount = gamma ** np.arange(r.shape[1])     # gamma^(k-1)
    weights = discount * rewards_to_go(r, gamma)  # (m, d)
    return (g * weights[:, :, None]).sum(axis=1).mean(axis=0)

def baseline_gradient(g: Array, r: Array, gamma: float) -> Array:
    """Reward-to-go minus, for each parameter i, the constant baseline that
    minimizes the estimate's variance: E[l_i^2 rtg] / E[l_i^2], where
    l_i = gamma^(k-1) d/d theta_i log pi. Pooled over all steps here."""
    discount = gamma ** np.arange(r.shape[1])
    ell = g * discount[None, :, None]              # (m, d, n)
    rtg = rewards_to_go(r, gamma)[:, :, None]      # (m, d, 1)
    base = (ell**2 * rtg).sum(axis=(0, 1)) / (ell**2).sum(axis=(0, 1))
    return (ell * (rtg - base)).sum(axis=1).mean(axis=0)


# g[i, k] is the score (a vector) of step k of trajectory i; R[i, k] its reward.
scores(θ, S, A) = [grad_log_policy(θ, S[i, k], A[i, k]) for i in axes(S, 1), k in axes(S, 2)]
discounts(d, γ) = γ .^ (0:d-1)

function rewards_to_go(R, γ)
    rtg, running = zero(R), zeros(size(R, 1))
    for k in size(R, 2):-1:1                          # sweep backward in time
        running = R[:, k] .+ γ .* running
        rtg[:, k] = running
    end
    return rtg
end

likelihood_ratio(g, R, γ) = mean(sum(g[i, :]) * (R[i, :] ⋅ discounts(size(R, 2), γ)) for i in axes(R, 1))

function reward_to_go(g, R, γ)
    w = discounts(size(R, 2), γ)' .* rewards_to_go(R, γ)
    return mean(sum(g[i, k] * w[i, k] for k in axes(R, 2)) for i in axes(R, 1))
end

function with_baseline(g, R, γ)
    disc, rtg = discounts(size(R, 2), γ), rewards_to_go(R, γ)
    ℓ = [disc[k] .* g[i, k] for i in axes(R, 1), k in axes(R, 2)]
    base = sum(ℓ[j] .^ 2 .* rtg[j] for j in eachindex(ℓ)) ./ sum(ℓ[j] .^ 2 for j in eachindex(ℓ))
    return mean(sum(ℓ[i, k] .* (rtg[i, k] .- base) for k in axes(R, 2)) for i in axes(R, 1))
end





Run them

PythonJulia



rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
S, A, R = sr.sample_trajectories(THETA, 100, rng)       # 100 episodes
g = sr.grad_log_policy(THETA, S, A)                      # scores, (100, 10, 2)
estimates = {"likelihood ratio": likelihood_ratio_gradient(g, R, GAMMA),
             "reward-to-go": reward_to_go_gradient(g, R, GAMMA),
             "baseline": baseline_gradient(g, R, GAMMA)}



rng = MersenneTwister(1)
reps = [begin
            S, A, R = sample_trajectories(θ, 10, rng)
            g = scores(θ, S, A)
            (likelihood_ratio(g, R, REGULATOR_γ), reward_to_go(g, R, REGULATOR_γ), with_baseline(g, R, REGULATOR_γ))
        end for _ in 1:300]
method_spread(j) = spread([r[j] for r in reps])
@assert method_spread(3) < method_spread(2) < method_spread(1)   # baseline < reward-to-go < likelihood ratio
S, A, R = sample_trajectories(θ, 100_000, rng)
@assert isapprox(reward_to_go(scores(θ, S, A), R, REGULATOR_γ), ∇U; atol = 0.3)

likelihood ratio    ( -1.33,  -7.94)
reward-to-go        ( -1.96,  -7.21)

NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






[f(i, k) for i in axes(S, 1), k in axes(S, 2)] builds a matrix, one entry per (i, k), like a nested list comprehension.

zero(R) makes an array of zeros shaped like R, like np.zeros_like(R).






Results

Finite differences: the step size, and shared noise








Figure 4: Finite-difference gradient error against the step δ (10 rollouts per evaluation of U, 300 repetitions). With fresh random numbers for each evaluation (orange), the noise is divided by δ and explodes for small steps. With shared random numbers (blue), the error is small until δ is large enough for curvature to bias the estimate. The dashed line is that bias alone (exact U, no noise).







Why reward-to-go works








Figure 5: The plain likelihood ratio’s terms for θ₁: step k’s score times the discounted reward at step ℓ, over 200,000 episodes. Left: average. Right: standard deviation. Terms on or below the diagonal (the reward came no later than the action) average to zero but are as noisy as the rest; reward-to-go drops those below the diagonal. The diagonal averages to zero too, because the regulator’s reward −s² is earned before the action takes effect.





The largest average of a term on or below the diagonal is 0.0052. That’s 2.2 standard errors from zero, about the largest you’d expect by chance among 55 terms that are truly zero. Their standard deviations, meanwhile, are as large as those of the terms that matter.


All estimators at equal cost








Figure 6: Three hundred gradient estimates at a budget of 30 episodes each, for six estimators, around the exact gradient (star). Plain finite differences use δ = 0.1 (smaller steps are far noisier without shared random numbers); with shared random numbers, δ = 0.01.













Figure 7: RMS error of each estimator against the simulation budget (episodes per gradient estimate), log-log. The lines fall with slopes near −1/2 (error ∝ 1/√budget), so a 25-fold budget buys a 5-fold smaller error. The ordering never changes: variance reduction is worth a fixed multiple of the budget. Plain finite differences would eventually level off at the bias of their step δ = 0.1 (about 0.8), but that’s below this range.







Does lower variance help learning?








Figure 8: Gradient ascent on the regulator from θ = (0, 1), using each estimator with 10 episodes per step (step size 0.2, gradient clipped to length 1): the exact value after each step, median of 20 runs. Lower-variance estimators climb faster and settle closer to the optimum (dashed).





After 10 steps (100 episodes), the median value is -0.58 with the plain likelihood ratio, -0.27 with reward-to-go and -0.23 with the baseline. The optimum is -0.155.

title: 11 · Policy Gradient Estimation
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: the cost of finite differences. A policy has 6 parameters, and each evaluation of \(U\) uses 20 rollouts. How many rollouts does one forward-difference gradient cost? What does a likelihood ratio estimate with the same total cost use?






TipSolution





One evaluation at \(\theta\) and one per parameter: \(7 \times 20 = 140\) rollouts. The likelihood ratio uses all 140 trajectories at the current \(\theta\) for a single estimate, and its cost doesn’t grow with the number of parameters. That’s why likelihood ratio methods dominate for policies with many parameters, such as neural networks.



Problem 2: parameters on different scales. A policy’s gain is stored as \(\theta_1\) in units of 1, and its noise level as \(\theta_2\) in hundredths (\(\sigma = \theta_2 / 100\)). With \(\partial U/\partial \sigma = -7\), what is \(\partial U / \partial \theta_2\)? Why does one finite-difference step \(\delta\) suit one parameter but not the other?






TipSolution





By the chain rule, \(\partial U/\partial\theta_2 = (\partial U/\partial\sigma)(d\sigma/d\theta_2) = -7 / 100 = -0.07\). A step \(\delta = 0.01\) in \(\theta_1\) is a small change, but in \(\theta_2\) it changes \(\sigma\) by only \(0.0001\). The change in \(U\) is then far smaller than the evaluation noise, so that component of the estimate is pure noise. Rescale parameters to comparable units, or use per-parameter steps.



Problem 3: a baseline doesn’t bias. A policy picks action 1 with probability \(p = \sigma(\theta)\) (the logistic function) and action 0 otherwise. Show that \(\mathbb{E}_a[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a) \cdot b] = 0\) for any constant \(b\).






TipSolution





For the logistic function, \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\log p = 1 - p\) and \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\log(1-p) = -p\). Then \(\mathbb{E}[\nabla \log \pi \cdot b] = b\,\big(p(1-p) + (1-p)(-p)\big) = 0\). In general, \(\sum_a \pi(a)\nabla\log\pi(a) = \sum_a \nabla\pi(a) = \nabla \sum_a \pi(a) = \nabla 1 = 0\).



Problem 4: the diagonal terms. In Figure 5, the diagonal terms (step \(k\)’s score times step \(k\)’s reward) also average to zero for the regulator. Why? Would that hold if the reward were \(-s^2 - a^2\)?






TipSolution





The regulator’s reward at step \(k\) is \(-s_k^2\), which is fixed before action \(a_k\) is chosen. Conditioning on \(s_k\), \(\mathbb{E}_{a_k}[\nabla\log\pi(a_k \mid s_k)] \cdot r_k = 0 \cdot r_k\). With an action cost \(-a_k^2\), the reward at step \(k\) depends on \(a_k\), so the diagonal terms carry signal and must be kept. That’s why the reward-to-go includes the current step’s reward.



Problem 5: which estimator? You tune a robot controller with 3 parameters on a physical robot, where you can’t replay the same random disturbances. Then you tune a 10,000-parameter neural network policy in a simulator. Which estimators suit each case?






TipSolution






The robot: there are few parameters, so perturbation methods are affordable, but common random numbers are unavailable. Use finite differences or the regression gradient with enough repetitions, or a likelihood ratio method with a baseline if the policy can be made stochastic. The likelihood ratio needs no model of the robot.
The network: finite differences would need 10,001 evaluations per gradient, which is hopeless. Use the likelihood ratio with reward-to-go and a baseline, whose cost doesn’t grow with the number of parameters. In a simulator you could also fix the random seeds, which helps any method.

title: 11 · Policy Gradient Estimation
text:
Recap

Policy gradient methods estimate \(\nabla U(\theta)\) from rollouts, and every estimate trades bias against variance. Why it matters: the gradient tells an optimizer which way to move (Chapter 12), but a noisy gradient wastes steps or misleads.
Finite differences nudge parameters and compare (Equation 1); common random numbers make them accurate. Why it matters: they need nothing but a simulator, but their cost grows with the number of parameters, and without shared noise, small steps drown in noise.
The likelihood ratio uses the policy’s own randomness: return times score (Equation 3). Why it matters: it needs no model and costs the same however many parameters there are. It’s the basis of REINFORCE and all modern policy gradient methods.
Reward-to-go and baselines remove noise without adding bias (Equation 4, Equation 5, Equation 6). Why it matters: here they cut the error at 30 episodes from 5.8 to 2.3, and they make learning faster and steadier.
The best baselines lead to the advantage function (Equation 7). Why it matters: learning \(A(s, a)\) alongside the policy is exactly what actor-critic methods do (Chapter 13).

text:
Cheat sheet & connections



Table 4: Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name).










Name
Formula

\(\big(U(\theta + \delta e_i) - U(\theta)\big)/\delta\)
Equation 1

Equation 2


★ Likelihood ratio
\(\mathbb{E}_\tau[\nabla\log p_\theta(\tau) R(\tau)]\), \(\nabla\log p_\theta(\tau) = \sum_k \nabla\log\pi_\theta(a^{(k)} \mid s^{(k)})\)
Equation 3


Reward-to-go
\(\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_k \nabla\log\pi_\theta\, \gamma^{k-1} r_{\text{to-go}}^{(k)}\big]\)
Equation 4


★ Baseline (REINFORCE)
\(\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_k \nabla\log\pi_\theta\, \gamma^{k-1} (r_{\text{to-go}}^{(k)} - r_{\text{base}}(s^{(k)}))\big]\)
Equation 5

\(\mathbb{E}[\ell_i^2 r_{\text{to-go}}] / \mathbb{E}[\ell_i^2]\)
Equation 6


Advantage form
\(\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_k \nabla\log\pi_\theta\, \gamma^{k-1} A_\theta(s^{(k)}, a^{(k)})\big]\)
Equation 7






Common pitfalls

Tiny finite-difference steps with fresh noise. The noise is divided by \(\delta\). Share random numbers, or use a larger step and accept some bias.
Crediting actions with past rewards. Always use reward-to-go. It’s free variance reduction.
A baseline that depends on the action. That biases the gradient. The baseline may depend on the state, not the action.
Deterministic policies with the likelihood ratio. There’s no action probability to differentiate. Add exploration noise, or use a model.
Mismatched parameter scales. Gradient components can differ by orders of magnitude. Rescale the parameters, or use natural gradients (Chapter 12).

Connections

Ch 12 · Policy Gradient Optimization: gradient ascent, natural gradients and trust regions using these estimates.
Ch 13 · Actor-Critic Methods: learn the advantage as a baseline.
Ch 3 · Inference: likelihood weighting uses the same kind of ratio of probabilities.

title: 9 · Online Planning
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 7 computed a policy for every state before acting, and Chapter 8 did the same with an approximate value function. Both are offline: all the work happens before the first move, and both struggle when the state space is huge. This chapter turns the problem around. An online planner waits until it knows the current state, then reasons only about the states reachable from there, picks one action, acts, and repeats. The same idea powers game-playing programs (Monte Carlo tree search was central to AlphaGo), robot controllers (model predictive control), and the online POMDP planners of Chapter 22.
The question: how do you choose a good action for the state you’re in right now, without solving the whole problem?
The short answer: look ahead from the current state, as far and as widely as you can afford, estimate what lies beyond, pick the best first action, then do it all again from the next state. The methods differ in how they spend a fixed amount of thinking: exhaustively, with bounds that prune, with random samples, or guided by optimism.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Every online planner works in the same receding-horizon loop and differs in how it explores the future: exhaustively, with pruning, by sampling, guided by an optimistic heuristic, or by optimizing a fixed sequence of actions.







The key ideas at a glance

Plan from where you are, then replan. From any one state, only a small part of the state space is reachable in a few steps. Receding horizon planning looks \(d\) steps ahead from the current state, takes the best first action, and repeats from wherever it lands. Replanning at every step makes up for a short horizon and for surprises.
Forward search: try everything, then estimate beyond the horizon. Expand every action and every possible outcome to depth \(d\), and put a value estimate \(U(s)\) at the leaves. The cost grows exponentially with depth, so the leaf values matter enormously. A good offline estimate, such as one from Chapter 8, makes a shallow search good. Combining the two is called hybrid planning.
Branch and bound: skip what can’t win. With a lower bound on values and an upper bound on action values, a branch whose best case is worse than something already found needn’t be explored. It returns exactly what forward search does, usually with far less work.
Sampling: simulate instead of enumerate. You only need a simulator, not the full transition table:

Rollouts estimate a state’s value by simulating some simple policy.
Sparse sampling follows only \(m\) sampled outcomes per action, so its cost no longer depends on the number of states.
Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) grows a search tree one simulation at a time. It chooses actions with an upper confidence bound (UCB1) that balances actions that look good against actions that haven’t been tried much, so effort flows to promising branches.

Heuristic search: be optimistic, then correct. Start from an optimistic value (an upper bound, also called an admissible heuristic). Repeatedly simulate the greedy policy, updating values along the way. Optimism lures the search into unexplored states, and each disappointment corrects a value. Labeled heuristic search marks states “solved” once their values stop changing, and stops when the current state is solved.
Open-loop planning: commit to a sequence. Instead of a plan that reacts to future outcomes, optimize a fixed sequence of actions, often as a fast continuous optimization. This is model predictive control (MPC). It ignores the chance to adapt later, which can cost a lot when outcomes are uncertain, but replanning at every step recovers much of that.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning

Receding horizon

Leaf value \(U(s)\)
