Hybrid planning
Online search plus an offline value estimate at the leaves


Rollout
A simulation of a simple policy, used to estimate a value


Generative model
A simulator that samples a next state and reward


Branch and bound
Search that prunes branches using upper and lower bounds


Sparse sampling
Search that follows \(m\) sampled outcomes per action


Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS)
Grow a search tree by repeated simulations, guided by UCB1


UCB1
Action score: estimated value plus a bonus for trying rarely tried actions


Admissible heuristic
An optimistic value estimate: never below the true optimal value


Open-loop plan
A fixed sequence of actions, chosen without reacting to outcomes


Model predictive control (MPC)
Optimize an open-loop plan, apply its first action, replan








After this chapter you can

Explain receding horizon planning, and why leaf values and depth trade off.
Run forward search, branch and bound, sparse sampling and MCTS, and compare their costs.
Compute UCB1 scores and explain the role of the exploration constant.
Use an admissible heuristic in heuristic search, and say when a state is “solved”.
Distinguish open-loop from closed-loop plans, and set up a simple model predictive controller.

title: 9 · Online Planning
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



A chess player doesn’t memorize the best move for every possible board. At the board, they think a few moves ahead from this position, judge the resulting positions with experience (“I’m up a knight, that’s good”), play a move, and think again after the reply.

Thinking through every reply is forward search.
Not bothering with a line once it’s clearly worse than one already found is branch and bound.
Thinking harder about the promising lines is Monte Carlo tree search.
“Experience” is the value estimate at the leaves.



We’ll use Hex World (Figure 2): 24 hexagonal tiles, three of them special (+5, −10, +10; landing on one ends the game after collecting it). Each move goes the intended way with probability 0.7, and veers to a neighboring direction otherwise. Bumping a wall costs 1, and future rewards are discounted by \(\gamma = 0.9\) per step. We know the exact optimal policy from Chapter 7, so we can score every planner against it.








Figure 2: Hex World, with the running example’s start (the middle tile, thick border). Numbers show how many steps it takes to first reach each tile from there. Within 3 steps only a handful of tiles can be reached, yet a full search tree of depth 3 has thousands of leaves, because it revisits the same tiles along different paths.






Plan from where you are
From the middle tile, only 11 of the 24 tiles can be reached within 3 steps. An online planner never needs values for the rest. Yet a complete search tree of depth 3 from there has 3,078 leaves: there are 6 actions and up to 3 outcomes each, so up to 18 branches per step, and the same tiles appear many times along different paths. See Equation 1.


Forward search and leaf values
Search 3 steps ahead from each of the 21 decision tiles, valuing the leaves at 0 (“I don’t know what happens after that”). This picks the optimal action on 81% of the tiles. Put a rough estimate at the leaves instead, the value of a simple heuristic policy, and even a 1-step search is optimal on 95%, while a 3-step search is optimal on all of them. The search fixes the estimate’s mistakes near the root, and the estimate stands in for everything beyond the horizon (Figure 6).


Pruning with bounds
Suppose the first action you examine is worth 3.2, and an upper bound says another action can be worth at most 2.9. There’s no need to look inside that other action at all. Branch and bound makes exactly the same choices as forward search here, but evaluates only 42% as many leaves at depth 3. See Equation 3.


Sampling and Monte Carlo tree search
Instead of weighing every outcome, simulate: take an action, sample where you land, keep going. Monte Carlo tree search does this again and again from the current state. At each state already in its tree, it picks the action with the best optimistic score: the average return seen so far, plus a bonus that is large for actions tried only a few times. After 500 simulations from each decision tile, it picks the optimal action 89% of the time with a well-scaled bonus (\(c = 10\)), but only 62% with a bonus 10 times too small (\(c = 1\)), because it then stops exploring too soon. See Equation 5.


Heuristic search: optimism, then correction
Start by believing every tile is as good as it could possibly be: the best reward, discounted by the fewest moves needed to reach it. Then walk the greedy path, and after each step replace the tile’s value with a one-step lookahead. Optimistic values pull the walk toward unexplored tiles, and every visit makes a value more realistic. With this heuristic, 20 walks from each tile pick the optimal action 99.5% of the time. With the lazy heuristic “every tile is worth 10”, it’s 87%: a looser heuristic needs more walks. See Equation 7.


Open loop vs. closed loop
A delivery drone can fly the valley route, worth 25 whatever happens, or the ridge route, where the wind turns out to blow left or right, 50/50. On the ridge, the matching turn earns 40 and the wrong turn 5.

Choosing a fixed sequence of actions in advance, the ridge is worth only \(0.5 \times 40 + 0.5 \times 5 = 22.5\), so the valley wins.
A closed-loop plan turns after seeing the wind, and the ridge is worth 40.

Open-loop planning is cheaper but can’t value the chance to react. See Equation 9.

title: 9 · Online Planning
text:
Formalism

Receding horizon and forward search
A receding horizon planner, at each time step, looks ahead \(d\) steps from the current state, takes the best first action, and replans from the next state (ADM §9.1). Forward search does the lookahead exhaustively (ADM §9.3):

\[
U_d(s) = \max_{a} \left( R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a)\, U_{d-1}(s') \right),
\qquad U_0(s) = U(s)
\tag{1}\]

In words. The value of a state with \(d\) steps to go is the best action’s reward plus the discounted average value, with \(d - 1\) steps to go, of where it leads. At the bottom of the tree, use the estimate \(U\).
Term by term.

\(U(s)\) is the leaf estimate: 0 if we just want the best \(d\)-step plan, or an offline approximation (Chapter 8) to account for what lies beyond.
The action chosen now is the maximizing \(a\) at the root.
The tree has up to \((|\mathcal{S}| \times |\mathcal{A}|)^d\) leaves, so the cost is exponential in the depth.

Why it holds. This is \(d\) steps of value iteration (Chapter 7), but computed only for states reachable from the root, recursively rather than for all states at once. If \(U = U^*\), the result is exactly optimal at any depth.


Rollouts
A rollout simulates a policy \(\pi\) (often random or a simple rule) for \(d\) steps using a generative model \(s' \sim T(s, a)\), and returns the discounted sum of rewards (ADM §9.2):

\[
\hat U^{\pi}(s) = \sum_{t=1}^{d} \gamma^{t-1} r_t,
\qquad a_t \sim \pi(s_t),\ \ (s_{t+1}, r_t) \sim \text{simulate}(s_t, a_t)
\tag{2}\]

In words. Play the game forward with a simple policy and add up the discounted rewards. Averaged over \(m\) rollouts, this estimates the policy’s value.
Term by term. A one-step lookahead on rollout values is an approximate policy improvement step (Chapter 7): it usually beats the rollout policy, but has no optimality guarantee. The cost is \(O(m \times |\mathcal{A}| \times |\mathcal{S}| \times d)\) with \(m\) rollouts per next state.


Branch and bound
With a lower bound \(\underline{U}(s) \le U^*(s)\) for the leaves and an upper bound \(\overline{Q}(s, a) \ge Q^*(s, a)\), examine actions from the highest upper bound down (ADM §9.4):

\[
\text{skip action } a \text{ (and all remaining ones) if } \ \overline{Q}(s, a) < \max_{a' \text{ examined}} \hat Q(s, a')
\tag{3}\]

In words. If even the most optimistic value of an action is below something you’ve already found, its subtree can’t change the answer.
Term by term.

\(\hat Q(s, a')\) is the value forward search computes for an action already examined, using \(\underline U\) at the leaves.
Sorting actions by \(\overline{Q}\) means that once one fails the test, every later one does too.
Worst case: nothing is pruned, and the cost equals forward search.

Why it holds. Backups preserve lower bounds, so every \(\hat Q\) computed with \(\underline U\) at the leaves is at most \(Q^*\), which is at most \(\overline Q\). An action with \(\overline{Q}(s, a) < \hat Q(s, a')\) therefore can’t have a larger \(\hat Q\) than \(a'\). On Hex World, the upper bound comes from the fewest moves to each positive reward, and the lower bound is the exact value of acting greedily on that upper bound: any policy’s value is a lower bound on the optimum.


Sparse sampling
Replace the sum over all next states with an average over \(m\) samples (ADM §9.5; M. Kearns, Y. Mansour and A. Ng, Machine Learning, 2002):

\[
\hat Q_d(s, a) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \Big( r^{(i)} + \gamma \max_{a'} \hat Q_{d-1}\big(s'^{(i)}, a'\big) \Big),
\qquad (s'^{(i)}, r^{(i)}) \sim \text{simulate}(s, a)
\tag{4}\]

In words. For each action, sample \(m\) outcomes and recurse on each. Average the results.
Term by term. The tree has \((m \times |\mathcal{A}|)^d\) leaves: still exponential in depth, but independent of the number of states. That’s what matters for huge or continuous state spaces. With \(\hat Q_0\) replaced by the leaf estimate \(U\), the estimate is noisy but converges to forward search as \(m\) grows.


Monte Carlo tree search
MCTS runs \(m\) simulations from the current state (ADM §9.6). Each simulation walks down the current tree choosing actions by UCB1, adds one new state when it leaves the tree, estimates that state’s value (by a rollout or a value function), and updates the statistics along the path. Inside the tree it chooses:

\[
a = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{a} \; Q(s, a) + c \sqrt{\frac{\log N(s)}{N(s, a)}},
\qquad N(s) = \sum_a N(s, a)
\tag{5}\]

In words. Prefer actions that have done well, but add a bonus that shrinks as an action is tried more often and grows (slowly) as the state is visited more. An action never tried gets an infinite bonus.
Term by term.

\(Q(s, a)\) is the average return seen after taking \(a\) in \(s\), and \(N(s, a)\) is how often that happened.
\(c\) sets the exploration strength. It must be on the scale of the values: too small and the search fixes on an early favorite, too large and it wastes simulations on bad actions.
After the simulations, act with \(\arg\max_a Q(s, a)\).

Why it holds. The bonus comes from a concentration bound (Chernoff–Hoeffding): with high probability the true mean is below \(Q + \sqrt{2 \log N / N(s, a)}\) for values in \([0, 1]\). Picking the highest upper confidence bound is optimism in the face of uncertainty, the same idea as in exploration (Chapter 15; P. Auer, N. Cesa-Bianchi and P. Fischer, Machine Learning, 2002). After each simulation returns \(q\), the statistics update as a running mean:

\[
N(s, a) \leftarrow N(s, a) + 1,
\qquad Q(s, a) \leftarrow Q(s, a) + \frac{q - Q(s, a)}{N(s, a)}
\tag{6}\]

In words. Count the visit, then move the average toward the new return by one over the count, which keeps \(Q\) equal to the mean of all returns seen.
Term by term. \(q = r + \gamma \times\) (the value returned by the rest of the simulation). For large or continuous spaces, progressive widening limits how many actions or next states each node may have, growing with its visit count.


Heuristic search and labeling
Heuristic search (ADM §9.7; A. Barto, S. Bradtke and S. Singh, Artificial Intelligence, 1995) keeps a value table \(U\), initialized to an upper bound \(\overline U \ge U^*\), and runs \(m\) greedy simulations of depth \(d\) from the current state, updating every visited state:

\[
U(s) \leftarrow \max_a \left( R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a)\, U(s') \right)
\quad \text{for each } s \text{ visited by the greedy policy}
\tag{7}\]

In words. Walk where the current values say is best, and correct each value you pass with a one-step lookahead.
Term by term.

An admissible heuristic \(\overline{U}\) (never below \(U^*\)) makes unexplored states look attractive, so they get visited and corrected.
Backups keep \(U\) above \(U^*\) throughout, and the values converge to \(U^*\) on the states the optimal policy reaches.
Tighter upper bounds need fewer simulations.

Labeled heuristic search (ADM §9.8; B. Bonet and H. Geffner, ICAPS, 2003) calls a state solved when every state in its greedy envelope (the states the greedy policy can reach from it) has a small residual:

\[
\big|\, U(s') - \max_a \big(R(s', a) + \gamma \textstyle\sum_{s''} T(s'' \mid s', a)\, U(s'')\big) \big| < \delta
\quad \text{for every } s' \text{ in the greedy envelope of } s
\tag{8}\]

In words. A state is solved when one more lookahead wouldn’t change any value it depends on by more than \(\delta\).
Term by term. Solved states are never updated again, and simulations stop when they reach one. The search ends when the current state is solved, so it spends effort only where values are still moving.


Open-loop planning and model predictive control
A closed-loop plan says what to do in every future state, so it can react to what happens. An open-loop plan is a fixed sequence of actions (ADM §9.9):

\[
\max_{a_{1:d}} \ U(a_{1:d}),
\qquad U(a_{1:d}) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \sum_{t=1}^{d} \gamma^{t-1} R(s_t, a_t) \right]
\tag{9}\]

In words. Choose the whole sequence of actions up front to maximize the expected return.
Term by term. \(U(a_{1:d})\) averages over outcomes but can’t condition later actions on them, so an open-loop plan can never beat the best closed-loop plan, and can be much worse (the drone example). Its advantage is that it’s often a fast continuous optimization.
Model predictive control makes it concrete by assuming deterministic dynamics (for example, the most likely outcome), solving the optimization, applying only the first action, and replanning:

\[
\max_{a_{1:d},\, s_{2:d}} \ \sum_{t=1}^{d} \gamma^{t} R(s_t, a_t)
\quad \text{subject to} \quad s_{t+1} = T(s_t, a_t),\ \ t = 1, \ldots, d-1
\tag{10}\]

In words. Pretend the future is predictable, find the best action sequence under that assumption, use its first step, and repeat as reality unfolds.
Term by term.

\(T(s, a)\) here is a deterministic function. With linear dynamics and a concave reward (a convex cost), the problem is convex and fast to solve.
Robust MPC instead maximizes the worst case over a set of possible outcomes, which is safer but often very conservative.
Multiforecast MPC plans against \(m\) sampled scenarios, either for the worst one or on average, with a separate action sequence per scenario but a shared first action. This is also called hindsight optimization.

title: 9 · Online Planning
text:
Algorithms & code

Exhaustive search: forward search and branch and bound

PythonJulia


def lookahead(mdp, U, s: int, a: int) -> float:
    """R(s, a) + gamma * sum_s2 T(s2 | s, a) U(s2), visiting only the
    next states that can actually happen."""
    p = mdp.T[s, a]
    future = sum(p[s2] * U(s2) for s2 in np.flatnonzero(p))
    return float(mdp.R[s, a] + mdp.gamma * future)

def forward_search(mdp, s: int, d: int, U) -> tuple[int | None, float]:
    """Best action and its value, searching every action and every
    possible next state to depth d, with U(s) at the leaves."""
    if d <= 0:
        return None, U(s)

    def U_next(s2):                   # value of s2 with d - 1 steps left
        return forward_search(mdp, s2, d - 1, U)[1]
    q = [lookahead(mdp, U_next, s, a) for a in range(mdp.T.shape[1])]
    a = int(np.argmax(q))
    return a, q[a]

def branch_and_bound(mdp, s: int, d: int, U_lo, Q_hi) -> tuple:
    """Forward search that skips actions which can't win: U_lo (a lower
    bound on U) values the leaves, and Q_hi (an upper bound on Q) says how
    good an action could possibly be."""
    if d <= 0:
        return None, U_lo(s)

    def U_next(s2):
        return branch_and_bound(mdp, s2, d - 1, U_lo, Q_hi)[1]
    best_a, best_u = None, -np.inf
    # Try the most promising actions first, so pruning starts early.
    for a in sorted(range(mdp.T.shape[1]), key=lambda a: -Q_hi(s, a)):
        if Q_hi(s, a) < best_u:
            break          # this action and all later ones can't do better
        u = lookahead(mdp, U_next, s, a)
        if u > best_u:
            best_a, best_u = a, u
    return best_a, best_u


using ADM, LinearAlgebra

# Hex World from the problem zoo: T[s, a, s′], R[s, a], γ. States and actions are indices.
mdp = hex_world()
nS, nA = size(mdp.R)

# R(s, a) + γ Σ T(s′ | s, a) U(s′), visiting only next states that can happen.
lookahead(mdp, U, s, a) = mdp.R[s, a] + mdp.γ * sum(mdp.T[s, a, s′] * U(s′) for s′ in findall(>(0), mdp.T[s, a, :]))

# Best action and its value, searching every action and outcome to depth d; U values the leaves.
function forward_search(mdp, s, d, U)
    d <= 0 && return (a = nothing, u = U(s))
    U′(s′) = forward_search(mdp, s′, d - 1, U).u      # value with d - 1 steps left
    q = [lookahead(mdp, U′, s, a) for a in 1:nA]
    a = argmax(q)
    return (a = a, u = q[a])
end

# Same answer as forward search, skipping actions whose upper bound Q_hi can't beat the best so far.
function branch_and_bound(mdp, s, d, U_lo, Q_hi)
    d <= 0 && return (a = nothing, u = U_lo(s))
    U′(s′) = branch_and_bound(mdp, s′, d - 1, U_lo, Q_hi).u
    best = (a = nothing, u = -Inf)
    for a in sort(1:nA, by = a -> -Q_hi(s, a))    # most promising first
        Q_hi(s, a) < best.u && break              # nothing left can win
        u = lookahead(mdp, U′, s, a)
        u > best.u && (best = (a = a, u = u))
    end
    return best
end

# Exact optimum (value iteration to a tight tolerance) to check against.
function solve(mdp; tol = 1e-12)
    U = zeros(nS)
    while true
        U′ = [maximum(lookahead(mdp, s′ -> U[s′], s, a) for a in 1:nA) for s in 1:nS]
        maximum(abs.(U′ - U)) < tol && return U′
        U = U′
    end
end
U_star = solve(mdp)
Q_star(s, a) = lookahead(mdp, s′ -> U_star[s′], s, a)





Sampling: rollouts, sparse sampling and Monte Carlo tree search

PythonJulia


def sample_step(mdp, s: int, a: int, rng) -> tuple[int, float]:
    """Generative model: draw s2 ~ T(. | s, a) and return (s2, reward)."""
    s2 = rng.choice(len(mdp.T), p=mdp.T[s, a])
    return int(s2), float(mdp.R[s, a])

def rollout(mdp, s: int, policy, d: int, rng) -> float:
    """Discounted return of one simulation of `policy` for d steps."""
    ret = 0.0
    for t in range(d):
        s, r = sample_step(mdp, s, policy(s, rng), rng)
        ret += mdp.gamma**t * r
    return ret

def rollout_lookahead(mdp, s: int, policy, d: int, m: int, rng) -> int:
    """Look one step ahead, valuing each next state by the average of m
    rollouts of `policy` (a one-step policy improvement, as in Ch 7)."""
    def U(s2):
        return np.mean([rollout(mdp, s2, policy, d, rng) for _ in range(m)])
    q = [lookahead(mdp, U, s, a) for a in range(mdp.T.shape[1])]
    return int(np.argmax(q))

def sparse_sampling(mdp, s: int, d: int, m: int, U, rng) -> tuple:
    """Forward search that follows only m sampled next states per action,
    so its cost no longer depends on the number of states."""
    if d <= 0:
        return None, U(s)
    best_a, best_u = None, -np.inf
    for a in range(mdp.T.shape[1]):
        u = 0.0
        for _ in range(m):
            s2, r = sample_step(mdp, s, a, rng)
            u += (r + mdp.gamma * sparse_sampling(mdp, s2, d - 1, m, U,
                                                  rng)[1]) / m
        if u > best_u:
            best_a, best_u = a, u
    return best_a, best_u

class MonteCarloTreeSearch:
    """Grow a search tree with m simulations from the current state, using
    UCB1 to balance trying promising actions against untried ones."""

    def __init__(self, mdp, d: int, m: int, c: float, U, rng):
        self.mdp, self.d, self.m, self.c, self.U = mdp, d, m, c, U
        self.rng = rng
        self.N = {}    # N[s][a]: how often action a was tried in state s
        self.Q = {}    # Q[s][a]: average return seen after doing so

    def __call__(self, s: int) -> int:
        for _ in range(self.m):
            self.simulate(s, self.d)
        return int(np.argmax(self.Q[s]))

    def simulate(self, s: int, d: int) -> float:
        if d <= 0:
            return self.U(s)
        n_actions = self.mdp.T.shape[1]
        if s not in self.N:           # a new leaf: add it, estimate its value
            self.N[s], self.Q[s] = np.zeros(n_actions), np.zeros(n_actions)
            return self.U(s)
        a = self.explore(s)
        s2, r = sample_step(self.mdp, s, a, self.rng)
        q = r + self.mdp.gamma * self.simulate(s2, d - 1)
        self.N[s][a] += 1
        self.Q[s][a] += (q - self.Q[s][a]) / self.N[s][a]  # running mean
        return q

    def explore(self, s: int) -> int:
        """UCB1: Q(s, a) + c sqrt(log N(s) / N(s, a)); untried actions
        get an infinite bonus, so each is tried once first."""
        N, Q = self.N[s], self.Q[s]
        bonus = np.full(len(N), np.inf)
        tried = N > 0
        if tried.any():
            bonus[tried] = np.sqrt(np.log(N.sum()) / N[tried])
        return int(np.argmax(Q + self.c * bonus))


using Random

# Generative model: sample s′ from T(· | s, a) by inverting the cumulative distribution.
sample_step(mdp, s, a, rng) = (findfirst(cumsum(mdp.T[s, a, :]) .>= rand(rng)), mdp.R[s, a])

function sparse_sampling(mdp, s, d, m, U, rng)
    d <= 0 && return (a = nothing, u = U(s))
    best = (a = nothing, u = -Inf)
    for a in 1:nA
        u = 0.0
        for _ in 1:m                               # m sampled outcomes per action
            s′, r = sample_step(mdp, s, a, rng)
            u += (r + mdp.γ * sparse_sampling(mdp, s′, d - 1, m, U, rng).u) / m
        end
        u > best.u && (best = (a = a, u = u))
    end
    return best
end

# Monte Carlo tree search: N and Q are dictionaries keyed by state, holding one entry per action.
struct MCTS
    mdp; d::Int; m::Int; c::Float64; U::Function; rng
    N::Dict{Int, Vector{Float64}}
    Q::Dict{Int, Vector{Float64}}
end
MCTS(mdp, d, m, c, U, rng) = MCTS(mdp, d, m, c, U, rng, Dict(), Dict())

function (π::MCTS)(s)
    for _ in 1:π.m
        simulate!(π, s, π.d)
    end
    return argmax(π.Q[s])
end

function simulate!(π::MCTS, s, d)
    d <= 0 && return π.U(s)
    if !haskey(π.N, s)                             # new leaf: add it and estimate its value
        π.N[s], π.Q[s] = zeros(nA), zeros(nA)
        return π.U(s)
    end
    N, Q = π.N[s], π.Q[s]
    # UCB1: untried actions (N = 0) get an infinite bonus.
    bonus = [n == 0 ? Inf : sqrt(log(sum(N)) / n) for n in N]
    a = argmax(Q .+ π.c .* bonus)
    s′, r = sample_step(π.mdp, s, a, π.rng)
    q = r + π.mdp.γ * simulate!(π, s′, d - 1)
    N[a] += 1
    Q[a] += (q - Q[a]) / N[a]                      # running mean of the returns
    return q
end





Heuristic search and labeled heuristic search

PythonJulia


def greedy(mdp, U: Array, s: int) -> tuple[int, float]:
    """Best action at s by one-step lookahead on a value table U."""
    q = mdp.R[s] + mdp.gamma * mdp.T[s] @ U     # one entry per action
    a = int(np.argmax(q))
    return a, float(q[a])

def heuristic_search(mdp, s: int, U_hi: Array, d: int, m: int, rng):
    """Run m greedy simulations of depth d from s, updating U by one-step
    lookahead along the way (real-time dynamic programming). Starting from
    an upper bound U_hi makes unexplored states look attractive."""
    U = np.array(U_hi, dtype=float)
    for _ in range(m):
        state = s
        for _ in range(d):
            a, U[state] = greedy(mdp, U, state)
            state, _ = sample_step(mdp, state, a, rng)
    return greedy(mdp, U, s)[0], U

def labeled_heuristic_search(mdp, s: int, U_hi: Array, d: int,
                             delta: float, rng, max_sims: int = 10_000):
    """Heuristic search that stops once s is 'solved': every state the
    greedy policy can reach from s has a residual below delta."""
    U, solved, sims = np.array(U_hi, dtype=float), set(), 0
    while s not in solved and sims < max_sims:
        visited, state = [], s
        for _ in range(d):           # a greedy simulation, as before
            if state in solved:
                break
            visited.append(state)
            a, U[state] = greedy(mdp, U, state)
            state, _ = sample_step(mdp, state, a, rng)
        # Try to label the visited states, last first; stop at the first
        # one whose greedy envelope still has a large residual.
        while visited and _label(mdp, U, solved, visited.pop(), delta):
            pass
        sims += 1
    return greedy(mdp, U, s)[0], U, sims
def _label(mdp, U: Array, solved: set, s: int, delta: float) -> bool:
    """Mark s and its greedy envelope solved if all residuals are below
    delta; otherwise update the envelope's values. True if solved."""
    if s in solved:
        return True
    envelope, to_expand, converged = [], [s], True
    while to_expand:                 # states reachable under greedy actions
        state = to_expand.pop()
        envelope.append(state)
        a, u = greedy(mdp, U, state)
        if abs(U[state] - u) > delta:
            converged = False
        else:                        # only expand states that look settled
            for s2 in np.flatnonzero(mdp.T[state, a]):
                if s2 not in solved and s2 not in envelope + to_expand:
                    to_expand.append(int(s2))
    if converged:
        solved.update(envelope)
    else:
        for state in reversed(envelope):
            U[state] = greedy(mdp, U, state)[1]
    return converged


# One-step lookahead on a value table U: best action and its value.
function greedy(mdp, U, s)
    q = [lookahead(mdp, s′ -> U[s′], s, a) for a in 1:nA]
    a = argmax(q)
    return a, q[a]
end

# Greedy simulations from s, correcting each visited value; U starts at an upper bound.
function heuristic_search(mdp, s, U_hi, d, m, rng)
    U = copy(U_hi)
    for _ in 1:m
        state = s
        for _ in 1:d
            a, U[state] = greedy(mdp, U, state)
            state, _ = sample_step(mdp, state, a, rng)
        end
    end
    return greedy(mdp, U, s)[1], U
end

# The optimistic heuristic: each positive reward discounted by the fewest moves to reach it.
function optimistic_values(mdp)
    tiles, U = ADM.HEX_STANDARD_TILES, zeros(nS)
    for (target, r) in ADM.HEX_STANDARD_REWARDS
        r > 0 || continue
        steps, frontier = Dict(target => 0), [target]
        while !isempty(frontier)                   # breadth-first search over neighbors
            next = []
            for t in frontier, dir in ADM.HEX_DIRECTIONS
                n = ADM.hex_neighbor(t, dir)
                if n in tiles && !haskey(steps, n)
                    steps[n] = steps[t] + 1
                    push!(next, n)
                end
            end
            frontier = next
        end
        for (t, k) in steps
            i = findfirst(==(t), tiles)
            U[i] = max(U[i], r * mdp.γ^k)
        end
    end
    return U
end





Model predictive control

PythonJulia


def double_integrator(s0: Array, a: Array) -> tuple[Array, Array]:
    """Positions and velocities after each action for a point that
    accelerates in 2-D: s0 = [x, y, vx, vy], a[t] = [ax, ay].
    Velocity changes first, then position moves by the new velocity."""
    v = s0[2:] + np.cumsum(a, axis=0)
    p = s0[:2] + np.cumsum(v, axis=0)
    return p, v

def mpc_plan(s0: Array, goal: Array, centers: Array, radius: float,
             a_max: float, weight: float = 50.0, warm: Array | None = None):
    """Open-loop plan for the double integrator: minimize effort
    sum ||a_t||^2 plus weight * (distance from the goal state at the end)^2,
    keeping each planned position outside a circle. centers[t] is where
    the planner expects the obstacle's center at step t + 1, so the plan has
    len(centers) steps. Returns the (d, 2) actions."""
    from scipy.optimize import minimize
    d = len(centers)

    def cost(x):
        a = x.reshape(d, 2)
        p, v = double_integrator(s0, a)
        miss = np.sum((p[-1] - goal[:2])**2) + np.sum((v[-1] - goal[2:])**2)
        return np.sum(a**2) + weight * miss

    def clearance(x):                # must be >= 0 at every step
        p, _ = double_integrator(s0, x.reshape(d, 2))
        return np.sum((p - centers)**2, axis=1) - radius**2
    x0 = np.zeros(2 * d) if warm is None else warm.ravel()
    result = minimize(cost, x0, method="SLSQP",
                      bounds=[(-a_max, a_max)] * (2 * d),
                      constraints=[{"type": "ineq", "fun": clearance}],
                      options={"maxiter": 300})
    return result.x.reshape(d, 2)


# The double integrator: velocity changes by the action, then position by the new velocity.
function double_integrator(s0, a)                 # a is d × 2
    v = s0[3:4]' .+ cumsum(a, dims = 1)
    p = s0[1:2]' .+ cumsum(v, dims = 1)
    return p, v
end
# Solving the MPC problem needs a constrained optimizer, typically JuMP.jl with Ipopt, which
# this site doesn't depend on; see the Python tab (SciPy's SLSQP) for the solver.

# The drone example: best open-loop plan versus the closed-loop plan.
payoff = Dict(("valley", :left) => [25, 25], ("valley", :right) => [25, 25],   # [wind left, wind right]
              ("ridge", :left) => [40, 5], ("ridge", :right) => [5, 40])
open_loop = maximum(sum(0.5 .* v) for v in values(payoff))
closed_loop = maximum(sum(0.5 .* max.(payoff[(route, :left)], payoff[(route, :right)])) for route in ("valley", "ridge"))
@assert (open_loop, closed_loop) == (25.0, 40.0)

Q_hi(s, a) = lookahead(mdp, s′ -> U_hi[s′], s, a)

The two best actions differ by only 0.35 in true value, and MCTS’s averages include the returns of its own exploratory moves deeper in the tree, so 1,000 simulations aren’t always enough to separate them. NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)

title: 9 · Online Planning
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: pruning by hand. At a state, the upper bounds on three actions are \(\overline{Q} = 5.0, 4.0, 2.0\). Branch and bound examines the first and finds it’s worth 3.5 (with lower-bound leaves). Which actions must still be examined?






TipSolution





Actions are examined in order of their upper bounds. The second action’s upper bound, 4.0, is above 3.5, so it could still win and must be examined. Suppose it turns out worth 3.8. Then the third action’s upper bound, 2.0, is below the best found, 3.8, so it and anything after it are pruned. If the second action had been worth less than 3.5, the third would still be pruned, since 2.0 < 3.5.



Problem 2: when sparse sampling saves nothing. In Hex World each action has at most 3 possible outcomes. Compare the number of leaves of forward search and of sparse sampling with \(m = 3\) at depth \(d\). When does sparse sampling pay off?






TipSolution





Forward search branches on 6 actions and at most 3 outcomes: up to \(18^d\) leaves. Sparse sampling with \(m = 3\) branches on 6 actions and 3 samples: exactly \(18^d\) leaves, and its values are noisy. On Hex World, sampling buys nothing. It pays off when actions have many possible outcomes (hundreds, or a continuum), since sparse sampling’s \((m|\mathcal{A}|)^d\) doesn’t grow with the number of outcomes, while forward search’s does.



Problem 3: combining heuristics. Hex World has two admissible heuristics: \(h_1(s) = 10\) everywhere, and \(h_2\), the reward discounted by the fewest moves. Is \(\min(h_1, h_2)\) admissible? Is it better than either? What about \(\max(h_1, h_2)\)?






TipSolution





Both are at least \(U^*\) everywhere, so their minimum is too: it’s admissible. It’s also at least as tight as each, since it’s never above either. Here \(h_2 \le 10 = h_1\) everywhere, so \(\min(h_1, h_2) = h_2\). The maximum is also admissible, but it’s the looser of the two, so it would slow the search down (compare the two curves in Figure 7).



Problem 4: the value of waiting to see. In the drone example, how large must the valley’s payoff be before closed-loop planning also prefers the valley? And below what valley payoff does open-loop planning choose the ridge?






TipSolution





Closed-loop planning values the ridge at 40 (it turns with the wind), so it prefers the valley only if the valley pays more than 40. Open-loop planning values the ridge at 22.5, so it chooses the ridge only if the valley pays less than 22.5. Between 22.5 and 40, the two disagree. That gap is the value of being able to react, the value of information from Chapter 6.



Problem 5: scaling the exploration constant. If every reward in Hex World were multiplied by 100, what should happen to MCTS’s exploration constant \(c\) to keep the same behavior? Why did \(c = 1\) work poorly here?






TipSolution





UCB1 adds \(Q(s, a)\), which would scale by 100, to \(c \sqrt{\log N(s)/N(s, a)}\), which doesn’t depend on the rewards. To keep the same balance, \(c\) must also be multiplied by 100. In Hex World, the action values differ by a few units, and \(c = 1\) adds a bonus below 1 after a few visits. So the search locks onto whichever action looked best early, and rarely revisits the others.

title: 9 · Online Planning
text:
Recap

Online planning chooses an action for the current state only, in a receding-horizon loop (Equation 1). Why it matters: it scales to problems where no offline policy fits, because only reachable states matter, and it’s how game engines, robots and POMDP planners (Chapter 22) act.
The deeper the search, the less the leaf values matter, but cost grows exponentially; good leaf values make shallow searches good. Why it matters: combining offline approximations (Chapter 8) with online search is the standard recipe for large problems.
Bounds prune (Equation 3), samples replace sums (Equation 4), and UCB1 steers simulations toward promising actions (Equation 5). Why it matters: each trades exactness for speed differently. MCTS’s exploration bonus is the same idea as in exploration (Chapter 15).
Optimistic values drive heuristic search, and labeling stops it when the answer has settled (Equation 7, Equation 8). Why it matters: tighter admissible heuristics mean less search, which is why designing good bounds is worth the effort.
Open-loop plans and MPC optimize action sequences quickly but can’t value reacting later (Equation 9, Equation 10). Why it matters: MPC is the workhorse of engineering control, and knowing its blind spot (and the model’s) tells you when replanning is enough.

Common pitfalls

Valuing leaves at zero when the goal is far away. Every plan then looks the same (the mountain car explorer), and the planner acts arbitrarily.
An exploration constant on the wrong scale. Set MCTS’s \(c\) relative to the spread of action values.
An “upper bound” that isn’t one. An inadmissible heuristic can make heuristic search settle on a suboptimal policy.
Trusting open-loop values under uncertainty. An open-loop plan undervalues actions whose payoff comes from reacting to what happens.
Replanning with the wrong model. MPC replans every step, but if it predicts the world wrongly (a static obstacle that actually moves), it can still crash.

title: 7 · Exact Solution Methods
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Part I ended with Chapter 6, which chose a single action to maximize expected utility. Most real problems are sequences: each action changes the situation, which changes what the next action should be. Part II (Chapters 7–14) handles such sequential decisions when the current state is always known. This chapter is its foundation: it solves them exactly, assuming the rules of the world are fully known. Every later chapter relaxes something: - huge state spaces (Ch 8, Ch 9); - searching over policies directly (Ch 10–13); - unknown rules that must be learned (Part III); - a hidden state (Part IV, starting at Ch 19).
The question: if you know exactly how the world responds to your actions (with probabilities) and what each outcome is worth, what should you do in every situation to collect the most reward over time?
The short answer: compute what every situation is worth when you act well from it, then in each situation take the action that leads to the best mix of immediate reward and future worth. Policy iteration and value iteration are two ways to compute those worths.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Both algorithms start from the MDP model and end with an optimal policy. Policy iteration loops between evaluating and improving a policy; value iteration repeats one backup until the values settle. The book also covers asynchronous value iteration, a linear-program formulation, and LQR (ADM §7.6–7.8).







The key ideas at a glance

A Markov decision process (MDP) describes the world. It lists:

the states (situations) and actions (choices);
a transition model giving the probability of each next state after each action;
a reward for each action in each state;
a discount factor \(\gamma\) (gamma) between 0 and 1, which makes a reward one step later worth \(\gamma\) times as much.

“Markov” means the next state depends only on the current state and action, not on the history.
A policy says what to do; its value says how good that is. A policy picks an action for every state. The value of a state under a policy is the expected total of discounted rewards from following it forever. A useful rule of thumb: \(1/(1-\gamma)\) is roughly how many steps ahead the agent effectively cares about. For \(\gamma = 0.9\) that’s about 10 steps.
A state’s value is reward now plus discounted value next. This self-consistency is the Bellman expectation equation. It turns an infinite sum into a one-step relation, so evaluating a policy means solving one linear system, or repeating the one-step relation until it settles.
Good values give good actions. Given values for every state, the one-step lookahead (the Q-value) of an action is its immediate reward plus the discounted average value of where it leads. Picking the best lookahead in each state is acting greedily.
Policy iteration: evaluate, improve, repeat. Start from any policy. Compute its values exactly, switch every state to its greedy action, and repeat. Each round is at least as good as the last, and after a handful of rounds nothing changes: the policy is optimal.
Value iteration: back up the best lookahead until the values settle. Start with all values 0. Repeatedly replace each state’s value with its best lookahead, a Bellman backup. Good news spreads outward from rewarding states, one step per sweep. Stop when the largest change in one sweep, the Bellman residual, is small enough to guarantee the values are within a chosen accuracy, then act greedily.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




State, action
A situation; a choice available in it


Transition model \(T(s' \mid s, a)\)
Probability of landing in \(s'\) after taking \(a\) in \(s\)


Reward \(R(s, a)\)
Expected immediate payoff for taking \(a\) in \(s\)


Discount factor \(\gamma\)
How much a reward one step later is worth compared to now


Policy \(\pi\)
A rule choosing an action in every state


Value \(U(s)\)
Expected discounted total reward from \(s\) onward


Q-value \(Q(s, a)\)
Value of taking \(a\) now, then continuing with the given values


Greedy
Picking the action with the best one-step lookahead


Bellman backup
Replace a state’s value with its best lookahead


Bellman residual
The largest change in any state’s value during one sweep








After this chapter you can

Write a sequential decision problem as an MDP: arrays of transition probabilities and rewards.
Compute the value of any policy, by iteration or by one linear solve.
Find an optimal policy with policy iteration or value iteration, and pick a stopping threshold with a guaranteed accuracy.
Predict how the discount factor changes what an agent is willing to go after.

title: 7 · Exact Solution Methods
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



A rover on a grid is looking for rock samples. It knows where the samples are, but its wheels slip: 30% of the time it moves in a direction it didn’t choose.
Imagine every cell holds a sticky note with one number: how much reward can I expect from here if I drive well? At first every note says 0. Then, in every round, each cell looks at its neighbors’ notes and updates its own: “If I head east, I usually land on the cell to my east, sometimes on another neighbor. Averaged over where I land, which direction gives me the best note, after discounting a little because it’s one step later?”
In round 1 only the cells with samples learn anything. In round 2 their neighbors notice. Good news spreads outward one cell per round, fading with distance, like a ripple. Once the notes stop changing, the best move from each cell is simply to head toward the best-looking neighbor.


That ripple is value iteration. Figure 2 shows it on the Rover grid used throughout this page. The top-right sample is worth +10, the crater beside it −10, and the rock at bottom left +3. The two gray cells are walls.








Figure 2: Value iteration on the Rover grid (γ = 0.9). After one sweep only the reward cells have value. Each later sweep spreads value one step further from the rewards, until the values stop changing.






Discounting: later rewards count for less
With \(\gamma = 0.9\), a reward worth 10 now is worth \(0.9 \times 10 = 9\) one step away, and \(0.9^{10} \times 10 \approx 3.5\) ten steps away. That’s why a far reward can lose to a near one. In the Rover grid, a small discount makes the rover settle for the nearby +3 rock, while a large one sends it all the way to the +10 site. Discounting also keeps the total of an endless stream of rewards finite. See Equation 1 and the γ slider.


Evaluating a plan: reward now plus what comes next
A delivery drone that always delivers, even on low battery, earns −6 per step once it’s low, and stays low forever. Its value when low is \(-6\) now plus \(0.9\) times its value when low. Solving \(U = -6 + 0.9\,U\) gives \(U = -60\): \(-6\) per step times an effective horizon of 10 steps. No infinite sum is needed, just a one-step relation that must hold. See Equation 2.


Acting on values: look one step ahead
Suppose you know every cell’s value. In a given cell, for each direction ask: “What do I get now, plus 0.9 times the average value of where I’ll probably land?” Take the direction with the best answer. You don’t need to plan the whole route. The values already summarize everything beyond one step. See Equation 4.


Value iteration: the ripple
That ripple in Figure 2 is value iteration. Each sweep lets every cell look one step further ahead. After sweep \(k\), a cell’s value is the best it can do in \(k\) steps, and sweeps continue until the values stop changing. The number of sweeps needed grows with \(\gamma\): the more the future matters, the further the ripple must travel before it settles. See Equation 7.


Policy iteration: measure the plan, fix every bad move
There is a second, more managerial way to get the same answer. Start with any plan, say “always drive north”. Measure exactly how good that plan is from every cell. Then fix every cell whose move is worse than the best alternative under those measurements. Repeat until no fix helps. That’s policy iteration. On the Rover grid it needs 3 rounds where value iteration needs 41 sweeps, but each round solves a linear system. See Policy iteration in the Formalism.


Knowing when to stop
Value iteration never exactly finishes, so when is it close enough? Watch the biggest change in any cell during a sweep. With \(\gamma = 0.9\), if nothing moved by more than \(0.001\), every value is within \(0.009\) of the true one. The factor \(\gamma/(1-\gamma) = 9\) comes from errors that shrink geometrically. See Equation 8.

title: 7 · Exact Solution Methods
text:
Formalism

Markov decision processes
An MDP (ADM §7.1) has:

a set of states \(\mathcal{S}\) and a set of actions \(\mathcal{A}\);
a transition model \(T(s' \mid s, a)\), the probability of landing in \(s'\) after taking \(a\) in \(s\);
a reward function \(R(s, a)\), the expected reward for taking \(a\) in \(s\);
a discount factor \(\gamma \in [0, 1)\), which makes a reward \(k\) steps away worth \(\gamma^k\) times as much as one received now.

A policy \(\pi\) maps each state to an action. How good is a policy? Follow it from \(s\) forever and add up the rewards, shrinking each by \(\gamma\) for every step of delay:

\[
U^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\, \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r_t \;\Big|\; s_0 = s,\ a_t = \pi(s_t) \Big]
\tag{1}\]

In words. Start in \(s\), follow \(\pi\) forever, and add up the rewards, each one shrunk by \(\gamma\) for every step you had to wait for it. The transitions are random, so average over every way the future could unfold.
Term by term.

\(r_t\) is the reward received at step \(t\). Here it equals \(R(s_t, \pi(s_t))\).
\(\gamma^t\) is the discount. With \(\gamma = 0.9\), a reward 10 steps away counts \(0.9^{10} \approx 0.35\) as much as one received now.
\(\mathbb{E}[\cdot \mid s_0 = s, \ldots]\) averages over the random transitions, given that you start in \(s\) and always act by \(\pi\).

Why discount? With \(\gamma < 1\) the infinite sum is always finite: if every reward is at most \(R_{\max}\), then \(|U^\pi(s)| \le R_{\max}/(1-\gamma)\). A useful rule of thumb is that \(1/(1-\gamma)\) is the effective horizon: about 10 steps for \(\gamma = 0.9\), and about 100 for \(\gamma = 0.99\).


Policy evaluation
Equation 1 is a definition, not a recipe: it has an infinite sum inside an average. The trick that makes it computable is to split off the first step (ADM §7.2).

\[
U^\pi(s) = R(s, \pi(s)) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \pi(s))\, U^\pi(s')
\tag{2}\]

In words. What a state is worth under \(\pi\) equals the reward you get right now, plus \(\gamma\) times the average worth of wherever you land next.
Term by term.

\(R(s, \pi(s))\) is the reward for the action the policy picks in \(s\).
\(T(s' \mid s, \pi(s))\) is the probability of landing in \(s'\).
\(\sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \pi(s))\, U^\pi(s')\) is the probability-weighted average of the next state’s value: what the future is worth, on average, one step from now.
\(\gamma\) discounts that future by one step.

Why it holds. In Equation 1, separate the \(t = 0\) term from the rest: \(\sum_{t \ge 0} \gamma^t r_t = r_0 + \gamma \sum_{t \ge 1} \gamma^{t-1} r_t\). The first part averages to \(R(s, \pi(s))\). The second part is \(\gamma\) times the discounted return starting from the next state \(s_1\). Because the process is Markov, the future after \(s_1\) depends only on \(s_1\), so that return averages to \(U^\pi(s_1)\). Averaging over \(s_1 \sim T(\cdot \mid s, \pi(s))\) gives the sum.
Try it. On the drone with “always deliver”, Low only ever returns to Low, so Equation 2 reads \(U(\text{Low}) = -6 + 0.9\, U(\text{Low})\), which gives \(U(\text{Low}) = -60\). That is \(-6\) per step times the effective horizon of 10.
There is one such equation per state, and every one is linear in the unknowns \(U^\pi(s')\). Stack them into vectors and matrices:

\[
\mathbf{U}^\pi = \mathbf{R}^\pi + \gamma \mathbf{T}^\pi \mathbf{U}^\pi
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{U}^\pi = (\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{T}^\pi)^{-1} \mathbf{R}^\pi
\tag{3}\]

In words. Policy evaluation is solving one linear system.
Term by term.

\(\mathbf{U}^\pi\) is the column of values, one entry per state.
\(\mathbf{R}^\pi\) is the column of rewards \(R(s, \pi(s))\).
\(\mathbf{T}^\pi\) is the \(|\mathcal{S}| \times |\mathcal{S}|\) matrix with entry \((s, s')\) equal to \(T(s' \mid s, \pi(s))\). Each row sums to 1.
\((\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{T}^\pi)\) is always invertible when \(\gamma < 1\), so there is exactly one solution.

There are two ways to solve it:

Exactly, with one linear solve. This costs about \(O(|\mathcal{S}|^3)\), which is fine for thousands of states and hopeless for billions (the subject of Chapter 8).
Iteratively: start with \(U = 0\) and keep replacing \(U\) with the right-hand side of Equation 2. Each pass shrinks the largest error by at least a factor \(\gamma\), and each pass costs only \(O(|\mathcal{S}|^2)\).



Acting on a value function
Values are only useful if they tell you what to do. Given any value function \(U\), not necessarily a correct one, ask of each action: “If I take \(a\) once and then collect \(U\), how well do I do?” (ADM §7.3).

\[
Q(s, a) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a)\, U(s')
\tag{4}\]

In words. Try action \(a\) once, then let \(U\) score wherever you land.
Term by term. It is Equation 2 with the policy’s action \(\pi(s)\) replaced by an arbitrary action \(a\), and \(U^\pi\) replaced by any value function \(U\). \(Q\) has one number per (state, action) pair, where \(U\) has one per state.
Acting well then means picking the action with the best lookahead:

\[
\pi(s) = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_a Q(s, a)
\tag{5}\]

In words. In each state, take the action whose one-step lookahead scores highest. \(\arg\max\) returns the action that attains the maximum, not the maximum value. Ties can be broken any consistent way; the code on this page takes the first.
The advantage \(A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - U(s)\) measures how much better \(a\) is than what \(U\) already expects. The greedy policy picks the action with the largest advantage.


Policy iteration
Policy iteration (ADM §7.4) alternates two steps until the policy stops changing:

Evaluate the current policy exactly with Equation 3.
Improve it by acting greedily on those values with Equation 5.

Why it improves. Suppose that in state \(s\) the greedy action beats the current policy’s action under \(U^\pi\). Switching to it, just once, beats sticking with \(\pi\). Switching in every state where it helps, every time you visit, is better still. This is the policy improvement theorem: the greedy policy is at least as good as \(\pi\) in every state.
Why it stops. Each round makes at least one state strictly better, unless the policy is already optimal. There are only \(|\mathcal{A}|^{|\mathcal{S}|}\) policies, so it can’t improve forever.


Value iteration
What does the best possible value function look like? Acting optimally from \(s\) means choosing the best first action and then continuing optimally from wherever you land. This is Bellman’s principle of optimality, and written out it gives:

\[
U^*(s) = \max_a \Big( R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a)\, U^*(s') \Big)
\tag{6}\]

In words. The best you can do from \(s\) equals the best, over all first actions, of the reward now plus \(\gamma\) times the average best value of where you land.
Compare with Equation 2. It is the same shape, with the fixed action \(\pi(s)\) replaced by a \(\max\) over actions. That \(\max\) makes the equations nonlinear, so there is no single linear solve for \(U^*\). Instead we iterate.
Term by term. The expression inside the parentheses is exactly \(Q(s, a)\) from Equation 4, computed with \(U^*\). So Equation 6 says \(U^*(s) = \max_a Q^*(s, a)\): acting greedily on \(U^*\) reproduces \(U^*\).
Value iteration (ADM §7.5) turns Equation 6 into an update: plug in the current guess on the right, read off a better guess on the left. Repeat for every state in each sweep, starting from \(U_0 = 0\).

\[
U_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \Big( R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a)\, U_k(s') \Big)
\tag{7}\]

In words. A new estimate of each state’s value is its best one-step lookahead on the old estimates.
What \(U_k\) means. \(U_k(s)\) is the best expected discounted reward achievable in exactly \(k\) steps from \(s\). Sweep 1 sees only immediate rewards, and sweep 2 sees two steps ahead. That is the ripple in Figure 2.
Why it converges. Two value functions that differ by at most \(e\) in every state give lookaheads that differ by at most \(\gamma e\), because the lookahead averages the difference and then multiplies it by \(\gamma\). So each backup shrinks the largest error by a factor \(\gamma\): \(\lVert U_{k+1} - U^* \rVert_\infty \le \gamma \lVert U_k - U^* \rVert_\infty\). In the jargon, the backup is a contraction.
When should it stop? We can’t measure the true error \(\lVert U_{k+1} - U^* \rVert_\infty\), the largest error in any state, because \(U^*\) is unknown. We can measure the Bellman residual \(\lVert U_{k+1} - U_k \rVert_\infty\), the largest change in one sweep. The two are linked:

\[
\lVert U_{k+1} - U_k \rVert_\infty < \delta,
\quad \delta = \frac{\epsilon(1-\gamma)}{\gamma}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\lVert U_{k+1} - U^* \rVert_\infty < \epsilon
\tag{8}\]

In words. If no state’s value moved by more than \(\delta\) in the last sweep, then every value is within \(\epsilon\) of the truth.
Term by term.

\(\lVert U \rVert_\infty = \max_s |U(s)|\), the worst case over states.
\(\epsilon\) is the accuracy you want.
\(\delta\) is the threshold that guarantees it. It shrinks as \(\gamma \to 1\), because far-sighted problems hide more error in the long tail of future rewards.







NoteWhy Equation 8 holds





Each backup shrinks the distance to \(U^*\) by a factor \(\gamma\): \(\lVert U_{k+1} - U^* \rVert \le \gamma \lVert U_k - U^* \rVert\). Split the right side with the triangle inequality:
\[
\lVert U_{k+1} - U^* \rVert \le \gamma \big( \lVert U_k - U_{k+1} \rVert + \lVert U_{k+1} - U^* \rVert \big)
\]
Collecting the \(\lVert U_{k+1} - U^* \rVert\) terms gives \(\lVert U_{k+1} - U^* \rVert \le \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma} \lVert U_{k+1} - U_k \rVert\). So a residual below \(\delta\) means an error below \(\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\delta = \epsilon\).





Elsewhere in the chapter
The book also covers asynchronous value iteration, which updates states in place, one at a time (ADM §7.6). It shows that the optimal values are the solution of a linear program (ADM §7.7). And it solves problems with linear dynamics and quadratic rewards in closed form (ADM §7.8). This page will add them later.

title: 7 · Exact Solution Methods
7 · Exact Solution Methods
text:
Algorithms & code
Every function below works on the array encoding from the worked example: T[s, a, s′], R[s, a], and a policy given as one action index per state.

Lookahead and the greedy policy
These implement Equation 4 for all states and actions at once, then Equation 5.

PythonJulia


def lookahead(T: Array, R: Array, gamma: float, U: Array) -> Array:
    """Q[s, a] = R(s, a) + gamma * sum_s2 T(s2 | s, a) * U(s2).

    Computed for every state s and action a at once.
    """
    # T has shape (S, A, S) and U has shape (S,). The @ sums over T's last
    # axis, giving an (S, A) array of expected next-state values.
    return R + gamma * T @ U

def greedy(T: Array, R: Array, gamma: float, U: Array) -> tuple[Array, Array]:
    """The greedy policy with respect to U, and each greedy action's value."""
    Q = lookahead(T, R, gamma, U)
    # axis=1 runs over actions: best action (and its value) in each state.
    # argmax breaks ties by taking the first action.
    return Q.argmax(axis=1), Q.max(axis=1)


using LinearAlgebra

# Q[s, a] = R(s, a) + γ Σ_s′ T(s′ | s, a) U(s′), for every s and a.
# A comprehension with two `for` clauses builds a matrix: rows are states, columns actions.
# dot(T[s, a, :], U) is the expected next-state value.
lookahead(T, R, γ, U) = [R[s, a] + γ * dot(T[s, a, :], U) for s in axes(R, 1), a in axes(R, 2)]

# The greedy policy with respect to U, and the value of each greedy action.
function greedy(T, R, γ, U)
    Q = lookahead(T, R, γ, U)
    # eachrow(Q) is one row per state; the dot applies argmax/maximum to every row.
    return argmax.(eachrow(Q)), maximum.(eachrow(Q))
end





Policy evaluation
The iterative version applies Equation 2 until nothing changes. The exact version solves Equation 3.

PythonJulia


def policy_matrices(T: Array, R: Array, policy: Array) -> tuple[Array, Array]:
    """T_pi[s, s2] and R_pi[s]: the MDP with the policy's action fixed."""
    # Paired indexing: row s of T_pi is T[s, policy[s], :], i.e. each state
    # keeps only the transition row of the action the policy picks there.
    s = np.arange(len(policy))
    return T[s, policy], R[s, policy]

def policy_evaluation_iterative(
    T: Array, R: Array, gamma: float, policy: Array,
    tol: float = 1e-10, k_max: int = 10_000,
) -> Array:
    """Apply U <- R_pi + gamma * T_pi @ U until U stops changing."""
    T_pi, R_pi = policy_matrices(T, R, policy)
    U = np.zeros(len(policy))
    for _ in range(k_max):
        U_next = R_pi + gamma * T_pi @ U
        if np.max(np.abs(U_next - U)) < tol:
            return U_next
        U = U_next
    return U

def policy_evaluation_exact(
    T: Array, R: Array, gamma: float, policy: Array,
) -> Array:
    """Solve the linear system (I - gamma * T_pi) U = R_pi."""
    T_pi, R_pi = policy_matrices(T, R, policy)
    return np.linalg.solve(np.eye(len(policy)) - gamma * T_pi, R_pi)


# T_π[s, s′] and R_π[s]: the MDP with the policy's action fixed in every state.
function policy_matrices(T, R, policy)
    S = eachindex(policy)
    # Row s keeps only the transitions of the action the policy picks in s.
    T_π = [T[s, policy[s], s′] for s in S, s′ in S]
    R_π = [R[s, policy[s]] for s in S]
    return T_π, R_π
end

# Apply U ← R_π + γ T_π U until U stops changing.
function policy_evaluation_iterative(T, R, γ, policy; tol=1e-10, k_max=10_000)
    T_π, R_π = policy_matrices(T, R, policy)
    U = zeros(length(policy))
    for _ in 1:k_max
        U′ = R_π + γ * T_π * U
        maximum(abs.(U′ - U)) < tol && return U′
        U = U′
    end
    return U
end

# Solve the linear system (I - γ T_π) U = R_π.
function policy_evaluation_exact(T, R, γ, policy)
    T_π, R_π = policy_matrices(T, R, policy)
    # A \ b solves A x = b. I is the identity; it takes whatever size the expression needs.
    return (I - γ * T_π) \ R_π
end





Value iteration
This applies the Bellman backup, Equation 7, to every state until the residual is below delta. It keeps every iterate so we can plot them.

PythonJulia


def value_iteration(
    T: Array, R: Array, gamma: float,
    delta: float = 1e-6, k_max: int = 10_000,
) -> tuple[Array, list[Array]]:
    """Apply Bellman backups until the Bellman residual is below delta.

    Returns the final U and the list of iterates [U_0, U_1, ...].
    """
    U = np.zeros(R.shape[0])
    history = [U]
    for _ in range(k_max):
        # Bellman backup: best one-step lookahead on the old estimate.
        U_next = lookahead(T, R, gamma, U).max(axis=1)
        history.append(U_next)
        # Bellman residual: the largest change in any state this sweep.
        if np.max(np.abs(U_next - U)) < delta:
            break
        U = U_next
    return history[-1], history


# Apply Bellman backups until the Bellman residual is below δ.
# Returns the final U and the vector of iterates [U₀, U₁, ...].
function value_iteration(T, R, γ; δ=1e-6, k_max=10_000)
    U = zeros(size(R, 1))
    history = [U]
    for _ in 1:k_max
        # Bellman backup: max over actions (dims=2) of the lookahead; vec turns the S×1 result into a vector.
        U′ = vec(maximum(lookahead(T, R, γ, U), dims=2))
        push!(history, U′)
        maximum(abs.(U′ - U)) < δ && break      # Bellman residual below δ: stop
        U = U′
    end
    return history[end], history
end





Policy iteration

PythonJulia


def policy_iteration(
    T: Array, R: Array, gamma: float, policy: Array, k_max: int = 100,
) -> tuple[Array, Array, list[Array]]:
    """Alternate exact evaluation and greedy improvement until stable.

    Returns the final policy, its value, and the list of policies visited.
    """
    history = [policy]
    U = policy_evaluation_exact(T, R, gamma, policy)
    for _ in range(k_max):
        improved, _ = greedy(T, R, gamma, U)
        # If acting greedily on the policy's own values changes nothing, the
        # policy satisfies the Bellman optimality equation: it is optimal.
        if np.array_equal(improved, policy):
            break
        policy = improved
        history.append(policy)
        U = policy_evaluation_exact(T, R, gamma, policy)
    return policy, U, history


# Alternate exact evaluation and greedy improvement until the policy stops changing.
# Returns the final policy, its value, and the vector of policies visited.
function policy_iteration(T, R, γ, policy; k_max=100)
    history = [policy]
    U = policy_evaluation_exact(T, R, γ, policy)
    for _ in 1:k_max
        improved, _ = greedy(T, R, γ, U)
        improved == policy && break    # greedy on its own values changes nothing: optimal
        policy = improved
        push!(history, policy)
        U = policy_evaluation_exact(T, R, γ, policy)
    end
    return policy, U, history
end





Run both on the drone

PythonJulia



U_star, history = value_iteration(T, R, gamma)
policy, U_pi, policies = policy_iteration(T, R, gamma, np.array([0, 0]))



U_star, history = value_iteration(T, R, γ)
policy, U_pi, policies = policy_iteration(T, R, γ, [1, 1])   # start: deliver in both states
@assert policy == [1, 2]                                       # deliver when High, charge when Low
@assert isapprox(U_star, U_pi; atol=1e-4)





Value iteration:  151 sweeps, U* = [69.492 61.017]
Policy iteration: 3 evaluations, policy = ['deliver', 'charge'], U = [69.492 61.017]








NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






Indices start at 1. State 1 is High and action 1 is deliver, where Python uses 0 for both.
The dot broadcasts. abs.(U′ - U) applies abs to every element, and argmax.(eachrow(Q)) applies argmax to every row. NumPy does this implicitly; Julia asks you to say so.
A \ b solves the linear system \(A x = b\), like np.linalg.solve(A, b). I is the identity matrix from LinearAlgebra, and it takes whatever size the expression needs.
cond && return x is a compact “if cond, return x”.
Unicode names such as γ, T_π and U′ are ordinary variable names. Type them in the REPL as \gamma<tab>, T_\pi<tab> and U\prime<tab>.






Results on the Rover grid
Figure 6 shows the converged values and greedy policy at \(\gamma = 0.9\). Cells beside the crater steer away from it even though that costs a step, because a slip toward the crater would be expensive. At this \(\gamma\), the whole grid heads for the +10 site.








Figure 6: Optimal values and policy on the Rover grid (γ = 0.9). Arrows show the optimal action; numbers are \(U^*(s)\).





Figure 7 compares how fast value iteration converges for three discount factors. The residual shrinks by about a factor \(\gamma\) per sweep, so a far-sighted rover (\(\gamma = 0.99\)) needs many more sweeps than a short-sighted one.








Figure 7: Bellman residual per sweep of value iteration on the Rover grid, for three discount factors. Value iteration stops when the residual falls below δ = 10⁻⁶ (dashed line).





Figure 8 shows policy iteration on the same grid. It starts from “always drive north” and reaches the optimal policy in 3 improvements. Value iteration needed 41 sweeps.








Figure 8: Policy iteration on the Rover grid (γ = 0.9), starting from ‘always drive north’. Each panel shows a policy and its exact value \(U^\pi\); the last panel is optimal.

text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: backups by hand. A factory machine is either Working or Broken. Each day you can run it or repair it, with \(\gamma = 0.9\):



State
Action
Reward
Next state




Working
run
+5
Working 0.9, Broken 0.1


Working
repair
−1
Working 1.0


Broken
run
0
Broken 1.0


Broken
repair
−4
Working 0.7, Broken 0.3



Starting from \(U_0 = 0\), compute \(U_1\), \(U_2\) and \(U_3\), and the greedy action in Broken after each sweep. What does the answer say about short planning horizons?






TipSolution





Sweep 1. Immediate rewards only: \(U_1(W) = \max(5, -1) = 5\) and \(U_1(B) = \max(0, -4) = 0\). Broken: run.
Sweep 2.

\(U_2(W) = \max\big(5 + 0.9(0.9 \cdot 5 + 0.1 \cdot 0),\; -1 + 0.9 \cdot 5\big) = \max(9.05,\, 3.5) = 9.05\)
\(U_2(B) = \max\big(0 + 0.9 \cdot 0,\; -4 + 0.9(0.7 \cdot 5 + 0.3 \cdot 0)\big) = \max(0,\, -0.85) = 0\). Broken: still run.

Sweep 3.

\(U_3(W) = \max\big(5 + 0.9(0.9 \cdot 9.05 + 0.1 \cdot 0),\; -1 + 0.9 \cdot 9.05\big) = \max(12.33,\, 7.145) = 12.33\)
\(U_3(B) = \max\big(0,\; -4 + 0.9(0.7 \cdot 9.05 + 0.3 \cdot 0)\big) = \max(0,\, 1.70) = 1.70\). Broken: repair.

\(U_k\) is the best value achievable in \(k\) steps. With only one or two days left, a repair costs more than the working days it buys back, so leaving the machine broken is right. From three days on, repairing pays. Stopping value iteration too early gives a policy that is optimal for the wrong horizon.



Problem 2: exact evaluation. A policy on two states has \(\gamma = 0.5\), rewards \(\mathbf{R}^\pi = (2, 1)\), and transitions: from state 1, stay with probability 0.5 or move to state 2 with probability 0.5; from state 2, stay with probability 1. Find \(U^\pi\) with Equation 3.






TipSolution





State 2 only ever returns to itself: \(U(2) = 1 + 0.5\, U(2)\), so \(U(2) = 2\). Then
\[
U(1) = 2 + 0.5\big(0.5\, U(1) + 0.5 \cdot 2\big) = 2.5 + 0.25\, U(1)
\quad\Rightarrow\quad U(1) = \tfrac{2.5}{0.75} = \tfrac{10}{3} \approx 3.33.
\]
In matrix form, \((\mathbf{I} - 0.5\,\mathbf{T}^\pi) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.75 & -0.25 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}\), and solving against \((2, 1)\) gives the same \((10/3, 2)\). The matrix is upper triangular because state 2 never returns to state 1, so back-substitution is all you need.



Problem 3: choosing the stopping threshold. You want value iteration’s answer to be within \(\epsilon = 0.1\) of \(U^*\) in every state. What residual threshold \(\delta\) guarantees this for \(\gamma = 0.9\), and for \(\gamma = 0.99\)? Why is the second so much smaller?






TipSolution





From Equation 8, \(\delta = \epsilon(1 - \gamma)/\gamma\):

\(\gamma = 0.9\): \(\delta = 0.1 \times 0.1 / 0.9 \approx 0.0111\)
\(\gamma = 0.99\): \(\delta = 0.1 \times 0.01 / 0.99 \approx 0.00101\)

With \(\gamma\) near 1, the rewards still to come beyond the current horizon are large. A tiny change in one sweep can still hide a big total error, because that change keeps compounding over many future steps. So the threshold has to be about ten times tighter, and since each sweep only shrinks the error by a factor \(\gamma\), it also takes many more sweeps (Figure 7).



Problem 4: when is the far reward worth it? Remove the slip, so moves are deterministic. From some cell, the +3 rock is 2 moves away and the +10 site is 5 moves away. A reward collected after \(d\) moves is worth \(\gamma^d\) times its face value. For which \(\gamma\) should the rover go for the +10?






TipSolution





Go for the +10 when \(10\gamma^5 > 3\gamma^2\). Dividing by \(\gamma^2\) gives \(\gamma^3 > 0.3\), so
\[
\gamma > 0.3^{1/3} \approx 0.669.
\]
Only the difference in distance (3 moves) matters, and the ratio of rewards. With slip, the risk along each route matters too, so there’s no simple formula. The γ slider above shows where the switch happens on the Rover grid.

title: 7 · Exact Solution Methods
text:
Recap
The key points of this chapter, and why each matters beyond it:

An MDP packs a sequential decision problem into five pieces: \(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, T, R, \gamma\). Why it matters: this is the common language of the rest of the book. Part II keeps the model and scales up the solution methods. Part III has to learn \(T\) and \(R\) from experience. Part IV hides the state behind noisy observations.
A policy’s value is its expected discounted return (Equation 1), and \(\gamma\) sets the effective horizon, about \(1/(1-\gamma)\) steps. Why it matters: \(\gamma\) is a modeling choice with real consequences for behavior. The γ slider showed the same rover taking the modest nearby reward or holding out for the big distant one.
The Bellman expectation equation (Equation 2) turns an infinite sum into a one-step recursion, and evaluating a policy becomes one linear solve. Why it matters: “reward now plus discounted value of what comes next” is the engine inside almost every algorithm ahead, including temporal-difference learning and Q-learning (Ch 17) and actor-critic methods (Ch 13).
Good values give good actions: act greedily on the one-step lookahead \(Q\) (Equation 4, Equation 5). Why it matters: it separates judging states from choosing actions. Later methods learn \(U\) or \(Q\) and derive the policy from it, or use the advantage \(Q - U\) to steer a policy directly (Ch 11–13).
The Bellman optimality equation (Equation 6) characterizes the best policy. Value iteration solves it by repeated backups, which converge because each one shrinks the error by a factor \(\gamma\). The residual rule (Equation 8) says when to stop. Why it matters: value iteration is the template for approximate value iteration (Ch 8) and for planning over beliefs (Ch 20).
Policy iteration takes few, expensive rounds, and value iteration takes many cheap sweeps. Both need the full model and touch every state. Why it matters: those two requirements fail for large or unknown problems. That failure motivates most of the book: approximation (Ch 8), planning only from the current state (Ch 9), and learning from experience (Ch 16–17).

Policy iteration or value iteration? Policy iteration takes few, expensive iterations (a linear solve each). Value iteration takes many cheap sweeps and slows down as \(\gamma \to 1\). For small problems, either works.
Common pitfalls

Stopping value iteration when the policy stops changing. The greedy policy often settles early, but nothing guarantees it is final. Problem 1 shows it can still flip. Stop on the residual (Equation 8).
Using \(\gamma = 1\) on a problem that never ends. The sums in Equation 2 can diverge. With \(\gamma = 1\), every policy must reach an absorbing state with zero reward.
Forgetting terminal states. In the Rover grid, collecting a reward moves the rover to an absorbing “done” state. Without it, the rover would collect the same reward forever.
Mixing up T[s, a, s′] index order between code and math. Write the convention next to the array, as in the worked example.

Connections

Ch 6 · Simple Decisions is the one-step case: choose the action with maximum expected utility.
Ch 8 · Approximate Value Functions handles state spaces too large to store \(U\) as a table.
Ch 9 · Online Planning applies lookahead from the current state only, instead of solving for every state.
Ch 16 · Model-Based Methods learns \(T\) and \(R\) from experience, then uses the methods on this page.
Ch 20 · Exact Belief State Planning runs value iteration over beliefs when the state isn’t observed.
Appendix A · Mathematical Concepts shows why value iteration converges: the Bellman backup is a contraction. Appendix E · Search Algorithms covers the deterministic special case.

title: 5 · Structure Learning
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 4 learned the numbers of a Bayesian network from data, but it was handed the graph: which variables point to which. Often nobody knows the graph either. Does roadwork affect lateness directly, or only through jams? Is the radio alert caused by the storm, or the other way around? This chapter learns the graph itself from data. That finishes Part I’s toolkit: represent (Ch 2), reason (Ch 3), learn the numbers (Ch 4), learn the structure (here). Chapter 6 then adds decisions on top.
The question: given data about several variables, which pattern of direct dependencies (which graph) best explains it?
The short answer: score every candidate graph by how probable it makes the data, averaged over all its possible parameters. That score automatically penalizes needless edges. Then search the space of graphs for a high score, because there are far too many to try them all.








ch05

Data

Bayesian score

evaluate

motivates






Figure 1: Map of this chapter. A score says how well a graph explains the data; search looks for a high-scoring graph among astronomically many; equivalence classes say which differences the data can’t resolve.







The key ideas at a glance

Score a graph by how well it predicts the data. The Bayesian score of a graph is the probability of the data under that graph, averaged over every possible set of numbers for its tables, weighted by a prior. It has a vivid equivalent: learn the tables one record at a time, as in Chapter 4, and multiply together the probability you gave each record just before seeing it. A graph with an unnecessary edge has more numbers to learn, so it predicts worse early on and pays for it. A graph missing a real edge predicts worse forever. The score balances fit against complexity without any tuning knob.
The score splits into one term per variable. Each variable’s term depends only on that variable and its parents. So changing one edge changes one or two terms, and a whole search can reuse a precomputed table of terms. That property, called decomposability, is what makes search affordable.
There are far too many graphs to try them all. Five variables allow 29,281 graphs without cycles; ten allow over \(10^{18}\). So we search. K2 takes a variable order and, variable by variable, greedily adds the earlier variable that most improves the score. It’s fast, but only as good as the order. Local search starts from any graph and repeatedly makes the single best edge change (add, remove or reverse) until no change helps. It can get stuck on a local maximum, so it’s restarted from different graphs.
Some graphs can never be told apart. “Storm causes alert” and “alert causes storm” imply exactly the same independences, so no data can distinguish them. Graphs like these are Markov equivalent: they have the same skeleton (edges ignoring direction) and the same v-structures (pairs of unlinked causes sharing an effect, \(a \to c \leftarrow b\)). With the right prior (BDeu), equivalent graphs get identical scores. Searching over whole equivalence classes, drawn as partially directed graphs, avoids wasting steps among equivalent graphs.
Data decides how much structure you can see. With little data, a simpler or look-alike story can outscore the graph that actually generated the data. In the commute example, the radio alert is such a reliable stand-in for the storm that a few hundred mornings often can’t tell “storms cause jams” from “alert days have jams”. In our simulations the true structure scored best in every dataset from about 1,000 mornings on, but not every time before that.



Vocabulary

K2

Skeleton

V-structure
