After this chapter you can

Compute a variable’s Bayesian score term from counts, and read it as “prediction while learning”.
Explain why the score resists extra edges without a penalty parameter.
Learn a graph with K2 or local search, and recognize their failure modes.
Decide whether two graphs are Markov equivalent, and explain what data can and can’t reveal about edge direction.

title: 5 · Structure Learning
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Three analysts each propose an explanation of your morning commutes. One says everything is unrelated; one draws exactly the true causal story; one connects everything to everything. How do you judge them fairly?
Make each one predict the mornings, one at a time, learning as they go. Before each morning is revealed, each analyst states a probability for what will happen; then they see it and update. Multiply up all the probabilities each analyst gave.

The “unrelated” analyst never catches on that jams make you late, and predicts badly all along.
The “everything” analyst has so many numbers to learn that it predicts clumsily for a long time, spreading its bets across combinations it has barely seen.
The analyst with the right structure learns fast and predicts well.

That product is the Bayesian score.



A score is prediction while learning
Take a single yes/no variable, and three records: late, on time, on time. Start with one pseudo-observation of each outcome, as in Chapter 4, and predict each record before seeing it:

first: “late” has probability \(1/2\);
then “on time”: \(1/3\), since you’ve seen one “late” plus the pseudocounts;
then “on time” again: \(2/4\).

The product is \(1/12\), and \(\ln(1/12)\) is exactly this variable’s score term. See Equation 1.


Why extra edges don’t win for free
Give “late” the parent “jam”, and the table splits into two rows, one per jam value, each learned only from its own mornings. If lateness really depends on jams, each row predicts its mornings much better, and the score rises. In the worked example, 30 mornings make the data about \(e^{2.76} \approx 16\) times more probable with the edge. If lateness didn’t depend on jams, splitting would just halve the data per row, each row would learn more slowly, and the score would drop. No penalty had to be added; slower learning is the penalty.


Search: K2 and hill climbing
With five variables, there are 29,281 possible graphs, and every added variable multiplies that enormously (Figure 4). K2 avoids the explosion by fixing an order. Each variable may only take parents from earlier in the order, and it greedily adds whichever one helps most. Give it the causal order (storm, roadwork, jam, late, alert) and it finds the true graph from 3,000 mornings. Give it the order backwards and it builds a wrong, lower-scoring graph. Local search needs no order. It keeps making the best single edge change, but it can reach a graph where every single change hurts even though a better graph exists. Restarting from random graphs is the simple cure. See Figure 6.


What data can’t tell you
Does the storm cause the alert, or the alert the storm? Either way, the two are strongly linked, and nothing else in the data distinguishes the directions. The two graphs make the same independence claims, so they’re Markov equivalent. The collider storm → jam ← roadwork is different. Reversing either arrow changes an independence claim (storm and roadwork would no longer be independent), and the data can see that. So some edge directions are learnable and others aren’t. See Equation 4 and Figure 2.


How much data you need
An alert is 95% likely in a storm and only 2% otherwise, so it’s almost a copy of the storm variable, and a small sample can’t always tell which of the two the jams really depend on. With 100–300 mornings, some other graph often scores best. In one of our simulated datasets, even 1,000 mornings weren’t enough: the best graph linked the jam to the alert instead of the storm. Across datasets, the true structure reliably wins from about 1,000 mornings on (Figure 5). Structure learning finds a graph that explains the data well. Whether it’s the causal truth depends on how much data you have and how distinguishable the alternatives are.

title: 5 · Structure Learning
text:
Formalism

The Bayesian score
For variable \(i\) with \(r_i\) values and parent combination \(j\), let \(m_{ijk}\) be the count of records where it takes value \(k\) (Ch 4), and \(\alpha_{ijk}\) the prior’s pseudocount for that cell. Write \(m_{ij0} = \sum_k m_{ijk}\) and \(\alpha_{ij0} = \sum_k \alpha_{ijk}\) for the row totals (ADM §5.1).

\[
\ln P(G \mid D) = \ln P(G) + \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j} \left[ \ln \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{ij0})}{\Gamma(\alpha_{ij0} + m_{ij0})} + \sum_{k=1}^{r_i} \ln \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{ijk} + m_{ijk})}{\Gamma(\alpha_{ijk})} \right]
\tag{1}\]

In words. The score of a graph \(G\) for data \(D\) is its prior plausibility, plus, for each variable and each parent combination, a term measuring how well that table row’s counts are predicted when the row’s probabilities are learned from those counts.
Term by term.

\(\Gamma\) is the gamma function, which extends the factorial: \(\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!\) for whole numbers. Ratios of gammas count how the Dirichlet prior’s pseudocounts combine with the real counts.
\(\ln P(G)\) is a prior over graphs. With a uniform prior over graphs it’s the same for every graph and can be dropped. That’s what this page does.
Each bracket is one row of one table. Rows never interact, so the score is a sum of per-variable terms (Equation 2).

Why it holds. The score is \(\ln P(D \mid G)\) with the parameters integrated out: \(P(D \mid G) = \int P(D \mid \theta, G)\, p(\theta \mid G)\, d\theta\). With Dirichlet priors, each row’s integral has a closed form, the ratio of gamma functions above. Equivalently, by the chain rule of probability, it’s the product of the posterior-predictive probabilities of the records taken in any order, which is exactly the “prediction while learning” reading.

\[
\ln P(D \mid G) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{score}\big(x_i, \mathrm{pa}_G(x_i); D\big)
\tag{2}\]

In words. A graph’s score is a sum of one term per variable, and each term depends only on that variable and its parents.
Term by term. \(\mathrm{pa}_G(x_i)\) is \(x_i\)’s parent set in graph \(G\). Adding or removing the edge \(a \to b\) changes only \(b\)’s term, and reversing it changes only \(a\)’s and \(b\)’s. So a search can score each possible (variable, parent set) pair once and reuse the numbers: 80 terms cover all 29,281 commute graphs.


Searching over graphs
The space is enormous. The number of DAGs on \(n\) labeled variables follows Robinson’s recurrence (R. W. Robinson, “Counting labeled acyclic digraphs,” 1973; the sequence is A003024 in the OEIS):

\[
a(n) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (-1)^{k+1} \binom{n}{k}\, 2^{k(n-k)}\, a(n-k), \qquad a(0) = 1
\tag{3}\]

In words. Count graphs by which \(k\) variables have no parents (the sources): choose them, let each point to any subset of the rest, and recurse on the remaining \(n - k\) variables. The alternating signs correct for graphs counted more than once.
Term by term. \(\binom{n}{k}\) chooses the sources; \(2^{k(n-k)}\) lets each of the \(k\) sources point or not to each of the other \(n - k\) variables; \(a(n-k)\) counts the graphs on the rest. The result: 1, 3, 25, 543, 29,281, then about 3.8 million for 6 variables and \(10^{18}\) for 10.
Two searches from the book (ADM §5.2):

K2 fixes a variable order and, for each variable, greedily adds parents from earlier in the order while the score improves, up to a maximum number of parents. Since parents always come earlier, cycles are impossible.
Local search (hill climbing) moves, at each step, to the best-scoring graph among those one edge change away (add, remove or reverse, skipping any that creates a cycle), and stops when no neighbor scores higher. It finds a local maximum. Random restarts, simulated annealing and other stochastic variants help it escape.



Markov equivalence
Two graphs are Markov equivalent if they encode the same conditional independences (ADM §5.3). There’s a simple test:

\[
G \equiv G' \iff \mathrm{skeleton}(G) = \mathrm{skeleton}(G') \ \text{ and } \ \mathrm{vstructs}(G) = \mathrm{vstructs}(G')
\tag{4}\]

In words. Two graphs are equivalent exactly when they have the same edges (ignoring direction) and the same “two unlinked causes, one shared effect” patterns.
Term by term. The skeleton is the undirected version of the graph. A v-structure is \(a \to c \leftarrow b\) with no edge between \(a\) and \(b\): a collider, from Ch 2. Reversing an edge that isn’t part of a v-structure, and doesn’t create one, leaves the class unchanged. This criterion is due to Verma and Pearl (1990).
Equivalent graphs can’t be distinguished by data, so a good score should give them the same value. The uniform prior (\(\alpha_{ijk} = 1\)) doesn’t quite do that. The BDeu prior does:

\[
\alpha_{ijk} = \frac{\kappa}{q_i\, r_i}
\tag{5}\]

In words. Spread a fixed total of \(\kappa\) pseudocounts evenly over each variable’s whole table.
Term by term. \(q_i\) is the number of parent combinations of variable \(i\) and \(r_i\) its number of values, so \(q_i r_i\) is its number of cells. \(\kappa\) (the equivalent sample size) says how many observations the prior is worth. Priors of this kind make the score score-equivalent: Markov-equivalent graphs get identical scores (Heckerman, Geiger and Chickering, 1995, cited in ADM §5.3). This page uses BDeu with \(\kappa = 1\) for its searches.
Searching directly over equivalence classes, each represented as a partially directed graph with the undeterminable edges left undirected, avoids moving between equivalent graphs that all score the same (ADM §5.4). This page doesn’t implement it.

Worked example

Scoring by hand

No jam: \(\ln \frac{\Gamma(2)}{\Gamma(22)} + \ln \frac{\Gamma(20)}{\Gamma(1)} + \ln \frac{\Gamma(2)}{\Gamma(1)} = \ln \frac{1! \cdot 19! \cdot 1!}{21!} = -\ln 420 = -6.04\).

title: 5 · Structure Learning
5 · Structure Learning
text:
Algorithms & code
A graph is a dictionary from each variable to the tuple of its parents. Data is a list of complete records, as in Chapter 4.

The Bayesian score

PythonJulia


def score_component(counts: np.ndarray, alpha) -> float:
    """One variable's term of the Bayesian score, from its counts m_ijk.

    counts has shape (parent values..., own values); alpha is a pseudocount
    per cell (a number, or an array of the same shape).
    """
    r = counts.shape[-1]
    m = counts.reshape(-1, r)              # one row per parent combination j
    a = np.broadcast_to(np.asarray(alpha, dtype=float), counts.shape)
    a = a.reshape(-1, r)
    # gammaln(x) = ln Gamma(x). Row j contributes
    #   ln G(a_j0) - ln G(a_j0 + m_j0)
    #   + sum_k [ln G(a_jk + m_jk) - ln G(a_jk)],
    # where a_j0 and m_j0 are the row totals.
    return float(np.sum(gammaln(a.sum(1)) - gammaln(a.sum(1) + m.sum(1)))
                 + np.sum(gammaln(a + m) - gammaln(a)))

def bayesian_score(card: dict, parents: dict, data: list,
                   prior: str = "uniform", kappa: float = 1.0) -> float:
    """ln P(data | graph): the Bayesian score with a uniform graph prior.

    prior="uniform" puts one pseudocount in every cell. prior="bdeu" spreads
    `kappa` pseudocounts evenly over each variable's table, which gives
    Markov-equivalent graphs exactly the same score.
    """
    total = 0.0
    for x, m in count_table(card, parents, data).items():
        if prior == "bdeu":
            alpha = kappa / m.size    # m.size = parent combos x values
        else:
            alpha = 1.0
        total += score_component(m, alpha)
    return total

def family_scores(card: dict, data: list, prior: str = "uniform",
                  kappa: float = 1.0) -> dict:
    """The score term of every (variable, parent set) pair.

    The Bayesian score is a sum of one term per variable, and each term
    depends only on that variable and its parents. So a graph's score is
    sum(table[x, parents[x]] for x), and whole searches reuse the table.
    Parent sets are stored as sorted tuples.
    """
    table = {}
    nodes = list(card)
    for x in nodes:
        others = [v for v in nodes if v != x]
        for k in range(len(others) + 1):
            for pa in combinations(others, k):
                # Score just the family x <- pa: a one-variable network.
                family = {x: pa, **{p: () for p in pa}}
                m = count_table(card, family, data)[x]
                alpha = kappa / m.size if prior == "bdeu" else 1.0
                table[x, tuple(sorted(pa))] = score_component(m, alpha)
    return table

def graph_score(table: dict, parents: dict) -> float:
    """A graph's Bayesian score, summed from precomputed family terms."""
    return sum(table[x, tuple(sorted(pa))] for x, pa in parents.items())


using ADM, Distributions, Random

# Counts m_ijk for variable x with parent tuple pa: axes (parent values..., own value).
function family_counts(card, x, pa, data)
    m = zeros(Int, (card[q] for q in pa)..., card[x])
    for r in data
        m[(r[q] for q in pa)..., r[x]] += 1
    end
    return m
end

# ln Γ(n) = ln((n - 1)!) for whole numbers n ≥ 1. With the uniform prior every
# pseudocount is 1, so all Γ arguments are whole numbers and no special functions are needed.
logΓ(n) = sum(log, 1:(n - 1); init = 0.0)

# One variable's term of the Bayesian score, uniform prior (α_ijk = 1).
function score_component(m)
    r = size(m, ndims(m))
    rows = reshape(m, :, r)          # one row per parent combination (Julia is column-major,
                                     # so the last axis becomes the columns)
    return sum(logΓ(r) - logΓ(r + sum(rows[j, :])) + sum(logΓ(1 + mjk) for mjk in rows[j, :])
               for j in axes(rows, 1))
end

bayesian_score(card, parents, data) =
    sum(score_component(family_counts(card, x, pa, data)) for (x, pa) in parents)





Searching: K2 and local search

PythonJulia


def is_acyclic(parents: dict) -> bool:
    """True if the graph has no directed cycle (repeatedly remove sources)."""
    remaining = dict(parents)
    while remaining:
        # A node whose parents have all been removed can't be on a cycle.
        free = [x for x, pa in remaining.items()
                if not any(p in remaining for p in pa)]
        if not free:
            return False                    # every node waits on another
        for x in free:
            del remaining[x]
    return True

def k2_search(score, order: list, max_parents: int = 2) -> dict:
    """K2: for each variable in order, greedily add the earlier variable
    that raises the score most, until no addition helps.

    `score` maps a graph to its score. Parents come only from earlier in
    the order, so no cycle can form.
    """
    parents = {x: () for x in order}
    for i, x in enumerate(order):
        best = score(parents)
        while len(parents[x]) < max_parents:
            options = [p for p in order[:i] if p not in parents[x]]
            scored = [(score({**parents, x: parents[x] + (p,)}), p)
                      for p in options]
            if not scored or max(scored)[0] <= best:
                break                       # no candidate improves the score
            best, p = max(scored)
            parents[x] = parents[x] + (p,)
    return parents

def neighbors(parents: dict):
    """Graphs one edit away: add, remove, or reverse a single edge."""
    nodes = list(parents)
    for a, b in combinations(nodes, 2):
        for u, v in ((a, b), (b, a)):
            if u in parents[v]:             # edge u -> v exists
                removed = tuple(p for p in parents[v] if p != u)
                yield {**parents, v: removed}                          # remove
                yield {**parents, v: removed, u: parents[u] + (v,)}   # reverse
            elif v not in parents[u]:       # no edge either way
                yield {**parents, v: parents[v] + (u,)}               # add

def local_search(score, start: dict, max_steps: int = 50):
    """Hill climbing: move to the best-scoring acyclic neighbor while that
    improves the score. Returns the final graph and the score after each
    step. `score` maps a graph to its score.
    """
    graph, scores = start, [score(start)]
    for _ in range(max_steps):
        candidates = [(score(g), i, g)
                      for i, g in enumerate(neighbors(graph)) if is_acyclic(g)]
        best_score, _, best = max(candidates)   # i breaks ties, never g
        if best_score <= scores[-1]:
            break                              # a local maximum
        graph = best
        scores.append(best_score)
    return graph, scores


# No directed cycle: keep removing nodes whose parents are all already removed.
function is_acyclic(parents)
    left = Set(keys(parents))
    while !isempty(left)
        free = [x for x in left if !any(p in left for p in parents[x])]
        isempty(free) && return false          # every remaining node waits on another
        setdiff!(left, free)
    end
    return true
end

# K2: along the order, greedily add the earlier variable that most improves the score.
function k2_search(score, order; max_parents = 2)
    parents = Dict{Symbol, Tuple}(x => () for x in order)
    for (i, x) in enumerate(order)
        best = score(parents)
        while length(parents[x]) < max_parents
            options = [p for p in order[1:i-1] if !(p in parents[x])]
            isempty(options) && break
            with(p) = merge(parents, Dict(x => (parents[x]..., p)))
            p = argmax(p -> score(with(p)), options)     # the option whose graph scores best
            score(with(p)) <= best && break          # no option improves the score
            parents = with(p)
            best = score(parents)
        end
    end
    return parents
end

# Graphs one edit away: add, remove, or reverse a single edge.
function neighbors(parents)
    nodes, out = collect(keys(parents)), Dict{Symbol, Tuple}[]
    for (i, a) in enumerate(nodes), b in nodes[i+1:end], (u, v) in ((a, b), (b, a))
        if u in parents[v]                                        # edge u → v exists
            removed = Tuple(p for p in parents[v] if p != u)
            push!(out, merge(parents, Dict(v => removed)))                                # remove
            push!(out, merge(parents, Dict(v => removed, u => (parents[u]..., v))))       # reverse
        elseif !(v in parents[u])                                 # no edge either way
            push!(out, merge(parents, Dict(v => (parents[v]..., u))))                     # add
        end
    end
    return out
end

# Hill climbing: take the best acyclic neighbor while it improves the score.
function local_search(score, start; max_steps = 50)
    graph, scores = start, [score(start)]
    for _ in 1:max_steps
        best = argmax(score, filter(is_acyclic, neighbors(graph)))
        score(best) <= scores[end] && break          # a local maximum
        graph = best
        push!(scores, score(best))
    end
    return graph, scores
end





Markov equivalence

PythonJulia


def skeleton(parents: dict) -> set:
    """The graph's edges with directions dropped."""
    return {frozenset((p, x)) for x, pa in parents.items() for p in pa}

def v_structures(parents: dict) -> set:
    """Triples a -> c <- b where a and b are not adjacent."""
    edges = skeleton(parents)
    return {(frozenset((a, b)), c) for c, pa in parents.items()
            for a, b in combinations(pa, 2) if frozenset((a, b)) not in edges}

def markov_equivalent(g1: dict, g2: dict) -> bool:
    """Same skeleton and same v-structures: the graphs encode exactly the
    same conditional independences, so no data can tell them apart."""
    return (skeleton(g1) == skeleton(g2)
            and v_structures(g1) == v_structures(g2))


# Edges with direction dropped: each edge becomes the set {parent, child}.
skeleton(g) = Set(Set([p, x]) for (x, pa) in g for p in pa)

# Colliders a → c ← b whose two causes a and b are not linked.
function v_structures(g)
    edges = skeleton(g)
    return Set((Set([pa[i], pa[j]]), c) for (c, pa) in g
               for i in eachindex(pa) for j in (i+1):length(pa) if !(Set([pa[i], pa[j]]) in edges))
end

markov_equivalent(g1, g2) = skeleton(g1) == skeleton(g2) && v_structures(g1) == v_structures(g2)





Run them on the commute data

PythonJulia



mornings = sample_dataset(COMMUTE, 3000, np.random.default_rng(1))
table = family_scores(COMMUTE.card, mornings, prior="bdeu")    # all 80 family terms
score = lambda g: graph_score(table, g)
k2_right = k2_search(score, ["S", "R", "J", "L", "A"])           # the causal order
k2_wrong = k2_search(score, ["L", "J", "A", "S", "R"])           # the order reversed
empty = {x: () for x in COMMUTE.parents}
found, steps = local_search(score, empty)



# Direct sampling, as in Ch 3 and Ch 4.
function topological_order(parents)
    order = Symbol[]
    while length(order) < length(parents)
        for (x, pa) in parents
            !(x in order) && all(p in order for p in pa) && push!(order, x)
        end
    end
    return order
end
function sample_dataset(bn, m, rng)
    order = topological_order(bn.parents)
    return map(1:m) do _
        r = Dict{Symbol, Int}()
        for x in order
            r[x] = rand(rng, Categorical(bn.cpt[x][(r[q] for q in bn.parents[x])..., :]))
        end
        r
    end
end

commute = commute_network()
mornings = sample_dataset(commute, 3000, MersenneTwister(1))
@assert isapprox(score_component([19 1; 5 5]), -13.9676; atol = 1e-4)    # the hand example
score(g) = bayesian_score(commute.card, g, mornings)
truth = commute.parents
@assert markov_equivalent(k2_search(score, [:S, :R, :J, :L, :A]), truth)
twin = merge(truth, Dict(:A => (), :S => (:A,)))
@assert markov_equivalent(truth, twin)
@assert !markov_equivalent(truth, merge(truth, Dict(:J => (:S,), :R => (:J,))))
found, steps = local_search(score, Dict{Symbol, Tuple}(x => () for x in keys(truth)))
@assert all(diff(steps) .> 0)                 # every step strictly improves the score





K2, causal order:   R→J, S→J, J→L, S→A
    equivalent to truth: True
K2, reversed order: L→J, J→A, A→S, J→S, J→R, S→R
    equivalent to truth: False, score -8.68 vs truth
Local search from the empty graph (5 steps): A→S, S→J, R→J, J→L
    equivalent to truth: True








NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






reshape(m, :, r) turns the count array into a matrix with r columns. Because Julia stores arrays column by column, the last axis, the variable’s own value, becomes the columns, just as m.reshape(-1, r) does in NumPy’s row-major layout.
argmax(f, xs) returns the element of xs that maximizes f, like Python’s max(xs, key=f).
with(p) = … inside a loop defines a small local function (a closure), like a Python lambda.
Set(Set([p, x]) …): a set of 2-element sets represents undirected edges, like a set of frozensets in Python.
merge(d, Dict(k => v)) returns a new dictionary with k replaced, like {**d, k: v}.






Results

The space of graphs








Figure 4: Number of directed acyclic graphs on n labeled variables (Equation 3), on a log scale. Five variables allow 29,281 graphs; ten allow over 10¹⁸.







How much data does the true structure need?
For each of 4 simulated datasets at each size, Figure 5 scores all 29,281 graphs and compares the true graph (or its equivalent twin) with the best graph that isn’t equivalent to it. Above zero, the truth wins.








Figure 5: Score of the true graph minus the score of the best non-equivalent graph, as the number of mornings grows (BDeu prior; each dot is one simulated dataset, the line is their average). Below zero, some other structure explains the data better; above zero, the true structure wins.







Search in action
On 3,000 mornings, local search from the empty graph finds the true structure’s class. On 10,000 mornings, the same search from the empty graph gets stuck. It ends on a graph that scores 10.7 below the truth, where no single edge change helps (Figure 6). Restarting from random graphs fixes it: 6 of 30 restarts reach the true class.








Figure 6: Local search on 10,000 mornings (BDeu prior). Left: how far each step’s score is below the true graph’s (log scale); the search stops at a local maximum about 10 points short. Middle: the graph it gets stuck on; orange arrows disagree with the true direction. Right: final scores of 30 restarts from random graphs, with the true graph’s score dashed; blue dots reached the true graph’s equivalence class.

title: 5 · Structure Learning
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: a score term by hand. A variable was observed 4 times: yes, yes, no, yes. Compute its score term with the uniform prior, both from Equation 1 and by sequential prediction.






TipSolution





Sequentially, starting from one pseudocount per value: yes \(1/2\), yes \(2/3\), no \(1/4\), yes \(3/5\). The product is \(\frac{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5} = \frac{6}{120} = \frac{1}{20}\).
By the formula, with 3 yes and 1 no: \(\ln \frac{\Gamma(2)}{\Gamma(6)} + \ln \frac{\Gamma(4)}{\Gamma(1)} + \ln \frac{\Gamma(2)}{\Gamma(1)} = \ln \frac{1 \cdot 3! \cdot 1!}{5!} = \ln \frac{6}{120} = \ln \frac{1}{20} \approx -3.00\).
Same answer. The order of the records doesn’t matter, only the counts.



Problem 2: equivalent or not? Which of these are Markov equivalent to \(X \to Y \to Z\)? (a) \(X \leftarrow Y \leftarrow Z\); (b) \(X \leftarrow Y \to Z\); (c) \(X \to Y \leftarrow Z\).






TipSolution





All four graphs share the skeleton \(X - Y - Z\). The original has no v-structure.

and (b) have none either, so both are equivalent: all three say \(X \perp Z \mid Y\).
is a v-structure (\(X\) and \(Z\) unlinked causes of \(Y\)), so it’s not equivalent: it says \(X \perp Z\) with nothing observed, and \(X\) and \(Z\) dependent once \(Y\) is known.

Of the 25 DAGs on three variables, 11 equivalence classes remain, which you can check with markov_equivalent and all_dags.



Problem 3: why K2 needs a good order. In the run above, K2 with the reversed order (late, jam, alert, storm, roadwork) produced a wrong graph. Explain why it can’t find the true graph from that order.






TipSolution





K2 only allows parents that come earlier in the order. In the true graph, storm and roadwork are parents of jam, but in the reversed order they come after jam, so those edges are forbidden. Even the true graph’s equivalence class needs the v-structure S → J ← R, which requires both arrows into jam. K2 can only approximate the dependencies with edges pointing the “wrong” way, which costs score. Orders are often taken from domain knowledge (causes before effects), or several random orders are tried.



Problem 4: counting DAGs. Use Equation 3 to compute \(a(3)\) from \(a(0) = 1\), \(a(1) = 1\) and \(a(2) = 3\).






TipSolution





\[
a(3) = \binom{3}{1} 2^{2} a(2) - \binom{3}{2} 2^{2} a(1) + \binom{3}{3} 2^{0} a(0) = 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 - 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 + 1 = 36 - 12 + 1 = 25.
\]

title: 5 · Structure Learning
text:
Recap

The Bayesian score (Equation 1) rates a graph by how probable it makes the data, with parameters averaged out. Equivalently, it measures how well the graph predicts each record while learning from the ones before. Why it matters: it compares structures of different complexity fairly, with no tuning knob. The same “marginal likelihood” idea is used to compare models throughout statistics and machine learning.
The score is decomposable (Equation 2): one term per variable and its parents. Why it matters: local changes are cheap to score, which is what makes any search feasible.
The space of graphs grows super-exponentially (Equation 3), so we search. K2 is fast but needs a good variable order; local search needs no order but finds local maxima, which restarts help escape. Why it matters: the same greedy-search trade-offs recur in policy search (Ch 10) and whenever a space is too big to enumerate.
Markov-equivalent graphs (Equation 4) can’t be distinguished by data; a BDeu prior (Equation 5) scores them identically. Why it matters: learned edge directions are only meaningful up to equivalence. Claiming “the data shows A causes B” needs more than a structure score.
How much structure you can recover depends on data. With too little, a simpler or proxy explanation wins. Why it matters: a learned structure is a hypothesis about dependencies, not proof of causation. Check how robust it is to the amount of data.

Cheat sheet & connections

Name
Formula

\(\ln P(G) + \sum_{i,j} \Big[\ln \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{ij0})}{\Gamma(\alpha_{ij0} + m_{ij0})} + \sum_k \ln \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_{ijk} + m_{ijk})}{\Gamma(\alpha_{ijk})}\Big]\)
Equation 1


Decomposability
\(\ln P(D \mid G) = \sum_i \mathrm{score}(x_i, \mathrm{pa}(x_i))\)
Equation 2


Counting DAGs
\(a(n) = \sum_k (-1)^{k+1} \binom{n}{k} 2^{k(n-k)} a(n-k)\)
Equation 3


★ Markov equivalence
same skeleton and same v-structures
Equation 4


BDeu prior
\(\alpha_{ijk} = \kappa / (q_i r_i)\): score-equivalent
Equation 5






Which search? Use K2 when you trust a variable order (causes before effects). Use local search with random restarts when you don’t. Search over equivalence classes when equivalent graphs are slowing the search down. Exhaustive search only works for about five variables or fewer.
Common pitfalls

Reading learned arrows as causation. Within an equivalence class, directions are arbitrary. Even across classes, with limited data a proxy variable can win.
Mixing priors when comparing. The uniform prior can give equivalent graphs different scores; use BDeu when directions shouldn’t matter.
Trusting one local search run. It stops at the first local maximum. Restart, or use stochastic moves.
Too many parents. Each extra parent doubles a binary variable’s table. Cap the number of parents, as K2 does, or the counts get too thin.

Connections

Ch 2 · Representation defines the graphs and v-structures (colliders) used here.
Ch 4 · Parameter Learning supplies the counts and Dirichlet priors inside the score.
Ch 6 · Simple Decisions builds decision networks on learned or designed structures.
Ch 10 · Policy Search uses the same local-search ideas to search over policies instead of graphs.
Appendix C · Computational Complexity: why finding the best structure is NP-complete, which is why this page searches locally.

title: 3 · Inference
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 2 built a language for beliefs: a Bayesian network stores a big joint distribution as small local tables, one per variable. This chapter uses that language. A model is only useful if you can ask it questions, and asking it a question is called inference. Every later chapter relies on it: - Ch 4 needs it to learn from incomplete data; - Ch 6 needs it to weigh the outcomes of decisions; - Ch 19 runs it at every time step to track a hidden state.
The question: given what you’ve observed, how likely is something you haven’t? You’re late and the radio warned of a storm. How likely is it that there actually was a storm? Written as a formula, \(P(\text{query} \mid \text{evidence})\).
The short answer: every such question is answered by adding up the joint distribution over the variables you don’t care about. Doing that naively takes exponential time, so you either organize the additions cleverly (variable elimination) or estimate them by simulation (sampling).

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Exact methods organize the sums; sampling methods estimate them. Two special structures, naive Bayes and Gaussian models, have fast closed forms.







The key ideas at a glance

Inference is summing and normalizing. Split the variables into three groups: the query (what you want to know), the evidence (what you’ve observed) and the hidden variables (everything else). The answer is the total probability of the situations where the query holds and the evidence matches, divided by the total over all situations where the evidence matches. That’s exact, but the number of situations doubles with every hidden yes/no variable.
Variable elimination organizes the sums. Most of the chain-rule product doesn’t involve any given hidden variable. So you can sum out one variable at a time, touching only the few tables that mention it, and keep the small result for later. The work depends on the order in which variables are eliminated. It’s efficient for many networks, although exact inference is intractable (NP-hard) in the worst case.
Naive Bayes is inference made trivial. If one hidden cause produces several observations that are otherwise unrelated, as a machine’s fault produces its symptoms, the posterior is just the prior times one likelihood per observation, normalized. That’s quick enough for diagnosis and classification.
Sampling estimates the sums. Simulate many situations from the model and count. Rejection sampling keeps only the simulations that match the evidence, which wastes most of them when the evidence is rare. Likelihood weighting forces the evidence into every simulation and weights each one by how plausible that forcing was. Gibbs sampling changes one variable at a time given everything else, and wanders through the plausible situations. More samples mean more accuracy, with error shrinking roughly like \(1/\sqrt{\text{samples}}\).
Gaussian models need no sums. When everything is jointly Gaussian, observing some variables shifts the others’ mean in proportion to how surprising the observation was, and shrinks their spread by a fixed amount. It’s a closed-form formula, and it’s the same update the Kalman filter uses.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning

Normalize
Rescale numbers so they add up to 1

A table over some variables: a CPT, or any partial product of CPTs


Elimination order
The order in which variable elimination sums variables out


Direct sampling
Drawing a full situation from the model, causes before effects


Likelihood weight
How plausible the observed evidence was in one weighted sample


Markov blanket
A variable’s parents, children and children’s other parents: all Gibbs needs


Burn-in
Early Gibbs samples thrown away while the chain forgets its starting point








After this chapter you can

Answer a query in a small Bayesian network by hand, summing in a smart order.
Implement variable elimination with factor products and sums.
Diagnose with naive Bayes.
Estimate queries by sampling, and pick a sampler based on how rare the evidence is.
Condition a Gaussian on an observation.

title: 3 · Inference
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



A detective asks: “Given the clues, how likely is it that the butler did it?”
The exact way: list every possible story consistent with the clues, weigh each by how plausible it is, and add up the weight of the stories in which the butler did it. That’s correct, but the number of stories explodes. Variable elimination is the detective who notices that many stories share sub-plots, and works each sub-plot out once instead of in every story.
The sampling way: run thousands of simulated evenings from the model and look at the ones that match the clues.

Rejection sampling throws away every simulation that doesn’t match. That’s wasteful when the clues are rare.
Likelihood weighting forces every simulation to match the clues, then gives less weight to the ones where that forcing was implausible.
Gibbs sampling starts from any story that matches the clues, then keeps revising one detail at a time. It wanders through the plausible stories in proportion to how plausible they are.




Summing and normalizing
You’re late and the radio issued an alert. There are only two possibilities for the storm: it happened or it didn’t. Add up the probability of every full morning with a storm, late and an alert: 0.0364. Do the same without a storm: 0.0025. Together they total 0.0389, the probability of the evidence. The storm’s share is \(0.0364 / 0.0389 = 0.935\). That’s all inference is. The difficulty is only that “every full morning” can be astronomically many. See Equation 1.


Sharing sub-plots (variable elimination)
To get those totals, you’d naively list all 8 combinations of the other variables for each storm value, and multiply 5 numbers for each. But “late, given the jam” doesn’t care about the storm or the roadwork. So first combine the jam and late tables into a small “chance of being late given storm and roadwork” table (4 entries). Then fold in the roadwork (2 entries), then the storm. You never build anything bigger than 4 entries. On a chain of 30 variables, the same trick replaces about half a billion terms with about 120 multiplications. See Equation 3.


One product for naive Bayes
A coffee machine is fine 80% of the time and has a worn pump 5% of the time. A worn pump makes a loud noise 80% of the time, a healthy machine only 10%. Hearing the noise multiplies each condition’s weight by its noise probability: fine becomes \(0.80 \times 0.1 = 0.08\) and pump becomes \(0.05 \times 0.8 = 0.04\). Scale buildup, the third condition, becomes \(0.15 \times 0.2 = 0.03\). Normalizing, one symptom raises the pump from 5% to \(0.04 / 0.15 \approx 27\%\). Each further symptom multiplies in again. See Equation 2.


Simulating instead of summing
Run the commute model 1,000 times. The evidence, late and an alert, shows up on only about 39 of those mornings. Rejection sampling estimates the storm probability from those 39 alone, a noisy answer. Likelihood weighting instead sets “late” and “alert” in all 1,000 runs, and weights each run by how likely that evidence was given its simulated storm and jam. Runs with a storm get weights hundreds of times larger than runs without, and all 1,000 runs contribute. Gibbs sampling fixes the evidence and repeatedly re-draws one unknown at a time given the rest. See Equation 4, Equation 5 and Equation 6.


Gaussians in closed form
Morning and evening commutes are correlated: bad days tend to be bad all day. This morning took 50 minutes, 15 more than usual. The model says each morning minute above average predicts 0.75 of an evening minute above average. So expect about 11 extra minutes tonight (51 instead of 40), with a spread that shrinks from 10 to 8 minutes, whatever this morning’s time was. See Equation 7.

title: 3 · Inference
text:
Formalism

Inference by enumeration
Split the variables into the query \(q\), the evidence \(e\) (observed values), and everything else, the hidden variables \(h\) (ADM §3.1).

\[
P(q \mid e) = \frac{P(q, e)}{P(e)} = \frac{\sum_{h} P(q, h, e)}{\sum_{q'} \sum_{h} P(q', h, e)}
\tag{1}\]

In words. Add up the probability of every complete situation that matches the query value and the evidence. Then divide by the same total taken over every query value.
Term by term.

\(P(q, h, e)\) is one entry of the joint, computed by the chain rule of Ch 2.
\(\sum_h\) marginalizes out the hidden variables: it adds up over all their values.
The denominator \(P(e)\) doesn’t depend on \(q\). In practice you compute the numerator for every value of \(q\) and normalize.

The cost is the problem: with \(n\) binary hidden variables, there are \(2^n\) terms.


Naive Bayes: one product
A naive Bayes model has one class variable \(C\) and observations \(o_1, \ldots, o_n\) that each depend only on \(C\) (ADM §3.2). The structure is shown in Figure 2. Enumeration then collapses to a single product.

\[
P(c \mid o_{1:n}) \;\propto\; P(c) \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(o_i \mid c)
\tag{2}\]

In words. Start from how common each class is, then multiply in how well each observation fits that class. Normalize at the end.
Term by term. \(P(c)\) is the class prior, and \(P(o_i \mid c)\) is the likelihood of observation \(i\) under class \(c\). The product is exact because the observations are assumed independent given the class. That is the “naive” part: it’s often not quite true, but it usually still ranks the classes well.

Condition (C)

C->F





N

C->N





W

C->W








Figure 2: The coffee-machine naive Bayes model: the machine’s condition C causes each symptom independently.







Variable elimination: pushing sums inside
Most joint entries share factors. Summing over a variable only involves the factors that mention it, so you can move each sum inward, past the factors that don’t depend on it (ADM §3.3). The tables involved are called factors \(\phi\): a CPT, a product of CPTs, or any partial result.

\[
P(l^1, a^1) = \sum_{s} P(s)\, P(a^1 \mid s) \sum_{r} P(r) \sum_{j} P(j \mid s, r)\, P(l^1 \mid j)
\tag{3}\]

In words. Instead of one giant sum over all combinations of \(s\), \(r\) and \(j\), do the innermost sum first (\(j\)), then use its result in the next sum out (\(r\)), and so on. Each step creates a small factor that replaces the variable it summed out.
Term by term.

The innermost \(\sum_j P(j \mid s, r) P(l^1 \mid j)\) multiplies the two factors that mention \(j\) and sums \(j\) out. The result is a new factor \(\phi_1(s, r)\) with 4 entries.
\(\sum_r P(r)\, \phi_1(s, r)\) does the same for \(r\), giving \(\phi_2(s)\).
The outer sum over \(s\) combines the rest.
The two operations throughout are factor product (multiply entries that agree on shared variables) and summing out. That’s where the name “sum-product” comes from.

The work depends on the elimination order: a bad order creates big intermediate factors. Finding the best order is itself hard. In fact, exact inference in general Bayesian networks is NP-hard (ADM §3.5). On tree-shaped networks, belief propagation passes messages along the edges and gets every marginal efficiently (ADM §3.4).


Sampling
When exact inference is too costly, estimate the answer from samples.
Direct sampling (ADM §3.6) draws a complete sample by visiting the variables in topological order, parents before children, and drawing each one from its CPT row given the parents already drawn. Rejection sampling keeps only the samples that match the evidence:

\[
\hat{P}(q \mid e) = \frac{\#\{\text{samples with } q \text{ and } e\}}{\#\{\text{samples with } e\}}
\tag{4}\]

In words. Among the simulated situations that match the evidence, the fraction where the query holds.
Term by term. Both counts come from the same stream of direct samples. The estimate converges to the truth as samples accumulate, but only the matching samples count. With evidence of probability \(P(e)\), you keep only about \(N \cdot P(e)\) of \(N\) samples. For “late and radio alert”, \(P(e) = 0.039\), so 96% are wasted.
Likelihood weighting (ADM §3.7) never wastes a sample. It sets the evidence variables to their observed values instead of sampling them, and corrects for that with a weight:

\[
w = \prod_{e_i \in e} P\big(e_i \mid \mathrm{pa}(e_i)\big)
\qquad
\hat{P}(q \mid e) = \frac{\sum_{\text{samples with } q} w}{\sum_{\text{all samples}} w}
\tag{5}\]

In words. A sample’s weight is how likely the observed evidence would have been, given the values sampled for its parents. Samples where the evidence was plausible count more.
Term by term. The product runs over the evidence variables only, and \(\mathrm{pa}(e_i)\) takes the values drawn in this sample. For example, if a sample drew “storm” and “jam”, its weight for evidence (late, alert) is \(P(l^1 \mid j^1)\, P(a^1 \mid s^1) = 0.5 \times 0.95 = 0.475\).
Gibbs sampling (ADM §3.8) builds a Markov chain. It starts from any assignment consistent with the evidence, then repeatedly resamples one hidden variable given all the others:

\[
P(x_i \mid x_{-i}) \;\propto\; P\big(x_i \mid \mathrm{pa}(x_i)\big) \prod_{c \,\in\, \mathrm{children}(x_i)} P\big(c \mid \mathrm{pa}(c)\big)
\tag{6}\]

In words. To resample \(x_i\), weigh each of its values by how well it fits its parents, and how well its children fit it.
Term by term.

\(x_{-i}\) is every variable except \(x_i\).
Only \(x_i\)’s Markov blanket matters: its parents, its children, and its children’s other parents. Every other factor of the joint is the same for all values of \(x_i\), so it cancels when you normalize.
Consecutive samples are correlated, and the chain needs time to forget its starting point. The early sweeps are discarded (burn-in), and sometimes only every \(k\)-th sweep is kept (thinning).



Gaussian models: conditioning in closed form
If the variables are jointly Gaussian, inference needs no sums at all (ADM §3.9). Split the variables into a query block \(\mathbf{a}\) and an observed block \(\mathbf{b}\):

\[
\boldsymbol{\mu}_{a \mid b} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_a + \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1} (\mathbf{b} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_b)
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{a \mid b} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{aa} - \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ba}
\tag{7}\]

In words. Seeing \(\mathbf{b}\) shifts your estimate of \(\mathbf{a}\) in proportion to how surprising \(\mathbf{b}\) was and how strongly the two are correlated. It also shrinks your uncertainty, by the same amount whatever value you saw.
Term by term.

\(\mathbf{b} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_b\) is the surprise: the observation minus its expected value.
\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ab} \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{bb}^{-1}\) is the regression coefficient: how far \(\mathbf{a}\) moves per unit of surprise. In 1D it is \(\rho\, \sigma_a / \sigma_b\).
\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{a \mid b}\) doesn’t depend on the observed value. In 1D it is \(\sigma_a^2 (1 - \rho^2)\).
This is exactly the Kalman filter’s correct step from Ch 19, with the prediction playing the role of the prior.

title: 3 · Inference
text:
Worked example

Exact inference by hand
Using the commute network from Ch 2 (its tables are also in the problem gallery): you’re late and the radio warned of a storm. How likely is a storm? Follow Equation 3, innermost sum first.
Step 1: sum out the jam \(j\), for each combination of storm and roadwork: \(\phi_1(s, r) = \sum_j P(j \mid s, r) P(l^1 \mid j)\).



Table 2: \(\phi_1(s, r)\): the probability of being late, given storm and roadwork.

\(r^1\)

\(0.1(0.5) + 0.9(0.05) = 0.095\)
\(0.6(0.5) + 0.4(0.05) = 0.320\)


\(s^1\)
\(0.7(0.5) + 0.3(0.05) = 0.365\)
\(0.9(0.5) + 0.1(0.05) = 0.455\)






Step 2: sum out roadwork \(r\): \(\phi_2(s) = \sum_r P(r) \phi_1(s, r)\). \(\phi_2(s^0) = 0.8(0.095) + 0.2(0.320) = 0.140\) and \(\phi_2(s^1) = 0.8(0.365) + 0.2(0.455) = 0.383\).
Step 3: combine with the storm prior and the radio:

\(P(s^1, l^1, a^1) = 0.1 \times 0.95 \times 0.383 = 0.03639\)
\(P(s^0, l^1, a^1) = 0.9 \times 0.02 \times 0.140 = 0.00252\)

Normalize: \(P(s^1 \mid l^1, a^1) = 0.03639 / (0.03639 + 0.00252) \approx\) 0.935. The radio alert is strong evidence: an alert without a storm happens only 2% of the time. Enumeration would have summed 8 full joint entries for each storm value. Variable elimination never built anything bigger than a 4-entry table.


Naive Bayes: diagnosing a coffee machine
A machine is fine 80% of the time, has scale buildup 15% of the time, and a worn pump 5% of the time. Each condition shows three symptoms with different probabilities:

The coffee flows slowly and the machine is loud, but the taste is fine. By Equation 2:

ok: \(0.80 \times 0.05 \times 0.10 \times 0.90 = 0.0036\)
scale buildup: \(0.15 \times 0.70 \times 0.20 \times 0.40 = 0.0084\)

These sum to \(0.0288\), so the posterior is \((0.125, 0.292, 0.583)\). The worn pump, the rarest condition a priori, is now the most likely, because the noise fits it so much better. Figure 3 shows the belief shifting as each symptom arrives.

Gaussian conditioning
Morning and evening commute times (in minutes) are jointly Gaussian: morning \(\mathcal{N}(35, 8^2)\), evening \(\mathcal{N}(40, 10^2)\), with correlation \(\rho = 0.6\) (bad traffic days tend to be bad all day). This morning took 50 minutes. By Equation 7, in 1D:

Shift: \(\rho\, \sigma_e / \sigma_m \times (50 - 35) = 0.6 \times \tfrac{10}{8} \times 15 = 11.25\), so the expected evening time is \(40 + 11.25 = 51.25\) minutes.
Spread: \(10^2 (1 - 0.6^2) = 64\), so the standard deviation is 8 minutes, down from 10.

title: 3 · Inference
3 · Inference
text:
Algorithms & code

Factors
A factor is a table with one named axis per variable. Everything else is built from three operations on factors: product, summing out, and conditioning.

PythonJulia


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Factor:
    variables: tuple
    table: np.ndarray

def cpt_factor(bn: BayesNet, x: str) -> Factor:
    """X's CPT as a factor over (parents..., X)."""
    return Factor(tuple(bn.parents[x]) + (x,), bn.cpt[x])

def factor_product(f: Factor, g: Factor) -> Factor:
    """phi(x, y, z) = f(x, y) * g(y, z), matching entries on shared variables."""
    variables = f.variables + tuple(v for v in g.variables if v not in f.variables)

    def expand(h: Factor) -> np.ndarray:
        # Reorder h's axes to follow `variables`, then insert a size-1 axis
        # for every variable h doesn't mention. NumPy broadcasting then lines
        # up shared variables and repeats h along the ones it lacks.
        order = [h.variables.index(v) for v in variables if v in h.variables]
        shape = [h.table.shape[h.variables.index(v)] if v in h.variables else 1
                 for v in variables]
        return np.transpose(h.table, order).reshape(shape)

    return Factor(variables, expand(f) * expand(g))

def sum_out(f: Factor, x: str) -> Factor:
    """Marginalize x away: add the table up along x's axis."""
    i = f.variables.index(x)
    return Factor(f.variables[:i] + f.variables[i + 1:], f.table.sum(axis=i))

def condition(f: Factor, evidence: dict) -> Factor:
    """Keep only entries that agree with the evidence, and drop those axes."""
    # An integer index picks one value (and removes the axis); slice(None)
    # keeps the whole axis, like `:` does.
    index = tuple(evidence.get(v, slice(None)) for v in f.variables)
    kept = tuple(v for v in f.variables if v not in evidence)
    return Factor(kept, np.asarray(f.table[index]))

def normalize(f: Factor, order=None) -> Factor:
    """Scale the table to sum to 1, optionally reordering its axes."""
    order = tuple(order or f.variables)
    table = np.transpose(f.table, [f.variables.index(v) for v in order])
    return Factor(order, table / table.sum())


using ADM, Distributions, Random

# A factor: a table with one named axis per variable.
struct Factor
    vars::Vector{Symbol}
    table::Array{Float64}
end

cpt_factor(bn, x) = Factor([bn.parents[x]..., x], bn.cpt[x])

function factor_product(f, g)
    vars = [f.vars; [v for v in g.vars if !(v in f.vars)]]
    # Put each table's axes in `vars` order, with a size-1 axis for every variable it
    # doesn't mention; broadcasting (.*) then matches shared variables and repeats the rest.
    function expand(h)
        axis(v) = findfirst(==(v), h.vars)
        t = isempty(h.vars) ? h.table : permutedims(h.table, [axis(v) for v in vars if v in h.vars])
        return reshape(t, Tuple(v in h.vars ? size(h.table, axis(v)) : 1 for v in vars))
    end
    return Factor(vars, expand(f) .* expand(g))
end

function sum_out(f, x)
    i = findfirst(==(x), f.vars)
    return Factor(deleteat!(copy(f.vars), i), dropdims(sum(f.table; dims = i); dims = i))
end

function condition(f, evidence)
    # An integer picks one value (dropping that axis); Colon() keeps the whole axis.
    idx = [haskey(evidence, v) ? evidence[v] : Colon() for v in f.vars]
    t = f.table[idx...]
    return Factor([v for v in f.vars if !haskey(evidence, v)], t isa Array ? t : fill(t))
end

# Scale to sum to 1, with axes in the given order. (Named `normalized` to avoid
# clashing with LinearAlgebra's `normalize`.)
function normalized(f, order = f.vars)
    t = permutedims(f.table, [findfirst(==(v), f.vars) for v in order])
    return Factor(collect(order), t ./ sum(t))
end





Exact inference and variable elimination
exact_inference multiplies every CPT into the full joint first. variable_elimination never does: before summing out each hidden variable, it multiplies only the factors that mention it.

PythonJulia


def exact_inference(bn: BayesNet, query, evidence: dict) -> Factor:
    """P(query | evidence) from the full joint: exact but exponential."""
    phi = reduce(factor_product, (cpt_factor(bn, x) for x in bn.parents))
    phi = condition(phi, evidence)
    for v in phi.variables:
        if v not in query:          # every hidden variable gets summed out
            phi = sum_out(phi, v)
    return normalize(phi, query)

def variable_elimination(bn: BayesNet, query, evidence: dict, order) -> Factor:
    """P(query | evidence), summing out hidden variables one at a time.

    `order` lists the hidden variables in the order to eliminate them.
    """
    factors = [condition(cpt_factor(bn, x), evidence) for x in bn.parents]
    for h in order:
        # Only the factors that mention h are multiplied before h is summed
        # out; every other factor is left alone. That is the whole saving
        # over building the full joint.
        involved = [f for f in factors if h in f.variables]
        factors = [f for f in factors if h not in f.variables]
        if involved:
            factors.append(sum_out(reduce(factor_product, involved), h))
    return normalize(reduce(factor_product, factors), query)


function exact_inference(bn, query, evidence)
    ϕ = reduce(factor_product, [cpt_factor(bn, x) for x in keys(bn.parents)])
    ϕ = condition(ϕ, evidence)
    for v in setdiff(ϕ.vars, query)       # sum out every hidden variable
        ϕ = sum_out(ϕ, v)
    end
    return normalized(ϕ, query)
end

function variable_elimination(bn, query, evidence, order)
    factors = [condition(cpt_factor(bn, x), evidence) for x in keys(bn.parents)]
    for h in order
        # Multiply only the factors that mention h, then sum h out;
        # every other factor is left alone.
        involved = filter(f -> h in f.vars, factors)
        filter!(f -> !(h in f.vars), factors)
        isempty(involved) || push!(factors, sum_out(reduce(factor_product, involved), h))
    end
    return normalized(reduce(factor_product, factors), query)
end





Rejection sampling and likelihood weighting

PythonJulia


def topological_order(parents: dict) -> list:
    """Variables ordered so that every parent comes before its children."""
    order = []
    while len(order) < len(parents):
        for x, pa in parents.items():
            if x not in order and all(p in order for p in pa):
                order.append(x)
    return order

def _cpt_row(bn: BayesNet, sample: dict, x: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """Distribution of x given the parents' values in `sample`."""
    return bn.cpt[x][tuple(sample[q] for q in bn.parents[x])]

def direct_sample(bn: BayesNet, rng, order=None) -> dict:
    """One joint sample: draw each variable given its already-drawn parents."""
    sample = {}
    for x in order or topological_order(bn.parents):
        row = _cpt_row(bn, sample, x)
        sample[x] = rng.choice(len(row), p=row)
    return sample

def rejection_sampling(bn, query, evidence, n, rng) -> Factor:
    """Draw n direct samples; keep those that match the evidence."""
    order = topological_order(bn.parents)
    counts = np.zeros([bn.card[q] for q in query])
    for _ in range(n):
        s = direct_sample(bn, rng, order)
        if all(s[v] == value for v, value in evidence.items()):
            counts[tuple(s[q] for q in query)] += 1
    if counts.sum() == 0:
        raise ValueError("no sample matched the evidence; draw more samples")
    return Factor(tuple(query), counts / counts.sum())

def likelihood_weighted_sampling(bn, query, evidence, n, rng) -> Factor:
    """Fix evidence variables instead of sampling them, and weight each
    sample by how likely that evidence was given its sampled parents."""
    order = topological_order(bn.parents)
    weights = np.zeros([bn.card[q] for q in query])
    for _ in range(n):
        s, w = {}, 1.0
        for x in order:
            row = _cpt_row(bn, s, x)
            if x in evidence:
                s[x] = evidence[x]
                w *= row[s[x]]       # P(observed value | sampled parents)
            else:
                s[x] = rng.choice(len(row), p=row)
        weights[tuple(s[q] for q in query)] += w
    return Factor(tuple(query), weights / weights.sum())


function topological_order(parents)
    order = Symbol[]
    while length(order) < length(parents)
        for (x, pa) in parents
            !(x in order) && all(p in order for p in pa) && push!(order, x)
        end
    end
    return order
end

# Distribution of x given the parents' values in sample s: index the CPT by the
# parents' values (splatted), then take the whole last axis.
cpt_row(bn, s, x) = bn.cpt[x][(s[q] for q in bn.parents[x])..., :]

function direct_sample(bn, rng, order = topological_order(bn.parents))
    s = Dict{Symbol, Int}()
    for x in order                      # parents are always drawn before children
        s[x] = rand(rng, Categorical(cpt_row(bn, s, x)))
    end
    return s
end

function rejection_sampling(bn, query, evidence, n, rng)
    order, counts = topological_order(bn.parents), zeros(bn.card[query])
    for _ in 1:n
        s = direct_sample(bn, rng, order)
        all(s[v] == val for (v, val) in evidence) && (counts[s[query]] += 1)   # keep matches only
    end
    return counts ./ sum(counts)
end

function likelihood_weighted_sampling(bn, query, evidence, n, rng)
    order, weights = topological_order(bn.parents), zeros(bn.card[query])
    for _ in 1:n
        s, w = Dict{Symbol, Int}(), 1.0
        for x in order
            p = cpt_row(bn, s, x)
            if haskey(evidence, x)
                s[x] = evidence[x]
                w *= p[s[x]]            # P(observed value | sampled parents)
            else
                s[x] = rand(rng, Categorical(p))
            end
        end
        weights[s[query]] += w
    end
    return weights ./ sum(weights)
end





Gibbs sampling

PythonJulia


def blanket_distribution(bn: BayesNet, sample: dict, x: str) -> np.ndarray:
    """P(x | all other variables), which depends only on x's Markov blanket:
    P(x | pa(x)) times P(c | pa(c)) for each child c of x."""
    children = [c for c, pa in bn.parents.items() if x in pa]
    p = np.empty(bn.card[x])
    for value in range(bn.card[x]):
        s = {**sample, x: value}      # try x = value, keep everything else
        p[value] = prod(_cpt_row(bn, s, y)[s[y]] for y in [x, *children])
    return p / p.sum()

def gibbs_sampling(bn, query, evidence, n, rng, burn_in=200, thin=1):
    """Markov chain: resample one hidden variable at a time from its
    distribution given everything else. Returns P(query | evidence)."""
    # Start anywhere consistent with the evidence.
    sample = {**direct_sample(bn, rng), **evidence}
    hidden = [x for x in bn.parents if x not in evidence]
    counts = np.zeros([bn.card[q] for q in query])
    for k in range(burn_in + n * thin):
        for x in hidden:
            p = blanket_distribution(bn, sample, x)
            sample[x] = rng.choice(len(p), p=p)
        # Skip the first `burn_in` sweeps (the chain hasn't forgotten its
        # start yet), then keep one sweep in every `thin`.
        if k >= burn_in and (k - burn_in) % thin == 0:
            counts[tuple(sample[q] for q in query)] += 1
    return Factor(tuple(query), counts / counts.sum())


# P(x | everything else): only x's own CPT row and its children's rows depend on x.
function blanket_distribution(bn, s, x)
    children = [c for (c, pa) in bn.parents if x in pa]
    p = map(1:bn.card[x]) do value
        t = merge(s, Dict(x => value))            # try x = value, keep the rest
        prod(cpt_row(bn, t, y)[t[y]] for y in [x; children])
    end
    return p ./ sum(p)
end

function gibbs_sampling(bn, query, evidence, n, rng; burn_in = 200)
    s = merge(direct_sample(bn, rng), evidence)   # any start consistent with the evidence
    hidden = [x for x in keys(bn.parents) if !haskey(evidence, x)]
    counts = zeros(bn.card[query])
    for k in 1:(burn_in + n)
        for x in hidden
            s[x] = rand(rng, Categorical(blanket_distribution(bn, s, x)))
        end
        k > burn_in && (counts[s[query]] += 1)    # skip the burn-in sweeps
    end
    return counts ./ sum(counts)
end





Naive Bayes and Gaussian conditioning

PythonJulia


def naive_bayes_posterior(prior, likelihoods, observations) -> np.ndarray:
    """P(c | o_1..o_n), proportional to P(c) * prod_i P(o_i | c).

    likelihoods[i][c, o] = P(feature i = o | class c).
    """
    p = np.array(prior, dtype=float)
    for L, o in zip(likelihoods, observations):
        p = p * L[:, o]
    return p / p.sum()

def gaussian_condition(mu, Sigma, a, b, values):
    """Mean and covariance of x_a given x_b = values, for a joint Gaussian.

    a and b are lists of indices into mu and Sigma.
    """
    S_ab, S_bb = Sigma[np.ix_(a, b)], Sigma[np.ix_(b, b)]
    # K = S_ab S_bb^-1: how far the query moves per unit of surprise in
    # the observed variables. solve() avoids forming the inverse.
    K = np.linalg.solve(S_bb, S_ab.T).T
    mu_a = mu[a] + K @ (np.asarray(values) - mu[b])
    Sigma_a = Sigma[np.ix_(a, a)] - K @ S_ab.T
    return mu_a, Sigma_a


function naive_bayes_posterior(prior, likelihoods, observations)
    p = copy(prior)
    for (L, o) in zip(likelihoods, observations)
        p .*= L[:, o]              # L[c, o] = P(feature = o | class c)
    end
    return p ./ sum(p)
end

function gaussian_condition(μ, Σ, a, b, values)
    K = Σ[a, b] / Σ[b, b]          # Σ_ab Σ_bb⁻¹, computed without forming the inverse
    return μ[a] + K * (values - μ[b]), Σ[a, a] - K * Σ[b, a]
end





Run them all

PythonJulia

NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






reduce(factor_product, factors) folds a list with a two-argument function, like Python’s functools.reduce.
filter(f -> cond, xs) keeps the matching items; filter! does it in place. f -> … is Julia’s lambda.
cond && action runs action only if cond is true. x || action runs it only if x is false.
map(1:n) do value … end is the same as map(value -> …, 1:n), written as a block.
merge(d1, d2) combines dictionaries, with d2 winning on shared keys, like {**d1, **d2}.
dropdims(sum(A; dims = i); dims = i): Julia’s sum keeps the summed axis with size 1, so dropdims removes it. NumPy’s sum drops it for you.






Results: how fast do the samplers converge?
Figure 7 measures each sampler’s average error on \(P(\text{storm} \mid \text{late}, \text{alert})\) as the number of samples grows, averaged over 10 independent runs. All three improve roughly like \(1 / \sqrt{N}\), the usual Monte Carlo rate: about 3 times less error for 10 times more samples. Rejection sampling pays for the evidence’s rarity and is the least accurate at every \(N\). Likelihood weighting is best for most sample sizes. Gibbs sampling starts behind, because of its correlated early samples, but catches up by \(N = 10{,}000\).








Figure 7: Mean absolute error of three samplers estimating P(storm | late, alert), over 10 runs per point, for a growing number of samples N (log-log axes). Rejection sampling keeps only about 4% of its samples; at N = 100 some runs keep none, which is why its error barely improves at first.





Figure 8 shows why Gibbs sampling needs a burn-in. Three chains start from different assignments. Their running estimates disagree at first, then settle on the same answer.








Figure 8: Running estimate of P(storm | late, alert) from three Gibbs chains with different starting points. The early sweeps depend on the start; that’s what burn-in throws away.

title: 3 · Inference
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: a query through a fork. In the commute network, the radio issues an alert. What’s the probability of a traffic jam, \(P(j^1 \mid a^1)\)?






TipSolution





First update the storm belief: \(P(s^1 \mid a^1) \propto 0.1 \times 0.95 = 0.095\) and \(P(s^0 \mid a^1) \propto 0.9 \times 0.02 = 0.018\), so \(P(s^1 \mid a^1) = 0.095 / 0.113 = 0.841\).
Then sum out storm and roadwork. \(P(j^1 \mid s^1) = 0.8(0.7) + 0.2(0.9) = 0.74\) and \(P(j^1 \mid s^0) = 0.8(0.1) + 0.2(0.6) = 0.20\). So
\[
P(j^1 \mid a^1) = 0.841 \times 0.74 + 0.159 \times 0.20 = \mathbf{0.654},
\]
up from the prior \(P(j^1) = 0.254\). Information flows from the alert, through the storm, to the jam: the fork pattern of Ch 2.



Problem 2: why elimination order matters. A chain of 30 binary variables, \(X_1 \to X_2 \to \cdots \to X_{30}\). How many joint entries does enumeration sum to get \(P(x_{30})\)? How big is the largest factor if you eliminate \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) in order?






TipSolution





Enumeration sums over the \(2^{29} \approx 5.4 \times 10^8\) combinations of the hidden variables, for each value of \(X_{30}\).
Eliminating in order: summing out \(X_1\) multiplies \(P(x_1)\) and \(P(x_2 \mid x_1)\), a factor over \((X_1, X_2)\) with 4 entries, and leaves \(\phi(x_2)\). Every later step is the same size. So the largest factor has 4 entries, and the total work is about \(29 \times 4\) multiplications: linear instead of exponential.
A bad order is costly. Eliminating \(X_{15}\) first leaves a factor linking \(X_{14}\) and \(X_{16}\), and each such choice can grow the factors further.



Problem 3: likelihood weights. With evidence “late and alert”, compute the weights of two samples: (a) storm = yes, jam = yes; (b) storm = no, jam = no. How many (b)-type samples equal one (a)-type sample?






TipSolution





By Equation 5, the weight is \(P(l^1 \mid j)\, P(a^1 \mid s)\):


\(0.5 \times 0.95 = 0.475\)


\(0.05 \times 0.02 = 0.001\)


One (a) sample counts as much as 475 (b) samples. Likelihood weighting still draws (b)-type samples often, since \(P(s^0, j^0) = 0.67\) a priori, but it nearly ignores them. When the evidence is very unlikely under the prior, most samples get tiny weights, and likelihood weighting degrades too. That’s one motivation for Gibbs sampling.



Problem 4: conditioning the other way. This evening’s commute took 60 minutes. What’s your belief about this morning’s?






TipSolution





Swap the roles in Equation 7. The shift is \(\rho\, \sigma_m / \sigma_e \times (60 - 40) = 0.6 \times \tfrac{8}{10} \times 20 = 9.6\), so the mean is \(35 + 9.6 =\) 44.6 minutes. The variance is \(8^2 (1 - 0.6^2) = 40.96\), a standard deviation of 6.4 minutes. The shrinkage factor \(1 - \rho^2 = 0.64\) is the same in both directions.

title: 3 · Inference
text:
Recap

Every inference query is a sum over the joint (Equation 1): fix the evidence, sum out the hidden variables, normalize. Why it matters: belief updates in Ch 19, the value of information in Ch 6, and learning with missing data in Ch 4 are all this computation.
Variable elimination (Equation 3) pushes sums inside products, so it only builds factors as big as each step needs. The elimination order sets the cost, and exact inference is NP-hard in general. Why it matters: it is the practical exact method, and the same “sum out one variable at a time” idea is the predict step of every filter.
Naive Bayes (Equation 2) is one product, exact when the observations are independent given the class. Why it matters: it’s a fast, surprisingly strong baseline for diagnosis and classification.
Sampling trades exactness for scalability. Rejection sampling wastes samples when the evidence is rare (Equation 4); likelihood weighting fixes the evidence and weights instead (Equation 5); Gibbs sampling walks a Markov chain using only each variable’s Markov blanket (Equation 6). Why it matters: sampling is how inference scales to large models, and the same ideas reappear in particle filters (Ch 19) and Monte Carlo planning (Ch 9).
Gaussian models condition in closed form (Equation 7): shift by the regression on the surprise, and shrink the variance by \(1 - \rho^2\). Why it matters: this is the Kalman filter’s update, and the backbone of estimation for continuous systems.

text:

Which method? Use variable elimination for small or tree-like networks. Use likelihood weighting when the evidence sits near the network’s roots and isn’t too surprising. Use Gibbs sampling for large networks with deep or surprising evidence. For Gaussian models, condition in closed form.
Common pitfalls

Forgetting to normalize. A sum over the joint gives \(P(q, e)\), not \(P(q \mid e)\).
Rejection sampling with rare evidence. The effective sample size is about \(N \cdot P(e)\). Check how many samples you actually kept.
Trusting early Gibbs samples. Discard a burn-in, and remember that consecutive samples are correlated, so \(N\) Gibbs samples are worth fewer than \(N\) independent ones.
A bad elimination order. Eliminate variables with few neighbors first, which keeps the factors small.

Connections

Ch 6 · Simple Decisions uses inference to compute expected utilities and the value of information.
Appendix C · Computational Complexity: why exact inference is NP-hard, via a reduction from 3SAT.
Ch 19 · Beliefs: the discrete filter is variable elimination over time, the Kalman filter is Gaussian conditioning, and the particle filter is likelihood weighting with resampling.

title: 1 · Introduction
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
This is the starting point of the book and of this site. It frames the whole subject: an agent repeatedly observes its environment and acts, and it must choose well despite several kinds of uncertainty. The rest of the book is organized around those kinds of uncertainty, one Part each. This page is also a map: each idea below points to the chapter that develops it.
The question: what does it mean to make good decisions when the world is uncertain, and what are the ways to build a system that does?
The short answer: choose actions that maximize expected utility over time, given everything observed so far; build such systems by programming, learning from examples, optimizing in simulation, planning with a model, or learning from experience.








loop



env

Environment
state, other agents



agent

Agent
policy



env->agent


observation oₜ



agent->env


action aₜ






Figure 1: The observe–act loop. At each step the agent receives an observation of its environment and chooses an action, which changes the environment.







The key ideas at a glance

The observe–act loop. An agent (a person, a robot, or software) receives an observation \(o_t\), chooses an action \(a_t\), and the environment responds. Observations can be noisy or incomplete, and actions can have uncertain effects. A policy says what to do given what has been observed.
Four sources of uncertainty. Outcome uncertainty: actions have random effects. Model uncertainty: we don’t know the rules of the environment exactly. State uncertainty: we can’t see the state directly. Interaction uncertainty: other agents are choosing too. The book’s Parts II–V each add one of these; Part I sets up the probability and utility needed to reason about any of them.
Maximize expected utility. A rational agent chooses the action with the highest expected utility, averaging over what it is uncertain about (Chapter 6). Over time, that becomes maximizing expected discounted reward (Chapter 7).
Five ways to build a decision maker. Write the rules by hand; learn from an expert’s examples; search over policies in simulation; plan with a model; or learn by trial and error. They differ in what the designer must supply: rules, examples, a simulator, a model, or only a reward.
Many fields contributed. Probability and statistics, economics (utility, games), psychology (reinforcement), neuroscience (neural networks), computer science, control engineering and operations research all built parts of the toolkit.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Agent
Anything that observes and acts: a person, a robot, a program


Observation \(o_t\)
What the agent perceives at time \(t\); possibly noisy or partial


Action \(a_t\)
What the agent does at time \(t\)


Policy \(\pi\)
A rule for choosing actions from what has been observed


Reward, utility
A number saying how good an outcome is


Discount factor \(\gamma\)
How much less a reward counts for each step it is delayed


Model
A description of how the environment responds to actions








After this chapter you can

Describe a decision problem as an observe–act loop, and name its sources of uncertainty.
Say which Part of the book, and which chapters of this site, address each source.
Compare the five ways to design a decision maker, and what each requires.
Compute a discounted return and a maximum-expected-utility decision by hand.

title: 1 · Introduction
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Learning to cook a new dish. You could follow a recipe exactly (explicit programming), copy what a friend does (learning from examples), try variations and keep what tastes better (optimization), reason from how ingredients behave (planning with a model), or cook it many times and learn from each result (reinforcement learning). The oven may run hot (outcome uncertainty), you don’t fully know the recipe’s quirks (model uncertainty), you can’t see inside the cake (state uncertainty), and someone else keeps adjusting the heat (interaction uncertainty).


We’ll use Hex World throughout this page (Appendix F.1; problem gallery): an agent moves across 24 hexagonal tiles, and each move goes the intended way only 70% of the time, veering to a neighboring direction otherwise. Three tiles end the episode with a reward: +10, +5 or −10. Bumping into the edge costs 1. We score every policy by its expected discounted reward (\(\gamma = 0.9\)) from a random ordinary tile.

Five designers, one problem
The five approaches, each implemented with this site’s code from later chapters:

Explicit programming: a hand-written rule “always head for the +10 tile” earns 2.77.
Learning from examples (behavioral cloning, Chapter 18): copying 5 expert demonstrations earns 1.62 on average; 20 demonstrations, 4.02.
Optimization (Chapter 10): trying random changes to a policy in a simulator, and keeping what helps, earns between 3.46 and 4.28.
Planning (Chapter 7): computing the best policy from the model earns 4.53, the optimum.
Reinforcement learning (Chapter 17): Q-learning by trial and error earns between 4.40 and 4.48 after 50,000 steps.

The less the designer knows, the more data the method needs, and planning is only possible with a model. See Figure 3.


Uncertainty changes the right answer
If moves always went the intended way, the best policy would be worth 5.87; at 70% reliability, 4.53; at 40%, 2.59. The best action changes too: at 40% reliability, 5 of the 21 ordinary tiles choose differently than at 70%. Accounting for uncertainty isn’t a correction to a deterministic plan; it changes the plan. See the interactive.

title: 1 · Introduction
text:
Formalism

The decision problem
At each step \(t\), the agent has seen \(o_1, \dots, o_t\) and chooses \(a_t\). A policy \(\pi\) maps what has been seen to an action. Its quality is the expected discounted sum of rewards it collects, and the goal is the best policy:

\[
\pi^* = \arg\max_\pi\ \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{t-1} r_t \ \Big|\ \pi\Big]
\tag{1}\]

In words. Pick the way of acting that collects the most reward on average, counting rewards less the later they come.
Term by term.

\(r_t\): the reward received at step \(t\), which depends on the state and the action.
\(\gamma \in [0, 1)\): the discount factor; a reward \(k\) steps away counts \(\gamma^k\) as much. With \(\gamma = 0.9\), a reward 10 steps away counts about a third.
\(\mathbb{E}[\cdot \mid \pi]\): the average over every source of randomness (outcomes, observations, other agents) when acting by \(\pi\).

Why it holds. It’s a definition, not a theorem, but a well-motivated one: the discounted sum is finite whenever rewards are bounded, and discounting captures both impatience and the risk that the process ends. Parts II–V are about computing or approximating \(\pi^*\) under different uncertainties.


Maximum expected utility
For a single decision, the principle is (developed in Chapter 6):

\[
a^* = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid a, o)\, U(s')
\tag{2}\]

In words. Choose the action whose possible outcomes, weighted by their probabilities, are best on average.
Term by term.

\(P(s' \mid a, o)\): the probability that action \(a\) leads to outcome \(s'\), given observation \(o\) (Chapters 2–3 compute such probabilities).
\(U(s')\): the utility, how much the agent values outcome \(s'\) (Chapter 6).
The sum is the expected utility of \(a\); the best action maximizes it.

Why it holds. Utility theory (J. von Neumann and O. Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, 1944) shows that if an agent’s preferences between uncertain outcomes satisfy a few consistency axioms, they can be described by a utility function, and the agent prefers exactly the options with higher expected utility. Over time, Equation 1 is this principle applied to whole sequences of decisions.
