title: 1 · Introduction
text:
Worked example

A discounted return
A hex-world agent bumps into the edge once (−1), takes two ordinary steps (0 each), then steps onto the +10 tile. With \(\gamma = 0.9\) and the reward counted when it acts on that tile at step 4:
\[
-1 + 0.9 \times 0 + 0.9^2 \times 0 + 0.9^3 \times 10 = -1 + 7.29 = 6.29
\]
Had it reached the +10 tile two steps later, the same reward would count \(0.9^5 \times 10 = 5.90\). Discounting is what makes the agent prefer short routes.


A maximum-expected-utility choice
The agent is on a tile with the −10 tile to the east and a safe ordinary tile to the west. A move goes the intended way with probability 0.7 and veers to each neighboring direction with probability 0.15. Heading east lands on the −10 tile with probability 0.7. Heading west lands there only if the move veers twice around, which can’t happen in one step: probability 0. If the ordinary tiles are worth about 4 and the −10 tile is worth −10:

east: \(0.7 \times (-10) + 0.3 \times 4 = -5.8\);
west: \(1.0 \times 4 = 4\).

Maximum expected utility picks west. With these numbers, even a 10% chance of the −10 tile would cost 1.4 in expected utility, so good policies weigh even small risks of landing there; the uncertainty dial below shows how the best actions shift as the risk of veering changes.
In Hex World itself, the best policy’s values range from 0.71 to 8.22 over the ordinary tiles; the rule “head for +10” chooses differently on 10 of them.

title: 1 · Introduction
1 · Introduction
text:
Algorithms & code

The explicit rule and the local search
The other three approaches use code shown on their own chapters’ pages (linked in Table 3).

PythonJulia


def head_for(tiles, target) -> Array:
    """Explicit programming: a hand-written rule. On every tile, pick the
    direction whose neighbor is fewest moves from `target` (ignoring that
    moves can veer). Reward tiles and the terminal state get action 0."""
    tiles = list(tiles)
    steps = hex_steps(tiles, target)
    policy = np.zeros(len(tiles) + 1, dtype=int)       # last entry: terminal
    for i, tile in enumerate(tiles):
        best = min(range(len(DIRECTIONS)),
                   key=lambda a: steps.get(neighbor(tile, DIRECTIONS[a]),
                                           np.inf))
        policy[i] = best
    return policy

def simulated_return(mdp, policy, b, seed, n=100, depth=40) -> float:
    """Average discounted return of a deterministic policy over n simulated
    episodes from b. The seed is fixed, so two policies are compared on the
    same random draws (common random numbers)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    total = 0.0
    for _ in range(n):
        s = rng.choice(len(b), p=b)
        for t in range(depth):
            a = policy[s]
            total += mdp.gamma ** t * mdp.R[s, a]
            s = rng.choice(len(b), p=mdp.T[s, a])
    return total / n

def local_search(mdp, b, rng, proposals=300, n=100, depth=40, seed=0):
    """Optimization: start from a random policy; repeatedly change one
    state's action at random and keep the change if the simulated return
    improves. It uses the simulator only as a black box, never T or R
    directly. Returns the policy and the simulated return after each
    proposal."""
    n_s, n_a = mdp.R.shape
    policy = rng.integers(n_a, size=n_s)
    best = simulated_return(mdp, policy, b, seed, n, depth)
    history = [best]
    for _ in range(proposals):
        trial = policy.copy()
        s = rng.integers(n_s)
        trial[s] = rng.integers(n_a)
        u = simulated_return(mdp, trial, b, seed, n, depth)
        if u > best:
            policy, best = trial, u
        history.append(best)
    return policy, history


using ADM, LinearAlgebra

p = hex_world()                     # Hex World (Appendix F.1); T[s, a, s′], R[s, a]
n = size(p.T, 1)

# Planning: value iteration on the model (Ch 7).
function plan(p; iters = 1000)
    U = zeros(size(p.T, 1))
    for _ in 1:iters
        U = [maximum(p.R[s, a] + p.γ * (p.T[s, a, :] ⋅ U) for a in 1:6) for s in axes(p.T, 1)]
    end
    return U, [argmax([p.R[s, a] + p.γ * (p.T[s, a, :] ⋅ U) for a in 1:6]) for s in axes(p.T, 1)]
end
U, policy = plan(p)

# Score a deterministic policy from a uniform start over the ordinary tiles.
start = [i for i in 1:n-1 if !all(p.T[i, :, n] .== 1)]   # tiles that don't end the episode
b = zeros(n); b[start] .= 1 / length(start)
function score(p, policy, b)
    Tπ = [p.T[s, policy[s], t] for s in 1:n, t in 1:n]
    Rπ = [p.R[s, policy[s]] for s in 1:n]
    return b ⋅ ((I - p.γ * Tπ) \ Rπ)
end
println("planning: ", round(score(p, policy, b); digits = 3))
@assert isapprox(score(p, policy, b), 4.526; atol = 1e-3)









NoteReading the Python code






head_for uses hex_steps, a breadth-first search that counts the fewest moves from every tile to the target, and picks the direction whose neighbor is closest. It knows the map and the goal, but nothing about veering or about the −10 tile.
simulated_return creates its random generator from a fixed seed each time, so two policies are scored on the same random draws. Differences between them then reflect the policies, not the luck of the draws.
local_search is a simple hill climber: it only ever looks at simulated returns, never at T or R.






Run them

game = hex_world()
rule = intro.head_for(STANDARD_TILES, (2, 9))               # head for the +10 tile
policy, U, _ = policy_iteration(game.T, game.R, game.gamma, np.zeros(len(game.R), int))
print("rule:", round(value(rule), 3), " planning:", round(value(policy), 3))

rule: 2.766  planning: 4.526




Results

Five ways to build a Hex World agent








Figure 3: Hex World: the expected discounted reward (from a random ordinary tile) of policies built five ways. Dots are individual runs (20 for behavioral cloning, 5 for local search and Q-learning); bars are averages. The dashed line is the optimum.






The rule is easy to write and mediocre. “Head for +10” ignores veering and the +5 tile, and chooses differently from the optimal policy on 10 of 21 ordinary tiles, for 2.77 against 4.53.
Copying needs enough examples. Tiles no demonstration visited get a random action. With 5 demonstrations (about 24 state–action pairs) the clones varied from 0.03 to 3.68; with 20, from 2.60 to 4.45.
Optimization in simulation works, at a cost. Each local search used 1,200,000 simulated steps to reach 3.97 on average.
Reinforcement learning needs no model, but needs experience. Q-learning’s policies averaged 3.87 after 5,000 steps and 4.45 after 50,000.
Planning is the most efficient, when a model exists. Policy iteration found the optimum, 4.53, with no simulation at all.



A short history

Applications and impact
The same framework covers very different problems (ADM §1.2): aircraft collision avoidance, where alerts must come early enough to act but not so early that pilots maneuver needlessly (this site’s Chapter 14 validates such a system); automated driving, with noisy sensors and unpredictable road users; medical screening schedules that trade detection against false alarms; saving and investing over a lifetime; teams of drones watching a wildfire; and planetary rovers that must act without waiting for Earth.
Decision-making algorithms bring real benefits, in medicine, infrastructure, energy and conservation among others. They also carry risks (ADM §1.5): an optimizer serves whatever objective it is given, data-driven methods inherit the biases of their data, and systems can be manipulated by adversaries. The validation methods of Chapter 14, and care in choosing the objective, are part of building them responsibly.

title: 1 · Introduction
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: name the uncertainty. Which source of uncertainty (outcome, model, state or interaction) dominates each situation? (a) A delivery drone is pushed off course by gusts. (b) A car’s camera can’t see a pedestrian behind a parked truck. (c) A trading algorithm faces other trading algorithms. (d) A new battery’s discharge curve hasn’t been measured.






TipSolution






Outcome: the effect of the chosen action is random. (b) State: the world’s current state is hidden. (c) Interaction: other agents choose too. (d) Model: the rules governing the system are unknown until learned. Real problems usually mix several; the book’s Parts add them one at a time.




Problem 2: discounting. With \(\gamma = 0.9\), what is a reward of 1 every step forever worth? And a single reward of 10, received 7 steps from now (at step 8)?






TipSolution





\(\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} 0.9^{t-1} = 1/(1 - 0.9) = 10\). The delayed reward: \(0.9^7 \times 10 \approx 4.78\). Waiting 7 steps costs more than half its value.



Problem 3: maximum expected utility. A hiker can take a short trail (arrives in 1 hour with probability 0.8; gets lost for 5 hours with probability 0.2) or a long trail (always 2 hours). Utility is minus the hours. Which does maximum expected utility choose? What if getting lost took 6 hours?






TipSolution





Short: \(0.8(-1) + 0.2(-5) = -1.8\); long: \(-2\). Short wins, barely. With 6 hours: \(0.8(-1) + 0.2(-6) = -2.0\), a tie. Maximum expected utility weighs how likely each outcome is and how bad it is.



Problem 4: pick an approach. For each case, which approach from Table 3 is most natural? (a) An accurate simulator exists, but no model you can write down. (b) An expert has logged thousands of decisions. (c) The dynamics are known exactly and the problem is small. (d) The system can be tried safely many times, but nothing is known about it.






TipSolution






Optimization (policy search) or reinforcement learning in the simulator. (b) Supervised learning (imitation), perhaps refined later. (c) Planning: exact methods such as value or policy iteration. (d) Reinforcement learning. On Hex World above, these gave very different results for the same amount of designer effort.




Problem 5: why does “head for +10” lose? Using the page’s numbers, explain why a rule that heads for the best reward does worse than the optimal policy.






TipSolution





The rule ignores two things the optimal policy weighs. Some tiles are much closer to the +5 tile than to the +10 tile, and with discounting a nearby +5 can be worth more than a distant +10. And moves veer 30% of the time, so paths that pass next to the −10 tile risk falling in. The optimal policy (worth 4.53) trades these off tile by tile; the rule (2.77) doesn’t, and differs on 10 tiles.

title: 1 · Introduction
text:
Recap

Decision making is an observe–act loop under uncertainty (Figure 1). Why it matters: every chapter of the book is a way of choosing actions in this loop.
There are four sources of uncertainty: outcome, model, state and interaction (Table 2). Why it matters: they organize the book; Parts II–V add them one at a time, on the foundations of Part I.
Rational choice means maximizing expected utility, and over time, expected discounted reward (Equation 2, Equation 1). Why it matters: this single principle underlies decision networks, MDPs, POMDPs and games alike.
There are five broad ways to build a decision maker (Table 3). Why it matters: they trade designer knowledge for data; on Hex World, planning with a model was optimal at once, while learning without one needed tens of thousands of steps.
Uncertainty changes the best action, not just its value (Figure 2). Why it matters: a plan made as if the world were deterministic can be wrong, which is why the book models uncertainty explicitly.

Cheat sheet & connections

Name
Formula
Ref




Discounted return
\(\sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \gamma^{t-1} r_t\)
Equation 1


★ Maximum expected utility
\(a^* = \arg\max_a \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid a, o)\, U(s')\)
Equation 2


Constant reward \(r\) forever
\(r / (1 - \gamma)\)
Problem 2






Common pitfalls

Planning as if the world were deterministic. Uncertainty changes which action is best.
Confusing the kinds of uncertainty. A noisy sensor (state) calls for different tools than an unknown model (model) or an adversary (interaction).
Choosing the method before the problem. The best approach depends on what you have: a model, a simulator, examples, or only experience.
Forgetting the objective. An optimizer delivers exactly what the reward asks for, which may not be what was meant.

title: Algorithms for Decision Making - Companion
text:
This site is an independent, unofficial companion to Algorithms for Decision Making by Mykel Kochenderfer, Tim Wheeler, and Kyle Wray (MIT Press, 2022), the textbook for Stanford AA228/CS238. The book is freely available at algorithmsbook.com.
Every chapter has a page with the big picture, intuition, the key equations explained term by term, worked examples with real numbers, interactive figures, tested code in Python and Julia, and solved problems.

title: Algorithms for Decision Making - Companion
text:
The book in one picture
The book is about one agent, or several, choosing actions under uncertainty. Part I builds the tools: probability to describe what we don’t know, and utility to say what we want. Parts II–V then each add one source of uncertainty (Figure 1): random outcomes of actions over time, an unknown model, a hidden state, and other agents. Within a Part, the chapters typically move from stating the problem, to solving it exactly, to approximating when exact is too expensive.

title: Algorithms for Decision Making - Companion
text:
How to use this site
Each chapter page is laid out the same way:

Big picture: where the chapter fits, its key ideas, and its vocabulary.
Intuition: a concrete story before any math.
Formalism: the definitions and key equations, in the book’s notation, each explained in words and term by term.
Worked example: the ideas applied to real numbers.
Interactive: figures you can change.
Algorithms & code: implementations in Python and Julia, side by side.
Solved problems: try each one before opening its solution.
Recap and Cheat sheet & connections: the key points, the key equations, and links to related chapters.

Big picture and Intuition are written to stand alone: reading just those two sections of every chapter gives a tour of the whole book.
Each page states which language was executed to produce its figures. The code in the other language is tested separately.
Three reference pages collect material from across the site:

Notation: every symbol, grouped by Part.
Cheat sheets: every chapter’s key equations in one place.
Problems: the gallery of problems, with loading code in both languages.

Name
Formula
Ref
Cost per iteration




Value of a policy
\(U^\pi(s) = \mathbb{E}\big[\sum_t \gamma^t r_t \mid s_0 = s\big]\)
eq.
—


★ Bellman expectation equation
\(U^\pi(s) = R(s,\pi(s)) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s,\pi(s))\, U^\pi(s')\)
eq.
\(O(\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert^2)\) per sweep


Matrix form (exact evaluation)
\(\mathbf{U}^\pi = (\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{T}^\pi)^{-1} \mathbf{R}^\pi\)
eq.
\(O(\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert^3)\)


★ Q-function (lookahead)
\(Q(s,a) = R(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s,a)\, U(s')\)
eq.
\(O(\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert^2 \lvert\mathcal{A}\rvert)\)


Greedy policy
\(\pi(s) = \arg\max_a Q(s,a)\)
eq.
\(O(\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert \lvert\mathcal{A}\rvert)\) given \(Q\)


★ Bellman optimality equation
\(U^*(s) = \max_a Q^*(s,a)\)
eq.
—


★ Bellman backup
\(U_{k+1}(s) = \max_a \big(R(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s,a)\, U_k(s')\big)\)

\(O(\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert^2 \lvert\mathcal{A}\rvert)\)


Residual stopping rule
\(\lVert U_{k+1} - U_k \rVert_\infty < \epsilon(1-\gamma)/\gamma\)

\(O(\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert)\)

title: 2 · Representation
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
The book is about agents that make good decisions when they are uncertain. Part I (Chapters 2–6) covers the first half of that: reasoning under uncertainty, before any decisions are made. Before an agent can reason about anything, it needs a way to write down what it believes. This chapter supplies that language. Chapter 3 uses it to answer questions, Chapters 4 and 5 learn it from data, and Chapter 6 adds decisions. Every later model on this site, including transition models in Part II and sensor models in Part IV, is built from the pieces introduced here.
The question: how can an agent describe what it believes about many uncertain quantities at once, compactly enough to store and use?
The short answer: a table of probabilities for every combination of many variables is far too large, but if each variable depends directly on only a few others, you can store the same information as small local tables, one per variable, arranged on a graph.








ch02

one->many

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Each step builds a bigger object out of the previous one, and the Bayesian network is the payoff: a compact joint distribution whose graph also answers independence questions.







The key ideas at a glance

Probability is a degree of belief, and a distribution spreads it over the possible values. For a quantity with separate values, like “number of late days this week”, a probability mass function (PMF) gives each value a probability, and those add up to 1. For a continuous quantity, like “commute time in minutes”, a probability density function (PDF) is a curve, and probabilities are areas under it: the chance of a 30–45 minute trip is the area between 30 and 45. The Gaussian (bell curve) is the standard continuous shape. A mixture of several bell curves handles quantities with several typical values.
A joint distribution describes many variables together, and it explodes. To describe several variables at once, you need a probability for every combination of their values. Five yes/no variables have \(2^5 = 32\) combinations; thirty have about a billion. Such a table can’t be stored, and there would never be enough data to fill it in.
Conditional distributions describe one variable given a few others. \(P(x \mid y)\) is the probability of \(x\) in the situations where \(y\) holds. It is computed as \(P(x, y) / P(y)\). For yes/no variables it’s a small table, a conditional probability table (CPT), such as “late 50% of the time if there’s a jam, 5% if not”. For continuous variables it’s a formula: a straight-line trend plus noise (linear Gaussian), or a smooth on/off switch (sigmoid).
A Bayesian network assembles conditionals into a full joint distribution. Draw a graph with an arrow from each variable to those it directly influences, with no loops. Give each variable one conditional table: its distribution given its parents (the variables pointing into it). Then the probability of any complete situation is the product of one entry from each table. This is the chain rule for Bayesian networks. The commute example needs 10 numbers instead of 31, and the savings grow exponentially with size.
The graph shows which variables can’t inform each other. Two variables are conditionally independent given some observations if learning one tells you nothing more about the other. You can read this off the graph with d-separation. Information flows along paths, a path through an observed middle variable is usually blocked, and one special case works the other way: two causes of a common effect become linked once the effect is observed. That effect is explaining away.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Random variable
An uncertain quantity, like “was there a storm?” or “commute time”


PMF / PDF
Probability of each value (discrete) / density curve whose areas are probabilities (continuous)


CDF, quantile
Chance of at most \(x\) / the value that is beaten a given fraction of the time


Joint distribution
Probabilities of every combination of values of several variables


Marginal
The distribution of some variables alone, found by summing the joint over the others


Conditional, CPT
Distribution of a variable given others; its table form for discrete variables


Parent / child
In a Bayesian network, a variable with an arrow into / out of another


Chain rule
The joint is the product of each variable’s conditional given its parents


Conditional independence
Once \(Z\) is known, learning \(Y\) tells you nothing more about \(X\)


d-separation
Reading conditional independence off the graph’s paths


Explaining away
Observing a common effect makes its independent causes compete








After this chapter you can

Describe an uncertain quantity with a PMF, PDF or mixture, and read probabilities as areas.
Count how many numbers a full joint table or a Bayesian network needs.
Build a small Bayesian network and compute the probability of any complete situation by the chain rule.
Tell from the graph alone whether two variables can inform each other, given what’s observed.

title: 2 · Representation
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Imagine describing every possible morning before work. You track five yes/no facts: was there a storm, roadwork, a traffic jam, were you late, and did the radio warn of a storm? Listing a probability for every combination takes \(2^5 = 32\) numbers. With 30 facts it would take about a billion.
But you don’t think that way. You think in local stories: storms and roadwork cause jams; jams make you late; storms trigger radio alerts. Each story needs only a few numbers (“if there’s a jam, I’m late half the time”). Chain the stories together and you can still recover the probability of any full morning, from just 10 numbers.


That “chain the local stories” idea is a Bayesian network. Figure 2 draws the one used throughout this page.








commute



S

Storm (S)



J

Traffic jam (J)



S->J





A

Radio alert (A)



S->A





R

Roadwork (R)



R->J





L

Late (L)



J->L








Figure 2: The morning-commute Bayesian network. Each arrow points from a cause to an effect; each variable is yes/no, and each comes with a small table of probabilities given its parents.






Probabilities as areas
Say your commute time is spread like a bell curve centered at 35 minutes. What’s the chance a trip takes exactly 35.000 minutes? Essentially zero: there are infinitely many possible times. The sensible question is about a range. The chance of 30–45 minutes is the area under the curve between 30 and 45, about 0.63. So the curve’s height (the density) is not itself a probability, and for a narrow curve it can be bigger than 1. Only areas are probabilities. See Equation 1 and Figure 3.


Why a full table explodes
Five yes/no facts give 32 combinations, which is manageable. Each extra fact doubles the count: 10 facts give about a thousand, 20 about a million, 30 about a billion. Even if you could store a billion numbers, you could never observe enough mornings to estimate them. The fix is not a bigger table but a different representation. See Figure 6.


Conditionals as local stories
“If there’s a jam, I’m late half the time; if not, one time in twenty.” That is a conditional distribution: two numbers, \(P(\text{late} \mid \text{jam}) = 0.5\) and \(P(\text{late} \mid \text{no jam}) = 0.05\). It mentions only the jam, because once you know about the jam, the storm and the roadwork don’t change your lateness. Each variable’s story involves only its direct causes, which keeps every story small. See Equation 5.


Multiplying the stories together
How likely is this particular morning: a storm, no roadwork, a jam, late, and a radio alert? Walk through the stories in cause-before-effect order and multiply:

storm: 0.1;
no roadwork: 0.8;
a jam, given storm and no roadwork: 0.7;
late, given the jam: 0.5;
an alert, given the storm: 0.95.

The product is 0.027. Every complete morning’s probability comes out this way, so the ten numbers in the stories carry the same information as the 31 in a full table. That’s the chain rule, Equation 8.


Reading independence off the picture
Storms and roadwork have nothing to do with each other: learning there’s roadwork tells you nothing about the weather. But suppose you’re stuck in a jam. Now a storm is a plausible explanation (29% likely). If you then see roadwork, the jam is already explained, and a storm drops to 14%. The two causes became linked because you observed their common effect. The opposite happens on a chain: once you know whether there was a jam, the storm no longer tells you anything about being late. The graph shows which case you’re in. See Figure 7.

title: 2 · Representation
text:
Formalism

Probability distributions (one variable)
A probability measures a degree of belief (ADM §2.1): 0 means certainly false, 1 means certainly true. A distribution assigns belief to every value a variable can take (ADM §2.2).

\[
\sum_{x} P(x) = 1 \quad\text{(discrete)}
\qquad\qquad
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} p(x)\, dx = 1 \quad\text{(continuous)}
\tag{1}\]

In words. For a discrete variable, the probabilities of all values add up to 1. For a continuous one, the density curve encloses an area of 1.
Term by term.

\(P(x)\) is a probability mass function (PMF): the probability that the variable equals \(x\) exactly.
\(p(x)\) is a probability density function (PDF). It is not a probability, and it can exceed 1. Probabilities come from areas: \(P(a \le x \le b) = \int_a^b p(x)\, dx\).
The distinction matters because a continuous variable takes any single exact value with probability 0.

The cumulative distribution function \(\operatorname{cdf}(x) = P(X \le x)\) answers “what’s the chance of at most \(x\)?”. Its inverse, the quantile function, answers “what value is exceeded only \(1 - \alpha\) of the time?”. For example, the 90% quantile of your commute time is the time you beat 9 days out of 10.
The most important continuous distribution:

\[
\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu, \sigma^2) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
\tag{2}\]

In words. A symmetric bell curve centered at \(\mu\), whose width is set by \(\sigma\).
Term by term.

\(\mu\) is the mean: the center and the most likely value.
\(\sigma\) is the standard deviation. About 68% of the probability lies within \(\mu \pm \sigma\), and about 95% within \(\mu \pm 2\sigma\).
\(\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\) penalizes distance from the mean, measured in units of \(\sigma\). The exponential turns that penalty into a density that falls off fast.
\(\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\) is just the constant that makes the area equal to 1 (Equation 1).

Two other workhorses are the uniform \(\mathcal{U}(x \mid a, b)\), which is flat on \([a, b]\), and the mixture, for data with several distinct modes:

\[
p(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \rho_i\, \mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_i, \sigma_i^2), \qquad \rho_i \ge 0,\ \ \sum_i \rho_i = 1
\tag{3}\]

In words. Pick one of \(n\) bell curves at random, with probability \(\rho_i\) for curve \(i\), then draw from it.
Term by term. \(\rho_i\) is the mixture weight, or how common component \(i\) is. The weights sum to 1, so the mixture still integrates to 1. Commute times are a natural example: normal days cluster around 30 minutes, jam days around 50. You can try it in the interactive below.
Figure 3 shows a PMF, a PDF and a CDF side by side.








Figure 3: Three ways to describe a distribution. Left: a PMF, the number of late days in a 5-day week. Middle: a PDF, commute time in minutes, where the shaded area is the probability of a 30–45 minute trip. Right: the CDF of the same commute time, with the 90% quantile marked.







Joint distributions (many variables)
A joint distribution \(P(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) gives the probability of every combination of values (ADM §2.3). For \(n\) binary variables, a full table has \(2^n\) entries, and \(2^n - 1\) free parameters, because the last entry is fixed by the rest summing to 1. That exponential growth is the central problem this chapter solves (Figure 6).
For continuous variables, the standard joint distribution is the multivariate Gaussian:

\[
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2} |\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|^{1/2}} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right)
\tag{4}\]

In words. A bell-shaped hill in \(n\) dimensions. The mean \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\) sets where the hill is; the covariance \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\) sets its width in each direction and how the variables move together.
Term by term.

\(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ii}\) is the variance of variable \(i\). \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{ij}\) is the covariance of \(i\) and \(j\): positive if they tend to rise together, negative if one tends to fall as the other rises.
\((\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\) is a squared distance from the mean that accounts for the variables’ spreads and correlations (the Mahalanobis distance). The contours of equal density are ellipses.
\(|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}|\), the determinant, measures the overall spread; it keeps the total volume equal to 1.
The joint needs only \(n\) means and \(n(n+1)/2\) covariances, far fewer than a table, because the Gaussian’s shape is fixed.









Figure 4: Density contours of a two-variable Gaussian with unit variances and three correlations. Correlation tilts and stretches the ellipses: with ρ = 0.7, a high x₁ makes a high x₂ likely.







Conditional distributions
The way out of the exponential table is to describe each variable given the few things it depends on (ADM §2.4).

\[
P(x \mid y) = \frac{P(x, y)}{P(y)}
\tag{5}\]

In words. Among the situations where \(y\) holds, what fraction also have \(x\)?
Term by term. \(P(x, y)\) is how often \(x\) and \(y\) happen together. Dividing by \(P(y)\) zooms in on the world where \(y\) happened, and rescales it so that it sums to 1 again. Rearranged, \(P(x, y) = P(x \mid y)\, P(y)\): a joint can be built from a conditional times a marginal. That identity is the seed of the Bayesian network.
A conditional probability table (CPT) stores \(P(x \mid y)\) for discrete variables: one distribution over \(x\) for each value of the parents \(y\). Continuous variables need a formula instead. Two common ones:

\[
p(x \mid y) = \mathcal{N}(x \mid m y + b,\ \sigma^2)
\tag{6}\]

In words. \(x\) is a straight-line function of \(y\), plus bell-shaped noise.
Term by term. \(m\) is the slope (how much \(x\) moves per unit of \(y\)), \(b\) is the intercept, and \(\sigma\) is the noise around the line. For example, trip time might be \(m = 1.2\) minutes per minute of delay, plus a baseline \(b\), plus noise.

\[
P(x^1 \mid y) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp\!\left(-2\,\frac{y - \theta_1}{\theta_2}\right)}
\tag{7}\]

In words. A smooth on/off switch. The probability that a binary \(x\) is “yes” rises from 0 to 1 as a continuous \(y\) passes a threshold.
Term by term.

\(x^1\) means “\(x\) takes value 1”, or yes. \(x^0\) is no.
\(\theta_1\) is the threshold: at \(y = \theta_1\), the probability is exactly 0.5.
\(\theta_2\) is the softness. A small \(\theta_2\) gives an abrupt switch, and a large one a gradual ramp.









Figure 5: Two conditional distributions for continuous parents. Left: a linear Gaussian, trip time given the delay at a bottleneck; the line is the mean and the band holds 95% of trips. Right: a sigmoid, the probability of being late given the delay, for three softness values θ₂ with threshold θ₁ = 10 minutes.







Bayesian networks
A Bayesian network is a directed acyclic graph with one node per variable, plus one conditional distribution per node given its parents (ADM §2.5). It encodes a joint distribution through one famous identity:

\[
P(x_{1:n}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P\big(x_i \mid \mathrm{pa}(x_i)\big)
\tag{8}\]

In words. The probability of a complete situation is the product of each variable’s probability given its parents’ values in that situation.
Term by term.

\(x_{1:n}\) is a full assignment: a value for every variable.
\(\mathrm{pa}(x_i)\) is the values of \(X_i\)’s parents in the graph.
Each factor comes straight out of a small CPT.

Why it holds. The general chain rule, which comes from applying Equation 5 repeatedly, says \(P(x_{1:n}) = \prod_i P(x_i \mid x_{1:i-1})\) for any ordering. Order the variables so that parents come before children. The network’s defining assumption is that each variable, given its parents, is independent of the other variables earlier in the order. So each factor shrinks to \(P(x_i \mid \mathrm{pa}(x_i))\).
What it saves. A node with \(k\) binary parents needs \(2^k\) numbers, one \(P(\text{yes})\) per parent combination. The commute network needs \(1 + 1 + 4 + 2 + 2 = 10\) numbers, where the full table needs 31. With 20 variables and at most two parents each, the difference is at most 80 against about a million (Figure 6).








Figure 6: Free parameters needed for n binary variables: a full joint table, a Bayesian network where each variable has at most 2 parents, and fully independent variables. The vertical axis is logarithmic, so the full table’s straight line is exponential growth.







Conditional independence
The graph also tells you, without any arithmetic, when learning one variable can’t change your belief about another (ADM §2.6).

\[
(X \perp Y \mid Z) \iff P(x, y \mid z) = P(x \mid z)\, P(y \mid z) \ \text{ for all } x, y, z
\tag{9}\]

In words. Once you know \(Z\), also learning \(Y\) tells you nothing more about \(X\).
Term by term. \(\perp\) reads “is independent of”. The right side says the joint of \(X\) and \(Y\), given \(Z\), splits into separate factors. Equivalently, \(P(x \mid y, z) = P(x \mid z)\).
Whether a path between two variables carries information depends on the middle node of each three-node segment. There are three patterns, shown in Figure 7.

Figure 7: The three building blocks of d-separation. Observing the middle node (shaded) blocks a chain and a fork, but opens a collider.






Chain \(S \to J \to L\): a storm makes a jam likelier, which makes being late likelier. If you already know whether there was a jam, the storm adds nothing about lateness. Observing the middle blocks.
Fork \(A \leftarrow S \to J\): a radio alert and a jam share a cause. The alert suggests a storm, and so a jam. Once you know whether there was a storm, the alert adds nothing. Observing the middle blocks.
Collider \(S \to J \leftarrow R\): storms and roadwork are unrelated, until you see a jam. Then learning there was roadwork explains away the jam and makes a storm less likely. Observing the middle, or any of its descendants, opens the path.

\(X\) and \(Y\) are d-separated by \(Z\) if every path between them is blocked somewhere. d-separation guarantees \((X \perp Y \mid Z)\) for every choice of CPTs.

text:
Worked example
The commute network’s tables, in code. (The network also has an entry in the problem gallery, where it can be loaded ready-made.)

PythonJulia



from adm.bayes_net import BayesNet

def binary(p_yes):
    """CPT with last axis (no, yes), from P(yes) for each parent combination."""
    p_yes = np.asarray(p_yes, dtype=float)
    return np.stack([1 - p_yes, p_yes], axis=-1)

parents = {"S": (), "R": (), "J": ("S", "R"), "L": ("J",), "A": ("S",)}
commute = BayesNet(
    card={x: 2 for x in parents},
    parents=parents,
    cpt={
        "S": binary(0.1),                     # P(storm)
        "R": binary(0.2),                     # P(roadwork)
        "J": binary([[0.1, 0.6], [0.7, 0.9]]),  # P(jam | S, R); rows S, columns R
        "L": binary([0.05, 0.5]),             # P(late | J)
        "A": binary([0.02, 0.95]),            # P(alert | S)
    },
)



# Values are 1 = no, 2 = yes (Julia counts from 1).
struct BayesNet
    card; parents; cpt      # Dicts keyed by variable name (a Symbol)
end

# CPT with last axis (no, yes), from P(yes) for each parent combination.
binary(p_yes) = cat(1 .- p_yes, p_yes; dims = ndims(p_yes) + 1)

parents = Dict(:S => (), :R => (), :J => (:S, :R), :L => (:J,), :A => (:S,))
commute = BayesNet(
    Dict(x => 2 for x in keys(parents)),
    parents,
    Dict(:S => binary(0.1),                   # P(storm)
         :R => binary(0.2),                   # P(roadwork)
         :J => binary([0.1 0.6; 0.7 0.9]),    # P(jam | S, R); rows S, columns R
         :L => binary([0.05, 0.5]),           # P(late | J)
         :A => binary([0.02, 0.95])),         # P(alert | S)
)



A full morning, by the chain rule. What’s the probability of a storm, no roadwork, a jam, being late, and a radio alert? By Equation 8, multiply one entry from each table:
\[
P(s^1, r^0, j^1, l^1, a^1) = \underbrace{0.1}_{P(s^1)} \times \underbrace{0.8}_{P(r^0)} \times \underbrace{0.7}_{P(j^1 \mid s^1, r^0)} \times \underbrace{0.5}_{P(l^1 \mid j^1)} \times \underbrace{0.95}_{P(a^1 \mid s^1)} = 0.0266
\]
How often is there a jam? Sum over the four combinations of its parents:
\[
P(j^1) = \sum_{s, r} P(s)\, P(r)\, P(j^1 \mid s, r) = 0.9(0.8)(0.1) + 0.9(0.2)(0.6) + 0.1(0.8)(0.7) + 0.1(0.2)(0.9) = 0.254
\]
Then \(P(l^1) = 0.254 \times 0.5 + 0.746 \times 0.05 = 0.164\): you’re late about one day in six. That number fed the PMF in Figure 3.
Explaining away, in numbers. You’re stuck in a jam. How likely is it that there was a storm?
\[
P(s^1 \mid j^1) = \frac{P(s^1, j^1)}{P(j^1)} = \frac{0.1\,(0.8 \times 0.7 + 0.2 \times 0.9)}{0.254} = \frac{0.074}{0.254} \approx 0.29
\]
Now you also see roadwork. The roadwork alone would explain the jam, so a storm becomes less likely:
\[
P(s^1 \mid j^1, r^1) = \frac{0.1 \times 0.9}{0.1 \times 0.9 + 0.9 \times 0.6} = \frac{0.09}{0.63} \approx 0.14
\]
Storm and roadwork are independent a priori, but dependent once the jam is known. That is the collider pattern at work. Table 2 confirms these numbers from the full joint table.

title: 2 · Representation
2 · Representation
text:
Algorithms & code

Chain rule, joint table, and parameter count
These implement Equation 8. joint_table applies it to every assignment, which is fine for 5 variables and hopeless for 50. Chapter 3 is about avoiding exactly that.

PythonJulia


def probability(bn: BayesNet, assignment: dict) -> float:
    """P(assignment) by the chain rule: one CPT entry per variable."""
    p = 1.0
    for x, pa in bn.parents.items():
        # CPT axes are (parents..., x), so index with the parents' values
        # first and x's own value last.
        index = tuple(assignment[q] for q in pa) + (assignment[x],)
        p *= bn.cpt[x][index]
    return p

def joint_table(bn: BayesNet) -> np.ndarray:
    """The full joint distribution as an array, axes in `bn.parents` order."""
    names = list(bn.parents)
    table = np.zeros([bn.card[x] for x in names])
    for values in product(*(range(bn.card[x]) for x in names)):
        table[values] = probability(bn, dict(zip(names, values)))
    return table

def num_parameters(bn: BayesNet) -> int:
    """Independent numbers in all the CPTs (each row loses one: it sums to 1)."""
    return sum(
        prod(bn.card[q] for q in pa) * (bn.card[x] - 1)
        for x, pa in bn.parents.items()
    )


# P(assignment) by the chain rule: one CPT entry per variable.
# `...` splats the parents' values into separate indices; x's own value comes last.
probability(bn, a) = prod(bn.cpt[x][(a[q] for q in pa)..., a[x]] for (x, pa) in bn.parents)

# The full joint distribution as an array, with axes in the given order.
function joint_table(bn, order)
    table = zeros(Tuple(bn.card[x] for x in order))
    for idx in CartesianIndices(table)
        table[idx] = probability(bn, Dict(zip(order, Tuple(idx))))
    end
    return table
end

# Independent numbers in all the CPTs (each row loses one: it sums to 1).
num_parameters(bn) = sum(prod((bn.card[q] for q in pa); init = 1) * (bn.card[x] - 1)
                         for (x, pa) in bn.parents)





d-separation by searching for an active trail
The search walks the graph from \(X\), keeping track of whether it arrived at each node from a child (“up”) or from a parent (“down”). That direction is what decides whether a node is a chain, fork or collider on the current path. If it ever reaches \(Y\), the path it followed is an active trail.

PythonJulia


def active_trail(parents: dict, x: str, y: str, given=()) -> list | None:
    """An active trail from x to y given the observed set, or None if none.

    Searches (node, direction) pairs: "up" means we arrived from a child,
    "down" means we arrived from a parent. A trail through a node is blocked
    if the node is observed, except at a v-structure (collider), which is
    active only if the collider or one of its descendants is observed.
    """
    given = set(given)
    children = {v: [c for c in parents if v in parents[c]] for v in parents}
    # A collider is active if it or a descendant is observed, i.e. if it is
    # an ancestor of (or in) the observed set.
    active_colliders, frontier = set(), list(given)
    while frontier:
        v = frontier.pop()
        if v not in active_colliders:
            active_colliders.add(v)
            frontier.extend(parents[v])
    came_from = {(x, "up"): None}
    queue = [(x, "up")]
    while queue:
        node, direction = state = queue.pop(0)
        if node == y and node not in given:
            trail = []
            while state is not None:
                trail.append(state[0])
                state = came_from[state]
            return trail[::-1]
        moves = []
        if direction == "up" and node not in given:
            moves += [(p, "up") for p in parents[node]]
            moves += [(c, "down") for c in children[node]]
        elif direction == "down":
            if node not in given:
                moves += [(c, "down") for c in children[node]]
            if node in active_colliders:
                moves += [(p, "up") for p in parents[node]]
        for move in moves:
            if move not in came_from:
                came_from[move] = state
                queue.append(move)
    return None

def d_separated(parents: dict, x: str, y: str, given=()) -> bool:
    """True if x and y are conditionally independent given `given`."""
    return active_trail(parents, x, y, given) is None


function active_trail(parents, x, y, given = ())
    given = Set(given)
    children = Dict(v => [c for c in keys(parents) if v in parents[c]] for v in keys(parents))
    # A collider is active if it or a descendant is observed.
    active_colliders, frontier = Set{Symbol}(), collect(given)
    while !isempty(frontier)
        v = pop!(frontier)
        v in active_colliders && continue
        push!(active_colliders, v)
        append!(frontier, parents[v])
    end
    came_from = Dict{Tuple{Symbol, Symbol}, Any}((x, :up) => nothing)
    queue = [(x, :up)]
    while !isempty(queue)
        state = popfirst!(queue)
        node, direction = state
        if node == y && !(node in given)
            trail = Symbol[]
            while state !== nothing
                push!(trail, state[1])
                state = came_from[state]
            end
            return reverse(trail)
        end
        moves = Tuple{Symbol, Symbol}[]
        if direction == :up && !(node in given)
            append!(moves, [(p, :up) for p in parents[node]], [(c, :down) for c in children[node]])
        elseif direction == :down
            node in given || append!(moves, [(c, :down) for c in children[node]])
            node in active_colliders && append!(moves, [(p, :up) for p in parents[node]])
        end
        for m in moves
            haskey(came_from, m) || (came_from[m] = state; push!(queue, m))
        end
    end
    return nothing
end

d_separated(parents, x, y, given = ()) = active_trail(parents, x, y, given) === nothing





Run them on the commute network

PythonJulia



p_morning = probability(commute, {"S": 1, "R": 0, "J": 1, "L": 1, "A": 1})
n_params = num_parameters(commute)
storm_roadwork = d_separated(parents, "S", "R")
storm_roadwork_given_late = d_separated(parents, "S", "R", ["L"])
trail = active_trail(parents, "A", "L")



p_morning = probability(commute, Dict(:S => 2, :R => 1, :J => 2, :L => 2, :A => 2))
@assert p_morning ≈ 0.1 * 0.8 * 0.7 * 0.5 * 0.95
@assert num_parameters(commute) == 10
joint = joint_table(commute, [:S, :R, :J, :L, :A])
@assert sum(joint) ≈ 1 && sum(joint[:, :, :, 2, :]) ≈ 0.1643
@assert d_separated(parents, :S, :R) && !d_separated(parents, :S, :R, (:L,))
@assert active_trail(parents, :A, :L) == [:A, :S, :J, :L]





P(storm, no roadwork, jam, late, alert) = 0.0266
Parameters: 10 in the network vs 31 in a full table
Storm ⊥ Roadwork: True;  Storm ⊥ Roadwork | Late: False
Active trail from Radio alert to Late: A → S → J → L








NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






Symbols like :S are lightweight names, a common choice for dictionary keys. They’re like interned strings.
cat(a, b; dims = k) stacks arrays along a new axis k, like np.stack([a, b], axis=-1) here.
Splatting: bn.cpt[x][(a[q] for q in pa)..., a[x]] expands the parents’ values into separate indices, like table[(*parent_values, x_value)] in Python.
CartesianIndices(table) loops over every index tuple of an array, like itertools.product(*map(range, table.shape)).
prod(...; init = 1) gives 1 for an empty product, which is needed for a node with no parents. Python’s math.prod does that automatically.

title: 2 · Representation
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: counting parameters. A network has six binary variables. \(A\) and \(B\) have no parents; \(C\) has parents \(A, B\); \(D\) has parent \(C\); \(E\) has parents \(C, D\); \(F\) has parents \(B, E\). How many free parameters does it need, and how many would a full joint table need?






TipSolution





Each binary node needs \(2^{k}\) numbers, where \(k\) is its number of parents: \(A\): 1, \(B\): 1, \(C\): 4, \(D\): 2, \(E\): 4, \(F\): 4. The total is 16. A full table needs $2^6 - 1 = $ 63.



Problem 2: reading independence off the graph. In the commute network, decide each of the following, and name the blocking or active pattern: (a) \(A \perp R\); (b) \(A \perp R \mid J\); (c) \(A \perp L \mid S\); (d) \(S \perp R \mid L\).






TipSolution






Independent. The only path is \(A \leftarrow S \to J \leftarrow R\), and the collider \(J\) is unobserved (as is its descendant \(L\)), so it blocks.
Dependent. Observing \(J\) opens the collider. The fork at \(S\) is unobserved, so it passes, and the trail \(A - S - J - R\) is active.
Independent. The path \(A \leftarrow S \to J \to L\) has a fork at \(S\), which is observed and so blocks.
Dependent. \(L\) is a descendant of the collider \(J\). Observing it opens \(S \to J \leftarrow R\). Intuitively, being late suggests a jam, which then needs an explanation.

Check them all in the explorer above.



Problem 3: a Gaussian probability. Commute time is \(\mathcal{N}(35, 8^2)\) minutes. Using the rule of thumb that about 95% of the probability lies within \(2\sigma\) of the mean, what range covers 95% of commutes? About what fraction of commutes take longer than 51 minutes?






TipSolution





\(35 \pm 2 \times 8\) gives 19 to 51 minutes. The remaining 5% is split evenly between the two tails, so about 2.5% of commutes take longer than 51 minutes. (The exact value is 2.3%.)



Problem 4: explaining away, from scratch. Change the commute network so that roadwork is common, \(P(r^1) = 0.5\), and keep everything else. Compute \(P(s^1 \mid j^1)\). Is it higher or lower than the original 0.29, and why?






TipSolution





\(P(s^1, j^1) = 0.1\,(0.5 \times 0.7 + 0.5 \times 0.9) = 0.08\), and \(P(s^0, j^1) = 0.9\,(0.5 \times 0.1 + 0.5 \times 0.6) = 0.315\). So \(P(s^1 \mid j^1) = 0.08 / 0.395 \approx\) 0.20, which is lower than 0.29. With roadwork common, a jam is more easily explained without a storm, so seeing a jam is weaker evidence for one. This is explaining away again, now working through the prior on the competing cause.

title: 2 · Representation
text:
Recap

Distributions describe belief about one quantity: a PMF for discrete values, a PDF for continuous ones, with probabilities as areas (Equation 1). The Gaussian (Equation 2) and mixtures (Equation 3) are the everyday building blocks. Why it matters: every model later in the book, whether transitions, observations or rewards, is built from these pieces.
Joint distributions over many variables grow exponentially: \(2^n - 1\) numbers for \(n\) binary variables. Why it matters: this is the core obstacle to reasoning about realistic systems, and every representation afterward is a way around it.
Conditional distributions describe one variable given a few others: tables, linear Gaussians (Equation 6), sigmoids (Equation 7). Why it matters: they are the “local stories” that stay small, and they reappear as transition models \(T(s' \mid s, a)\) in Ch 7 and observation models \(O(o \mid a, s')\) in Ch 19.
A Bayesian network multiplies those local stories into a full joint (Equation 8), with far fewer parameters. Why it matters: it is the representation that Ch 3 (inference), Ch 4 (learning parameters) and Ch 5 (learning structure) all work on, and decision networks in Ch 6 extend it.
The graph reveals independence through d-separation: chains and forks are blocked by observing the middle; colliders are opened by it. Why it matters: independence is what makes inference and learning tractable, and explaining away is a real, often counterintuitive effect in diagnosis.

d-separation in one line: a path is blocked if it has an observed chain or fork node, or an unobserved collider with no observed descendants.
Common pitfalls

Treating a density as a probability. \(p(x) = 2\) is fine for a narrow distribution; only areas are probabilities.
Forgetting that CPT rows sum to 1. Store \(P(\text{yes})\) and derive \(P(\text{no})\), or check each row.
Reading arrows as proof of causation. A Bayesian network only encodes independence. Arrows drawn from cause to effect make the tables small and easy to fill in, but the math doesn’t require it.
Assuming observed evidence can only reduce dependence. Observing a collider or one of its descendants creates dependence (explaining away).

title: 4 · Parameter Learning
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 2 described a world with a Bayesian network: a graph, plus a table of probabilities for each variable. Chapter 3 used those tables to answer questions. Both chapters simply assumed the numbers were known: \(P(\text{storm}) = 0.1\), \(P(\text{jam} \mid \text{storm}) = 0.7\), and so on. In practice nobody hands you those numbers. You have data: a log of past mornings. This chapter turns data into the numbers.
The structure of the graph is still assumed known here; Chapter 5 learns that too. And the same ideas come back whenever an agent must learn a model from experience, most directly in model-based reinforcement learning (Ch 16), which learns transition probabilities by counting.
The question: given a record of past observations, what should the probabilities in my model be, and how sure should I be about them?

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Data comes in on the left. Depending on how much you trust the data, what shape you assume, and whether values are missing, a different method turns it into model parameters.







The key ideas at a glance

Parameters and the likelihood. A model’s numbers are its parameters, written \(\theta\) (theta). The likelihood of a set of parameters is the probability they assign to the data you actually saw. Good parameters make the observed data likely. Because the probabilities of independent records multiply, and multiplying many small numbers is awkward, we work with the log-likelihood, a sum of logs.
Maximum likelihood (ML) is counting. The parameters that make the data most likely are just the observed frequencies. If a jam happened on 3 of 5 roadwork mornings, the estimate of \(P(\text{jam} \mid \text{roadwork})\) is \(3/5\). For a Bayesian network, every row of every table is estimated separately, from the records that match that row’s parent values. For a Gaussian, ML gives the sample mean and the average squared deviation. ML is simple and becomes exact with enough data. With little data it overreacts: a combination seen once gets probability 1, and one never seen gets no estimate at all.
Bayesian learning adds prior knowledge as pretend data. Instead of a single best number, keep a whole distribution over the parameter. For a yes/no probability that distribution is the Beta distribution, and updating it is just adding: start with \(\alpha\) pretend “yes” and \(\beta\) pretend “no” observations (the pseudocounts), then add the real counts. The estimate becomes (yes + pseudo-yes) / (all + pseudo-all). It never reaches exactly 0 or 1, and it is sensible even with no data. The Dirichlet distribution does the same for variables with more than two values.
Nonparametric learning lets the data set the shape. Sometimes no simple shape fits. Commute times are a lump of normal days plus a lump of jam days, and a single bell curve would sit between the lumps. Kernel density estimation puts a small bump on every data point and adds them up. The only choice is the bump width, the bandwidth: too narrow and you get spikes, too wide and you blur the lumps together.
Missing data: don’t guess once, guess softly and repeat. Real logs have gaps: some mornings nobody recorded whether there was a storm. Dropping incomplete records wastes data. Filling each gap with the most common value biases the answer. Expectation-maximization (EM) fills each gap with fractional counts (“this morning was 97% storm, 3% no storm”, computed by inference from Chapter 3). It then re-estimates the parameters from those counts and repeats. Each round can only make the data more likely, and it settles close to what complete data would have given.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Parameters \(\theta\)
The numbers in a model, such as the entries of a CPT


Likelihood
How probable the observed data is under particular parameters


Maximum likelihood estimate
The parameters that make the data most probable: observed frequencies


Prior / posterior
Belief about the parameters before / after seeing the data


Pseudocounts
The prior, expressed as pretend observations added to the real counts


Conjugate prior
A prior whose posterior has the same form, like Beta → Beta, so updating is just adding counts


Bandwidth
The width of each bump in kernel density estimation


Imputation
Filling in missing values


E-step / M-step
EM’s two halves: Expected counts from the current model, then Maximum-likelihood re-estimation








After this chapter you can

Estimate every table of a Bayesian network from data by counting, and know when that goes wrong.
Choose a prior, read it as pseudocounts, and see how much it matters for a given amount of data.
Fit a Gaussian by maximum likelihood, or a shape-free density with a kernel.
Learn from records with missing values using EM, and explain why it beats dropping or guessing.

title: 4 · Parameter Learning
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



You’re judging a new café from its customer ratings.

Maximum likelihood: average the ratings. With 200 ratings that’s excellent. With one rating of 5 stars, it claims the café is perfect.
Bayesian: start from what a typical café scores, say 3.5 stars, and count that as if it were a few ratings. One 5-star review nudges you up a little; 200 of them overwhelm your starting belief. The more data, the less the prior matters.
Kernel density: instead of one average, draw the whole spread of ratings, smoothing the raw tally so that a 4.5 also lends a little weight to 4 and 5.
Missing data: some reviews lost their star rating but kept their text. Rather than ignore them, you read each text, estimate “probably 4 stars, maybe 3”, count each review fractionally, and refine your reading of the texts as your picture of the café sharpens. That is EM.




Maximum likelihood: the frequencies you saw
Suppose 20 logged mornings split by storm and roadwork like this: 12 mornings with neither (1 jam), 5 with roadwork only (3 jams), 3 with a storm only (2 jams), and none with both. Maximum likelihood estimates \(P(\text{jam})\) for each combination as jams / mornings: \(1/12\), \(3/5\), \(2/3\), and for “both”, \(0/0\), no estimate at all. The first three are sensible, if noisy. The last shows ML’s weak spot: it has nothing to say about situations the data never covered. Formally, this is Equation 2.


Bayesian learning: pseudocounts pull toward the prior
Add one pretend jam and one pretend no-jam to every row, a uniform prior. The estimates become \(2/14 = 0.14\), \(4/7 = 0.57\), \(3/5 = 0.60\), and \(1/2 = 0.50\) for the never-seen row. Rows with lots of data barely move; rows with little data move toward 0.5; the empty row gets a cautious 0.5 instead of nothing. Stronger priors (more pseudocounts) pull harder. That’s Equation 4 and Equation 5.


Kernel density: a bump on every point
With 200 recorded commute times, a single Gaussian fit centers near 35 minutes. Yet almost no commute takes 35 minutes: normal days cluster near 30, jam days near 50. A kernel density estimate puts a small bell curve on each of the 200 times and adds them up, and the two clusters appear on their own. Try the bandwidth slider below. That’s Equation 6.


EM: soft guesses, refined
A morning’s record says “late, radio alert, jam, no roadwork”, but the storm entry is blank. Given the current model, a storm explains that record far better than no storm: \(P(\text{storm} \mid \text{the rest}) \approx 0.97\) (see the worked example). So EM counts this morning as 0.97 of a storm morning and 0.03 of a calm one. After doing that for every blank, it re-estimates the tables from these fractional counts, which changes the next round’s guesses slightly, and so on until nothing changes. That’s Equation 7.

title: 4 · Parameter Learning
text:
Formalism

The likelihood
Let the data be \(m\) independent records \(x_1, \ldots, x_m\) and the parameters \(\theta\) (ADM §4.1).

\[
\ell(\theta) = \log P(x_{1:m} \mid \theta) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \log P(x_i \mid \theta)
\tag{1}\]

In words. Score a set of parameters by how probable they make the observed data. Use logs so the product over records becomes a sum.
Term by term.

\(P(x_i \mid \theta)\) is the probability of record \(i\) under the parameters \(\theta\). For a Bayesian network, it’s the chain-rule product from Ch 2.
The records are assumed independent, so their probabilities multiply. The log turns that product into a sum, which is numerically safer and easier to maximize.
Maximizing \(\ell\) and maximizing the likelihood itself give the same \(\theta\), because log is increasing.



Maximum likelihood
For a discrete variable in a Bayesian network, let \(m_{ijk}\) be the number of records in which variable \(i\) takes its \(k\)-th value while its parents take their \(j\)-th combination of values.

\[
\hat\theta_{ijk} = \frac{m_{ijk}}{\sum_{k'} m_{ijk'}}
\tag{2}\]

In words. The estimated probability of each value, for each combination of parent values, is how often it happened divided by how often that parent combination happened.
Term by term.

\(i\) picks the variable (say, “jam”), \(j\) the parent combination (say, “storm, no roadwork”), \(k\) the value (say, “yes”).
The denominator counts every record with that parent combination. If it’s 0, the estimate is undefined (0/0).
The hat on \(\hat\theta\) marks an estimate.

Why it holds. The log-likelihood of a Bayesian network splits into one separate term per table row: \(\sum_{ijk} m_{ijk} \log \theta_{ijk}\). Each row’s probabilities must sum to 1. Maximizing \(\sum_k m_k \log \theta_k\) subject to \(\sum_k \theta_k = 1\) (with a Lagrange multiplier) gives \(\theta_k \propto m_k\): proportional to the counts.
For continuous data assumed Gaussian, the same principle gives:

\[
\hat\mu = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} x_i
\qquad
\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} (x_i - \hat\mu)^2
\tag{3}\]

In words. The best-fitting bell curve is centered at the average, and its variance is the average squared distance from that average.
Term by term. \(\hat\sigma^2\) divides by \(m\), not \(m - 1\). It’s slightly too small on average, because \(\hat\mu\) was fitted to the same data, a bias that fades as \(m\) grows. The familiar “sample variance” divides by \(m - 1\) to remove it.


Bayesian parameter learning
Treat the unknown parameter itself as uncertain, and keep a distribution over it (ADM §4.2). For a probability \(\theta\) of “yes”:

\[
\mathrm{Beta}(\theta \mid \alpha, \beta) \propto \theta^{\alpha - 1} (1 - \theta)^{\beta - 1}
\quad\xrightarrow{\;m_1 \text{ yes},\ m_0 \text{ no}\;}\quad
\mathrm{Beta}(\theta \mid \alpha + m_1,\ \beta + m_0),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\theta] = \frac{\alpha + m_1}{\alpha + \beta + m_1 + m_0}
\tag{4}\]

In words. A Beta distribution describes belief about a probability. Seeing data just adds the counts of yes and no to its two parameters. Its mean is “yes” counts over total counts, real plus pretend.
Term by term.

\(\theta^{\alpha - 1}(1-\theta)^{\beta-1}\) is the shape: it peaks near \(\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha + \beta - 2}\), and it is flat when \(\alpha = \beta = 1\).
The data’s likelihood is \(\theta^{m_1}(1-\theta)^{m_0}\). Multiplying it into the prior adds the exponents, and that’s the whole update. A prior that stays in the same family after updating is called conjugate.
\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) act as pseudocounts: pretend observations of yes and no. \(\alpha + \beta\) is how many observations the prior is “worth”.
\(\mathbb{E}[\theta]\) is the posterior mean, the usual single-number estimate. It lies between the prior mean \(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}\) and the ML estimate \(\frac{m_1}{m_1 + m_0}\), moving toward the latter as data accumulates.

For a variable with \(n\) values, the Beta generalizes to the Dirichlet:

\[
\mathrm{Dir}(\theta_{1:n} \mid \alpha_{1:n}) \propto \prod_{k=1}^{n} \theta_k^{\alpha_k - 1}
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\theta_k \mid \text{data}] = \frac{\alpha_k + m_k}{\sum_{k'} (\alpha_{k'} + m_{k'})}
\tag{5}\]

In words. Same idea, more categories: one pseudocount per value, and the estimate is (pseudocount + count) over the total.
Term by term. \(\theta_{1:n}\) are the \(n\) probabilities, summing to 1. \(\alpha_k\) is value \(k\)’s pseudocount. With every \(\alpha_k = 1\) (the uniform prior), the posterior mean is Laplace smoothing: add one to every count. For a Bayesian network, each row of each table gets its own Dirichlet, updated with that row’s counts \(m_{ijk}\).


Nonparametric learning
When no fixed shape is right, let the data define the density (ADM §4.3):

\[
\hat p(x) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \phi(x - x_i),
\qquad
\phi(d) = \mathcal{N}(d \mid 0, h^2)
\tag{6}\]

In words. Place a small bell curve on every data point, and average them.
Term by term.

\(\phi\) is the kernel, the shape of each bump; here a Gaussian.
\(h\) is the bandwidth, the bump width. It trades detail against noise: small \(h\) follows every quirk of the sample, large \(h\) blurs real structure away.
Averaging \(m\) densities that each integrate to 1 gives a density that integrates to 1.
Nothing is fitted, but every data point must be kept, and evaluating \(\hat p\) costs \(O(m)\).



Learning with missing data
When some values are missing (ADM §4.4), the likelihood sums over every way the missing values could have been filled in. There’s no counting formula for it any more. Expectation-maximization climbs it by alternating two easy steps:

\[
\text{E-step: } \hat m_{ijk} = \sum_{\text{records } r} P\big(x_i = k,\ \mathrm{pa}_i = j \mid \text{observed part of } r,\ \theta\big)
\qquad
\text{M-step: } \theta_{ijk} \leftarrow \frac{\hat m_{ijk}}{\sum_{k'} \hat m_{ijk'}}
\tag{7}\]

In words. E-step: using the current parameters, work out how likely each possible fill-in of each record’s gaps is, and add up fractional counts. M-step: re-estimate the parameters from those counts exactly as in Equation 2. Repeat.
Term by term.

For a record with nothing missing, the probability is 1 for the observed values and 0 otherwise, so it contributes whole counts, as before.
For a record with gaps, it’s an inference query from Ch 3: \(P(\text{missing} \mid \text{observed})\).
\(\hat m_{ijk}\) are expected counts, possibly fractional.

Why it works. Each EM iteration never decreases the log-likelihood of the observed data. It stops at a (possibly local) maximum, so different starting points can end in different places.
Two simpler alternatives are dropping incomplete records, which is unbiased when values go missing at random but wastes data, and imputation, filling each gap with a single guess. Imputing the most common value is simplest, but it systematically distorts the data.

A new bus route has been late on 3 of its first 10 runs.

Uniform prior Beta(1, 1): the posterior is Beta(4, 8), with mean \(4/12 = 0.33\).
A prior centered on 50%, worth 10 runs, Beta(5, 5): the posterior is Beta(8, 12), with mean \(8/20 = 0.40\).

The stronger the prior, the more 10 runs are pulled toward its center. Try other values in the interactive below.


Gaussian maximum likelihood by hand
Five commutes: 30, 34, 29, 52 and 35 minutes. By Equation 3, \(\hat\mu = 180/5 = 36\) and \(\hat\sigma^2 = (36 + 4 + 49 + 256 + 1)/5 = 69.2\), a standard deviation of 8.3 minutes. The single 52-minute trip, likely a jam day, pulls the mean up and inflates the spread. That’s a hint that one bell curve is the wrong shape here.


One EM step by hand
A record has the storm value missing: late, radio alert, jam, no roadwork. Under the true tables, the probability of each fill-in is proportional to the chain-rule product. Factors that don’t involve the storm are the same for both fill-ins and cancel.

Storm: \(P(s^1)\, P(j^1 \mid s^1, r^0)\, P(a^1 \mid s^1) = 0.1 \times 0.7 \times 0.95 = 0.0665\)
No storm: \(P(s^0)\, P(j^1 \mid s^0, r^0)\, P(a^1 \mid s^0) = 0.9 \times 0.1 \times 0.02 = 0.0018\)

So \(P(s^1 \mid \text{record}) = 0.0665 / 0.0683 = 0.974\). This record adds 0.974 to the storm counts and 0.026 to the no-storm counts, in every table the storm variable appears in.
