Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Demonstrations can be copied directly (behavioral cloning, improved interactively by DAgger and SMILe), explained by a reward (inverse reinforcement learning), or matched adversarially (GAIL).







The key ideas at a glance

Behavioral cloning. Fit a policy \(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) that maximizes the likelihood of the expert’s actions in the demonstrated states: ordinary supervised learning. With a table of states, it simply counts the expert’s choices in each state.
Cascading errors. A clone is only trained where the expert went. One slip, from the clone’s own mistake or from randomness in the world, puts it somewhere unfamiliar. There it acts poorly, which takes it somewhere even less familiar. Errors compound over the length of an episode.
Interactive demonstrations. DAgger runs the current learner, asks the expert what it would have done in each state the learner visited, adds those labels to the data set, and retrains. The data then cover the states the learner actually reaches. SMILe trains a new policy on each round’s data and mixes it with the earlier ones, gradually phasing out the expert.
Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL). Assume the expert optimizes an unknown reward, here a weighted sum of features, \(R_\phi(s, a) = \phi^\top\beta(s, a)\). Find weights under which the expert’s behavior looks optimal, then plan. Maximum margin IRL picks weights that make the expert beat every policy found so far by as much as possible. Maximum entropy IRL picks the reward under which the demonstrations are most likely, with trajectories exponentially more likely the more reward they earn.
Rewards transfer; copied policies don’t. A reward over features (“mud is bad, paths are good”) applies anywhere those features appear. A cloned table of actions is tied to the states it was trained on.
Generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL). Train a discriminator to tell the learner’s state-action pairs from the expert’s, and train the policy to fool it. It matches the expert’s behavior without ever writing down a reward.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




Expert demonstrations \(\mathcal{D}\)
Recorded states and the expert’s actions in them


Behavioral cloning
Learning the expert’s action from the state by supervised learning


Cascading errors
Small mistakes leading to unfamiliar states and bigger mistakes


DAgger
Data set aggregation: the expert labels the learner’s own states


SMILe
Stochastic mixing iterative learning: a growing mixture of trained policies


Inverse reinforcement learning
Inferring the reward that the expert’s behavior optimizes


Features \(\beta(s, a)\), weights \(\phi\)
A description of each situation, and the reward’s weight on each part


Feature expectations \(\mu_\pi\)
Expected discounted total of each feature under policy \(\pi\)


Maximum entropy principle
Among distributions consistent with the data, choose the least committal


GAIL
Matching the expert’s behavior through a policy-versus-discriminator game








After this chapter you can

Train a policy by behavioral cloning and explain why its errors cascade.
Improve a cloned policy with DAgger or SMILe, and say what each asks of the expert.
Recover a linear reward from demonstrations by maximum margin or maximum entropy IRL.
Explain when a learned reward transfers to a new environment and a cloned policy doesn’t.
Describe GAIL’s adversarial setup.

title: 18 · Imitation Learning
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



You’re learning to drive by watching an instructor.

Cloning: you copy what they did on the lessons you watched. But they never drifted onto the shoulder, so when you do, you have no idea what to do.
DAgger: you drive, and the instructor calls out what they would do at every moment, including your drifts. Now you learn how to recover.
Inverse RL: instead of memorizing moves, you work out what the instructor cares about: staying centered, keeping distance, smoothness. That understanding carries over to roads you’ve never driven.



Our running example is a park: an 8 × 8 grid of paths, grass and mud, with a gate in the top-right corner. Walkers enter from the left edge. Each step goes where intended 80% of the time and slips sideways or back otherwise. The true reward, which the learners never see, is −1 per step on a path, −2 on grass, −6 in mud, and +10 at the gate, with discount 0.95. The expert walks optimally for that reward, and is worth -9.31 on average from the left edge. Walking at random is worth -45.43.

Copy what you saw
From 3 demonstrated walks, behavioral cloning sees the expert’s choice in 20 of the 63 cells where a choice is made, and acts at random everywhere else. Its policy is worth -19.11. With 100 walks it covers 44 cells and is worth -9.48 (Figure 4). See Equation 1.


When you slip, you’re lost
The expert rarely leaves its preferred routes, so the clone never learns what to do off them. But the park is slippery, so the clone does leave them. Every slip lands it in a cell where it acts at random, and random steps take it further into unfamiliar cells. With few demonstrations, much of the clone’s lost value comes from these cascades.


Ask the expert about your own mistakes
DAgger lets the clone walk, and the expert labels every cell the clone visits, including the unfamiliar ones. Starting from the same 3 walks and adding 3 labeled walks per round, the policy’s value rose from -19.11 to -9.84 in 7 rounds (Figure 5). See Equation 2.


Explain the walks with a reward
The expert avoids mud and prefers paths. Inverse reinforcement learning turns that into numbers: weights on “path”, “grass”, “mud” and “gate” under which the expert’s walks look optimal. Maximum entropy IRL, given demonstrations starting from every cell, ranked path above grass above mud in 100% of 10 trials. Given only walks from the left edge, which rarely go near mud, it got the ranking right in 70% (Figure 6). See Equation 6.


A reward carries over
Move to a new park, layout B, with the same kinds of terrain in a different arrangement. The cloned policy’s table of “what to do in cell (3, 4)” means nothing there; it scores -22.27. Planning with the reward learned in park A scores -12.82 on average, against -12.07 for an expert who knows the true reward (Figure 7).

title: 18 · Imitation Learning
text:
Formalism

Behavioral cloning
Given expert state-action pairs \(\mathcal{D}\), maximize the likelihood of the expert’s actions (ADM §18.1; D. A. Pomerleau, Neural Computation, 1991):

\[
\max_\theta \prod_{(s, a) \in \mathcal{D}} \pi_\theta(a \mid s)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\max_\theta \sum_{(s, a) \in \mathcal{D}} \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)
\tag{1}\]

In words. Choose the policy under which the expert’s recorded choices were most likely.
Term by term.

\(\pi_\theta(a \mid s)\) is a stochastic policy with parameters \(\theta\): a table, a softmax over features, a neural network, or a Bayesian network (Chapter 2).
For a table, the maximizer is the count ratio \(\pi(a \mid s) = N(s, a)/\sum_{a'} N(s, a')\). States never demonstrated have no data; here they get a uniform policy.
For a differentiable \(\pi_\theta\), gradient ascent on the log-likelihood does the fitting.

Why it holds. It is maximum likelihood estimation (Chapter 4) of a conditional distribution. The states are treated as given inputs, which is exactly where cloning goes wrong: at test time, the states come from the clone’s own behavior, not the expert’s.
The cost of that mismatch grows with the horizon. Roughly: if the clone errs with probability \(\epsilon\) in the expert’s states, its expected cost over \(h\) steps can grow like \(\epsilon h^2\), because each error can send it off course for the rest of the episode (S. Ross and J. A. Bagnell, AISTATS, 2010).


Data set aggregation (DAgger)
Alternate between acting and asking (ADM §18.2; S. Ross, G. J. Gordon and J. A. Bagnell, AISTATS, 2011):

\[
\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \mathcal{D} \cup \big\{(s, \pi_E(s)) : s \text{ visited by rollouts of } \pi_{\theta^{(k)}}\big\},
\qquad
\theta^{(k+1)} = \arg\max_\theta \sum_{(s, a) \in \mathcal{D}} \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)
\tag{2}\]

In words. Let the learner act, record the expert’s answer for every state the learner reaches, add those examples to everything collected so far, and retrain.
Term by term.

\(\pi_E(s)\) is the expert’s action in \(s\). The expert is consulted, not followed: the learner’s own actions decide which states are visited.
The data set aggregates all rounds, so later rounds change the policy less and less.
The original algorithm executes a mix of the expert and the learner; executing the learner alone, as here and in the book, is the extreme case.

Why it holds. The training distribution becomes the learner’s own state distribution, the one that matters at test time. Ross and colleagues show that DAgger’s error then grows only linearly with the horizon, \(O(\epsilon h)\), instead of quadratically. The catch is practical: the expert must be available to answer questions about states it would never have reached itself.


Stochastic mixing iterative learning (SMILe)
Start with the expert’s policy, \(\pi^{(1)} = \pi_E\). In round \(k\), run \(\pi^{(k)}\), have the expert label the states it visits, and train a new component \(\hat\pi^{(k)}\) on that round’s data only. Then mix (ADM §18.3; S. Ross and J. A. Bagnell, AISTATS, 2010):

\[
\pi^{(k+1)} = (1 - \beta)^k\, \pi_E + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \beta (1 - \beta)^{i-1}\, \hat\pi^{(i)}
\tag{3}\]

In words. Act like the expert with a probability that shrinks every round, and otherwise like one of the trained components, favoring earlier ones.
Term by term.

\(\beta \in (0, 1)\) is the mixing rate; small \(\beta\) changes the policy slowly.
The weights sum to 1: \((1 - \beta)^k + \beta\sum_{i \le k}(1 - \beta)^{i-1} = 1\).
The final policy drops the expert and renormalizes the components’ weights.

Why it holds. Each round changes the state distribution only a little, because each new component carries weight at most \(\beta\). So every component is trained on states close to those it will face. Earlier components get more weight because they were trained on states most like the expert’s. The components have to generalize from their own round’s data, though. With a table, which can’t generalize, each component acts at random in every state its round didn’t visit, as the results below show.


Inverse reinforcement learning: feature expectations
Assume a linear reward, \(R_\phi(s, a) = \phi^\top\beta(s, a)\) (ADM §18.4). Then a policy’s expected return is linear in its feature expectations:

\[
\mathbb{E}_{s \sim b}[U^\pi(s)] = \mathbb{E}_\tau\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{d} \gamma^{k-1} R_\phi(s^{(k)}, a^{(k)})\Big] = \phi^\top \mu_\pi,
\qquad
\mu_\pi = \mathbb{E}_\tau\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{d} \gamma^{k-1}\beta(s^{(k)}, a^{(k)})\Big]
\tag{4}\]

In words. Everything a linear reward can say about a policy is summarized by how much of each feature the policy racks up, discounted.
Term by term.

\(\beta(s, a)\) is a vector of features; in the park, one-hot indicators of path, grass, mud and gate.
\(\mu_\pi\) is estimated from rollouts, or computed exactly for a known model by treating each feature as a reward.
For the expert, \(\mu_E\) comes from the demonstrations.
Why it matters: if a policy’s feature expectations equal the expert’s, it earns the same return as the expert under every reward of this form, including the unknown true one.

Why it holds. Expectation is linear, and \(\phi\) doesn’t depend on the trajectory, so it factors out of the sum.


Maximum margin IRL
Iterate (P. Abbeel and A. Y. Ng, ICML, 2004): find weights under which the expert beats every policy found so far by the largest margin, compute the optimal policy for those weights, add it, and repeat.

\[
\max_{t,\,\phi}\ t
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\phi^\top\mu_E \ge \phi^\top\mu^{(i)} + t\ \ \text{for } i = 1, \ldots, k - 1,
\qquad \|\phi\|_2 \le 1
\tag{5}\]

In words. Find the reward direction that best separates the expert from every policy tried so far.
Term by term.

\(\mu^{(i)}\) are the feature expectations of earlier policies; the first is a random policy.
The norm bound fixes the scale, since scaling a reward doesn’t change the optimal policy.
When the margin \(t\) is small, some combination of the policies found matches the expert’s feature expectations. The output is a mixture: follow \(\pi^{(i)}\) with probability \(\lambda_i\), where \(\lambda\) minimizes \(\|\mu_E - \sum_i \lambda_i\mu^{(i)}\|\) over the simplex.
The weights \(\phi\) are a means to that end. They need not resemble the true reward.

Why it holds. If \(\mu_\lambda\) is within \(\epsilon\) of \(\mu_E\), then for every \(\phi\) with \(\|\phi\| \le 1\), the returns differ by at most \(|\phi^\top(\mu_E - \mu_\lambda)| \le \epsilon\) by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. That includes the true reward, scaled to unit norm.


Maximum entropy IRL
Many rewards, and many trajectory distributions, match the same feature expectations. The maximum entropy principle picks the least committal distribution consistent with them, which has an exponential form (ADM §18.5; B. D. Ziebart et al., AAAI, 2008):

\[
P_\phi(\tau) = \frac{\exp R_\phi(\tau)}{Z(\phi)},
\qquad
\nabla_\phi \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{D}} \log P_\phi(\tau)
= \underbrace{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{D}} \sum_k \gamma^{k-1}\beta(s^{(k)}, a^{(k)})}_{\text{demonstrations}}
- \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim P_\phi}\Big[\sum_k \gamma^{k-1}\beta(s^{(k)}, a^{(k)})\Big]}_{\text{model}}
\tag{6}\]

In words. Trajectories are exponentially more likely the more reward they earn. Adjust the reward until the feature counts it predicts match the ones demonstrated.
Term by term.

\(R_\phi(\tau) = \sum_k \gamma^{k-1} R_\phi(s^{(k)}, a^{(k)})\) is a trajectory’s discounted reward, and \(Z(\phi)\) normalizes.
The gradient is “demonstrated feature counts minus expected feature counts”. At the optimum they match, as in Equation 4.
The expectation needs the policy induced by \(\phi\) and its state visitation. The book uses the optimal policy. Here we use the soft (maximum entropy) optimal policy, \(\pi(a \mid s) = \exp(Q(s, a) - V(s))\) with \(V(s) = \log\sum_a \exp Q(s, a)\), which is what the maximum entropy model implies for stochastic dynamics. The visitation comes from pushing the start distribution forward \(d\) steps (eq. 18.18).
Unlike maximum margin, it gives one reward, and the log-likelihood is concave in \(\phi\) for a linear reward, so gradient ascent finds its maximum.

Why it holds. \(\log P_\phi(\tau) = R_\phi(\tau) - \log Z(\phi)\). The gradient of \(R_\phi(\tau)\) is its discounted feature count. The gradient of \(\log Z\) is \(\sum_\tau P_\phi(\tau)\nabla R_\phi(\tau)\), the expected feature count: the familiar property of log-normalizers.


Generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL)
Train a policy \(\pi_\theta\) and a discriminator \(C_\phi(s, a)\), the probability that a pair came from the learner rather than the expert, as a game (ADM §18.6; J. Ho and S. Ermon, NeurIPS, 2016):

\[
\min_\theta \max_\phi\ \ \mathbb{E}_{(s, a) \sim \pi_\theta}\big[\log C_\phi(s, a)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{(s, a) \sim \mathcal{D}}\big[\log\big(1 - C_\phi(s, a)\big)\big]
\tag{7}\]

In words. The discriminator learns to tell the learner’s behavior from the expert’s; the policy learns to make that impossible.
Term by term.

The discriminator is trained by classification: high \(C\) on the learner’s pairs, low on the expert’s.
The policy is trained by reinforcement learning (for example, the policy gradient methods of Chapters 11–12) with reward \(-\log C_\phi(s, a)\): pairs that look expert-like pay more.
Both are usually neural networks. This page does not implement GAIL; it needs the machinery of Appendix D and much more computation than the other methods here.

Why it holds. At the game’s equilibrium, the learner’s distribution of state-action pairs matches the expert’s (as in generative adversarial networks). GAIL can be seen as inverse reinforcement learning whose “reward” is the discriminator’s opinion, followed immediately by reinforcement learning on it.

title: 18 · Imitation Learning
text:
Worked example

Cloning by counting
Suppose the demonstrations visit cell (3, 2) four times, with the expert going east three times and north once, and never visit cell (5, 5). The cloned policy is

at (3, 2): east 0.75, north 0.25, south and west 0;
at (5, 5): all four actions 0.25.

The clone reproduces the expert’s frequencies where it has data, and is clueless where it doesn’t.


Feature expectations by hand
A walk with \(\gamma = 0.95\) crosses a path cell, a grass cell, then a path cell, then reaches the gate and ends. Its discounted feature counts are

path: \(1 + 0.95^2 = 1.9025\);
grass: \(0.95\);
mud: 0;
gate: \(0.95^3 = 0.857\).

Under the true weights \((-1, -2, -6, 10)\), its discounted return is \(-1.9025 - 1.9 + 8.57 = 4.77\). Any policy whose average counts equal these earns the same, whatever the weights.


One maximum margin step
The expert’s feature expectations from the demonstrations are \(\mu_E =\) (8.37, 1.68, 0.39, 0.48) for (path, grass, mud, gate). A uniformly random walker’s are \(\mu^{(1)} =\) (8.13, 7.90, 3.61, 0.02). With a single constraint, the best unit \(\phi\) points along \(\mu_E - \mu^{(1)}\), and the margin is its length, 7.02. That first reward is \(\phi =\) (0.04, -0.89, -0.46, 0.07): mostly “less grass, less mud”. It penalizes grass more than mud, because the random walker spends much more time on grass than the expert does. Maximum margin weights describe how the expert differs from the policies found so far, not the true reward.

title: 18 · Imitation Learning
18 · Imitation Learning
text:
Algorithms & code

Cloning and interactive learning

PythonJulia


def rollouts(T, probs, b, m, d, rng, label=None, end=None):
    """m trajectories of up to d steps from b, acting with `probs`. Each
    trajectory is a list of (s, a). If label(s) is given, the recorded
    action is label(s) (the expert's choice) while the action taken still
    comes from probs, as in DAgger. Rollouts stop at the state `end`."""
    trajs = []
    n_s, n_a = probs.shape
    for _ in range(m):
        s, traj = rng.choice(n_s, p=b), []
        for _ in range(d):
            if s == end:
                break
            a = rng.choice(n_a, p=probs[s])
            traj.append((s, a if label is None else label(s)))
            s = rng.choice(n_s, p=T[s, a])
        trajs.append(traj)
    return trajs

def behavioral_cloning(pairs, n_states, n_actions):
    """Maximum likelihood tabular policy (eq. 18.1): action counts per
    state, normalized. States never demonstrated get a uniform policy."""
    N = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
    for s, a in pairs:
        N[s, a] += 1
    seen = N.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    return np.where(seen > 0, N / np.maximum(seen, 1), 1 / n_actions)

def dagger(T, expert, b, demos, k_max, m, d, rng, end=None):
    """Data set aggregation (algorithm 18.2): clone, run the clone, have
    the expert label the states it visits, add them, clone again.
    expert[s] is the expert's action. Returns the policies after each
    iteration (the first is plain behavioral cloning)."""
    n_s, n_a = T.shape[0], T.shape[1]
    data = [pair for traj in demos for pair in traj]
    policies = [behavioral_cloning(data, n_s, n_a)]
    for _ in range(k_max - 1):
        new = rollouts(T, policies[-1], b, m, d, rng, label=lambda s: expert[s], end=end)
        data += [pair for traj in new for pair in traj]
        policies.append(behavioral_cloning(data, n_s, n_a))
    return policies

def smile(T, expert, b, k_max, m, d, beta, rng, end=None):
    """Stochastic mixing iterative learning (algorithm 18.3). Iteration k
    runs the current mixture, has the expert label the visited states,
    clones only that new data, and mixes the clone in. The expert keeps
    weight (1 - beta)^k and clone i gets beta (1 - beta)^(i-1). Returns the
    mixtures after each iteration and the final one with the expert's share
    renormalized away."""
    n_s, n_a = T.shape[0], T.shape[1]
    expert_probs = greedy_probs(expert, n_a)
    clones, mixtures = [], []
    current = expert_probs
    for k in range(1, k_max + 1):
        new = rollouts(T, current, b, m, d, rng, label=lambda s: expert[s], end=end)
        clones.append(behavioral_cloning([p for tr in new for p in tr], n_s, n_a))
        w = np.array([beta * (1 - beta) ** (i - 1) for i in range(1, k + 1)])
        current = (1 - beta) ** k * expert_probs + np.tensordot(w, np.array(clones), axes=1)
        mixtures.append(current)
    final = np.tensordot(w / w.sum(), np.array(clones), axes=1)
    return mixtures, final

def policy_value(T, R, gamma, probs, b):
    """Expected discounted return of a stochastic policy from start
    distribution b: b . (I - gamma T_pi)^-1 R_pi."""
    T_pi = np.einsum("sa,sat->st", probs, T)         # average T over actions
    R_pi = (probs * R).sum(axis=1)
    return b @ np.linalg.solve(np.eye(len(b)) - gamma * T_pi, R_pi)


using ADM, Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra
import Distributions

p, β = park("A")
nS, γ = size(p.R, 1), p.γ
b = park_left_starts("A")
stop = nS                                           # the end state

# Exact value of a stochastic policy P[s, a] from start distribution b.
function value(P)
    Tπ = [sum(P[s, a] * p.T[s, a, s′] for a in 1:4) for s in 1:nS, s′ in 1:nS]
    Rπ = [sum(P[s, a] * p.R[s, a] for a in 1:4) for s in 1:nS]
    return b ⋅ ((I - γ * Tπ) \ Rπ)
end

# Expert: optimal policy, by value iteration.
function expert_policy()
    U = zeros(nS)
    for _ in 1:2000
        U = [maximum(p.R[s, a] + γ * (p.T[s, a, :] ⋅ U) for a in 1:4) for s in 1:nS]
    end
    return [argmax([p.R[s, a] + γ * (p.T[s, a, :] ⋅ U) for a in 1:4]) for s in 1:nS]
end
πE = expert_policy()

# m walks of up to d steps acting with P; record (s, label(s)) — the expert's label.
function walks(P, m, d, rng; label = s -> πE[s])
    data = Tuple{Int,Int}[]
    for _ in 1:m
        s = rand(rng, Distributions.Categorical(b))
        for _ in 1:d
            s == stop && break
            a = rand(rng, Distributions.Categorical(P[s, :]))
            push!(data, (s, label(s)))
            s = rand(rng, Distributions.Categorical(p.T[s, a, :]))
        end
    end
    return data
end

# Behavioral cloning with a table: action counts per state; uniform where unseen.
function clone(data)
    N = zeros(nS, 4)
    for (s, a) in data
        N[s, a] += 1
    end
    return [sum(N[s, :]) > 0 ? N[s, a] / sum(N[s, :]) : 0.25 for s in 1:nS, a in 1:4]
end

PE = [πE[s] == a ? 1.0 : 0.0 for s in 1:nS, a in 1:4]
function dagger_run(seed; rounds = 8, m = 3)
    rng = MersenneTwister(seed)
    data = walks(PE, m, 60, rng)
    values = [value(clone(data))]
    for _ in 2:rounds
        append!(data, walks(clone(data), m, 60, rng))   # the learner acts; the expert labels
        push!(values, value(clone(data)))
    end
    return values
end
v = mean(dagger_run(seed) for seed in 1:10)
println("expert ", round(value(PE); digits = 2), "; DAgger by round ", round.(v; digits = 2))
@assert v[end] > v[1] + 3





Inverse reinforcement learning

PythonJulia


def feature_expectations(T, beta, gamma, probs, b):
    """mu_pi = E[sum_k gamma^(k-1) beta(s_k, a_k)] from b (eq. 18.5), exactly:
    the value of each feature treated as a reward."""
    T_pi = np.einsum("sa,sat->st", probs, T)
    beta_pi = np.einsum("sa,sak->sk", probs, beta)   # expected features per state
    return b @ np.linalg.solve(np.eye(len(b)) - gamma * T_pi, beta_pi)

def demo_feature_expectations(demos, beta, gamma):
    """mu_E from trajectories: average of sum_k gamma^(k-1) beta(s_k, a_k)."""
    return np.mean([sum(gamma**k * beta[s, a] for k, (s, a) in enumerate(traj))
                    for traj in demos], axis=0)

def max_margin_weights(mu_E, mus):
    """Solve eq. 18.6: maximize t subject to phi.mu_E >= phi.mu_i + t for
    every earlier policy i and ||phi|| <= 1. Returns (t, phi)."""
    k = len(mu_E)
    cons = [{"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda x, mu=mu: x[:k] @ (mu_E - mu) - x[k]} for mu in mus]
    cons.append({"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda x: 1 - x[:k] @ x[:k]})
    x0 = np.r_[(mu_E - np.mean(mus, axis=0)) / (np.linalg.norm(mu_E - np.mean(mus, axis=0)) + 1e-12), 0.0]
    res = minimize(lambda x: -x[k], x0, constraints=cons, method="SLSQP",
                   options={"ftol": 1e-12, "maxiter": 500})
    return res.x[k], res.x[:k]

def max_margin_irl(T, beta, gamma, mu_E, b, eps=1e-3, k_max=30):
    """Maximum margin inverse reinforcement learning (algorithm 18.5), with
    exact planning and exact feature expectations. Starts from a uniformly
    random policy. Returns (lam, policies, mus, margins, phis)."""
    n_s, n_a = T.shape[0], T.shape[1]
    policies = [np.full((n_s, n_a), 1 / n_a)]
    mus = [feature_expectations(T, beta, gamma, policies[0], b)]
    margins, phis = [], []
    for _ in range(k_max):
        t, phi = max_margin_weights(mu_E, mus)
        margins.append(t)
        phis.append(phi)
        if t <= eps:
            break
        pi, _, _ = policy_iteration(T, beta @ phi, gamma, np.zeros(n_s, int))  # plan for R_phi
        policies.append(greedy_probs(pi, n_a))
        mus.append(feature_expectations(T, beta, gamma, policies[-1], b))
    return mixture_weights(mu_E, mus), policies, mus, margins, phis

def soft_policy(T, R, gamma, iters=2000, tol=1e-10):
    """Maximum entropy ("soft") optimal policy: Q = R + gamma T V with
    V(s) = log sum_a exp Q(s, a), and pi(a | s) = exp(Q(s, a) - V(s))."""
    V = np.zeros(T.shape[0])
    for _ in range(iters):
        Q = R + gamma * T @ V
        Qmax = Q.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        V_new = (Qmax + np.log(np.exp(Q - Qmax).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)))[:, 0]
        if np.max(np.abs(V_new - V)) < tol:
            V = V_new
            break
        V = V_new
    Q = R + gamma * T @ V
    return np.exp(Q - V[:, None])

def horizon_feature_expectations(T, beta, gamma, probs, b, d):
    """Expected sum_{k=1}^{d} gamma^(k-1) beta(s_k, a_k) by pushing the
    state distribution forward d steps (the dynamic program of eq. 18.18)."""
    dist, mu = b.copy(), np.zeros(beta.shape[2])
    T_pi = np.einsum("sa,sat->st", probs, T)
    beta_pi = np.einsum("sa,sak->sk", probs, beta)
    for k in range(d):
        mu += gamma**k * dist @ beta_pi
        dist = dist @ T_pi
    return mu

def max_entropy_irl(T, beta, gamma, demos, b, d, alpha, k_max, phi0=None):
    """Maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning (algorithm 18.6), per
    demonstration: ascend the log-likelihood, whose gradient is the
    demonstrations' discounted feature counts minus those expected under
    the maximum entropy policy for the current reward (eq. 18.17).
    Returns (phi, policy, history of gradient norms)."""
    mu_D = demo_feature_expectations(demos, beta, gamma)
    phi = np.zeros(beta.shape[2]) if phi0 is None else phi0.copy()
    norms = []
    for _ in range(k_max):
        probs = soft_policy(T, beta @ phi, gamma)
        grad = mu_D - horizon_feature_expectations(T, beta, gamma, probs, b, d)
        norms.append(np.linalg.norm(grad))
        phi += alpha * grad
    return phi, soft_policy(T, beta @ phi, gamma), norms


using ADM, Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra
import Distributions

p, β = park("A")
nS, γ = size(p.R, 1), p.γ
# Demonstrations start from every cell except the gate and the end state.
gate = findfirst(s -> β[s, 1, 4] == 1, 1:nS)
b = [s in (gate, nS) ? 0.0 : 1.0 for s in 1:nS]
b ./= sum(b)
Rφ(φ) = [β[s, a, :] ⋅ φ for s in 1:nS, a in 1:4]          # linear reward

# One transition matrix per action, so each backup is four matrix-vector products.
Ta = [p.T[:, a, :] for a in 1:4]

# Soft (maximum entropy) optimal policy: V = log Σₐ exp Q, π(a | s) = exp(Q - V).
function soft_policy(R; iters = 400)
    V = zeros(nS)
    Q = zeros(nS, 4)
    for _ in 1:iters                                # 0.95^400 ≈ 1e-9: converged
        Q = R .+ γ .* hcat((Ta[a] * V for a in 1:4)...)
        m = maximum(Q; dims = 2)
        V = vec(m .+ log.(sum(exp.(Q .- m); dims = 2)))   # log-sum-exp, shifted for stability
    end
    return exp.(Q .- V)
end

# Expected discounted feature counts over d steps: push the state distribution forward.
function feature_counts(P, d)
    dist, μ = copy(b), zeros(4)
    Tπ = sum(P[:, a] .* Ta[a] for a in 1:4)         # row s weighted by π(a | s)
    βπ = sum(P[:, a] .* β[:, a, :] for a in 1:4)    # expected features per state, nS × 4
    for k in 0:d-1
        μ .+= γ^k .* (βπ' * dist)
        dist = Tπ' * dist
    end
    return μ
end

# The expert's feature counts: here computed exactly from the true reward's soft-greedy
# expert (a sharpened soft policy), standing in for many demonstrations.
μE = feature_counts(soft_policy(20 .* p.R), 80)
φ = zeros(4)
for _ in 1:400
    global φ += 0.05 .* (μE .- feature_counts(soft_policy(Rφ(φ)), 80))   # demos minus model
end
println("recovered weights (path, grass, mud, gate): ", round.(φ ./ norm(φ); digits = 2))
@assert φ[1] > φ[2] > φ[3]                         # path better than grass better than mud









NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






b ⋅ ((I - γ * Tπ) \ Rπ): ⋅ (typed \cdot) is the dot product, and A \ x solves a linear system like np.linalg.solve(A, x).
[... for s in 1:nS, a in 1:4] with two loops builds a matrix directly: rows by s, columns by a.
global φ += ... is needed to update a top-level variable inside a top-level loop.
s in (gate, nS) ? 0.0 : 1.0 tests membership in a tuple.
Tπ' * dist pushes the distribution forward one step: ' transposes, so this is dist @ T_pi in NumPy.
exp.(Q .- V) broadcasts: V is a vector, so it is subtracted from every column of Q, row by row.






Run them

mdp, beta = park("A")
starts = left_edge_starts("A")
expert, _, _ = policy_iteration(mdp.T, mdp.R, mdp.gamma, np.zeros(len(mdp.R), int))
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
demos = im.rollouts(mdp.T, im.greedy_probs(expert, 4), starts, 3, 60, rng, end=len(mdp.R) - 1)
policies = im.dagger(mdp.T, expert, starts, demos, 8, 3, 60, rng, end=len(mdp.R) - 1)



DAgger, value by round: -21.48 -11.10 -10.91 -10.79 -10.79 -10.79 -10.13 -10.13 (expert -9.31)




Results

The parks and the expert








Figure 3: The two park layouts and the expert’s policy in each (arrows: the intended move; walkers enter from the left edge). Park A provides the demonstrations; park B tests whether what was learned transfers.







Behavioral cloning needs coverage








Figure 4: Behavioral cloning in park A against the number of demonstrated walks (20 trials each): the cloned policy’s exact value from the left edge (left), and the number of cells where the expert’s choice was seen (right).





Even with 100 walks, the expert’s choice is known in only 44 of 63 cells: the expert simply never goes to some parts of the park. The clone survives that because the expert’s routes, and slips from them, rarely reach those cells either.


Asking the expert: DAgger and SMILe








Figure 5: Value from the left edge by round: DAgger (starting from 3 demonstrated walks, adding 3 expert-labeled walks of the learner per round; 20 trials) and SMILe (mixing rate β = 0.2, with 3, 10 or 30 labeled walks per round; 10 trials; the SMILe curves are the mixtures, which still include the expert).






DAgger needs little data because it aggregates: every labeled walk ever collected trains every later policy.
SMILe trains each component only on its own round’s walks. With a table, which can’t generalize, a component trained on 3 walks acts at random in most cells. As the expert’s weight decays, those random components take over: after 10 rounds the mixture without the expert is worth -17.62 with 3 walks per round, -11.88 with 10, and -9.93 with 30.
SMILe’s design assumes a policy class that generalizes from each round’s data, like the feature-based policies in the book’s mountain car example, and it trades data efficiency for gradual, stable changes to the policy.



Inverse reinforcement learning








Figure 6: Left: maximum margin IRL’s margin by iteration, from 30 demonstrated walks from the left edge. Right: reward weights for path, grass, mud and the gate, scaled to unit length: the true reward, and maximum entropy IRL’s estimates (averaged over 10 trials) from 30 walks starting at the left edge or at every cell.






Maximum margin needed 15 new policies. Its margin levels off near 0.20 rather than reaching 0: the expert’s feature expectations are estimated from 30 walks, and no policy matches that noisy estimate exactly. The final mixture uses 4 of the policies and is worth -10.36, against the expert’s -9.31.
Maximum entropy from walks starting at every cell recovers the right ordering of the terrains (100% of trials), and planning with its reward in park A is worth -9.51.
From the left edge only, the walks rarely go near mud, so the data barely distinguish grass from mud. The average weights (orange) have the right order, but individual trials ranked the terrains correctly in only 70% of cases.
Both put little weight on the gate, far less than the true reward. Every step off the gate costs something, so ending the walk is already valuable, and the demonstrations can’t separate “the gate is great” from “walking is costly”. Rewards are identified only up to such trade-offs, which matter less than the terrain ranking for choosing routes. The planned policy is still decent in park A (-9.65), where the demonstrations’ routes decide most things. The difference shows up when the reward is used somewhere new.



Transfer to a new park








Figure 7: Values in park B (from its left edge) of an expert who knows the true reward, of planning with rewards learned by maximum entropy IRL in park A (10 trials each), of the policy cloned in park A (applied to the same cell numbers), and of a random walker.





The learned reward is three numbers about terrain plus one about the gate, so it means the same thing in any park. Planned with in park B, the reward learned from walks starting at every cell was worth -12.82 on average, close to the expert’s -12.07. The reward learned from left-edge walks, which sometimes ranks grass and mud the wrong way round, was worth -13.94. The cloned policy is a table about park A’s cells; in park B it scored -22.27, only better than random because both parks have their gate in the same corner.

title: 18 · Imitation Learning
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: cloning from counts. In one state the expert chose left 6 times, straight 3 times and right once. What does behavioral cloning with a table predict? If the clone always takes its most likely action instead, what fraction of the expert’s behavior in that state does it reproduce?






TipSolution





\(\pi(\text{left}) = 0.6\), \(\pi(\text{straight}) = 0.3\), \(\pi(\text{right}) = 0.1\). Always taking left matches the expert’s action 60% of the time, if the expert’s choices there are random. If the expert’s choices depend on something the state description leaves out (for example, traffic behind), no policy of this state can do better. Cloning can only be as good as the state representation.



Problem 2: quadratic versus linear. A clone makes a mistake with probability 0.01 per step in states the expert visits, and after a mistake it never recovers (every later step is costly). Over a 100-step episode, roughly how many costly steps does it incur? How does DAgger’s guarantee compare?






TipSolution





The first mistake happens at step \(k\) with probability about \(0.01\) each step, and then costs \(100 - k\) steps. The expected cost is about \(\sum_{k=1}^{100} 0.01(100 - k) \approx 0.01 \times 4950 \approx 50\) steps: of order \(\epsilon h^2/2\). DAgger trains on the learner’s own states, so its error per step stays about \(\epsilon\) everywhere, giving about \(\epsilon h = 1\) costly step. The quadratic-versus-linear gap grows with the horizon.



Problem 3: a margin by hand. Two features. The expert’s feature expectations are \(\mu_E = (3, 1)\), and the only policy so far has \(\mu^{(1)} = (1, 2)\). Find the maximum margin weights and the margin.






TipSolution





With one constraint, \(\phi^\top(\mu_E - \mu^{(1)}) \ge t\), and \(\|\phi\| \le 1\), the best \(\phi\) points along \(\mu_E - \mu^{(1)} = (2, -1)\), so \(\phi = (2, -1)/\sqrt5 \approx (0.894, -0.447)\). The margin is \(t = \|(2, -1)\| = \sqrt 5 \approx 2.24\). The reward says “the first feature is good, the second bad”. The next step finds the optimal policy for it and adds its feature expectations as a new constraint.



Problem 4: the maximum entropy gradient. Demonstrations average the discounted feature counts (4, 1, 0.5). Under the current reward, the maximum entropy model expects (3, 2, 0.5). Which way does gradient ascent move each weight?






TipSolution





The gradient is demonstrations minus model: \((1, -1, 0)\). The first weight rises: the expert collects more of feature 1 than the model predicts, so feature 1 must be more rewarding. The second falls, and the third stays put because it is already matched. Ascent stops when the counts match, which is Equation 4’s condition.



Problem 5: why transfer needs identifiable rewards. In park A, walks from the left edge rarely pass near mud. Why does the learned reward then transfer less well to park B, even though the policy it gives in park A is fine?






TipSolution





If the demonstrations never face a choice involving mud, any mud weight that keeps mud unattractive enough fits the data equally well. The data don’t pin down how bad mud is compared with grass. In park A that doesn’t matter, because the routes avoid both anyway. In park B, a route that must choose between mud and grass depends on exactly that comparison, and the learned reward can choose wrong. Demonstrations must exercise the features whose weights will matter later. Starting walks from every cell did that here.

title: 18 · Imitation Learning
text:
Recap

Behavioral cloning is supervised learning of the expert’s actions (Equation 1). Why it matters: it is often the first thing to try and needs no environment model or reward. But it learns only where the expert went. With 3 walks, the clone was worth -19.11 against the expert’s -9.31.
Errors cascade because the learner’s states differ from the expert’s; interactive methods fix the data (Equation 2, Equation 3). Why it matters: DAgger’s labels on the learner’s own states brought it to -9.84. It is the principle behind training driving policies with corrective demonstrations.
A linear reward sees a policy only through its feature expectations (Equation 4). Why it matters: matching the expert’s feature expectations guarantees matching its return under every linear reward, including the true one. That is the basis of maximum margin IRL (Equation 5).
Maximum entropy IRL finds the reward under which the demonstrations are most likely (Equation 6). Why it matters: it resolves the ambiguity of many rewards fitting the same behavior, and handles noisy, suboptimal demonstrations gracefully. It underlies much of modern reward learning.
A reward transfers; a copied policy doesn’t, but only if the demonstrations exercise the features. Why it matters: planning with the reward learned in park A was worth -12.82 in park B, against -12.07 for the expert. Learning why generalizes further than learning what.

Common pitfalls

Evaluating a clone on the expert’s states. Its accuracy there says little about how it behaves once its own mistakes take it elsewhere; evaluate by running it.
A state description that hides what the expert sees. If the expert reacts to information the learner doesn’t observe, the best clone is only a blurred average.
Demonstrations that don’t exercise the features. Inverse RL can’t learn weights for situations the expert never faced; the result may look fine where the demos were and fail elsewhere.
Reading maximum margin weights as the true reward. They are a device for finding a matching policy mixture, and may look nothing like the real reward.
Assuming the expert is optimal. Real demonstrations are noisy; maximum entropy IRL tolerates that better than methods that assume perfect optimality.

title: 20 · Exact Belief State Planning
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 19 kept track of where the agent probably is: a belief, updated after every action and observation. Now we decide what to do with it. A partially observable MDP (POMDP) is an MDP whose state the agent can’t see; it sees only noisy observations. The key move is to treat the belief itself as the state. A POMDP then becomes an ordinary MDP over beliefs, with a continuous state space. This chapter solves that MDP exactly, for finite horizons, by exploiting a special structure: the value function over beliefs is piecewise linear and convex. Chapters 21 and 22 approximate it when exact solutions are too expensive.
The question: how do we choose actions optimally when we only have a belief about the state, not the state itself?
The short answer: plan over beliefs. A policy can be written as a conditional plan, a tree of actions that branches on what you observe. Each plan’s expected utility is linear in the belief, given by an alpha vector of per-state utilities. The best achievable utility is the upper surface of those lines (planes in higher dimensions), so it’s piecewise linear and convex. Value iteration builds longer plans from shorter ones and prunes the plans that are never the best, keeping the problem small enough to solve.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. Treating the belief as the state turns a POMDP into a belief-state MDP; conditional plans and their alpha vectors make it solvable exactly by value iteration with pruning.







The key ideas at a glance

The belief-state MDP. A belief summarizes everything the agent knows. Its reward is the expected reward over the belief, and it moves according to Bayes’ rule after each action and observation. So the POMDP is an MDP whose states are beliefs. That MDP has infinitely many states, but a lot of structure.
Conditional plans. With a finite horizon, a policy can be written as a tree: take this action; if you observe this, do that; if you observe the other, do something else. A plan’s utility from each true state can be computed recursively.
Alpha vectors. A plan’s utility from a belief is the belief-weighted average of its utilities from each state: a dot product \(\alpha^\top b\). Each plan is a line over the belief (a plane in higher dimensions). The best value over all plans is the upper surface of these lines, which is piecewise linear and convex.
Pruning. Most plans are never the best at any belief. A linear program finds, for each alpha vector, the belief where it beats the others by the most. If it never beats them, the plan is dropped. For the crying baby, only 2 or 3 plans of each horizon survive.
Value iteration. Build every \((k+1)\)-step plan from a first action and a choice of pruned \(k\)-step subplan after each observation, compute their alpha vectors from the subplans’ vectors, and prune. The number of all plans explodes doubly exponentially with the horizon; pruning keeps the working set small.
Linear policies. With linear-Gaussian dynamics and quadratic rewards, the belief is a Gaussian and the optimal action is the fully observed optimal controller applied to the belief’s mean: certainty equivalence.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




POMDP
An MDP whose state is hidden; the agent receives observations instead


Observation model \(O(o \mid a, s')\)
Probability of observing \(o\) after taking \(a\) and arriving in \(s'\)


Belief \(b\)
A probability distribution over states (Chapter 19)


Belief-state MDP
The MDP whose states are beliefs and whose transitions are belief updates


Conditional plan \(\pi\)
A tree: an action, then a subplan for each possible observation


Alpha vector \(\alpha_\pi\)
A plan’s expected utility from each state; its value at a belief is \(\alpha_\pi^\top b\)


Piecewise linear and convex
The shape of the optimal value over beliefs: the upper surface of lines


Dominated alpha vector
One that is never the best at any belief


Pruning
Removing dominated alpha vectors (and their plans)


Certainty equivalence
Acting as if the belief’s mean were the true state (optimal in the linear-Gaussian case)








After this chapter you can

Write down the belief-state MDP of a discrete POMDP.
Evaluate a conditional plan and compute its alpha vector.
Act from a set of alpha vectors, directly or by one-step lookahead.
Detect dominated alpha vectors with a linear program, and prune them.
Run POMDP value iteration and read off the optimal policy for a small problem.
Explain when acting on the belief’s mean is optimal.

title: 20 · Exact Belief State Planning
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



You’re looking after a baby who can’t say “I’m hungry”. You only hear whether it cries.

Belief: after an hour of quiet, you think it’s probably still content; a cry makes hunger much more likely. Your confidence is the belief.
A plan: “Wait. If it cries, feed it; if not, keep waiting, and feed it at the next cry.” That’s a strategy that responds to what you hear, not a fixed schedule.
Plans are straight lines: how well a plan does depends on how likely the baby is to be hungry right now, and that dependence is linear. Feeding is costly if the baby is sated, but pays if it’s hungry.
The best strategy depends on your current belief: ignore while hunger seems unlikely, feed when it seems likely. The crossing point is the decision threshold.



Our running example is the crying baby (ADM Appendix F.7, in the problem gallery). The baby is sated or hungry. Each hour the caregiver can feed it (cost 5, always sates it), sing (cost 0.5), or ignore it. A sated baby becomes hungry 10% of the time unless fed. Hunger costs 10 per hour. A hungry baby cries 80% of the time, a sated one 10% (when sung to: 90% and 0%). The discount is 0.9.

The belief is the state
If you’re 30% sure the baby is hungry and you ignore it, next hour’s expected cost is \(0.3 \times 10 = 3\). Whatever you hear next, you can work out your new belief with Chapter 19’s filter. So “30% sure” behaves exactly like a state of an MDP, one with a continuum of values. See Equation 1.


A plan is a tree
“Ignore. If it cries, feed; if it’s quiet, ignore. Then feed only if it cries.” That three-hour plan chooses among 2 × 2 = 4 possible action sequences depending on what it hears. Its expected cost can be worked out for a baby that is sated now (-3.17) and one that is hungry now (-25.19). See Equation 2.


Plans are lines over the belief
For a belief \(P(\text{hungry}) = x\), the plan’s value mixes those two numbers in proportion: \((1 - x)\) times -3.17 plus \(x\) times -25.19, a straight line in \(x\). “Always feed” and “always ignore” are two other lines. The best three-hour value is the upper surface of all such lines (Figure 3). See Equation 3.


Most plans are never best
There are 2187 three-step plans: three actions at each of the tree’s 7 nodes. But only 3 of them are best at some belief. The rest can be discarded without losing anything (Figure 5). See Equation 5.


Build long plans from short ones
A \((k+1)\)-step plan is a first action plus a surviving \(k\)-step plan after each observation. Pruning at every step, value iteration reaches 30 hours with at most 27 plans to check per step, although the number of 30-step plans has hundreds of millions of digits. The resulting policy: ignore the baby until \(P(\text{hungry})\) reaches about 0.28, then feed it (Figure 6). See Equation 6.

title: 20 · Exact Belief State Planning
text:
Formalism

POMDPs and the belief-state MDP
A POMDP adds to an MDP an observation space \(\mathcal{O}\) and an observation model \(O(o \mid a, s')\) (ADM §20.1; Chapter 19). Treating beliefs as states gives an MDP with reward and transition

\[
R(b, a) = \sum_s R(s, a)\, b(s),
\qquad
T(b' \mid b, a) = \sum_o \mathbb{1}\big[b' = \text{Update}(b, a, o)\big]\ \sum_{s'} O(o \mid a, s') \sum_s T(s' \mid s, a)\, b(s)
\tag{1}\]

In words. The reward of acting on a belief is the belief-weighted average reward. The next belief is the Bayes update for whichever observation arrives, and each observation arrives with its predicted probability.
Term by term.

\(\sum_s T(s' \mid s, a) b(s)\) is the predicted distribution of the next state; weighting by \(O(o \mid a, s')\) and summing gives \(P(o \mid b, a)\).
\(\text{Update}(b, a, o)\) is the discrete filter of Chapter 19: predict, weight by the observation’s likelihood, normalize.
The indicator says the belief transition is deterministic given the observation; only the observation is random.

Why it holds. The belief is a sufficient statistic: the probability of every future observation and reward, given the whole history, depends on the history only through \(b\) (K. J. Åström, J. Math. Anal. Appl., 1965). So an optimal policy can map beliefs to actions, and the belief evolves as a Markov process.
The belief space is continuous, so the tabular methods of Chapter 7 don’t apply directly. The rest of the chapter exploits its structure instead.


Conditional plans
A conditional plan \(\pi\) has a root action \(\pi()\) and a subplan \(\pi(o)\) for each observation (ADM §20.2). Its utility from state \(s\) is

\[
U^\pi(s) = R\big(s, \pi()\big) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T\big(s' \mid s, \pi()\big) \sum_o O\big(o \mid \pi(), s'\big)\, U^{\pi(o)}(s')
\tag{2}\]

In words. Take the root action, collect its reward, then average over where you end up and what you observe, following the matching subplan.
Term by term.

A leaf’s utility is just its reward.
An \(h\)-step plan with \(|\mathcal{O}|\) observations has \((|\mathcal{O}|^h - 1)/(|\mathcal{O}| - 1)\) nodes, and any action can go at each node, so there are \(|\mathcal{A}|^{(|\mathcal{O}|^h - 1)/(|\mathcal{O}| - 1)}\) plans: doubly exponential in \(h\).
The best \(h\)-step value from belief \(b\) is \(U^*(b) = \max_\pi U^\pi(b)\).

Why it holds. It is the Bellman expectation equation (Chapter 7) for the fixed plan, with the observation choosing which subplan applies.


Alpha vectors
A plan’s utility from a belief averages its utility from each state (ADM §20.3):

\[
U^\pi(b) = \sum_s b(s)\, U^\pi(s) = \alpha_\pi^\top b,
\qquad
U^*(b) = \max_\pi\ \alpha_\pi^\top b
\tag{3}\]

In words. Each plan’s value is linear in the belief. The optimal value is the maximum of these linear functions: piecewise linear and convex.
Term by term.

\(\alpha_\pi = (U^\pi(s))_s\) is the plan’s alpha vector. Its entries are utilities, not probabilities.
With two states, a belief is one number, \(x = P(\text{hungry})\), and \(\alpha_\pi^\top b = (1 - x)\alpha_\pi(\text{sated}) + x\,\alpha_\pi(\text{hungry})\): a line from \(\alpha_\pi(\text{sated})\) at \(x = 0\) to \(\alpha_\pi(\text{hungry})\) at \(x = 1\).
A set \(\Gamma\) of alpha vectors, each labeled with its plan’s root action, is a policy: at belief \(b\), take the action of the vector with the largest \(\alpha^\top b\).

Why it holds. Utility is an expectation over the unknown current state, and expectation is linear in the probabilities. A maximum of linear functions is convex: mixing two beliefs can’t give a higher best value than the mix of their best values. Intuitively, being uncertain never beats knowing, on average.
With a set \(\Gamma\) we can also act by one-step lookahead (ADM eqs. 20.13–20.15):

\[
\pi_\Gamma(b) = \arg\max_a\Big[R(b, a) + \gamma \sum_o P(o \mid b, a)\, U^\Gamma\big(\text{Update}(b, a, o)\big)\Big],
\qquad
P(o \mid b, a) = \sum_s b(s) \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a)\, O(o \mid a, s')
\tag{4}\]

In words. Try each action: its expected reward now, plus, for each observation it might produce, the value of the belief you’d then hold.
Term by term. \(U^\Gamma(b) = \max_{\alpha \in \Gamma}\alpha^\top b\). This needs no action labels on the vectors, and it works with any value function over beliefs, which the approximate methods of Chapters 21–22 rely on.


Pruning
An alpha vector \(\alpha\) is dominated if no belief makes it the best. Find the belief where it beats the others by the most (ADM §20.4):

\[
\max_{\delta,\, b}\ \delta
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
b \ge 0,\quad \mathbf 1^\top b = 1,\quad
\alpha^\top b \ge \alpha'^\top b + \delta\ \ \text{for all } \alpha' \in \Gamma
\tag{5}\]

In words. Search over all beliefs for the one where \(\alpha\) has the biggest lead over every other vector. If even the biggest lead is not positive, \(\alpha\) is never needed.
Term by term.

\(\delta\) is the lead; \(b\) is a probability distribution.
The objective and constraints are linear, so it’s a small linear program. The book uses a general LP solver. This site’s code uses a few lines of the simplex method, after relaxing \(\mathbf 1^\top b = 1\) to \(\le 1\) and requiring \(\delta \ge 0\). That makes \(b = 0\) a starting corner and doesn’t change the answer when the lead is positive, since scaling \(b\) up to sum to 1 only increases \(\delta\). The test suite checks it against a brute-force search over beliefs.
Pruning a whole set compares each candidate only with the vectors already kept (algorithm 20.7): a candidate that wins somewhere brings in whichever vector is best at that belief.

Why it holds. The optimal value is the maximum over the set. Removing a vector that is never the maximum changes the maximum nowhere.


Value iteration
Build \((k + 1)\)-step plans from a root action \(a\) and one \(k\)-step subplan per observation, with alpha vectors computed from the subplans’ (ADM §20.5):

\[
\alpha(s) = R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) \sum_o O(o \mid a, s')\, \alpha_o(s')
\tag{6}\]

In words. A new plan’s utility from each state is the first action’s reward plus the discounted, observation-weighted utility of the subplan chosen for each observation.
Term by term.

\(\alpha_o\) is the alpha vector of the subplan chosen for observation \(o\).
Each step creates \(|\mathcal{A}| \times |\Gamma_k|^{|\mathcal{O}|}\) plans, which are then pruned.
It is Equation 2 with the subplans’ utilities already computed, so no tree is re-evaluated.
Only pruned subplans are needed: a dominated subplan can always be replaced by one that is at least as good at the belief that follows.

Why it holds. It is Chapter 7’s Bellman backup, carried out on whole plans. The Bellman backup of a piecewise linear convex function is again piecewise linear and convex, and its pieces are exactly these combinations (R. D. Smallwood and E. J. Sondik, Operations Research, 1973).


Linear policies
If the dynamics and observations are linear with Gaussian noise and the reward is quadratic, the belief is a Gaussian \(\mathcal{N}(\mu_b, \Sigma_b)\), tracked exactly by the Kalman filter of Chapter 19 (ADM §20.6):

\[
a = -K\,\mu_b
\tag{7}\]

In words. Use the fully observed optimal controller (the linear feedback gain \(K\) of the linear quadratic regulator, Chapter 7), and feed it the belief’s mean as if it were the true state.
Term by term.

\(K\) comes from the Riccati recursion of the fully observed problem, and doesn’t depend on the observation noise.
\(\mu_b\) comes from the Kalman filter, which doesn’t depend on the rewards. Estimation and control separate.

Why it holds. With a quadratic reward, the expected cost of a Gaussian belief is the cost at its mean plus a term that depends only on the covariance. The covariance evolves the same way whatever the agent does, so it can’t affect the choice of action. This is special to the linear-quadratic-Gaussian case; in general, beliefs matter beyond their mean.

title: 20 · Exact Belief State Planning
text:
Worked example

A plan’s alpha vector by hand
Take the two-step plan “ignore; then feed if crying, ignore if quiet”. The subplans are one-step leaves: feed has \(\alpha = R(\cdot, \text{feed}) = (-5, -15)\) for (sated, hungry), and ignore has \((0, -10)\).

From sated: ignoring costs nothing now. The baby stays sated (0.9) or becomes hungry (0.1). If sated, it cries 10% of the time: \(0.1(-5) + 0.9(0) = -0.5\). If hungry, it cries 80% of the time: \(0.8(-15) + 0.2(-10) = -14\). So \(\alpha(\text{sated}) = 0 + 0.9\,[0.9(-0.5) + 0.1(-14)] = -1.665\).
From hungry: \(-10\) now; it stays hungry, so \(\alpha(\text{hungry}) = -10 + 0.9(-14) = -22.6\).

The code agrees: alphavector gives (-1.665, -22.6).


Lookahead from an even belief
At \(b = (0.5, 0.5)\), use the two-step value function \(U^\Gamma\) (the 2 vectors that survive pruning at horizon 2) and look one step ahead:



Table 2: One-step lookahead at b = (0.5, 0.5).











Action
R(b, a)
Each observation
Q(b, a)




feed
-10.0
crying: P = 0.1, b′(hungry) = 0.0, U = -0.9; quiet: P = 0.9, b′(hungry) = 0.0, U = -0.9
-10.81


sing
-5.5
crying: P = 0.495, b′(hungry) = 1.0, U = -15.0; quiet: P = 0.505, b′(hungry) = 0.109, U = -2.87
-13.49


ignore
-5.0
crying: P = 0.485, b′(hungry) = 0.907, U = -14.07; quiet: P = 0.515, b′(hungry) = 0.214, U = -4.77
-13.35






Feeding costs the most now, but leaves the baby sated whatever is heard, so its future is cheap. Ignoring saves the 5 now, but a hungry baby stays hungry, and the likely cry makes the next belief bad. At an even belief, feeding wins.


Is a vector dominated?
Three vectors over (sated, hungry): \(\alpha_1 = (-3, -18)\), \(\alpha_2 = (-6, -12)\), \(\alpha_3 = (-5, -16)\). The lines of \(\alpha_1\) and \(\alpha_2\) cross where \(-3 - 15x = -6 - 6x\), at \(x = 1/3\), both worth \(-8\). There, \(\alpha_3\) is worth \(-5 - 11/3 = -8.67\), worse than both. Being a line, it can’t beat the upper envelope anywhere else either: it’s dominated. The linear program finds the same:
find_maximal_belief returns nothing for α₃ against {α₁, α₂}, and belief (1.0, 0.0) for α₁ against α₂: α₁ leads most when the baby is surely sated.

title: 20 · Exact Belief State Planning
20 · Exact Belief State Planning
text:
Algorithms & code

Conditional plans, alpha vectors and lookahead

JuliaPython


# Conditional plans and alpha vectors (ADM §20.2-20.3).
# A POMDP p has p.T[s, a, s′], p.R[s, a], p.O[a, s′, o] and discount p.γ.

# A plan: an action at the root and one subplan per observation (none at a leaf).
struct ConditionalPlan
    a::Int
    subplans::Vector{ConditionalPlan}      # subplans[o] follows observation o
end
ConditionalPlan(a::Int) = ConditionalPlan(a, ConditionalPlan[])

# Utility of plan π from state s (eq. 20.8): the root action's reward, then the
# discounted average over next states s′ and observations o of subplan π(o) from s′.
function evaluate_plan(p, π::ConditionalPlan, s)
    r = p.R[s, π.a]
    isempty(π.subplans) && return r
    nS, nO = size(p.T, 3), size(p.O, 3)
    future = sum(p.T[s, π.a, s′] * p.O[π.a, s′, o] *
                 evaluate_plan(p, π.subplans[o], s′) for s′ in 1:nS, o in 1:nO)
    return r + p.γ * future
end

# Alpha vector: the plan's utility from every state (algorithm 20.3).
# A belief's utility is then the dot product α ⋅ b (eq. 20.11).
alphavector(p, π) = [evaluate_plan(p, π, s) for s in axes(p.T, 1)]

# The same alpha vector built from the subplans' alpha vectors αs[o]
# (eq. 20.17), without re-evaluating the whole tree.
function combine_alpha(p, a, αs)
    nS, nO = size(p.T, 1), size(p.O, 3)
    return [p.R[s, a] + p.γ * sum(p.T[s, a, s′] * p.O[a, s′, o] * αs[o][s′]
                                  for s′ in 1:nS, o in 1:nO) for s in 1:nS]
end

# P(o | b, a) (eqs. 20.14-20.15): move with T, then observe with O.
function observation_probability(p, b, a, o)
    nS = length(b)
    return sum(b[s] * p.T[s, a, s′] * p.O[a, s′, o] for s in 1:nS, s′ in 1:nS)
end

# One-step lookahead from a belief with value function U (eq. 20.13):
# expected reward now plus the discounted value of each updated belief.
function lookahead_belief(p, U, b, a)
    r = sum(p.R[s, a] * b[s] for s in eachindex(b))
    future = 0.0
    for o in axes(p.O, 3)
        po = observation_probability(p, b, a, o)
        po > 0 || continue                 # impossible observations add nothing
        future += po * U(update_discrete(b, p.T, p.O, a, o))
    end
    return r + p.γ * future
end

# The best action and its value by one-step lookahead on U.
function greedy_belief(p, U, b)
    q = [lookahead_belief(p, U, b, a) for a in axes(p.R, 2)]
    return (a = argmax(q), u = maximum(q), q = q)
end

# The value function of a set of alpha vectors Γ: the upper surface (eq. 20.12).
utility(Γ, b) = maximum(α ⋅ b for α in Γ)


import numpy as np

from adm.problems.crying_baby import belief_update, crying_baby

p = crying_baby()                     # states: sated, hungry; actions: feed, sing, ignore


class Plan:
    """An action at the root and one subplan per observation (none at a leaf)."""
    def __init__(self, a, subplans=()):
        self.a, self.subplans = a, list(subplans)


def evaluate_plan(p, plan, s):
    """U^pi(s) (eq. 20.8): reward now, then the subplan chosen by the observation."""
    r = p.R[s, plan.a]
    if not plan.subplans:
        return r
    nS, nO = p.T.shape[2], p.O.shape[2]
    return r + p.gamma * sum(p.T[s, plan.a, s2] * p.O[plan.a, s2, o]
                             * evaluate_plan(p, plan.subplans[o], s2)
                             for s2 in range(nS) for o in range(nO))


def alphavector(p, plan):
    return np.array([evaluate_plan(p, plan, s) for s in range(p.T.shape[0])])


def lookahead(p, U, b, a):
    """Q(b, a) (eq. 20.13): expected reward, plus each observation's updated belief's value."""
    q = p.R[:, a] @ b
    for o in range(p.O.shape[2]):
        po = (b @ p.T[:, a, :]) @ p.O[a, :, o]           # P(o | b, a)
        if po > 0:
            q += p.gamma * po * U(belief_update(p, b, a, o))
    return q


FEED, SING, IGNORE = 0, 1, 2
plan2 = Plan(IGNORE, [Plan(FEED), Plan(IGNORE)])            # ignore; feed if crying
alpha = alphavector(p, plan2)
assert np.allclose(alpha, [-1.665, -22.6])
U = lambda b: max(a @ b for a in [p.R[:, IGNORE], alpha])   # a tiny value function
print("Q at an even belief:", [round(lookahead(p, U, np.array([0.5, 0.5]), a), 3) for a in range(3)])





Pruning and value iteration

JuliaPython


# Pruning and value iteration for POMDPs (ADM §20.4-20.5).

# Largest utility gap of α over the vectors in Γ at any belief (eq. 20.16):
#   maximize δ  subject to  (α - γ′) ⋅ b ≥ δ for all γ′ in Γ,  b ≥ 0,  Σb = 1.
# Solved here with Σb = 1 relaxed to Σb ≤ 1 and δ ≥ 0, which keeps the origin
# feasible (so one phase of the simplex method suffices) and changes nothing
# when the best gap is positive: rescaling b up to Σb = 1 only raises δ.
# Returns the belief where α gains most, or nothing if α never beats Γ.
function find_maximal_belief(α, Γ; tol = 1e-9)
    m = length(α)
    isempty(Γ) && return fill(1 / m, m)
    # Variables x = [b_1..b_m, δ]. Rows: δ - (α - γ′) ⋅ b ≤ 0, and Σb ≤ 1.
    A = vcat([[-(α .- g)' 1.0] for g in Γ]..., [ones(1, m) 0.0])
    rhs = [zeros(length(Γ)); 1.0]
    x = simplex_max([zeros(m); 1.0], A, rhs)
    δ, b = x[end], x[1:m]
    return δ > tol ? b ./ sum(b) : nothing
end

# Maximize c ⋅ x subject to A x ≤ rhs, x ≥ 0, for rhs ≥ 0 (so x = 0 is a
# starting corner). Tableau simplex with Bland's rule, which cannot cycle.
function simplex_max(c, A, rhs; tol = 1e-12)
    m, n = size(A)
    tab = [A Matrix(1.0I, m, m) rhs; -c' zeros(1, m) 0.0]   # last row: -c
    basis = collect(n+1:n+m)               # slack variables start basic
    while true
        # Entering column: the first with a negative reduced cost.
        j = findfirst(<(-tol), tab[end, 1:end-1])
        j === nothing && break             # optimal
        # Leaving row: smallest ratio; ties go to the smallest basic index.
        rows = [i for i in 1:m if tab[i, j] > tol]
        isempty(rows) && error("unbounded linear program")
        ratio(i) = tab[i, end] / tab[i, j]
        best = minimum(ratio, rows)
        i = argmin(i -> basis[i], [i for i in rows if ratio(i) <= best + tol])
        tab[i, :] ./= tab[i, j]            # pivot on (i, j)
        for k in axes(tab, 1)
            k == i || (tab[k, :] .-= tab[k, j] .* tab[i, :])
        end
        basis[i] = j
    end
    x = zeros(n + m)
    x[basis] = tab[1:m, end]
    return x[1:n]
end

# Keep only alpha vectors that are best at some belief (algorithm 20.7).
# A candidate that never beats the current dominating set is dropped; if it
# does beat it somewhere, the candidate best at that belief is added.
function find_dominating(Γ)
    n = length(Γ)
    candidates, dominating = trues(n), falses(n)
    while any(candidates)
        i = findfirst(candidates)
        b = find_maximal_belief(Γ[i], Γ[dominating])
        if b === nothing
            candidates[i] = false
        else
            k = argmax([candidates[j] ? b ⋅ Γ[j] : -Inf for j in 1:n])
            candidates[k], dominating[k] = false, true
        end
    end
    return dominating
end

function prune(plans, Γ)
    keep = find_dominating(Γ)
    return plans[keep], Γ[keep]
end

# Every (k+1)-step plan: a first action, then any k-step plan after each
# observation (|A| × |plans|^|O| of them), with alpha vectors from eq. 20.17.
function expand(plans, Γ, p)
    nA, nO = size(p.R, 2), size(p.O, 3)
    new_plans, new_Γ = ConditionalPlan[], Vector{Float64}[]
    for a in 1:nA, pick in Iterators.product(fill(eachindex(plans), nO)...)
        # pick[o] is the index of the subplan followed after observation o.
        push!(new_plans, ConditionalPlan(a, [plans[i] for i in pick]))
        push!(new_Γ, combine_alpha(p, a, [Γ[i] for i in pick]))
    end
    return new_plans, new_Γ
end

# POMDP value iteration (algorithm 20.8): start from the one-step plans,
# then alternate expanding and pruning. Returns the pruned (plans, Γ) for
# every horizon 1..k_max, and how many plans each expansion produced.
function value_iteration_pomdp(p, k_max)
    plans = [ConditionalPlan(a) for a in axes(p.R, 2)]
    Γ = [p.R[:, a] for a in axes(p.R, 2)]
    counts = [length(plans)]
    plans, Γ = prune(plans, Γ)
    history = [(plans, Γ)]
    for k in 2:k_max
        plans, Γ = expand(plans, Γ, p)
        push!(counts, length(plans))
        plans, Γ = prune(plans, Γ)
        push!(history, (plans, Γ))
    end
    return history, counts
end


from itertools import product

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog

from adm.problems.crying_baby import crying_baby

p = crying_baby()
nS, nA, nO = p.T.shape[0], p.T.shape[1], p.O.shape[2]


def maximal_belief(alpha, Gamma):
    """eq. 20.16 with SciPy's LP solver: variables (b, delta); maximize delta."""
    if not Gamma:
        return np.full(len(alpha), 1 / len(alpha))
    m = len(alpha)
    # (alpha' - alpha) . b + delta <= 0 for each alpha' in Gamma, written as A_ub x <= 0.
    A_ub = np.array([np.r_[g - alpha, 1.0] for g in Gamma])
    res = linprog(c=np.r_[np.zeros(m), -1.0], A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=np.zeros(len(Gamma)),
                  A_eq=[np.r_[np.ones(m), 0.0]], b_eq=[1.0],
                  bounds=[(0, None)] * m + [(None, None)])
    return res.x[:m] if -res.fun > 1e-9 else None


def prune(Gamma, actions):
    """Keep the vectors that are best somewhere (algorithm 20.7)."""
    candidates, keep = set(range(len(Gamma))), []
    while candidates:
        i = min(candidates)
        b = maximal_belief(Gamma[i], [Gamma[k] for k in keep])
        if b is None:
            candidates.discard(i)
        else:
            k = max(candidates, key=lambda j: Gamma[j] @ b)
            candidates.discard(k)
            keep.append(k)
    return [Gamma[k] for k in keep], [actions[k] for k in keep]


def backup(a, subalphas):
    """eq. 20.17: alpha(s) = R(s, a) + gamma sum_s2 T sum_o O alpha_o(s2)."""
    # sum over o of O[a, s2, o] * alpha_o[s2], for every s2:
    future = sum(p.O[a, :, o] * subalphas[o] for o in range(nO))
    return p.R[:, a] + p.gamma * p.T[:, a, :] @ future


Gamma, actions = prune([p.R[:, a] for a in range(nA)], list(range(nA)))
for h in range(2, 31):
    new = [(backup(a, [Gamma[i] for i in pick]), a)
           for a in range(nA) for pick in product(range(len(Gamma)), repeat=nO)]
    Gamma, actions = prune([g for g, _ in new], [a for _, a in new])

x = np.linspace(0, 1, 1001)
best = [actions[int(np.argmax([g @ [1 - xi, xi] for g in Gamma]))] for xi in x]
switch = x[best.index(0)]                                # first belief where feeding is best
print(f"30 steps: {len(Gamma)} alpha vectors; feed once P(hungry) >= {switch:.3f}")
assert abs(switch - 0.283) < 0.002 and 1 not in best     # never sing









NoteReading the Julia code (for Python programmers)






struct ConditionalPlan ... end with a second constructor ConditionalPlan(a::Int) = ... is how Julia gives a type a convenience constructor; ConditionalPlan[] is an empty vector of plans.
sum(f(x, y) for x in 1:n, y in 1:m) sums over both loops, like a nested generator in Python.
Iterators.product(fill(eachindex(plans), nO)...) is itertools.product(range(len(plans)), repeat=nO): fill(x, n) makes n copies, and ... splats them as arguments.
[A Matrix(1.0I, m, m) rhs; -c' zeros(1, m) 0.0] builds a block matrix: spaces put blocks side by side, ; stacks rows. I is the identity from LinearAlgebra.
argmin(i -> basis[i], rows) returns the element of rows that minimizes the function, like min(rows, key=lambda i: basis[i]).
k == i || (...) runs the right side only when k != i: short-circuit evaluation used as a one-line if.






Run them

p = crying_baby()
history, counts = value_iteration_pomdp(p, 30)
plans, Γ = history[end]
decide(b) = p.actions[plans[argmax([α ⋅ b for α in Γ])].a]

decide (generic function with 1 method)




30-step plans kept: 2; at P(hungry) = 0.2: ignore, at P(hungry) = 0.4: feed




Results

Plans as lines







Figure 3: Utility against the belief P(hungry) of three 3-step plans: always feed, always ignore, and the plan “ignore; feed after a cry, else ignore; then feed only after a cry”. The black curve is the best achievable 3-step value, the upper surface of the pruned alpha vectors.




The conditional plan beats both fixed plans over a middle range of beliefs, but not everywhere: it is itself only one of the lines. The best 3-step value is higher still, because a different plan is best at each end.


Pruning keeps the problem small







Figure 4: Number of plans by horizon (log scale): all possible h-step plans, the plans created by each expansion step (from the pruned plans of the previous horizon), and the plans kept after pruning.






Value iteration step by step







Figure 5: POMDP value iteration on the crying baby: the alpha vectors kept at horizons 1–6, colored by the plan’s first action. The upper surface is the optimal value for that horizon.





Horizon 1: ignoring beats feeding and singing at every belief, because feeding and singing only add cost now: \((0, -10)\) is componentwise better than \((-5, -15)\) and \((-0.5, -10.5)\).
Horizon 2: feeding now pays off at the next step, and wins once \(P(\text{hungry})\) exceeds 0.51.
From horizon 3 on: the threshold settles near 0.28, and only 2 or 3 plans survive each round.
Singing is never optimal here, at any horizon from 1 to 30. The page checks every belief on a grid of 1,001 points, and the test suite checks that at horizon 3 the pruned surface matches the one from all 2,187 plans exactly. Ignoring is nearly as informative (a hungry baby cries 80% of the time, a sated one 10%), so singing’s sharper evidence isn’t worth its cost. The book’s appendix remarks that singing is optimal at some finite horizons. With the problem as written there, and also with the hunger cost charged after the transition instead of before, we found no such horizon.



The policy in action







Figure 6: Left: the 30-step optimal value and policy over the belief (ignore below the threshold, feed above). Right: 30 hours of care under this policy (acting on the belief, one seed): the belief P(hungry) (line), the true state (shaded when hungry), feeds (orange ticks) and cries (dots).




The caregiver never sees the true state (the shaded hours).

Quiet hours barely move the belief. The 10% chance of becoming hungry is mostly cancelled by the quiet, since a hungry baby would probably have cried. The belief levels off near 0.032.
A cry pushes it past the threshold, and the policy feeds. Feeding always sates the baby, so the belief drops to 0.
Some feeds are false alarms. In this run, 2 of the 5 feeds followed a cry from a baby that wasn’t hungry. The policy accepts that: a hungry hour costs 10, a feed only 5.

title: 20 · Exact Belief State Planning
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: counting plans. How many 3-step conditional plans are there with 2 actions and 3 observations? How many nodes does each plan have?






TipSolution





A 3-step plan has \(1 + 3 + 9 = 13\) nodes, which is \((3^3 - 1)/(3 - 1)\). Each node takes one of 2 actions, so there are \(2^{13} = 8{,}192\) plans. With 4 steps: \(40\) nodes and \(2^{40} \approx 10^{12}\) plans. Enumerating plans is hopeless beyond tiny horizons; pruning is what makes exact solution possible.



Problem 2: a belief update. The caregiver believes \(P(\text{hungry}) = 0.2\), ignores the baby, and hears crying. What is the new belief?






TipSolution





Predict: \(P(\text{hungry}') = 0.2 + 0.8 \times 0.1 = 0.28\). Weight by the cry’s likelihood: hungry \(0.28 \times 0.8 = 0.224\), sated \(0.72 \times 0.1 = 0.072\). Normalize: \(0.224/0.296 \approx 0.757\). One cry moves the belief from 0.2 to about 0.76, past the feeding threshold of about 0.28.



Problem 3: dominance by hand. Over (sated, hungry), is \(\alpha = (-4, -14)\) dominated by \(\{(-2, -20), (-7, -11)\}\)?






TipSolution





With \(x = P(\text{hungry})\): the lines are \(-2 - 18x\), \(-7 - 4x\), and \(\alpha\)’s \(-4 - 10x\). The first two cross at \(x = 5/14 \approx 0.357\), where both are worth \(-8.43\). There \(\alpha\) is worth \(-7.57\), higher. So \(\alpha\) is best near \(x = 0.357\), and not dominated. Its lead is largest at that crossing: 0.86.



Problem 4: is singing worth it? At \(P(\text{hungry}) = 0.3\), compare what one hour of singing versus ignoring tells you: the probability of hearing a cry, and the belief after each observation.






TipSolution





Predicted \(P(\text{hungry}') = 0.3 + 0.7 \times 0.1 = 0.37\) for both. Ignoring: cry probability \(0.37 \times 0.8 + 0.63 \times 0.1 = 0.359\); after a cry, \(0.296/0.359 = 0.82\); after quiet, \(0.074/0.641 = 0.12\). Singing: cry probability \(0.37 \times 0.9 = 0.333\); after a cry the belief is 1 (a sated baby never cries when sung to); after quiet, \(0.037/0.667 = 0.055\). Singing sharpens the evidence, but ignoring already separates the cases well (0.82 versus 0.12). The value of that extra sharpness is less than singing’s 0.5 cost, which is why value iteration never chooses to sing.



Problem 5: certainty equivalence. A robot’s position is tracked by a Kalman filter with mean \(\mu_b = 2\) and variance \(\Sigma_b = 0.5\). The fully observed optimal controller is \(a = -0.8x\). What action does the LQG policy take? Would a larger variance change it?






TipSolution





\(a = -0.8 \times 2 = -1.6\). A larger variance wouldn’t change the action. It would raise the expected cost, but by a term the action can’t influence. That separation holds only for linear dynamics, Gaussian noise and quadratic costs. With a cliff near the robot, say, uncertainty would call for caution, and certainty equivalence would fail.

title: 20 · Exact Belief State Planning
text:
Recap

A POMDP is an MDP over beliefs (Equation 1). Why it matters: every method in Part IV plans on beliefs; the price is a continuous state space, handled exactly here and approximately in Chapters 21–22.
Finite-horizon policies are conditional plans, and each plan’s value is linear in the belief (Equation 2, Equation 3). Why it matters: the optimal value is the upper surface of those lines: piecewise linear and convex. That structure is what makes POMDPs tractable at all.
One-step lookahead turns any value function over beliefs into a policy (Equation 4). Why it matters: it needs only a way to value beliefs, so it reappears with the approximate value functions of Chapter 21 and the online planners of Chapter 22.
Pruning with a linear program keeps value iteration small (Equation 5, Equation 6). Why it matters: the number of 3-step plans is 2187, but only 3 matter. In larger problems the surviving sets still grow quickly, motivating point-based methods (Chapter 21).
In the linear-quadratic-Gaussian case, acting on the belief’s mean is optimal (Equation 7). Why it matters: it justifies the common practice of estimating then controlling, and marks its limits: in general, the uncertainty itself should shape the action.

text:
Cheat sheet & connections



Table 3: Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name).

\(U^\pi(s) = R(s, \pi()) + \gamma\sum_{s'}T\sum_o O\,U^{\pi(o)}(s')\)

\(U^\pi(b) = \alpha_\pi^\top b\); \(U^*(b) = \max_\pi \alpha_\pi^\top b\)

Equation 5

Equation 6

\(a = -K\mu_b\)
Equation 7






Common pitfalls

Planning on the most likely state. Acting as if the likeliest state were certain ignores both risk and the value of information. It’s optimal only in special cases like LQG.
Mixing up O’s arguments. Here the observation depends on the action and the next state, \(O(o \mid a, s')\). Using the current state instead gives different beliefs and plans.
Forgetting impossible observations. An observation with \(P(o \mid b, a) = 0\) can’t be used to update the belief (division by zero); it contributes nothing to the lookahead.
Expanding unpruned sets. Without pruning, the number of plans explodes after two or three steps even for two states.
Reading alpha vectors as probabilities. Their entries are utilities per state; only the belief is a distribution.

Connections

Ch 7 · Exact Solution Methods: value iteration and the Bellman backup, here applied to whole plans; the linear quadratic regulator behind certainty equivalence.
Ch 15 · Exploration and Exploitation: the Bayes-optimal bandit, a POMDP whose hidden state is the arms’ payoff probabilities.
Ch 21 · Offline Belief State Planning: approximate value functions over beliefs, including point-based value iteration.
Ch 22 · Online Belief State Planning: planning from the current belief only, with lookahead and tree search.
Appendix C · Computational Complexity: why exact finite-horizon POMDP planning is PSPACE-complete.
