Best response, and when it’s enough
If driver 2 goes with probability \(q\), driver 1’s expected reward is \(3 - 13q\) for going and \(q - 1\) for stopping, so driver 1 should go when \(q\) is below \(2/7\) and stop otherwise. That’s a best response. In the prisoner’s dilemma, defecting is best whatever the other does (0 > −1 and −3 > −4): a dominant strategy. See Equation 2.


Nobody wants to switch: Nash equilibria
The intersection has three Nash equilibria. Two are pure: one driver goes and the other stops. The third is mixed: each goes with probability 0.286 (that is, 2/7), exactly the value that leaves the other indifferent. The mixed one is worth −0.714 to each: better than both waiting (−1), but far worse than taking turns. Rock-paper-scissors has only a mixed equilibrium: play each action a third of the time. See Equation 4.


A traffic light: correlated equilibrium
A light that tells one driver “go” and the other “stop”, each way half the time, is a correlated equilibrium: whoever is told to go gains 3 by going and would get −1 by stopping; whoever is told to stop gets 0, and would crash for −10 by going. Each driver earns 1.5 on average, far more than the mixed Nash equilibrium’s −0.714. See Equation 5.


Learning by playing
Agents that don’t know the equilibrium can learn by playing repeatedly. In the traveler’s dilemma, each round of best responses undercuts the last by $1, and the claims fall all the way to the Nash equilibrium of $2 by round 95. In rock-paper-scissors, best responses chase each other forever: rock, paper, scissors, rock, … . Fictitious play best-responds to observed frequencies instead; in the intersection, two drivers who start alike stay alike, going together and stopping together. Their frequencies approach the mixed equilibrium, but they earn −3.57 per round. See Equation 6.


How people actually play
In experiments, many people playing the traveler’s dilemma claim near the top of the range, not the minimum (K. Basu, American Economic Review, 1994; C. M. Capra, J. K. Goeree, R. Gomez and C. A. Holt, American Economic Review, 1999). A hierarchical softmax model explains this: a player who reasons a couple of levels deep, and makes cheap mistakes more often than costly ones, claims about $91 on average (precision 0.3, level 2). See Equation 3.

title: 24 · Multiagent Reasoning
text:
Formalism

Simple games and utilities
A simple game (ADM §24.1) has agents \(\mathcal{I} = \{1, \dots, k\}\), joint actions \(\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}^1 \times \dots \times \mathcal{A}^k\) and rewards \(R^i(\boldsymbol{a})\). If agents act independently with policies \(\pi^j\), agent \(i\)’s expected reward is

\[
U^i(\boldsymbol{\pi}) = \sum_{\boldsymbol{a} \in \mathcal{A}} R^i(\boldsymbol{a}) \prod_{j \in \mathcal{I}} \pi^j(a^j)
\tag{1}\]

In words. Average agent \(i\)’s reward over all joint actions, weighting each by how likely it is when every agent chooses independently.
Term by term.

\(R^i(\boldsymbol{a})\): agent \(i\)’s reward when the agents play \(\boldsymbol{a}\).
\(\prod_j \pi^j(a^j)\): the probability of \(\boldsymbol{a}\), since the choices are independent.
We write \(\boldsymbol{a} = (a^i, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i})\) and \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i})\), where \(-i\) means “everyone but \(i\)”.

Why it holds. It’s the expectation of \(R^i\) under the product distribution of independent choices.


Best and softmax responses

\[
\pi^i \text{ is a best response to } \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i} \iff U^i(\pi^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}) \ge U^i(\pi^{i\prime}, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}) \text{ for all } \pi^{i\prime}
\tag{2}\]

A pure best response is \(\arg\max_{a^i} U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i})\).
In words. Against fixed opponents, the game is just a single-agent decision: pick the action with the highest expected reward.
Term by term.

\(U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i})\) is Equation 1 with \(\pi^i\) putting all its weight on \(a^i\).
A mixed policy is a best response only if every action it uses has the highest expected reward, so some pure action is always a best response.
Dominant: a best response to every \(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}\); it’s enough to check every pure \(\boldsymbol{a}^{-i}\).

Why it holds. \(U^i\) is linear in \(\pi^i\), so its maximum over the simplex is at a vertex: a pure action.
People aren’t perfect optimizers. The softmax (logit, quantal) response (ADM §24.2.2; R. D. McKelvey and T. R. Palfrey, Games and Economic Behavior, 1995) makes each action more likely the better it is:

\[
\pi^i(a^i) \propto \exp\big(\lambda\, U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i})\big)
\tag{3}\]

In words. Better actions are exponentially more likely; how much more depends on the precision \(\lambda\).
Term by term.

\(\lambda = 0\): every action equally likely. \(\lambda \to \infty\): the best response.
Mistakes that cost little are common; mistakes that cost a lot are rare.
Hierarchical softmax (level-\(k\); D. O. Stahl and P. W. Wilson, 1994): level 0 plays uniformly; level \(k\) softmax-responds to everyone else playing level \(k - 1\).

Why it holds. It’s a model, not a theorem. It is the choice rule of an agent who adds independent, Gumbel-distributed noise to each action’s value and then picks the best, a standard model of noisy choice.


Dominant strategy and Nash equilibria

\[
\boldsymbol{\pi} \text{ is a Nash equilibrium} \iff U^i(\boldsymbol{\pi}) \ge U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}) \text{ for every agent } i \text{ and action } a^i
\tag{4}\]

In words. Nobody can gain by changing their own policy while the others keep theirs.
Term by term.

Each agent’s policy is a best response (Equation 2) to the others’.
Checking pure deviations \(a^i\) suffices, since \(U^i\) is linear in \(\pi^i\).
Regret here is \(\max_i \big(\max_{a^i} U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}) - U^i(\boldsymbol{\pi})\big)\), which is zero exactly at an equilibrium.
In a mixed equilibrium, every action an agent uses must have the same expected reward (otherwise it would drop the worse one). That indifference condition is how small games are solved by hand.

Why it holds. Every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium (J. Nash, Annals of Mathematics, 1951), by a fixed-point argument on the best-response map. Finding one is PPAD-complete (C. Daskalakis, P. W. Goldberg and C. H. Papadimitriou, 2009), so no polynomial-time algorithm is known.
As an optimization problem (ADM eq. 24.5):
\[
\min_{\boldsymbol{\pi},\, U}\ \sum_i \big(U_i - U^i(\boldsymbol{\pi})\big) \quad \text{s.t.}\quad U_i \ge U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i})\ \ \forall i, a^i, \qquad \pi^i \text{ distributions}
\]
The constraints force \(U_i\) above every action’s value; the objective pulls it down to the policy’s own value. The minimum, 0, is attained exactly at Nash equilibria. The products of policies make it nonconvex, so the page’s solver (SciPy’s SLSQP, several starts) can stop at local solutions. For two-agent games with few actions, support enumeration finds every equilibrium exactly: guess which actions each agent uses, solve the indifference equations, and check the rest.


Correlated equilibrium
A correlated joint policy \(\pi(\boldsymbol{a})\) is one distribution over joint actions, as if a mediator draws \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and privately tells each agent its part (ADM §24.5; R. J. Aumann, Journal of Mathematical Economics, 1974). It is an equilibrium if no agent gains by disobeying:

\[
\sum_{\boldsymbol{a}^{-i}} R^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i})\, \pi(a^i, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i}) \;\ge\; \sum_{\boldsymbol{a}^{-i}} R^i(a^{i\prime}, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i})\, \pi(a^i, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i})
\quad \text{for all } i,\ a^i,\ a^{i\prime}
\tag{5}\]

In words. When told to play \(a^i\), agent \(i\) expects to do at least as well by obeying as by switching to any \(a^{i\prime}\).
Term by term.

\(\pi(a^i, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i})\): how often the mediator recommends this joint action. Summing over \(\boldsymbol{a}^{-i}\) with \(a^i\) fixed covers every situation in which \(i\) is told \(a^i\).
The left side is what obeying earns in those situations; the right side is what switching to \(a^{i\prime}\) would earn.
Every constraint is linear in \(\pi\), so with a linear objective (for example total reward, “utilitarian”, or the worst-off agent’s reward, “egalitarian”) this is a linear program.

Why it holds. Dividing both sides by the probability that \(i\) is told \(a^i\) turns them into conditional expectations given the recommendation. Any Nash equilibrium is a correlated equilibrium with \(\pi(\boldsymbol{a}) = \prod_j \pi^j(a^j)\), so the set of correlated equilibria is never empty, and it is convex: the region of payoffs it reaches can include points no Nash equilibrium reaches.


Learning in repeated play
Iterated best response (ADM §24.6) has every agent best-respond to the others’ previous policies. It converges in some games (for example potential games) and cycles in others.
Fictitious play (ADM §24.8; G. W. Brown, 1951; J. Robinson, Annals of Mathematics, 1951) has each agent \(i\) count how often each other agent \(j\) played each action, and best-respond to the frequencies:

\[
\hat{\pi}^j(a^j) = \frac{N^i(j, a^j)}{\sum_{a'} N^i(j, a')}, \qquad a^i_t = \arg\max_{a^i} U^i(a^i, \hat{\boldsymbol{\pi}}^{-i})
\tag{6}\]

In words. Assume each opponent is a random player who plays actions as often as they have been seen so far, and best-respond to that.
Term by term.

\(N^i(j, a^j)\): agent \(i\)’s count of how often \(j\) played \(a^j\), usually started at 1.
\(\hat{\pi}^j\) is the maximum likelihood estimate of \(j\)’s policy (Chapter 16), treating it as fixed.
The actions played are always pure; it’s the frequencies that may converge to a mixed equilibrium.

Why it holds. If the frequencies converge, their limit is a Nash equilibrium: each agent’s frequent actions are best responses to the others’ limiting frequencies. Robinson proved convergence for two-agent zero-sum games; in general it can fail.
Gradient ascent (ADM §24.9) nudges each policy along the gradient of its own reward. If the others are assumed to repeat their last actions, the gradient is simply \(R^i(\cdot, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i}_t)\) (ADM eq. 24.12; M. Zinkevich, ICML, 2003). The policy then moves by \(\alpha_t\) times that gradient, with \(\alpha_t \propto 1/\sqrt{t}\), and is projected back onto the probability simplex (Chapter 23).

title: 24 · Multiagent Reasoning
text:
Worked example

The mixed equilibrium of the intersection
Let driver 2 go with probability \(q\). For driver 1:

going earns \(-10\,q + 3\,(1 - q) = 3 - 13q\);
stopping earns \(0 \cdot q + (-1)(1 - q) = q - 1\).

Driver 1 is willing to mix only if these are equal: \(3 - 13q = q - 1\), so \(q = 4/14 = 2/7\). By symmetry driver 1 also goes with probability \(2/7\), and each earns \(q - 1 = -5/7 \approx -0.714\).
Support enumeration finds 3 equilibria; the mixed one has P(go) = 0.2857 for both, worth −0.7143 each.
That beats both drivers always waiting (−1 each), but it is far worse than taking turns: with probability \((2/7)^2 \approx 0.08\) both go and nearly crash, and with probability \((5/7)^2 \approx 0.51\) both wait.


Checking the traffic light
The light recommends (go, stop) or (stop, go), each with probability \(1/2\). Check driver 1’s constraints (Equation 5):

Told “go” (so driver 2 was told “stop”): obeying earns 3; stopping instead earns −1. Obey.
Told “stop” (driver 2 goes): obeying earns 0; going instead earns −10. Obey.

The same holds for driver 2, so it is a correlated equilibrium, worth \(\tfrac12 \cdot 3 + \tfrac12 \cdot 0 = 1.5\) to each.
The egalitarian linear program returns π = [0.0, 0.5, 0.5, 0.0] over (go, go), (go, stop), (stop, go), (stop, stop), worth 1.500 and 1.500. The utilitarian objective instead picks (go, stop) outright: total 3.0, but all of it to driver 1.


A softmax response by hand
In rock-paper-scissors, suppose the opponent plays rock, paper, scissors with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. Your expected rewards are: rock \(0.2 - 0.3 = -0.1\); paper \(0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3\); scissors \(0.3 - 0.5 = -0.2\). With precision \(\lambda = 2\), the softmax response is proportional to \(e^{-0.2}, e^{0.6}, e^{-0.4}\):
The code: rock 0.247, paper 0.550, scissors 0.202. Paper, the best response, is most likely, but not certain.

title: 24 · Multiagent Reasoning
24 · Multiagent Reasoning
text:
Algorithms & code

Responses, equilibria and learning

PythonJulia


def action_values(game, policies, i) -> Array:
    """U^i(a_i, pi^-i) for every action a_i of agent i.

    R[i] has one axis per agent. Contract every other agent's axis with
    its policy, from the last axis down, so the axis numbers stay valid.
    """
    Ri = game.R[i]
    for j in reversed(range(len(policies))):
        if j != i:
            Ri = np.tensordot(Ri, policies[j], axes=([j], [0]))
    return Ri

def utility(game, policies, i) -> float:
    """eq. 24.1: agent i's expected reward under independent policies."""
    return float(action_values(game, policies, i) @ policies[i])

def best_response(game, policies, i) -> Array:
    """eq. 24.3: a deterministic best response (ties: lowest index)."""
    n = game.R.shape[i + 1]
    return np.eye(n)[np.argmax(action_values(game, policies, i))]

def softmax_response(game, policies, i, lam) -> Array:
    """eq. 24.4: pi^i(a) proportional to exp(lam U^i(a, pi^-i))."""
    u = lam * action_values(game, policies, i)
    p = np.exp(u - u.max())           # subtract the max: exp can't overflow
    return p / p.sum()

def regret(game, policies) -> float:
    """The most any one agent could gain by switching alone: 0 exactly at
    a Nash equilibrium."""
    return max(action_values(game, policies, i).max()
               - utility(game, policies, i) for i in range(len(policies)))

def dominant_actions(game, i) -> list:
    """Actions of agent i that are a best response to every pure joint
    action of the others (so to every mixed one too)."""
    # Rows: agent i's actions; columns: every joint action of the others.
    Ri = np.moveaxis(game.R[i], i, 0).reshape(game.R.shape[i + 1], -1)
    return [a for a in range(len(Ri)) if np.all(Ri[a] >= Ri.max(axis=0))]

def nash_equilibrium(game, rng, starts=10):
    """eq. 24.5 by SLSQP from random starts: minimize sum_i (U_i - U^i(pi))
    subject to U_i >= U^i(a_i, pi^-i) for every action. Returns the best
    run's policies and its regret (0 at an equilibrium)."""
    sizes = game.R.shape[1:]
    cuts = np.cumsum(sizes)[:-1]
    k = len(sizes)

    def unpack(z):                     # z = [pi^1, ..., pi^k, U_1..U_k]
        return np.split(z[:-k], cuts), z[-k:]

    def objective(z):
        pis, U = unpack(z)
        return sum(U[i] - utility(game, pis, i) for i in range(k))

    def gaps(z):                       # >= 0 when no action beats U_i
        pis, U = unpack(z)
        return np.concatenate([U[i] - action_values(game, pis, i)
                               for i in range(k)])

    cons = [{"type": "ineq", "fun": gaps}]
    cons += [{"type": "eq", "fun": lambda z, i=i: unpack(z)[0][i].sum() - 1}
             for i in range(k)]
    bounds = [(0, 1)] * sum(sizes) + [(None, None)] * k
    best = None
    for _ in range(starts):
        pis0 = [rng.dirichlet(np.ones(n)) for n in sizes]
        U0 = [action_values(game, pis0, i).max() for i in range(k)]
        z0 = np.concatenate(pis0 + [np.array(U0)])
        res = minimize(objective, z0, method="SLSQP", bounds=bounds,
                       constraints=cons,
                       options={"maxiter": 500, "ftol": 1e-12})
        pis = [np.clip(p, 0, None) for p in unpack(res.x)[0]]
        pis = [p / p.sum() for p in pis]
        r = regret(game, pis)
        if best is None or r < best[1]:
            best = (pis, r)
    return best

def support_enumeration(game, tol=1e-9) -> list:
    """Every Nash equilibrium of a nondegenerate two-player game, exactly.

    For each pair of equal-size supports, solve for the mixes that make
    the other agent indifferent across its support; keep the solution if
    the mixes are valid and no outside action does better. Exponential in
    the number of actions: for validating small games only.
    """
    A, B = game.R[0], game.R[1]        # rows = agent 1's action
    n1, n2 = A.shape
    found = []

    def indifferent(M, rows, cols):
        """Mix x over `rows` making x @ M[rows][:, cols] constant (v)."""
        s = len(rows)
        lhs = np.zeros((s + 1, s + 1))
        # One equation per column c: sum_r x_r M[r, c] - v = 0.
        lhs[:s, :s] = M[np.ix_(rows, cols)].T
        lhs[:s, s] = -1
        lhs[s, :s] = 1                 # and the mix sums to 1
        rhs = np.zeros(s + 1)
        rhs[s] = 1
        try:
            return np.linalg.solve(lhs, rhs)[:s]
        except np.linalg.LinAlgError:
            return None

    for s in range(1, min(n1, n2) + 1):
        for S1 in combinations(range(n1), s):
            for S2 in combinations(range(n2), s):
                # Agent 1 mixes to make agent 2 indifferent, and vice versa.
                xs = indifferent(B, list(S1), list(S2))
                ys = indifferent(A.T, list(S2), list(S1))
                if xs is None or ys is None or min(xs.min(), ys.min()) < -tol:
                    continue
                x, y = np.zeros(n1), np.zeros(n2)
                x[list(S1)], y[list(S2)] = xs, ys
                new = not any(np.allclose(x, fx) and np.allclose(y, fy)
                              for fx, fy in found)
                if regret(game, [x, y]) <= 1e-7 and new:
                    found.append((x, y))
    return found

def correlated_equilibrium(game, objective="utilitarian", agent=0) -> Array:
    """eq. 24.8 by linear programming; returns pi[a1, ..., ak], a
    distribution over joint actions. Objectives (Table 24.1):
    "utilitarian" (total reward), "egalitarian" (the worst-off agent),
    "dictatorial" (agent `agent`), or a weight vector w (maximize
    sum_i w_i U^i: used to trace the payoffs equilibria can reach)."""
    k, shape = game.R.shape[0], game.R.shape[1:]
    joints = list(np.ndindex(*shape))
    n = len(joints)
    rows = []
    # For each agent i, recommendation a_i and alternative b: the gain
    # from switching to b, over the joint actions that recommend a_i, <= 0.
    for i in range(k):
        for ai in range(shape[i]):
            for b in range(shape[i]):
                if b == ai:
                    continue
                row = np.zeros(n)
                for idx, a in enumerate(joints):
                    if a[i] == ai:
                        alt = a[:i] + (b,) + a[i + 1:]
                        row[idx] = game.R[(i,) + alt] - game.R[(i,) + a]
                rows.append(row)
    rows = np.array(rows)
    # U[i, joint]: agent i's reward for each joint action.
    U = np.array([[game.R[(i,) + a] for a in joints] for i in range(k)])
    if objective == "egalitarian":
        # Variables (pi, t): maximize t with t <= every agent's reward.
        c = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n), [-1.0]])
        A_ub = np.vstack([np.hstack([rows, np.zeros((len(rows), 1))]),
                          np.hstack([-U, np.ones((k, 1))])])
        b_ub = np.zeros(len(rows) + k)
        A_eq = np.concatenate([np.ones(n), [0.0]])[None, :]
        bounds = [(0, None)] * n + [(None, None)]
    else:
        if isinstance(objective, str):
            w = np.ones(k) if objective == "utilitarian" else np.eye(k)[agent]
        else:
            w = np.asarray(objective, dtype=float)
        c = -(w @ U)                   # linprog minimizes
        A_ub, b_ub = rows, np.zeros(len(rows))
        A_eq, bounds = np.ones((1, n)), [(0, None)] * n
    res = linprog(c, A_ub=A_ub, b_ub=b_ub, A_eq=A_eq, b_eq=[1.0],
                  bounds=bounds, method="highs")
    return np.clip(res.x[:n], 0, None).reshape(shape)

def iterated_best_response(game, k_max, policies=None) -> list:
    """§24.6: all agents best-respond at once to the others' previous
    policies. Returns the joint policy after each round (0 = start)."""
    policies = uniform_policies(game) if policies is None else policies
    history = [policies]
    for _ in range(k_max):
        policies = [best_response(game, policies, i)
                    for i in range(len(policies))]
        history.append(policies)
    return history

def hierarchical_softmax(game, lam, k, policies=None) -> list:
    """§24.7: level 0 plays uniformly; level k softmax-responds (precision
    lam) to everyone else playing level k - 1."""
    policies = uniform_policies(game) if policies is None else policies
    for _ in range(k):
        policies = [softmax_response(game, policies, i, lam)
                    for i in range(len(policies))]
    return policies

def fictitious_play(game, k_max, counts=None) -> dict:
    """§24.8: each agent counts the others' actions (eq. 24.9) and best-
    responds to those frequencies (ties: lowest index). counts[i][j] is
    agent i's count vector for agent j (default: ones). Returns each
    round's actions and each agent's model of the others."""
    k, sizes = game.R.shape[0], game.R.shape[1:]
    if counts is None:
        N = [[np.ones(sizes[j]) for j in range(k)] for _ in range(k)]
    else:
        N = [[np.array(c, dtype=float) for c in row] for row in counts]
    actions, models = [], []
    for _ in range(k_max):
        model = [[N[i][j] / N[i][j].sum() for j in range(k)]
                 for i in range(k)]
        a = [int(np.argmax(action_values(game, model[i], i)))
             for i in range(k)]
        for i in range(k):             # everyone sees the joint action
            for j in range(k):
                N[i][j][a[j]] += 1
        actions.append(a)
        models.append(model)
    return {"actions": np.array(actions), "models": models}

def gradient_ascent_play(game, k_max, rng, policies=None, rate=1.0):
    """§24.9: each agent samples an action, then steps its policy along
    R^i(., a^-i), the gradient if the others repeat their last action
    (eq. 24.12), with step rate / sqrt(t), and projects back onto the
    simplex. Returns the joint policy after each round."""
    if policies is None:
        policies = uniform_policies(game)
    policies = [np.array(p, dtype=float) for p in policies]
    history = [policies]
    for t in range(1, k_max + 1):
        a = [rng.choice(len(p), p=p) for p in policies]
        new = []
        for i, p in enumerate(policies):
            # Others as their last actions (one-hot); agent i as itself.
            others = [np.eye(len(q))[a[j]] for j, q in enumerate(policies)]
            others[i] = p
            step = rate / np.sqrt(t) * action_values(game, others, i)
            new.append(project_simplex(p + step))
        policies = new
        history.append(policies)
    return history


using ADM, LinearAlgebra

g = intersection()                 # R[i, a1, a2]; actions 1 = go, 2 = stop

# Expected reward of each of agent i's actions, when the other plays policy p.
action_values(g, i, p) = i == 1 ? g.R[1, :, :] * p : g.R[2, :, :]' * p

# Correlated equilibrium (eq. 24.8) with ADM's simplex method: maximize
# total reward subject to "obeying is no worse" for every recommendation.
# Adding a constant to all rewards changes no constraint, and makes every
# reward positive, so maximizing pushes Σπ up to its limit of 1.
function correlated_equilibrium(g)
    n1, n2 = size(g.R, 2), size(g.R, 3)
    R = g.R .- minimum(g.R) .+ 1
    joint = [(a1, a2) for a1 in 1:n1 for a2 in 1:n2]      # π's variables
    rows = Vector{Float64}[]
    for (i, n) in ((1, n1), (2, n2)), ai in 1:n, b in 1:n
        b == ai && continue
        # Gain from switching ai → b, over joint actions that recommend ai.
        push!(rows, [a[i] != ai ? 0.0 :
                     R[i, (i == 1 ? (b, a[2]) : (a[1], b))...] - R[i, a...]
                     for a in joint])
    end
    A = vcat(reduce(vcat, permutedims.(rows)), ones(1, length(joint)))
    rhs = [zeros(length(rows)); 1.0]                        # gains ≤ 0, Σπ ≤ 1
    c = [R[1, a...] + R[2, a...] for a in joint]
    return Dict(zip(joint, simplex_max(c, A, rhs)))
end

light = correlated_equilibrium(g)
total = sum(p * (g.R[1, a...] + g.R[2, a...]) for (a, p) in light)
println("utilitarian correlated equilibrium: total reward ", round(total; digits = 3))
@assert isapprox(total, 3.0; atol = 1e-9)

# Fictitious play with identical starting counts: the drivers move in lockstep.
function fictitious_play(g, rounds)
    N = [ones(2), ones(2)]                     # N[j]: counts of agent j's actions
    acts = Tuple{Int,Int}[]
    for _ in 1:rounds
        a1 = argmax(action_values(g, 1, N[2] / sum(N[2])))
        a2 = argmax(action_values(g, 2, N[1] / sum(N[1])))
        N[1][a1] += 1; N[2][a2] += 1
        push!(acts, (a1, a2))
    end
    return acts
end
acts = fictitious_play(g, 2000)
go = count(a -> a[1] == 1, acts) / length(acts)
println("P(go) = ", round(go; digits = 3), ", lockstep: ", all(a -> a[1] == a[2], acts))
@assert abs(go - 2 / 7) < 0.01 && all(a -> a[1] == a[2], acts)









NoteReading the Python code






np.tensordot(Ri, p, axes=([j], [0])) sums agent \(j\)’s axis of the reward array against its policy. Doing this for every other agent leaves a vector over agent \(i\)’s own actions: Equation 2’s \(U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i})\).
np.ndindex(*shape) walks every joint action as a tuple, like nested loops.
linprog minimizes, so maximization objectives are negated. A_ub @ x <= b_ub holds the “obeying is no worse” constraints of Equation 5.
minimize(..., method="SLSQP") handles the nonconvex Nash program: it finds a local solution, so the code tries several random starts and keeps the one with the smallest regret.






Run them

game = intersection()
print("dominant strategies:", G.dominant_strategy_equilibrium(game))
for x, y in G.support_enumeration(game):
    print("Nash:", np.round(x, 3), np.round(y, 3))
light = G.correlated_equilibrium(game, "egalitarian")
print("traffic light:", np.round(light.ravel(), 3), G.correlated_utilities(game, light))

dominant strategies: None
Nash: [1. 0.] [0. 1.]
Nash: [0. 1.] [1. 0.]
Nash: [0.286 0.714] [0.286 0.714]
traffic light: [0.  0.5 0.5 0. ] [1.5 1.5]




Results

What equilibria can achieve at the intersection








Figure 3: The intersection’s payoff plane. Gray: every payoff pair any joint-action distribution can give. Blue: the pairs that correlated equilibria give. Points: the three Nash equilibria (black) and the traffic light, the egalitarian correlated equilibrium (orange).






The three Nash equilibria give (3, 0), (0, 3) and (−0.714, −0.714). Only the pure ones are efficient, and each favors one driver.
The correlated equilibria (blue) reach exactly the triangle whose corners are the three Nash equilibria. So in this game, a correlated equilibrium is a public coin flip among Nash equilibria. That’s still worth having: the traffic light’s (1.5, 1.5) is on the efficient edge and fair, which no single Nash equilibrium is.



Iterated best response and the traveler’s dilemma








Figure 4: The traveler’s dilemma. Left: claims under iterated best response from uniform play, by round. Right: the hierarchical softmax model’s distribution of claims at levels 1-4, precision 0.3.






Best responses unravel. Against uniform claims, the best claim is $96. Against any claim \(c\), the best response is \(c - 1\) (earning \(c + 1\)). So each round undercuts the last by $1, reaching the unique Nash equilibrium of $2 at round 95, where both earn $2.
Levels of reasoning don’t unravel. With precision 0.3, the mean claim is $84 at level 1, $91 at level 2 and $93 at level 4. Undercutting by $1 gains little, and the softmax model’s noise keeps high claims attractive.
A numerical solver can stop far away. Started at random, SLSQP on the Nash program returned policies with regret 4.4e-07: nobody could gain more than that by deviating. Yet its most likely claim is $51, and each traveler expects $51.88. It is an approximate equilibrium, held up by tiny probabilities on high claims. The exact equilibrium, $2, is unique.



Can behavior data pin down the model?








Figure 5: Fitting the hierarchical softmax model to 200 simulated claims (true precision 0.3, level 2). Left: log-likelihood of one dataset over precision and level (darker is higher; the true values are circled). Right: three (precision, level) pairs predict almost the same claims.





Across 30 simulated datasets of 200 claims each, maximum likelihood recovered the true level in only 9 of 30. The fits spread along a ridge: a low precision at a high level predicts nearly the same claims as a high precision at level 1. The mean claims of the three pairs on the right are $90.9, $91.2 and $91.1. To separate depth of reasoning from precision, you need data from several different games.


Fictitious play and gradient ascent








Figure 6: Learning by play. Left: fictitious play in rock-paper-scissors (identical starting counts): each action’s running frequency. Middle: fictitious play at the intersection with identical starting counts: the running frequency of going and the running average reward. Right: gradient ascent (step 0.1/√t) in rock-paper-scissors from three random starts, plotted as P(rock) against P(paper) over 2000 rounds.






Fictitious play finds the mixed equilibrium of rock-paper-scissors in frequency. After 2000 rounds from equal counts, the frequencies are within 0.008 of a third; from 100 random starting counts, the median largest gap was 0.014. The actions themselves cycle in ever-longer runs.
Converging frequencies aren’t converging play. At the intersection, two drivers with identical counts make identical choices every round. Their frequency of going approaches 0.285 (the mixed equilibrium’s 2/7), but every round is a near-crash or a double wait: −3.57 per round, against −0.714 for independent mixing. With random starting counts, 99 of 100 runs settled into a pure equilibrium, one driver always going.
Gradient ascent keeps circling in rock-paper-scissors. After 2000 rounds, the three runs still had regret 0.32, 0.56, 0.38: the policies drift around the uniform equilibrium rather than settling at it. At the intersection, all 20 of 20 runs reached a pure equilibrium.

title: 24 · Multiagent Reasoning
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: dominance. In a game, agent 1 chooses up or down, agent 2 left or right. Agent 1’s rewards are (up, left) 4, (up, right) 1, (down, left) 3, (down, right) 0. Agent 2’s are 2, 3, 1, 5 in the same order. Does either agent have a dominant strategy? What will they play?






TipSolution





Agent 1: up beats down against both (4 > 3 and 1 > 0), so up is dominant. Agent 2: against up it prefers right (3 > 2), and against down also right (5 > 1), so right is dominant too. Both play their dominant strategies: (up, right), with rewards (1, 3). Check that it is a Nash equilibrium: agent 1 would get 0 by switching, agent 2 would get 2.



Problem 2: a mixed equilibrium. A penalty kicker aims left or right; the goalkeeper dives left or right. The kicker scores with probability 0.9 if the keeper dives the wrong way, 0.4 if the keeper guesses right (either side). Rewards are the scoring probability for the kicker and its negative for the keeper. Find the equilibrium.






TipSolution





Let the keeper dive left with probability \(p\). Kicking left scores \(0.4p + 0.9(1 - p)\), kicking right \(0.9p + 0.4(1 - p)\). Indifference gives \(p = 1/2\). By symmetry the kicker also aims left half the time. The kicker scores \(0.65\) on average. No pure equilibrium exists: any predictable choice is exploited.



Problem 3: check a correlated equilibrium. At the intersection, a light shows (go, stop) with probability 0.4, (stop, go) 0.4 and (stop, stop) 0.2. Is it a correlated equilibrium, and what does each driver earn?






TipSolution





Driver 1 told “go” (probability 0.4, always facing “stop”): obey 3, deviate −1. Fine. Told “stop” (probability 0.6: driver 2 goes with probability \(0.4/0.6\), stops with \(0.2/0.6\)): obeying earns \(\tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 0 + \tfrac{1}{3}(-1) = -\tfrac13\); going earns \(\tfrac23(-10) + \tfrac13 \cdot 3 = -\tfrac{17}{3}\). Obey. By symmetry it is a correlated equilibrium. Each earns \(0.4 \cdot 3 + 0.4 \cdot 0 + 0.2 \cdot (-1) = 1.0\): worse than the traffic light (1.5), because it sometimes wastes a round.



Problem 4: fictitious play by hand. Two agents play the prisoner’s dilemma with fictitious play, counts starting at 1. What do they play in the first three rounds, and why does fictitious play settle immediately here?






TipSolution





With counts (1, 1), each models the other as 50/50 and computes cooperate: \(0.5(-1) + 0.5(-4) = -2.5\); defect: \(0.5 \cdot 0 + 0.5(-3) = -1.5\). Both defect. The counts become (1, 2), so each thinks the other defects 2/3 of the time, and defecting is still better; it always will be, since defecting is dominant: it’s best against any belief. Fictitious play reaches the dominant strategy equilibrium in round 1 and stays.



Problem 5: how long does unraveling take? In the traveler’s dilemma, if both travelers start at $100 and best-respond to each other each round, when do they reach $2?






TipSolution





Against a claim of \(c > 2\), claiming \(c - 1\) earns \(c + 1\), the most possible: claiming \(c\) earns \(c\), and claiming lower earns at most \(c\). So both claim $99 in round 1, $98 in round 2, …, $2 in round 98. Against $2, the best response is $2 (claiming $2 earns $2, anything higher earns $0). The page’s run started from uniform play, whose best response is $96, so it took 95 rounds.

title: 24 · Multiagent Reasoning
text:
Recap

With several agents, “optimal” becomes “equilibrium” (Equation 2, Equation 4). Why it matters: every later chapter in Part V asks the same question, in richer settings: which joint policies leave no agent wanting to deviate?
Nash equilibria always exist, but may be random, multiple, inefficient and hard to compute (Equation 4). Why it matters: the prisoner’s dilemma and the intersection show that self-interested best responses can leave everyone worse off; numerical solvers can stop at approximate equilibria.
Correlated equilibria coordinate through a shared signal, and are computed by a linear program (Equation 5). Why it matters: the traffic light earns each driver 1.5, against −0.71 for the mixed Nash equilibrium; mediated coordination is often both fairer and more efficient.
Learning dynamics can reach equilibria, but can also cycle or miscoordinate (Equation 6). Why it matters: agents that learn from play are the multiagent version of reinforcement learning (Chapter 25’s Nash Q-learning builds on this), and convergence is the exception rather than the rule.
Behavioral models predict people better than equilibria do (Equation 3). Why it matters: systems that interact with humans need a predictive model of them. But depth of reasoning and precision trade off, so one game’s data can’t separate them.

title: 24 · Multiagent Reasoning
text:
Cheat sheet & connections



Table 4: Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name).










Name
Formula
Ref




Utility
\(U^i(\boldsymbol{\pi}) = \sum_{\boldsymbol{a}} R^i(\boldsymbol{a}) \prod_j \pi^j(a^j)\)
Equation 1


Best response
\(\arg\max_{a^i} U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i})\)
Equation 2


Softmax response
\(\pi^i(a^i) \propto \exp(\lambda U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}))\)
Equation 3


★ Nash equilibrium
\(U^i(\boldsymbol{\pi}) \ge U^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i})\) for all \(i, a^i\)
Equation 4


★ Correlated equilibrium
\(\sum_{\boldsymbol{a}^{-i}} [R^i(a^i, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i}) - R^i(a^{i\prime}, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i})]\,\pi(a^i, \boldsymbol{a}^{-i}) \ge 0\)
Equation 5


Fictitious play
best-respond to \(\hat{\pi}^j \propto N(j, \cdot)\)
Equation 6






Common pitfalls

Expecting one right answer. Games can have several equilibria; say which one, and why (an objective, a convention, a learning rule).
Trusting a solver’s “equilibrium”. Check the regret, and remember that a small regret doesn’t mean the policies are near an exact equilibrium.
Confusing frequency convergence with policy convergence. Fictitious play’s frequencies can match an equilibrium while the actual play is disastrous.
Treating people as Nash players. In the traveler’s dilemma the equilibrium predicts $2; people claim near $100.
Over-interpreting fitted behavioral parameters. Level and precision are hard to separate from one game’s data.

Connections

Ch 6 · Simple Decisions: the single-agent version (maximize expected utility), and bounded rationality.
Ch 15 · Exploration and Exploitation: softmax action selection.
Ch 16 · Model-Based Methods: maximum likelihood models, used by fictitious play.
Ch 23 · Controller Abstractions: projection onto the simplex, used by gradient ascent.
Ch 25 · Sequential Problems: games with states: Markov games and Nash Q-learning.
Appendix C · Computational Complexity: computing a Nash equilibrium is PPAD-complete, which is why this page searches numerically on small games.

title: 26 · State Uncertainty
text:
Big picture

Where this chapter fits
Chapter 25’s agents all saw the state. Here each agent sees only its own observations, as in a POMDP (Chapter 19–23), while the others act on theirs. The result, a partially observable Markov game (POMG), is the most general model in the book: an MDP, a POMDP, a simple game and a Markov game are all special cases. Chapter 27 specializes it to agents that share one reward.
The question: how do we evaluate and find equilibrium policies when no agent sees the state, and no agent sees what the others see or do?
The short answer: give up on beliefs, and work with whole policies (conditional plans or controllers) as the objects that agents choose between.

A single agent can’t keep a useful belief: the state depends on the others’ actions, which depend on their observations.
Evaluation of a joint policy is still exact: a recursion over conditional plans, or a linear solve for controllers.
A POMG with \(h\)-step plans is a simple game whose actions are plans: its Nash equilibria are the POMG’s.
Dynamic programming grows plans one step at a time and prunes plans that are never a best response, which keeps the game small.

Figure 1: Map of this chapter. With partial observability, agents choose among whole policies (conditional plans or controllers). Evaluating joint policies turns the POMG into a simple game over plans, whose equilibria are found as in Chapter 24; dynamic programming prunes plans to keep that game small.







The key ideas at a glance

A POMG has a hidden state \(s\), joint actions \(\boldsymbol{a}\), transitions \(T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a})\), a joint observation \(\boldsymbol{o} = (o^1, \dots, o^k)\) drawn with probability \(O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{a}, s')\), and a reward \(R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})\) per agent. Agent \(i\) sees only \(o^i\).
No beliefs. In a POMDP the agent updates a belief using its own action and observation. In a POMG the state also depends on the others’ actions, which depend on observations it never sees. So policies are written as conditional plans (a tree of actions, branching on one’s own observations) or controllers (a graph of nodes), as in Chapters 20 and 23.
Joint evaluation is exact: follow every agent’s plan together through every state and joint observation (a recursion), or solve linear equations over (joint node, state) pairs for controllers.
Equilibria via a game of plans. Treat each agent’s \(h\)-step plans as its actions and the joint plans’ utilities as rewards: a simple game. Its Nash equilibria are the POMG’s \(h\)-step equilibria. But the number of plans grows doubly exponentially with \(h\).
Prune what’s never a best response. Build plans one step at a time, and after each step drop any plan that isn’t a best response for any distribution over the other agent’s plans and the state (a linear program). Equilibria survive; the game stays small.



Vocabulary



Table 1: Terms used on this page.









Term
Plain meaning




POMG (partially observable stochastic game)
A Markov game where each agent sees only its own observations


Joint observation \(\boldsymbol{o}\)
Everyone’s observations together; agent \(i\) receives \(o^i\)


Conditional plan
A tree: an action, then a subplan for each of one’s own observations


Controller
A finite graph of nodes with actions and observation-labeled edges


Game over plans
A simple game whose actions are whole conditional plans


Dominated plan
A plan that is never a best response, whatever the others do and whatever the state


Volunteer’s dilemma
Everyone wants the job done but would rather someone else did it








After this chapter you can

Write down a POMG, and explain why an agent can’t simply keep a belief.
Evaluate joint conditional plans by recursion and joint controllers by a linear solve.
Turn \(h\)-step plans into a simple game, and find its equilibria.
Prune dominated plans with a linear program, and explain why pruning keeps every equilibrium.
Recognize coordination problems (who acts?) that partial observability makes harder.

title: 26 · State Uncertainty
text:
Intuition






TipAnalogy



Two parents share night duty with a baby. Neither sees whether the baby is hungry; both hear it cry, but neither knows whether the other has already got up to feed it. Feeding costs parent 1 less effort than parent 2. The best rule for each depends on the other’s rule, and each rule is a plan: “if I hear crying, get up; otherwise sleep”.


We use the multicaregiver crying baby (Appendix F.14; problem gallery). A baby is sated or hungry; each of two caregivers can feed, sing or ignore it each hour. Either one feeding sates the baby; otherwise a sated baby turns hungry half the time. Both hear the same thing: a hungry baby cries 90% of the time, a sated one never. Both pay 10 per hour of hunger; feeding costs caregiver 1 an extra 2.5 and caregiver 2 an extra 5; singing costs 0.5 and 0.25. Both start believing the baby is hungry with probability 0.5.

One hour: nobody feeds
With one hour to go, feeding can’t help: this hour’s hunger cost is already set, and there’s no next hour. So both ignore, each paying the expected hunger cost of 5. Planning ahead is what makes feeding worthwhile.


Plans are the actions
With two hours, each caregiver has 27 two-step plans: a first action, then an action for each thing they might hear. Every pair of plans has a value for each caregiver, so the whole problem becomes a 27 × 27 simple game. Its pure Nash equilibria (there are 18, many of them differing only on branches that can’t happen) give one of two outcomes: caregiver 1 feeds first (payoffs −7.5, −5) or caregiver 2 does (−5, −10). It’s a volunteer’s dilemma: each would rather the other get up. See Equation 1.


Throw away what’s never best
Plans grow fast: 2,187 three-step plans per caregiver, and 14,348,907 four-step ones. But most are never a best response. At the last step, feeding and singing only cost effort, so only “ignore” survives. Growing plans one step at a time and pruning at each step left 4 three-step and 32 four-step plans per caregiver. See Equation 3.


Controllers run forever
With no deadline, a caregiver can follow a small controller. If caregiver 2 never feeds, caregiver 1’s best 2-node controller feeds every hour (worth −30.0): the baby turns hungry half the time, and an hour of hunger (10) costs more than a feed (2.5). Feeding only after crying is worth −47.6. Against that, caregiver 2’s best response is to never feed, which earns −5.0: the cost of the first hour’s hunger, and nothing after. See Equation 2.

title: 26 · State Uncertainty
text:
Formalism

Partially observable Markov games
A POMG (ADM §26.1; E. A. Hansen, D. S. Bernstein and S. Zilberstein, AAAI, 2004) has agents \(\mathcal{I}\), states \(\mathcal{S}\) with initial distribution \(b\), joint actions \(\boldsymbol{a}\), transitions \(T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a})\), joint observations \(\boldsymbol{o} \in \mathcal{O}^1 \times \dots \times \mathcal{O}^k\) with probability \(O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{a}, s')\), and rewards \(R^i(s, \boldsymbol{a})\). After acting, agent \(i\) receives only \(o^i\).
It generalizes everything before it: one agent gives a POMDP; observations that reveal the state give a Markov game; a single state gives a repeated simple game. An agent can’t maintain a belief, because updating it would need the other agents’ actions and observations, which depend on what those agents believe, and so on. So policies are conditional plans or controllers.


Evaluating joint conditional plans
Let \(\boldsymbol{\pi} = (\pi^1, \dots, \pi^k)\) be conditional plans, with root actions \(\boldsymbol{\pi}()\) and subplans \(\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{o}) = (\pi^1(o^1), \dots, \pi^k(o^k))\). Their joint utility from state \(s\) is (ADM eqs. 26.1–26.2)

\[
U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s) = R\big(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}()\big) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T\big(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{\pi}()\big) \sum_{\boldsymbol{o}} O\big(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{\pi}(), s'\big)\, U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{o})}(s')
\tag{1}\]

and from the initial distribution, \(U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(b) = \sum_s b(s)\, U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(s)\).
In words. Take everyone’s first action, collect the reward, then for each next state and joint observation, let each agent follow the branch for its own observation.
Term by term.

\(R(s, \boldsymbol{\pi}())\) is the vector of every agent’s reward for the joint root action.
\(\boldsymbol{\pi}(\boldsymbol{o})\): each agent moves down its own tree using only its own \(o^i\). The sum over joint observations accounts for what the others see.
A plan with no subplans ends: its value is just the reward.
The recursion visits every joint path through the trees: \((|\mathcal{S}||\mathcal{O}|)^h\) paths for \(h\) steps.

Why it holds. It is Chapter 20’s plan evaluation (eq. 20.8), with joint actions and joint observations: given the state and everyone’s plan, the future is fully determined in distribution.


Evaluating joint controllers
For controllers with action distributions \(\psi^i(a^i \mid x^i)\) and successor distributions \(\eta^i(x^{i\prime} \mid x^i, a^i, o^i)\), the value of joint node \(\boldsymbol{x}\) in state \(s\) is (ADM eq. 26.3)

\[
\begin{aligned}
U(\boldsymbol{x}, s) = \sum_{\boldsymbol{a}} \prod_i \psi^i(a^i \mid x^i) \Big[ R(s, \boldsymbol{a})
&+ \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, \boldsymbol{a}) \sum_{\boldsymbol{o}} O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{a}, s') \\
&\times \sum_{\boldsymbol{x}'} \prod_i \eta^i(x^{i\prime} \mid x^i, a^i, o^i)\, U(\boldsymbol{x}', s') \Big]
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]

In words. Chapter 23’s controller evaluation, with everyone’s nodes moving together.
Term by term.

The products over \(i\) say that agents choose actions and move nodes independently, each on its own observation.
There are \(|\mathcal{S}| \prod_i |X^i|\) unknowns: \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\) for two 2-node controllers here.
\(U(\boldsymbol{x}, b) = \sum_s b(s) U(\boldsymbol{x}, s)\) gives the value from the initial distribution.

Why it holds. The joint node and the state together form a Markov chain, as in Chapter 23, so this is its Bellman expectation equation: one linear solve.


Nash equilibria as a game over plans
Build a simple game (ADM §26.3) whose actions for agent \(i\) are its \(h\)-step plans \(\Pi^i\) and whose rewards are \(U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(b)\) from Equation 1. A Nash equilibrium of this game, in pure or mixed plans, is an \(h\)-step Nash equilibrium of the POMG. The catch is size: with \(|\mathcal{A}|\) actions and \(|\mathcal{O}|\) observations, \(|\Pi_h| = |\mathcal{A}|\,|\Pi_{h-1}|^{|\mathcal{O}|}\). For the caregivers that is 3, 27, 2,187 and 14,348,907 plans for \(h = 1, \dots, 4\).


Dynamic programming with pruning
Grow plans one step at a time (ADM §26.4): the \(h\)-step plans are a first action followed by surviving \((h-1)\)-step plans. After each step, drop any plan that is never a best response. Plan \(\pi^i\) survives only if some distribution \(b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s)\) over the other agents’ plans and the state makes it at least as good as every alternative:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\max_{\delta,\, b \ge 0}\ \ & \delta \\
\text{s.t.}\ \ & \textstyle\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s} b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s) = 1 \\
& \textstyle\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s} b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s)\big(U^{\pi^i, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, i}(s) - U^{\pi^{i\prime}, \boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, i}(s)\big) \ge \delta \ \ \text{for all } \pi^{i\prime}
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]

In words. Look for a situation, meaning a mix of what the others might do and what the state might be, in which this plan is at least as good as every other. If there’s none (the best \(\delta\) is negative), prune it.
Term by term.

\(b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s)\): a distribution over the others’ plans and the state, playing the role of a belief. No agent computes it; the LP searches over all of them.
\(\delta\): the plan’s smallest margin over the alternatives, under \(b\). Maximizing it finds the most favorable situation.
It’s Chapter 20’s alpha-vector pruning LP (eq. 20.16), with “state” replaced by “state and the others’ plan”.

Why it holds. A plan that is never a best response can’t be used in any Nash equilibrium: an agent would switch away from it whatever the others do. Removing it never removes an equilibrium, and every equilibrium of the pruned game is one of the full game. Pruning is repeated over agents until nothing changes, since removing one agent’s plans can make more of the other’s prunable.

title: 26 · State Uncertainty
text:
Worked example

Two hours with the baby
Take caregiver 1’s plan “feed now; then ignore whatever you hear” and caregiver 2’s plan “ignore twice”. Starting 50–50:

Hour 1. Caregiver 1 pays 2.5 for feeding; both pay 10 if the baby is hungry now (probability 0.5). Rewards: caregiver 1 \(-2.5 - 5 = -7.5\), caregiver 2 \(-5\).
Hour 2. The feed sated the baby, so it can’t be hungry and never cries; both ignore, paying nothing.

So the plan pair is worth \((-7.5, -5)\). Can caregiver 1 do better alone? Ignoring twice would leave the baby hungry in hour 2 with probability \(0.5 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75\), costing \(-5 + 0.9 \times 0.75 \times (-10) = -11.75\). Any plan that feeds in hour 2 only adds cost, since the game ends after hour 2 and feeding then helps no one. And caregiver 2 is paying nothing extra, so it can’t gain either. It’s an equilibrium, one of the two outcomes found by brute force above.
The code: (−7.500, −5.000) for the pair, and −11.750 for caregiver 1 if it ignores twice instead.


Is “sing, then ignore” ever worth it?
For caregiver 1 at the last step, compare singing, feeding and ignoring for any belief over the state and the other’s plan: singing costs 0.5 and feeding 2.5 more than ignoring, and none changes the reward of this hour. So in Equation 3, \(\delta\) for “sing” is at most \(-0.5\) whatever \(b\) is. Pruned. That’s why the one-step plans shrink from 3 to 1 for each caregiver.

title: 26 · State Uncertainty
26 · State Uncertainty
text:
Algorithms & code

Plans, evaluation, pruning and controllers

PythonJulia


def all_plans(n_actions, n_obs, horizon) -> list:
    """Every conditional plan of the given horizon: an action, then a
    (horizon - 1)-step plan for each observation."""
    plans = [(a,) for a in range(n_actions)]
    for _ in range(horizon - 1):
        plans = expand(plans, n_actions, n_obs)
    return plans

def expand(plans, n_actions, n_obs) -> list:
    """All plans one step longer: any first action, then any plan from
    `plans` after each observation (|A| |plans|^|O| of them)."""
    return [(a, subs) for a in range(n_actions)
            for subs in product(plans, repeat=n_obs)]

def plan_evaluator(game):
    """Returns U(p1, p2, s): both agents' utilities when they follow plans
    p1 and p2 from state s (eq. 26.1), cached across calls."""
    nS = game.T.shape[0]

    @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
    def U(p1, p2, s) -> tuple:
        a1, a2 = p1[0], p2[0]
        r = game.R[:, s, a1, a2].copy()
        if len(p1) == 1:                   # last step: reward only
            return tuple(r)
        n1, n2 = game.O.shape[3:]
        for s2 in range(nS):
            p = game.T[s, a1, a2, s2]
            if p == 0:
                continue
            for o1 in range(n1):
                for o2 in range(n2):
                    q = game.O[a1, a2, s2, o1, o2]
                    if q > 0:              # each agent follows its own branch
                        sub = U(p1[1][o1], p2[1][o2], s2)
                        r += game.gamma * p * q * np.array(sub)
        return tuple(r)

    return U

def utility(U, b, p1, p2) -> Array:
    """eq. 26.2: both agents' utilities from the state distribution b."""
    return sum(b[s] * np.array(U(p1, p2, s)) for s in range(len(b)))

def plan_game(game, b, plans1, plans2, U=None) -> SimpleGame:
    """§26.3: the simple game whose actions are whole conditional plans and
    whose rewards are their utilities from b."""
    U = plan_evaluator(game) if U is None else U
    R = np.zeros((2, len(plans1), len(plans2)))
    for k1, p1 in enumerate(plans1):
        for k2, p2 in enumerate(plans2):
            R[:, k1, k2] = utility(U, b, p1, p2)
    labels = (tuple(map(str, plans1)), tuple(map(str, plans2)))
    return SimpleGame(R, labels)

def pure_equilibria(g) -> list:
    """Every pure Nash equilibrium of a two-player simple game: each row
    is a best response to its column and vice versa (ties allowed)."""
    A, B = g.R
    best1 = A >= A.max(axis=0, keepdims=True) - 1e-9   # agent 1 can't gain
    best2 = B >= B.max(axis=1, keepdims=True) - 1e-9   # agent 2 can't gain
    return [tuple(map(int, k)) for k in np.argwhere(best1 & best2)]

def is_dominated(game, plans, i, k, U) -> bool:
    """eq. 26.6: is agent i's plan plans[i][k] dominated? Look for a
    distribution over (the other's plan, state) under which plan k beats
    every alternative by delta; if the best delta is negative, no such
    distribution exists, and the plan can go."""
    mine, theirs = plans[i], plans[1 - i]
    nS = game.T.shape[0]

    def u(pi, pj, s):                      # agent i's value, either role
        return U(pi, pj, s)[0] if i == 0 else U(pj, pi, s)[1]

    # Variables: b over (other plan, state) pairs, then delta.
    pairs = [(pj, s) for pj in theirs for s in range(nS)]
    n = len(pairs)
    rows = []
    for alt in mine:
        if alt == mine[k]:
            continue
        # delta - sum_b b (u(k) - u(alt)) <= 0
        diff = [u(mine[k], pj, s) - u(alt, pj, s) for pj, s in pairs]
        rows.append(np.concatenate([-np.array(diff), [1.0]]))
    if not rows:
        return False
    res = linprog(np.concatenate([np.zeros(n), [-1.0]]),     # maximize delta
                  A_ub=np.array(rows), b_ub=np.zeros(len(rows)),
                  A_eq=np.concatenate([np.ones(n), [0.0]])[None, :],
                  b_eq=[1.0], bounds=[(0, None)] * n + [(None, None)],
                  method="highs")
    return -res.fun < -1e-9                # the best delta is negative

def prune_dominated(game, plans, U, rng) -> list:
    """Remove dominated plans, agent by agent in random order, until a
    full pass removes nothing (§26.4)."""
    plans = [list(p) for p in plans]
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for i in rng.permutation(2):
            for k in rng.permutation(len(plans[i])):
                if len(plans[i]) > 1 and is_dominated(game, plans, i, k, U):
                    del plans[i][k]
                    changed = True
                    break
    return plans

def dynamic_programming(game, horizon, rng, U=None):
    """Algorithm 26.4's loop: start from one-step plans; expand and prune,
    horizon - 1 times. Returns the surviving plans and, for each horizon,
    how many plans each agent had before and after pruning."""
    U = plan_evaluator(game) if U is None else U
    nA = game.T.shape[1:3]
    nO = game.O.shape[3:]
    plans = [[(a,) for a in range(nA[i])] for i in range(2)]
    plans = prune_dominated(game, plans, U, rng)
    counts = [(tuple(nA), tuple(map(len, plans)))]
    for _ in range(horizon - 1):
        grown = [expand(plans[i], nA[i], nO[i]) for i in range(2)]
        plans = prune_dominated(game, grown, U, rng)
        counts.append((tuple(map(len, grown)), tuple(map(len, plans))))
    return plans, counts

def evaluate_controllers(game, c1, c2) -> Array:
    """eq. 26.3 by one linear solve. Each controller is (psi, eta) with
    psi[x, a] and eta[x, a, o, x2], as in Ch. 23. Returns
    U[x1, x2, s]: the joint value of each pair of nodes in each state."""
    (psi1, eta1), (psi2, eta2) = c1, c2
    n1, n2, nS = len(psi1), len(psi2), game.T.shape[0]
    idx = lambda x1, x2, s: (x1 * n2 + x2) * nS + s     # flatten (x1, x2, s)
    m = n1 * n2 * nS
    M, r = np.eye(m), np.zeros((2, m))
    for x1, x2, s in product(range(n1), range(n2), range(nS)):
        i = idx(x1, x2, s)
        for a1, a2 in product(range(psi1.shape[1]), range(psi2.shape[1])):
            w = psi1[x1, a1] * psi2[x2, a2]    # both act independently
            if w == 0:
                continue
            r[:, i] += w * game.R[:, s, a1, a2]
            for s2, o1, o2 in product(range(nS), *map(range, game.O.shape[3:])):
                p = w * game.T[s, a1, a2, s2] * game.O[a1, a2, s2, o1, o2]
                if p == 0:
                    continue
                # Each agent moves its own node on its own observation.
                nxt = np.outer(eta1[x1, a1, o1], eta2[x2, a2, o2])
                for y1, y2 in zip(*np.nonzero(nxt)):
                    M[i, idx(y1, y2, s2)] -= game.gamma * p * nxt[y1, y2]
    U = np.linalg.solve(M, r.T).T
    return U.reshape(2, n1, n2, nS)


using ADM

g = multicaregiver()          # T[s, a1, a2, s′], O[a1, a2, s′, o1, o2], R[i, s, a1, a2]
b = [0.5, 0.5]

# A plan is (a,) at the last step, or (a, (plan after crying, plan after quiet)).
function plans(h)
    h == 1 && return [(a,) for a in 1:3]
    return [(a, (p, q)) for a in 1:3 for p in plans(h - 1) for q in plans(h - 1)]
end

# eq. 26.1: both agents' utilities when following plans p1 and p2 from state s.
function evaluate(g, p1, p2, s)
    a1, a2 = p1[1], p2[1]
    u = g.R[:, s, a1, a2]
    length(p1) == 1 && return u
    for s′ in 1:2, o1 in 1:2, o2 in 1:2
        w = g.T[s, a1, a2, s′] * g.O[a1, a2, s′, o1, o2]
        # Each agent takes the branch for its own observation.
        w > 0 && (u = u .+ g.γ * w .* evaluate(g, p1[2][o1], p2[2][o2], s′))
    end
    return u
end
utility(g, p1, p2) = sum(b[s] * evaluate(g, p1, p2, s) for s in 1:2)

# The two-step game over plans, and its pure Nash equilibria by brute force.
Π = plans(2)
Ugame = [utility(g, p1, p2) for p1 in Π, p2 in Π]     # Ugame[k1, k2] = [u1, u2]
isnash(k1, k2) = all(Ugame[j, k2][1] <= Ugame[k1, k2][1] + 1e-9 for j in eachindex(Π)) &&
                 all(Ugame[k1, j][2] <= Ugame[k1, k2][2] + 1e-9 for j in eachindex(Π))
payoffs = unique([round.(Ugame[k1, k2]; digits = 4) for k1 in eachindex(Π), k2 in eachindex(Π)
                  if isnash(k1, k2)])
println(length(Π), " plans each; equilibrium payoffs: ", payoffs)
@assert sort(payoffs) == [[-7.5, -5.0], [-5.0, -10.0]]









NoteReading the Python code






Plans as nested tuples. (0, ((2,), (2,))) means “feed, then ignore after crying, ignore after quiet”. Tuples are hashable, so functools.lru_cache can remember each (plan, plan, state) value and reuse it whenever the same subplans meet again.
product(plans, repeat=n_obs) gives every way to assign a subplan to each observation.
The pruning LP puts \(\delta\) last among the variables; linprog minimizes, so the objective is \(-\delta\), and the “at least \(\delta\)” constraints are rewritten as \(\delta - (\dots) \le 0\).
evaluate_controllers flattens (node 1, node 2, state) into one index and fills the matrix \(I - \gamma T\) entry by entry.






Run them

game = multicaregiver()
plans, counts = P.dynamic_programming(game, 3, np.random.default_rng(0))
for h, (grown, kept) in enumerate(counts, start=1):
    print(f"horizon {h}: {grown} candidate plans, {kept} kept")

horizon 1: (3, 3) candidate plans, (1, 1) kept
horizon 2: (3, 3) candidate plans, (2, 2) kept
horizon 3: (12, 12) candidate plans, (4, 4) kept




Results

How many plans survive








Figure 3: Plans per caregiver by horizon: all conditional plans (gray), the candidates dynamic programming builds from the previous step’s survivors (light blue), and those that survive pruning (blue). Log scale.





Pruning at each step keeps the candidate sets tiny: 48 four-step candidates instead of 14,348,907, and 32 of those survive. The last step is where most of the pruning happens: at the final hour only “ignore” is worth considering.


The volunteer’s dilemma








Figure 4: Every pair of surviving plans, plotted by the two caregivers’ expected rewards (gray), with pure Nash equilibria (black) and, for three steps, the mixed equilibria (orange). Left: three steps. Right: four steps.






Three steps. The pure equilibria are (−9.75, −5.00) and (−7.25, −10.00): one caregiver does the feeding, the other free-rides. The mixed equilibria, where each sometimes feeds, are worth (−9.75, −10.00): no better than the worse pure outcome for either caregiver.
Four steps. Four kinds of pure equilibrium appear: (−11.78, −5.00); (−9.53, −9.50); (−9.28, −10.00); (−7.03, −14.50). Besides the lopsided ones, one splits the cost almost evenly between the two caregivers.
Pruning kept the equilibria. For two steps, the full 27 × 27 game and the pruned one have exactly the same equilibrium payoffs.



Controllers: who gets up?








Figure 5: Infinite-horizon values (from the 50–50 start) of five pairs of 2-node controllers for the caregivers.






Somebody has to feed. If nobody does, each pays −90.9: the baby ends up hungry forever.
Feeding on crying is a poor rule here. A sated baby turns hungry half the time, so waiting for a cry lets hunger (10 per hour) pile up while a feed costs caregiver 1 only 2.5. Caregiver 1 does better feeding every hour: −30.0 instead of −47.6. Brute force over all 144 deterministic 2-node controllers confirms that “always feed” is caregiver 1’s best response to an idle partner.
Free-riding is the other’s best response. Against a caregiver who always feeds, caregiver 2’s best controller never feeds and earns −5.0. So (always feed, never feed) is an equilibrium among 2-node controllers, and a lopsided one.

title: 26 · State Uncertainty
text:
Solved problems
Problem 1: special cases. Show that a POMDP and a Markov game are both POMGs.






TipSolution





A POMDP is a POMG with one agent: its observations are the joint observations. A Markov game is a POMG whose observations reveal the state: \(\mathcal{O}^i = \mathcal{S}\) and \(O(\boldsymbol{o} \mid \boldsymbol{a}, s') = 1\) when every \(o^i = s'\). With both, and one agent, it’s an MDP.



Problem 2: counting plans. Each of two agents has 2 actions and 3 observations. How many 1-, 2- and 3-step conditional plans does each have? How many joint plans at 3 steps?






TipSolution





\(|\Pi_1| = 2\); \(|\Pi_2| = 2 \times 2^3 = 16\); \(|\Pi_3| = 2 \times 16^3 = 8192\). Joint plans at 3 steps: \(8192^2 \approx 6.7 \times 10^7\), each needing an evaluation over every state and joint observation path. That is why pruning is essential.



Problem 3: evaluate a joint plan. For the caregivers, starting 50–50: caregiver 1 ignores then ignores; caregiver 2 ignores then ignores. What does each earn over two hours?






TipSolution





Hour 1: both pay 10 with probability 0.5: \(-5\) each. With nobody feeding, the baby is hungry in hour 2 with probability \(0.5 \times 1 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75\), costing \(0.9 \times 0.75 \times 10 = 6.75\). Each earns \(-11.75\). Either caregiver could improve by feeding in hour 1, which makes this plan pair not an equilibrium.



Problem 4: prune by hand. At the last step, caregiver 2’s options are feed (extra −5), sing (−0.25) and ignore (0), and none affects this step’s hunger cost. Write the pruning LP for “sing”, and solve it.






TipSolution





For any distribution \(b\) over caregiver 1’s plan and the state, “sing” minus “ignore” is \(-0.25\) exactly (hunger costs cancel). The constraint against “ignore” is \(-0.25 \ge \delta\), so \(\delta \le -0.25 < 0\): “sing” is dominated and pruned. “Feed” is pruned the same way, with \(\delta \le -5\).



Problem 5: why can’t caregiver 1 keep a belief? Caregiver 1 hears “quiet” after ignoring. Why can’t it update \(P(\text{hungry})\) with the Chapter 19 filter?






TipSolution





The filter needs the transition model for the action taken, and here the transition depends on the joint action: if caregiver 2 fed, the baby is certainly sated. Caregiver 1 doesn’t see whether caregiver 2 fed. It could average over caregiver 2’s policy, but that policy depends on what caregiver 2 heard and believes, which depends on caregiver 1’s policy, and so on. Committing to whole plans or controllers sidesteps the regress: every agent’s behavior is fixed in advance, and evaluation averages over everything.

title: 26 · State Uncertainty
text:
Recap

A POMG is the most general model in the book (Equation 1). Why it matters: MDPs, POMDPs, simple games and Markov games are all special cases; the difficulty comes from each agent seeing only part of the picture.
Without shared information, agents choose whole policies instead of acting on beliefs. Why it matters: conditional plans and controllers (Chapters 20, 23) become the objects of the game, and their evaluation stays exact.
A POMG over \(h\)-step plans is a simple game over plans. Why it matters: Chapter 24’s equilibrium methods apply directly, but the number of plans explodes: 14,348,907 four-step plans per caregiver.
Pruning never-best plans keeps the game small without losing equilibria (Equation 3). Why it matters: for the caregivers, 32 plans survive at four steps; the same idea drives Chapter 27’s methods for cooperative teams.
Coordination is the hard part. Why it matters: the caregivers’ equilibria are all “one works, the other free-rides” or worse; partial observability makes it harder to share the work, which is what shared rewards (Chapter 27) change.

text:
Cheat sheet & connections

Name

Equation 1


Joint controller evaluation
\(U(\boldsymbol{x}, s) = \sum_{\boldsymbol{a}} \prod_i \psi^i [R + \gamma \sum T \sum O \sum_{\boldsymbol{x}'} \prod_i \eta^i\, U(\boldsymbol{x}', s')]\)
Equation 2

actions \(\Pi^i_h\), rewards \(U^{\boldsymbol{\pi}, i}(b)\)
§26.3


Pruning LP
\(\max \delta\): some \(b(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{-i}, s)\) makes \(\pi^i\) beat every alternative by \(\delta\)
Equation 3






Common pitfalls

Letting an agent use information it doesn’t have. Plans branch only on the agent’s own observations, never on the others’ or on the state.
Enumerating plans naively. Their number is doubly exponential in the horizon; grow and prune instead.
Counting equivalent plans as different equilibria. Plans that differ only on impossible branches earn the same; the page reports distinct payoffs.
Forgetting that pruning must repeat. Removing one agent’s plans can make more of the other’s prunable.

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Executed in: Python · Book: ADM Appendix A
This appendix collects the mathematics used across the site, each idea with a small computed example and a pointer to where it is used. It follows the topics of ADM Appendix A.

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Spaces: measuring size and distance
A probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{E}, P)\) has a set of outcomes \(\Omega\), a collection \(\mathcal{E}\) of events (subsets of \(\Omega\) we can assign probabilities to), and a probability measure \(P\) with \(P(\Omega) = 1\) that adds up over disjoint events (ADM §A.1–A.2). A metric \(d(x, y)\) measures distance: it is zero only when \(x = y\), symmetric, and obeys the triangle inequality (§A.3). On vectors, distances usually come from a norm:

\[
\|\mathbf{x}\|_p = \Big(\sum_i |x_i|^p\Big)^{1/p}, \qquad \|\mathbf{x}\|_\infty = \max_i |x_i|
\tag{1}\]

In words. A norm measures a vector’s size; \(p\) decides how much the largest component dominates.
Term by term.

\(p = 1\): the sum of absolute values (“taxicab” length); \(p = 2\): the ordinary Euclidean length; \(p = \infty\): the largest component only.
The distance between two vectors is the norm of their difference, \(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|_p\).
Example: \(\mathbf{x} = (3, -4)\) has norms 7, 5 and 4 for \(p = 1, 2, \infty\).

Why it holds. Each is a norm: zero only for the zero vector, scales with \(|c|\) when the vector is multiplied by \(c\), and satisfies the triangle inequality (Minkowski’s inequality). The max norm is the limit of \(\|\mathbf{x}\|_p\) as \(p \to \infty\). It is the norm in which the Bellman backup contracts (see below).

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Positive definiteness
A symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is positive definite if (ADM §A.5)

\[
\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{A}\, \mathbf{x} > 0 \quad \text{for every } \mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}
\tag{2}\]

In words. The quadratic form \(\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\) is a bowl: positive in every direction away from the origin.
Term by term.

\(\mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \sum_{i,j} A_{ij} x_i x_j\), a number for each \(\mathbf{x}\).
Equivalently, all eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\) are positive. ≥ 0 instead of > 0 gives positive semidefinite.
Example: \(\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1\\1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\) has eigenvalues 1, 3: positive definite. \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2\\2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\) has −1, 3: indefinite, a saddle.

Why it holds. Writing \(\mathbf{x}\) in the eigenvector basis turns the form into \(\sum_i \lambda_i y_i^2\), which is positive for every nonzero \(\mathbf{y}\) exactly when every \(\lambda_i > 0\). Covariance matrices (Chapter 19’s Kalman filter) are positive semidefinite; a positive definite Hessian means a strict local minimum.

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Convexity
A function \(f\) is convex if the chord between any two points lies on or above the graph (ADM §A.6):

\[
f\big(\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) y\big) \le \lambda f(x) + (1 - \lambda) f(y) \quad \text{for all } x, y \text{ and } \lambda \in [0, 1]
\tag{3}\]

In words. The function at a weighted average is at most the weighted average of the function.
Term by term.

\(\lambda x + (1 - \lambda) y\): a point on the segment between \(x\) and \(y\).
The right side is the height of the chord above that point.
A set is convex if it contains every segment between its points; \(f\) is concave if \(-f\) is convex.

Why it holds. It’s a definition. Its use: a convex function’s local minima are global, and it lies above its tangent lines. On this site: the optimal value function of a POMDP is convex in the belief (Chapter 20), which makes alpha vectors and the sawtooth and triangulated bounds of Chapter 21 work.

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Information and entropy
The information content of an outcome with probability \(P(x)\) is \(-\log P(x)\): rare outcomes are more surprising (ADM §A.7). Averaging gives entropy, and using the wrong model gives cross entropy (§A.8–A.10):

\[
H(P) = -\sum_x P(x) \log P(x), \qquad
H(P, Q) = -\sum_x P(x) \log Q(x), \qquad
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P \,\|\, Q) = H(P, Q) - H(P) = \sum_x P(x) \log \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}
\tag{4}\]

In words. Entropy is the average surprise of outcomes from \(P\). Cross entropy is the average surprise if you expected \(Q\) instead. Their difference, the KL divergence, is the extra surprise from using the wrong model.
Term by term.

With \(\log_2\) the units are bits: a fair coin has \(H = 1\) bit; a coin with \(P(\text{heads}) = 0.9\) has 0.469 bits.
For \(P = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\) and \(Q = (0.4, 0.4, 0.2)\): \(H(P) =\) 1.485 bits; \(H(P, Q) =\) 1.522; \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) =\) 0.0365 but \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P) =\) 0.0372: it isn’t symmetric.
\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) is infinite if \(Q(x) = 0\) for some \(x\) with \(P(x) > 0\).

Why it holds. \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} \ge 0\), with equality only when \(P = Q\) (Gibbs’ inequality): since \(\log\) is concave, Jensen’s inequality gives \(\sum_x P(x)\log\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)} \le \log \sum_x Q(x) = 0\). Used on this site: maximum likelihood minimizes cross entropy to the data (Chapter 4), Bayesian scores (Chapter 5), trust regions (Chapter 12), and maximum entropy IRL (Chapter 18).

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Gradient ascent
To climb a differentiable function \(f\), repeatedly step uphill (ADM §A.11):

\[
\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + \alpha\, \nabla f(\mathbf{x})
\tag{5}\]

In words. Move a small step in the direction in which \(f\) increases fastest.
Term by term.

\(\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\): the gradient, the vector of partial derivatives; it points uphill.
\(\alpha > 0\): the step size. Too small is slow; too large overshoots and can diverge.
For a quadratic with curvature \(c\) along some direction, the iteration is stable only if \(\alpha < 2/c\).

Why it holds. By Taylor’s theorem, \(f(\mathbf{x} + \alpha\nabla f) \approx f(\mathbf{x}) + \alpha\|\nabla f\|^2\), which increases \(f\) for small enough \(\alpha\). Along a direction with curvature \(c\) the error is multiplied by \(1 - \alpha c\) each step, which shrinks only if \(|1 - \alpha c| < 1\), that is \(\alpha < 2/c\). The example in Figure 3 has curvatures 2 and 4, so the limit is 0.5. Used for policy gradients (Chapters 11–13), controllers (Chapter 23) and games (Chapter 24).

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Taylor expansion
A smooth function near a point \(a\) is approximated by a polynomial (ADM §A.12):

\[
f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}\,(x - a)^n \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) + \tfrac{1}{2} f''(a)(x - a)^2
\tag{6}\]

In words. Near \(a\), a function looks like its value, plus its slope times the distance, plus half its curvature times the distance squared, and so on.
Term by term.

\(f^{(n)}(a)\): the \(n\)-th derivative at \(a\); \(n!\) keeps the terms matched.
Truncating after the linear term gives the first-order approximation used for gradients; after the quadratic term, the second-order one used in Newton’s method and trust regions.
Example: \(\cos(0.5) =\) 0.8776; the approximations of order 0, 2 and 4 around 0 give 1.0000, 0.8750, 0.8776.

Why it holds. For analytic functions the series converges to \(f\) near \(a\); for functions differentiable enough, the error after the order-\(n\) term is proportional to \((x - a)^{n+1}\) (Taylor’s theorem with remainder).

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
section: Monte Carlo estimation and importance sampling
text:
Monte Carlo estimation and importance sampling
Expectations that can’t be computed exactly can be estimated by sampling (ADM §A.13–A.14):

\[
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim P}[f(x)] \approx \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x^{(i)}),\ x^{(i)} \sim P
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\approx \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x^{(i)})\, \frac{P(x^{(i)})}{Q(x^{(i)})},\ x^{(i)} \sim Q
\tag{7}\]

In words. Average the function over samples. If you can only (or would rather) sample from \(Q\), reweight each sample by how much more likely it was under \(P\).
Term by term.

The plain estimate is unbiased, with standard error \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\): ten times the samples buys about three times the accuracy.
The weights \(P(x)/Q(x)\) correct for sampling from \(Q\); \(Q\) must be positive wherever \(P f\) is nonzero.
A good \(Q\) puts samples where \(f(x)P(x)\) is large. Example: \(P(X > 3)\) for \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) is 0.00135. With 1000 samples, plain Monte Carlo’s estimates had a standard deviation of 0.00117; sampling from \(\mathcal{N}(3, 1)\) and reweighting, 0.000078.

Why it holds. \(\mathbb{E}_Q\big[f(x) P(x)/Q(x)\big] = \sum_x Q(x) f(x) P(x)/Q(x) = \mathbb{E}_P[f(x)]\), so both are unbiased; the law of large numbers makes the averages converge, and the central limit theorem gives the \(1/\sqrt{n}\) rate. Used for inference (Chapter 3), online planning (Chapter 9), policy gradients (Chapter 11) and validation (Chapter 14).

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Contraction mappings
A function \(B\) is a contraction in a norm if it brings every two points closer by at least a fixed factor (ADM §A.15):

\[
\|B U - B V\| \le \gamma\, \|U - V\| \quad \text{for all } U, V, \text{ with } \gamma < 1
\tag{8}\]

In words. Applying \(B\) shrinks every distance by at least a factor \(\gamma\).
Term by term.

For MDPs, \(B\) is the Bellman backup \((BU)(s) = \max_a [R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a) U(s')]\) and the norm is the max norm.
Consequence (the Banach fixed-point theorem): \(B\) has exactly one fixed point \(U^*\), and iterating \(B\) from anywhere converges to it, the error shrinking by \(\gamma\) each step. That is why value iteration works (Chapter 7).
Check on Hex World: over 1000 random pairs of value functions, the largest ratio \(\|BU - BV\|_\infty / \|U - V\|_\infty\) was 0.9000, never above \(\gamma = 0.9\).

Why it holds. For each state, the difference of two maxima is at most the largest difference of their terms, \(|\max_a g(a) - \max_a h(a)| \le \max_a |g(a) - h(a)|\). Each term differs by \(\gamma \sum_{s'} T(s' \mid s, a)(U(s') - V(s'))\), an average of differences scaled by \(\gamma\), so at most \(\gamma \|U - V\|_\infty\).

title: A · Mathematical Concepts
text:
Graphs
A graph has nodes and edges between them (ADM §A.16). In a directed graph each edge points from a parent to a child; a directed graph with no cycles is a DAG, and its nodes can be put in a topological order in which every parent comes before its children. Bayesian networks (Chapter 2) are DAGs; search trees (Appendix E) and coordination graphs (Chapter 27) are graphs too.

title: C · Computational Complexity
text:
Executed in: Python · Book: ADM Appendix C
Complexity theory measures how the time or memory an algorithm needs grows with the size of its input. On this site it explains why some methods are exact but useless beyond toy problems, and why later chapters turn to approximations. This appendix follows ADM Appendix C: asymptotic notation, time and space complexity classes, and decidability, with original examples.

title: C · Computational Complexity
text:
At a glance



Table 1: The ideas on this page.





Idea
Meaning
Example on this site




\(O(g)\)
grows no faster than \(g\), up to a constant
value iteration: \(O(\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert^2\lvert\mathcal{A}\rvert)\) per sweep (Ch 7)

solvable in polynomial time
solving an MDP by linear programming (Ch 7)

a proposed solution can be checked in polynomial time
3SAT: checking an assignment is quick


NP-hard
at least as hard as every problem in NP
exact inference in Bayesian networks (Ch 3)

solvable with polynomial memory, however long it takes
finite-horizon POMDP planning (Ch 20)
